Hæc Antoninus, vt iam dubium nemini esse debeat, quin Christiani omnes, præsertim hoc Monacho Franciscano in ecclesia dominante, compa-rati esse debeant, vel ad subeunda supplicia schismaticis & hæreticis constituta: vel ad ista Franciscanorum commenta pro diuinis oraculis, ab ecclesia Romana traditis, amplectenda. Atque vt maior & commodior optionis facultas sit, non alienum videtur, alia quædam ex eodem Conformitatum volumine insignia proferre, quale illud est, sol. 66. Quidam ciuis, inquit, dormiuit, & raptus in cœlum vidit Christum, B. Mariam, & alios sanctos, qui processionaliter ibant omnes,Christo & matri reverentiam exhiben-tes.Sed cum B.Franciscum non videret, Angelo ipsum ducenti dixit,Ubi est B.Franciscus cum suis in isto loco? Angelus respondit, Expecta & videbis B. Franciscum, & quem statum habet, & vidit,& ecce: Christus elevavit brachium dextrum,& de ipsius vulnere laterali exi-vit B. Franciscus cum vexillo crucis explicito in mani-bus,& post ipsum maxima multitudo fratrum, & alio-rum. Tunc cuius ille bona sua dedit fratribus, & factus est frater minor. Item sol.2.B.Franciscus repræsentatio-nem faciens Natiuitatis,Christum in vlnis habuit:& du orñaret[?] Virginem, ut sibi consolationem de Iesu paruulo faceret,Virgo ipsa pulcherrima astitit, & in brachiis B. Francisci a principio noctis usque ad diem, tenendum & osculandum præbuit & concessit. Ridicula hæc sunt, dicet aliquis: & plane nugatoria: sed hæ nugæ ( ut quondam dictum est)seria ducunt.nam qui de illa-rū fide dubitat,pro hæretico haberi iubetur. simul ex iis intelligitur,quàm impie Papæ illi superiores ecclesiæ Christianæ in confingendis religionibus illuserint,cùm Bartholomæi nescio cuius Pisani o-pera in his consarcinandis fabulis,& S. scripturæ loco imperitæ multitudini obtrudendis sint usi. Quid?utrum hæc ludicra dicenda sunt,an vero ne-faria,detestanda,& execrabilia, quæ sol.18. his ver-bis scripta sunt: Franciscus plus fuit quàm Iohannes Baptista,quia Iohannes Baptista tantum fuit pœni-tentiæ prædicator,Franciscus fuit prædicator, & ordinis pœni-tentiæ instituitor.Ille fuit præcursorChristi: hic prædicator &signifer Christi,qua in re Iohannem ipsum excedit.I-tem,Iohannem Franciscus præcedit,quia plures adDo-minum convertit, & pluribus in locis , videlicet in toto mundo.Johannes duos annos& parum plus prædicauit: Franciscus xviii.annos. Johannes verbum de pœnitetia accepit à Domino: Franciscus à Domino & à Papa: quod plus est.Johannes Baptista qualis essetfuturus,per Angelum patri ,per Spiritum sanctum, & Prophetas fuit declaratus. S. Franciscus verò à Prophetis ,à D. Jesu Christo,item per Angelum matri & famulis in spe-cie peregrini declaratus. S. Joannes in utero & extra prophetauit: B. Franciscus in utero , id est , in carcere apud Perusium captus,cum gaudio se magnum futurum prædixit. S.Joannes amicus sponsi: B. Franciscus similis Domino Jesu Christo. Joannes mundo singularissi-mus fuit sanctitate : Franciscus excellentissimus fuit ad Christum præ aliis,stigmatisationis conformitate.S.Joan-nes in ordine Serafico sublimatus : B.Franciscus in ipso ordine in sede Luciferi collocatus. Quid est Chri-stianam religionem , & sacram de Joanne Bapti-sta historiam irridere,si hoc non est? O Deus, vl-tionum (ut Scriptura loquitur) domine ! quandiu monstra ista P parum sacrosanctæ Maiestati tuæ, tam contumeliose illudere patiere? quandiu eos impunè in templo tuo sanctissimo debacchari si-nes? At enim locus est , in eodem illo blasphemia-rum promptuario alius prope detestabilior. nam pag.39. Franciscus, inquit, est melior apostolis, quia illi nauem tantum & alia reliquerunt, non tamen vestime-tum, quod in dorso habebant. B. vero Franciscus non so-lum omnium terrenorum facultati abrenuntiauit: sed e-tiam pannos & fœmoralia reiecit, atque mundum corpo-re & mente se obtulit brachiis Crucifixi: quod de nullo alio sancto legimus. unde bene poterat Christo dicere, Reliqui omnia, & secutus sum te. Vbi sunt Pharaones, & Pharaonum deteriores satrapæ, qui Magorum præstigias Mosis miraculis potiores ducunt: & his se monachalibus portentis obleƈtari simulant, vt plebem imperitā à Scripturæ sacræ lectione ac studio remoueant:&suis ciuibus quasi pro pecudibus ac brutis abutantur? Credita tamen hæc sunt superioribus sæculis. nec mirum, cùm Paulus tam aperte prædixerit, Antichristum venturum cum efficacia Satanæ, cum omni potentia, & signis, & pro digiis mendacibus: & cum omni fraude iniustitiæ in iis qui pereunt, pro eo quòd amorem veritatis non receperunt, vt salui fierent. Propterea igitur mittet illis Deus efficaciam deceptionis, vt credant mendacio: vt omnes qui non crediderunt veritati damnentur. 2 Thes. 2.
units.tr: Now, so that anyone can understand what kind of stigmatisation the Roman Church has decreed must be believed by all the faithful, it is worth attending to the author's own words, or rather to those of our monk Pope Sixtus, who has decreed that public faith and authority be given to that writer. For he says: Not only were the hands and feet pierced, but they were nailed through, so that the nails appeared in them. Then the heads of the nails were black, though they ought to have been like flesh or sinews, from which they were made. Third, the heads of the nails were elongated and beaten back, though no hammer or blow was present. Fourth, the stigmata were impressed in a bony place, not a soft one. Fifth, although the nails were of flesh or sinew, they were nevertheless hard, strong and solid like iron. Sixth, the nails themselves were not short, having only points or heads, but were long and protruded on the other side. Seventh, on the other side the nails did not stand out long, but were bent back, so that a finger could be inserted into their arched curve. Eighth, although the nails were made of flesh or sinew and protruded and projected on both sides of the feet and hands, the feet and hands were certainly not deformed or contracted. Ninth, the nails were separated on all sides from the other flesh, so that a piece was placed all around them, on account of the restriction of the blood. Tenth, the nails moved, and yet they could not be removed from the hands or feet, although Blessed Clare and others had attempted to do so. Eleventh, the scars of the nails and of the side did not rot for so long a time, namely for two years and more. Twelfth, the wound in the side was like the wound of Christ. Moreover, it was a miracle how Blessed Francis, who had the greatest pain from the opening of his body in five places, namely the hands, feet and side, and from which blood continually flowed from the aforementioned places, could live for so long, namely for the two years he survived after receiving the stigmata. Do you hear these things, you bard-cowled monk of ours? For although you handed down these fables in your schools for so many years as the general head and chief master of the Franciscan order, now that you have become the pillar of that same order and, as you say, the minister of the whole Church, do you try to hand these same monstrosities to us as divine oracles? What then? If any shame or modesty remained in you or your Franciscans, would that infamous epitaph about Francis Bernardone, carved openly on the gates of Blois, a noble city of Gaul, remain: "His sin shall be sought, and it shall not be found"? But it is worth our while to explain briefly from where he derives authority for these oracles. For a few verses later he speaks thus: The devil said that Christ, seeing that Francis had been given to him as standard-bearer of so great an order, impressed on him the stigmata of his wounds, and the nails in the hands and feet, and the wound in the right side. This is what the devil said, and why it was done: the devil, being adjured by a certain priest to tell the truth, said, after much, through the mouth of a woman living at Ravenna named Zantese: "In heaven there are only two marked ones, namely Christ and the peevish Francis. Christ, therefore, knowing that he would give to that peevish one the seal of his stigmata, did not allow him to receive from the Pope a seal made by human hand." This is what the devil said. These words are copied out letter for letter from the same Conformitatum, folio 230 [?], column 4, and folio 231, column 1. From these it can be understood how much authority is due to these oracles and to this splendid testimony of theirs, brought forward by Satan, since neither Christ nor the apostles could have endured that he should offer any testimony to himself. Now let the noble and illustrious counsellors of the King of France deliberate, in their wisdom, whether these fabricated and blasphemous fables, which Sixtus the Fourth and Sixtus the Fifth, both Franciscans and leaders of the Franciscans, along with several other Popes, have introduced into the Church and confirmed for so long by their authority, and which are today confirmed so zealously, are rightly or wrongly condemned as wicked and impious by the greatest part of the Christian world. So that they may deliberate on this more conveniently, we shall add another passage from the same book, folio 231, where it is written thus: Francis was bodily lifted up on the sacred mountain of Alvernia, as Brother Leo, his companion, saw. For at one time he found him lifted up in the air to such a height that he could scarcely touch his feet, and then he embraced them with tears. At another time he found him lifted from the earth up to the middle of the beeches. At another time he found him raised to such a height that he could scarcely see him. And Brother Leo often found him speaking with Christ. O good Jesus! Who, on hearing these monstrous words, does not shudder with his whole body? For what else is it to hand such things to the people in a sermon than to make Francis a corporeal God, and to set him before the Christian people to be adored in place of Christ? And yet there follow even more loathsome and foul things. For at folio 232 Francis himself is introduced speaking these words: After this, the crucified Lord Jesus applied his hands to my body, and first with the hands, second with the feet, third I felt the stigma of the side with most violent pain; and with a loud cry of mine he impressed it each time, and he spoke to me certain secret words, which I have not yet revealed to any man. Does our Cowled Sixtus think there will be anyone in this age so dull as to give credence to these blasphemous and wicked fables? Does he suppose that the counsellors of the King of France and the senators of the Parlements are so stupid and dull-witted that they will not execrate these impious inventions along with their author, the son of Pietro Bernardone? Unless perhaps someone should say that these things were born in the cloisters and prisons of monks, and that these same things are shut up there in secret and kept like the mysteries of Ceres, and that there is no one today so lacking in wit as not to know they are old wives' fables and the dreams of madmen. But on the other side, see, we have in our hands the dreadful decrees of the Popes, by which they most severely forbid anyone to dare to doubt the truth of these stories, and they decree that they be received in the Roman Catholic Church as sacred oracles, and that whoever thinks otherwise is to be held a heretic and a schismatic. For in the same book, folio 234, column 3, it is written thus: Pope Gregory IX issued several bulls concerning the holiness of Blessed Francis and his stigmata, in which he asserts that Blessed Francis truly had the stigmata of the Lord Jesus impressed in his body by Christ: AND HE ORDERS THIS TO BE HELD BY THE FAITHFUL, and to be believed, and to be punished under the mark of heresy, whoever thinks the opposite. Lord Alexander IV, who saw the stigmata of Blessed Francis with his own eyes, while Blessed Francis was still living, who says in the bull: "The eyes, looking on faithfully, saw the stigmata in the body of this saint while it was still cherished by the living spirit, and the fingers of those touching it most surely felt them." Third, Lord Pope Nicholas III issued a similar bull; fourth, Lord Pope Benedict XII. And since the determination of the holy Roman Church is most true and most certain (for the Roman Church itself is to be followed as teacher in all things, dist. 11, at the end; dist. 12, c. 1 and following; and dist. 22, c. reputatur; dist. 22, c. omnes, at the end; and whoever speaks against it is considered a heretic, dist. 22, c. omnes; because it has never strayed from the path of apostolic tradition, 24 q. 1; to which one must have recourse in doubtful and difficult matters, dist. 11, c. palam; dist. 12, praeceptis; 24 q. 1, c. quoties; and it has power to judge all men, and it is not permitted for anyone to judge it, 11 q. 3, episcopo, §. Sola; 17 q. 4, nemini), and the Roman Church itself has declared Blessed Francis to have been stigmatised by Christ, as is clear from the aforementioned bulls. Therefore this must be held most firmly, as true, and whoever holds the opposite must be despised by all as a HERETIC, especially since the two supreme Pontiffs, Gregory and Alexander, not only saw with their own eyes, but expressly say that this has been attested by trustworthy witnesses. And soon after, column 3: Sixth, the stigmatisation of Blessed Francis is also authenticated by the testimony of malignant spirits, of whom it was spoken above. Thus far from the book of the Conformitatum, folio 234, as I said, so that it may now be plain to everyone that it is not for nothing that we press these things so hard before the counsellors of the King of France and the senators of the Parlements. For our monk, the excommunicator of kings and princes, will not allow these things to be held as trifles or as the playful tales of poets, especially since he, having wallowed so long in the mire of the Franciscans, now professes himself their chief patron and defender, and orders those to be held as heretics who do not fully attach faith and authority to the Roman Church. Lest anyone doubt this, these things are handed down not in one place of that book, that is, folio 234, but also in the very beginning of the book, folio 3, in these words: In which saint was the prodigious stigmatisation made? Certainly in no other than our blessed father Francis, as the ROMAN CHURCH asserts, and imposes on the faithful to believe. Then also Pope Benedict granted the order a feast to be kept in honour of the stigmata. Moreover, Antoninus, bishop of Florence, in his Historia, book 3, title 24, §. 10, speaks thus: Pope Alexander IV, in the year 1254, took the mountain of Alvernia under his special protection immediately, on account of the sacred stigmata impressed there on the body of St. Francis, placing it directly under the Roman Church, extolling Blessed Francis with many praises, and by an effective precept he ordered that the sacred mountain never be abandoned by the brothers. In the same year, while at Anagni, he sent a servant of Christ carrying letters to the faithful, in accordance with the sequence of the letters of Gregory IX concerning the sacred stigmata of Blessed Francis, in which he hinted that he had seen them with his own eyes. He also sent other letters to the Archbishop of Genoa, commanding that those who had maliciously erased the stigmata from the image of St. Francis in the church of St. Mary and in the ministry of Christ should be summoned personally before him, to receive vengeance according to their deserts, forbidding under threat of anathema that anyone should henceforth attempt similar things. Pope Nicholas III, about the year 1280, sent letters to all the faithful of Christ, containing sure testimony concerning the sacred stigmata of Francis. These things Antoninus says, so that now no one ought to doubt that all Christians, and especially those under this Franciscan monk who dominates the Church, must be prepared either to undergo the punishments appointed for schismatics and heretics, or to embrace those Franciscan inventions as divine oracles handed down by the Roman Church. And so that there may be a greater and more convenient freedom of choice, it does not seem out of place to bring forward certain other notable passages from the same volume of the Conformitatum, such as this one, folio 66: A certain citizen, he says, fell asleep, and, being caught up into heaven, saw Christ, Blessed Mary, and other saints, who were all going in procession, paying reverence to Christ and the Mother. But when he did not see Blessed Francis, he said to the angel leading him: "Where is Blessed Francis with his people in this place?" The angel replied: "Wait and you will see Blessed Francis, and what state he is in." And he looked, and behold: Christ raised his right arm, and from his side wound came out Blessed Francis, with the banner of the cross unfurled in his hands, and after him a very great multitude of brothers and others. Then that citizen gave his goods to the brothers and became a Lesser Brother. Likewise, folio 2: Blessed Francis, making a representation of the Nativity, had Christ in his arms; and wishing to console himself concerning the little Jesus, the most beautiful Virgin herself stood by, and she allowed and granted him to hold and kiss the child in the arms of Blessed Francis from the beginning of the night until day. These things are ridiculous, someone will say, and plainly trifling; but these trifles (as was said once before) lead to serious consequences, for whoever doubts their truth is ordered to be held a heretic. At the same time it is understood from them how impiously those former Popes of the Christian Church have mocked religion in inventing these things, since they used the labour of I know not what Bartholomew of Pisa in patching together these fables and in foisting them on the unlearned multitude in place of Holy Scripture. What then? Are these things to be called playful, or rather wicked, detestable and execrable, which are written in folio 18 in these words: Francis was greater than John the Baptist, because John the Baptist was only a preacher of repentance, but Francis was a preacher and the founder of the order of penitence. John was the forerunner of Christ; Francis was the preacher and standard-bearer of Christ, in which respect he surpasses John himself. Again, Francis precedes John, because he converted more people to the Lord, and in more places, namely in the whole world. John preached for two years and a little more; Francis for eighteen years. John received the word of repentance from the Lord; Francis from the Lord and from the Pope, which is greater. John the Baptist was declared by an angel to his father, by the Holy Spirit and by the prophets, as to what he was to be. But St. Francis was declared by the prophets, by the Lord Jesus Christ, and likewise by an angel to his mother and to his servants, in the likeness of a pilgrim. St. John prophesied in the womb and outside it; Blessed Francis, in the womb, that is, when he was captured in the prison at Perugia, foretold with joy that he would be great. St. John was the friend of the bridegroom; Blessed Francis was like the Lord Jesus Christ. John was the most singular in sanctity to the world; Francis was the most excellent in his conformity to Christ in the stigmatisation, beyond others. St. John was exalted in the Seraphic order; Blessed Francis, in the same order, was placed in the seat of Lucifer. What is this, if it is not to mock the Christian religion and the sacred history of John the Baptist? O God, Lord of vengeances (as Scripture says), how long will you suffer these monsters to mock your most holy Majesty so insolently? How long will you allow them to rage with impunity in your most holy temple? But, in truth, there is in that same storehouse of blasphemies another passage, nearly more detestable. For on page 39 he says: Francis is better than the apostles, because they left only ships and other things, but not the garment they wore on their backs. But Blessed Francis not only renounced the use of all earthly goods, but also cast off his cloths and breeches, and offered himself naked in body and mind to the arms of the Crucified; which we read of no other saint. Whence he could well say to Christ: "I have left all things and followed you." Where are the Pharaohs and the worse satraps of the Pharaohs, who count the sorceries of the magicians as superior to the miracles of Moses, and who pretend to be seduced by these monastic monstrosities, so that they may keep the unlearned people away from the reading and study of Holy Scripture, and abuse their citizens as if they were cattle and brutes? Yet these things were believed in earlier ages. Nor is it surprising, since Paul so plainly foretold that Antichrist would come with the working of Satan, with all power, and signs, and lying wonders, and with all deceit of unrighteousness among those who perish, because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved. Therefore God will send them a strong delusion, that they should believe a lie, that all may be damned who did not believe the truth. 2 Thess. 2.
THE FICTION OF THE DOMINICAN RELIGION.

units.la: Dominum natum non alia persona quàm mater sua virgo Maria pannis involuit: & jam adulto tunicam suam inconsutilem, & alias vestes mater ipsa cōsilio manuum suarum texuit: cuius autem coloris fuerit non invenitur, ne videlicet eo noto falsi Prophetæ induti minus agnos-cerentur esse lupi rapaces. Dominico & ordini suo Bea-tissima virgo Maria habitum gestandum ostendit, ac etiam colorem. Nam beato Reginaldo graviter infirmati apparuit, & sanavit, habitum ostendens quo Dominicus cum filiis suis esset induendus: Cappa videlicet magna, & tunica cum scapulari, albis. 12. Dominus & Do-minicus virgo uterque mente & corpore, & humilis valde, ut Scripturæ conclamant: sic Dominicus virgo purissimus & humilis multum. 13. Dominicus cum Chri-sto proprium non possidebat lectulum, post lachrymarum fluvium vix humi dans corpusculum. 14.
units.tr: The newborn Lord was wrapped in swaddling clothes by no other person than his mother, the Virgin Mary; and when he was grown, the mother herself wove his seamless tunic and his other garments with her own hands. But what colour they were is not found, lest, forsooth, the false prophets, having been clothed with that known colour, might be recognised less easily as ravening wolves. The most blessed Virgin Mary showed the habit to be worn by Dominic and his order, and also its colour. For she appeared to the blessed Reginald when he was gravely ill, and healed him, showing the habit in which Dominic with his sons was to be clothed: namely a great cape and a tunic with a scapular, in white. 12. The Lord and Dominic were both virgins in mind and body, and very humble, as the Scriptures proclaim; so Dominic, most pure virgin and very humble. 13. Dominic, with Christ, did not possess a bed of his own, scarcely laying his little body on the ground after a flood of tears. 14.

units.la: Domini ora-tio semper fuit exaudita, cum voluit: unde & Patri dixit: Ego sciebam, quia semper me audis. nam etsi in horto cum orauit calicem à se transferri, non fuerit exauditus: hoc ideo, quia secundum sensualitatem postulans secun-dum rationem exaudiri nolebat. Dominicus autem cui-dam religioso viro sibi familiari in dominica locutione insinuavit, nunquam se à Deo aliquid postulasse, quod ad votum non obtinuerit. 15. Dominus Apostolos sui exemplo ad vitam mixtam, id est, contemplativam & activam prædicando dedicavit: matrem eius Virginem & Magdalenam ad contemplativam. Maria enim sta-bat secundum pedes Domini, & audiebat verbum eius. Luc.10. Martham verò, & alias mulieres ad activam. Sic Patriarcha Dominicus, vt alter Noe, arcam suæ religionis ex lignis bitumine charitatis coaglutinatis tricameratam fecit. Fratres vnà secum ad contemplanda cœlestia, & prædicanda salutis proficua in vna collocans: moniales reclusas ad contemplationem assumens, in secunda: vtriusque sexus homines ad actiuam applicans, qui dicerentur de pœnitentia fratres & sorores, seu militia Iesu Christi in terra mansione. 16. Discipuli Christi scilicet LXXii. semel scandalizati ex doctrina Christi quam non intelligebant, recesserunt ab eo: quibus recedentibus Christus remanentibus secum, ait, Nunquid, & vos vultis abire? At Petrus pro omnibus respondit, Domine, ad quem ibimus? Et B. Dominicus, cùm secum haberet aliquos discipulos, vna die tentati recesserunt ab eo: tantum remanentibus tribus, quibus Dominicus, ait: Nunquid, & vos vultis recedere? Cui vnus respondit, Absit pater vt relicto capite sequamur pedes. Demum sicut & discipuli Christi, qui recesserant, redierunt ad eum, ita & discipuli Dominici oratione eius reuersi sunt. 17. Dominus multas derisiones, detractiones, & persecutiones vsque ad mortem fortiter tolerauit, quaerentium eum in verbo capere, aliquando lapidare, ali-quādo præcipitare. Dominicus contumelias, subsannatio-nes, & oblocutiones non curauit: ita vt quidam paleas à tergo ei pro derisu alligarent: alii lutum & alia in eum vilia iacerent. 18. Dominus dilexit nos, & lauit nos à peccatis nostris in sanguine suo. Dominicus verò charitatis perfectione non vacuus, noctem impendebat Deo, meditationi & orationi vacans. Trinam disciplinam quasi quotidie de manu propria, non cordula, sed catena ferrea vsque ad sanguinis effusionem capiebat: pro suis culpis vnam, quæ minima erant: pro in purgatorio existentibus, aliam: tertiam pro iis qui versantur in mundo. 19. Dominus cum iterfaceret[?] versus Hierusalem, videns civitatem fleuit super eam, multaque praedixit occulta cordium, & eventus futurorum, propter quod in laudem eius dicebatur, Propheta magnus surrexit in nobis. Dominicus cum civitatibus propinquaret, cernens mente, amare flebat propter peccata eorum, multaque ut verus Propheta occulta & futura revelavit: sicut mortem Regis Arragonum in bello: connersionem haeretici Adiu futuram, quem propterea liberari iussit ab incendio. Hactenus Antoninus: Ex quibus potentissimi Regis Galliarum Consiliarij existi-mare poterunt: utrum iure an iniuria maxima Christianitatis pars figmenta ista religionum a Papis inducta repudiarit: cum adeo nefarie ac scelerate ausi sunt monachum Dominicum, tanquam idolum, in Ecclesia Dei adorandum proponere, cumque cum Christo Deo & Conservatore nostro contendere. Neque enim audiendus erit, si quis dicat, monachales istas esse quisquilias, quas eruditi viri & graves aspernantur. Quod enim superius de Franciscanicis eiusdem generis nugamentis dictum est, idem hoc loco de Dominicanis dicimus: cum in Ecclesia Romana pro divinis oraculis receptae sint, aut eas Christianis omnibus venerandas esse, aut constituta haereticis supplicia ab isto furcifero, Regum & principum excommunicatore monacho, expectanda. Sed iam alia audiamus. Nihil videtur ad hanc impietatem addi posse. Verum tamen experiamur. Nam idem Antoninus capite sequenti ubi Christi & Dominici miracula inter se comparat, pag. 187. ita loquitur,{1} Dominicus tres in urbe Roma resuscitavit filium viduae, quod Pontifici notum publicari noluit: sed præ humilitate omnino Dominicus recusauit. Architectum à fratribus conductum, & à muro super eum diruto conquassatum: & Neapoleonem Cardinalem de fossa noua nepotem, ex equo lapsum & totum dilaceratum. Satis credo & alios Dominum suscitasse, propter quod dicit in plurali, Math.II. Mortui resurgent, scilicet per me: cum tamen adhuc non nisi filiam Archisynagogi rediuiuam fecisse habeatur, secundum Euangelia. Sic & B. Dominicus alios mortuos, etsi non ita notorios, viuificasse inuenitur. Quid enim illos XL. peregrinos, qui in flumine magno, iuxta Tholosam nauigio ferebantur, cum nauis submerga sub aquis diu stetissent, sacra oratione à B. Dominico ex aquis exierunt sospites: nisi vitae redditos existimemus, vel in aquis vt pisces conseruatos? 2. Deus bis famelicos pane multiplicato satiauit, aquámque conuertit in vinum. Dominicus bis panes diuinitus fratribus procurauit, Romæ & Bononiæ: deferentibus angelis à pane cœlesti: vnde & suauissimos. Vegetem vacuam vino redundare fecit, & vice altera lympham in vinum suaue convertit. 3. Christus febricitantem Simonis socrum febri perfecte sanauit, & languidos multos. Dominicus mulierem quartanariam ex toto liberam reddidit. 4. Exibant daemonia à multis, clamantia & dicentia, Quia tu es filius Dei: Dominicus à daemonibus vexatos in anima & corpore plurimos liberatos effecit. 5. Christus immortalis effectus bis ianuis clausis ad discipulos intrauit: Dominicus verò adhuc mortalis (quod mirabilius est) in Ecclesiam clausam noctu ingressus est, ne fratres excitaret. 6. Dominus postquam transiuit ex hoc mundo, innumerabiles homines ad viam veritatis attraxit: Dominicus quanuis millia haereticorum ab erroribus renocasset, tamen post transitum eius multo plures. Ospem[?] miram quam dedisti (canit ecclesia de B. Dominico) mortis hora te flenti-bus, Dum post mortem promisisti, Te profuturum fratri-bus. 7. Et vt perueniamus ad calcem, Dominus ait, Data est mihi potestas in coelo & in terra. Hac potestas non parum est communicata Dominico, coelestium, terre-strium, & inferorum. Nam angelos sanctos in sui minis-terium habebat. sed & ipsi angeli accedentes in humana specie ad fratres, panes & escam ministrabant eis. Si de elementis loquimur, vim virtutis sua oblitus est ignis: quando ter libellus eius doctrina in flammas tra-ditus, ter exiuit illaesus penitus, libris aduersantium haereticorum subito combustis. Signo crucis obedit plu-uia ex aere copiose descendens, dum nec gutta vna eum itinerantem tangit, tota regione illo imbre inundata. Aqua fluminis in quod libri eius per ipsum transeuntis ceciderant, nec humectare valuit: sed post dies a piscatoribus loco piscis de aquis extracti illaesi & sicci, ac si in capsa fuissent, ei sunt restituti. Terra quoque quae metalla continet, in pecunia sibi necessaria non defecit. nam cum flumine quodam transito per nauiculam nauclerus naulum postularet a B. Dominico, illeque vt pauper se pecuniam non habere asseueraret importuniusque nauclerus ille per cappam tenens naulum peteret, B. Dominicus oratione facta in terram aspiciens vidit pecuniam sibi necessariam ibi iacentem, qua illi oblata, se liberauit: sed & (quod maius est) cum quidam clericus continere non posset, osculata manu B. Dominici a missa redeuntis cum odore suaui, tantus constitutus vigor in mentem eius diffusus est, vt postea facile contineret. Quid de infernalibus dicam? Certe ad nutum eius daemones contremiscebant, nec imperium eius recusare valebant. Quod patet: quando apparentem ipsum in for-ma frama fratris secum duxit per conuentus officina, scilicet dormitorii, thori, refectorii, locutorii, & postea capituli, & interrogauit de singulis locis, quid cum fratribus ibi lucraretur? quae omnia coactus est explicare.Hæc Anto-ninus.Ex quibus diiudicandum iisdem Regiis consiliariis relinquimus, utrumne hæc vera Christi religio sit Ecclesiæ ab Apostolis tradita, an vero commentitia Sathanæ fabula, consultò à Papis in Ecclesiam inducta, vt vel Scripturæ sacræ legendæ studium extingueretur, vel certè par vtrique fides atque auctoritas tribueretur? Sanè dubium nemini fore speramus, quin iam Papatus ementitarum & confictarum religionum apertissimè sit conuictus: ac proinde si Regem Nauarrum ac Principe Con-dæum ex eius Ecclesiæ communione, quæ porten-ta illa peperit, eiiciat, non illos ex Christi Ecclesia, sed ex Dominicanorum & Franciscanorum cloa-ca, vel potius ex Satanæ synagoga eiicere. Quod vt planius ac certius etiam confirmetur, consimile Papalis ecclesiæ figmentum ex eodem Antonino pro-feremus.Nám cap.sequenti pag.190.ita scribit,Dominicus, inquit, Romæ noctè quadam orationi incumbes, vidit ad patris dexteram exurgere filium in irasua[?], vt interficeret omnes peccatores terræ: & disperderet omnes operantes iniquitatem.Stabat autem in æthere, a-spectu terribilis, & contra mundum in maligno positum lanceas tres vibrabat, quarum prima superborum cervi-ces erectas transfigeret: altera cupidorum viscera effunderet: tertia concupiscentiis carnis deditos perforaret. Cuius iræ dum nemo posset resistere occurrit propi-tia Virgo mater, & pedes amplectens eius, rogauit, vt parceret eis quos redemerat, & iustitiam misericordia temperaret. Ad quam filius, Nónne vides, inquit, quanta mihi irrogentur iniuria? Tunc mater, Tu scis ait, qui omnia nosti, quia hæc est via per quam eos ad te reduces. Habeo seruum fidelem quem mittes in mundum vt verba tua annuntiet eis, & convertentur ad te omnium saluatorem. Alium quoque habeo seruum, quæ dabo ei adiutorem, vt similiter operetur. Filius dixit, Ecce placatus suscepi faciem tuam, verumtamen offende mihi quos velis ad tantum officium destinare. Tunc domina mater obtulit B. Dominicum Iesu Christo: & ait Dominus matri, Bene & studiose faciet quod dixisti. Obtulit quoque & S. Franciscum, quem similiter Dominus laudauit. Sanctus ergo Dominicus in visione considerans socium diligenter, quem prius non nouerat, in crastinum eum in Ecclesia, ex eis quæ in nocte videbat, recognouit, & in osculâ sancta ruens, & sinceros amplexus, dixit, Tu es socius meus: tu curres pariter mecum. Item paulo post: Dominicus orabat noctu in Ecclesia, & ecce repente facta manu Domini super eum raptus est in spiritu ante Deum, & vidit Deum sedentem, & matrem eius quæ sedebat ad dextram eius, amictam cappa, coloris saphirini. Aspiciens autem in circuitu vidit ex omni natione spiritualium patrum, qui ex sacris religionibus Christo & filios & filias spirituales genuerunt, multitudines innumeras in conspectu altissimi gloriantes. Et cum nullum ibi conspiceret suorum filiorum, erubescens, compunctus ex intimis amarissime flere cœpit. Exterritus ergo a gloria maiestatis domini, stetit a longe, nec audebat vultui gloriæ, & Virginis excellentiæ propinquare. Innuit autem ei manu domina, vt ad se veniret. At ille tremens & pauens, non præsumpsit accedere, quousque eum similiter vocauit Dominus maiestatis: accessit itaque homo compunctus, & humilis spiritu, & contrito suis lachrymis filii & matris propitiis pedibus demississime & humillime se prostrauit. At consolator flebilium Dominus gloriæ dixit ei, Surge. qui cum staret coram Domino, interrogauit, dicens, Cur sic amarissime ploras? qui ait: Quia in conspectu tuæ gloriæ omnis religionis homines intueor: de mei vero ordinis filiis hic, proh dolor! nullũ aspicio. Cui Dominus, Vis videre ordinem tuum? At ille, Hoc desidero Domine. Tunc filius manum suam sub scapulari Virginis matris suæ ponens, dixit ad illum, Ordinem tuum matri commisi. Et cum hoc pio haberet affectu, ordinem suum videre desiderans, Dominus iterum dixit ei: Omnino vis eum videre? Respondit, Hoc affecto mi Domine. Et ecce mater Domini complacuit filio: cappámque deauratam, qua operiri videbatur, euidenter patefaciens aperuit: & expandens coram lachrymoso Dominico seruo suo, erátque hoc tâta capacitatis, & immensitatis vestimentum, quod totam cœlestem patriam amplexando dulciter continebat. Sub hoc securitatis tegmento, in hoc pietatis gremio, vidit ille contemplator sublimium, & perspector domini secretorum Dominicus, fratrum sui ordinis innumeram multitudinem. Conuersus est ergo luctus in gaudium, & lamentum in jubilum.
units.tr: The Lord's prayer was always heard whenever he wished, and so he said to the Father: "I knew that you always hear me." For although in the garden, when he prayed that the cup might be taken from him, he was not heard, this was because, asking in accordance with the flesh, he did not wish to be heard in accordance with reason. Dominic, however, once told a religious man who was close to him, in an informal conversation, that he had never asked God for anything that he did not obtain as he wished. 15. The Lord dedicated his Apostles to a mixed life, that is, contemplative and active, by his own example in preaching; he dedicated his mother, the Virgin, and Magdalene to the contemplative life. For Mary sat at the feet of the Lord and heard his word (Luke 10). He dedicated Martha and the other women to the active life. Thus Dominic, the Patriarch, like a second Noah, made the ark of his religion, three-storeyed, of wood joined together with the pitch of charity. He placed the brothers together with himself, in the lower storey, to contemplate heavenly things and to preach what is profitable for salvation; in the second he took in enclosed nuns for contemplation; and to the active life he assigned men and women of both sexes, who were called brothers and sisters of penance, or soldiers of Jesus Christ, remaining in the world. 16. The disciples of Christ, namely seventy-two, once offended by the teaching of Christ, which they did not understand, withdrew from him; and when they withdrew, Christ, remaining with them, said: "Do you also wish to go away?" But Peter answered for all: "Lord, to whom shall we go?" And Blessed Dominic, when he had some disciples with him, on one day they were tempted and withdrew from him; with only three remaining, Dominic said to them: "Do you also wish to withdraw?" One of them answered: "Far be it, Father, that we should leave the head and follow the feet." At last, just as the disciples of Christ who had withdrawn returned to him, so too the disciples of Dominic returned at his prayer. 17. The Lord bravely endured many mockings, slanders and persecutions, even to death, from those who sought to catch him in his words, at times to stone him, at times to hurl him down. Dominic did not care for insults, scoffing and reproaches: so much so that some tied chaff to his back as a mockery, and others threw mud and other filthy things at him. 18. The Lord loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood. Dominic, not lacking in the perfection of charity, spent the night giving himself to God, devoted to meditation and prayer. Almost every day he took a threefold discipline with his own hand, not with a cord but with an iron chain, until blood flowed: one for his own faults, which were the least; another for those who were in purgatory; and a third for those who were living in the world. 19. When the Lord was going towards Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it, and he foretold many hidden things of hearts and the outcomes of future events; for which reason in his praise it was said: "A great prophet has arisen among us." When Dominic drew near to cities, seeing in his mind, he wept bitterly over their sins, and, like a true prophet, he revealed many hidden and future things: such as the death of the King of Aragon in battle; and the future conversion of the heretic Adius, whom for that reason he ordered to be freed from the fire. So far Antoninus. From these things the councillors of the most powerful King of France will be able to judge whether the greatest part of Christendom rightly or wrongly rejected these monkish fictions, brought in by the Popes, since they have dared so wickedly and criminally to set forth the monk Dominic, as an idol, to be worshipped in the Church of God, and to contend with Christ, our God and Saviour. For no one should be heard if he says that these monkish trifles are trivia which learned and serious men despise. What was said above about the Franciscan trifles of the same kind, we say here about the Dominicans: since they have been received in the Roman Church as divine oracles, either all Christians must venerate them, or heretics must expect punishment established by that gallows-bird, that monk who excommunicates kings and princes. But let us now hear other things. Nothing seems able to be added to this impiety. Yet let us test it. For the same Antoninus, in the following chapter, where he compares the miracles of Christ and Dominic, page 187, speaks thus: {1} Dominic raised a widow's son three times in the city of Rome, which he did not wish to be made known to the Pontiff, but out of humility Dominic refused altogether. He was struck by an architect hired by the brothers, when a wall fell upon him; and Cardinal Neapoleon of Fossa Nova, a nephew, fell from his horse and was completely torn apart. I believe that others also were raised by Christ, for which reason he says in the plural, Matthew 11: "The dead shall rise," namely through me; although it is held, according to the Gospels, that he had restored to life only the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue. So also Blessed Dominic is found to have revived other dead, though not so notorious. For what of those forty pilgrims who were carried in a boat on a great river near Toulouse, when the ship had sunk and remained under the water for a long time, and who came out from the waters safe and sound by the holy prayer of Blessed Dominic? Unless we think they were restored to life, or preserved in the waters like fish? 2. God satisfied the hungry twice with multiplied bread, and turned water into wine. Dominic twice procured bread for the brothers by divine means, at Rome and at Bologna, the angels bringing it down from heavenly bread, whence it was also most sweet. He made an empty jar overflow with wine, and on another occasion turned water into sweet wine. 3. Christ perfectly healed Simon's mother-in-law of her fever, and many who were sick. Dominic freed a woman with quartan fever completely. 4. Demons came out of many, crying out and saying, "You are the Son of God." Dominic made many who were vexed by demons, in soul and body, to be set free. 5. Christ, having become immortal, entered to his disciples twice with the doors shut; but Dominic, still mortal (which is more wonderful), entered into a closed church at night, so as not to wake the brothers. 6. After the Lord passed out of this world, he drew countless people to the way of truth; Dominic, although he had called back many thousands of heretics from their errors, nevertheless after his passing many more. "The wondrous hospitality which you gave," the Church sings of Blessed Dominic, "at the hour of death, while those who wept for you, when after death you promised that you would profit the brothers." 7. And to come to the sum: the Lord said, "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth." This power was not a little communicated to Dominic, of heavenly, earthly and infernal things. For he had holy angels for his ministry; and the angels themselves, coming in human form to the brothers, served them bread and food. If we speak of the elements, fire forgot its power: when three times his little book of doctrine was committed to the flames, it came out three times completely unharmed, while the books of the opposing heretics were suddenly burned. Rain falling copiously from the air obeyed the sign of the cross, so that not a drop touched him as he travelled, while the whole region was flooded with that rain. The water of the river into which his books had fallen, when he himself passed through it, could not wet them; but days later they were drawn out of the water by fishermen in place of a fish, unharmed and dry, as if they had been in a box, and were restored to him. The earth also, which holds metals, did not fail him in money he needed. For when he was crossing a certain river by boat, the ferryman demanded the fare from Blessed Dominic; and when he, claiming as a poor man that he had no money, and the ferryman, more insistent, held him by his cloak and demanded the fare, Blessed Dominic, after prayer, looked down at the ground and saw money lying there that he needed; when it was offered to the ferryman, he was freed. But (what is greater) when a certain cleric could not restrain himself, and kissed the hand of Blessed Dominic as he was returning from Mass, with its sweet odour, such strength was established and poured into his mind that afterwards he could easily restrain himself. What shall I say of the infernal powers? Surely at his nod the demons trembled, nor could they refuse his command. This is clear: when the devil, appearing to him in the form of a brother, he led him through the workshops of the convent, namely the dormitory, the bed-chamber, the refectory, the parlour, and afterwards the chapter-house, and asked him about each place, what was gained there by the brothers; all of which he was compelled to explain. So Antoninus. From these things we leave it to the same royal councillors to judge whether this is the true religion of Christ handed down to the Church by the Apostles, or rather a fabricated fable of Satan, deliberately brought into the Church by the Papists, either so that the study of reading Holy Scripture might be extinguished, or at least that equal faith and authority might be given to both? We hope that no one will doubt that the Papacy has now been clearly convicted of invented and fabricated religions; and therefore if it expels the King of Navarre and the Prince of Condé from the communion of its Church, which bore those monsters, it expels them not from the Church of Christ, but from the sewer of the Dominicans and Franciscans, or rather from the synagogue of Satan. So that this may be made clearer and more certainly confirmed, we will bring forward from the same Antoninus a similar fiction of the Papal Church. For in the following chapter, page 190, he writes thus: Dominic, he says, was praying one night at Rome, and saw the Son rising at the right hand of the Father in wrath, to kill all the sinners of the earth and destroy all who work iniquity. He stood in the air, terrible in appearance, and against the world placed in evil, he brandished three lances: the first would pierce the raised necks of the proud; the second would pour out the bowels of the covetous; the third would pierce those given over to the desires of the flesh. While no one could resist his anger, the propitious Virgin Mother ran to him, and embracing his feet, asked him to spare those whom he had redeemed, and to temper justice with mercy. To her the Son said: "Do you not see what injuries are being done to me?" Then the Mother said: "You know all things, and you know that this is the way by which you will lead them back to you. I have a faithful servant whom you will send into the world to announce your words to them, and they will be converted to you, the Saviour of all. I have also another servant, whom I will give as a helper, so that he may work in the same way." The Son said: "Behold, I have received your face appeased; but name to me whom you wish to send for such a great office." Then the Lady Mother presented Blessed Dominic to Jesus Christ; and the Lord said to the Mother: "He will do well and diligently what you have said." She presented also Saint Francis, whom the Lord likewise praised. Therefore Saint Dominic, considering in the vision the companion whom he had not known before, the next day recognised him in the church, from what he had seen in the night; and rushing into a holy kiss and sincere embraces, he said: "You are my companion; you shall run together with me." Again, a little later: Dominic was praying at night in the church, and behold, suddenly, the hand of the Lord being laid upon him, he was caught up in spirit before God, and saw God sitting, and his mother sitting at his right hand, wrapped in a cloak of sapphire colour. Looking round, he saw from every nation spiritual fathers, who by sacred religions had begotten sons and daughters for Christ, innumerable multitudes glorifying before the face of the Most High. And when he saw none of his own sons there, blushing and pricked in his inmost heart, he began to weep most bitterly. Terrified therefore by the glory of the majesty of the Lord, he stood afar off, and did not dare to approach the countenance of the glory and the excellence of the Virgin. But the Lady beckoned to him with her hand, that he should come to her. But he, trembling and fearful, did not presume to approach, until the Lord of majesty likewise called him; so the man, pricked in heart and humble in spirit, approached, and, with tears, prostrated himself most humbly and lowly at the gracious feet of the Son and the Mother. But the Lord of glory, the consoler of the weeping, said to him: "Rise." And when he stood before the Lord, he asked, saying: "Why do you weep so bitterly?" He answered: "Because in the sight of your glory I look upon men of every religion; but of the sons of my order, alas! I see none here." The Lord said to him: "Do you wish to see your order?" "This is what I desire, Lord." Then the Son, placing his hand beneath the scapular of his Mother the Virgin, said to him: "I have committed your order to my mother." And since he had this pious affection, desiring to see his order, the Lord again said to him: "Do you truly wish to see it?" He answered: "This is my desire, Lord." And behold, the Mother of the Lord was pleased with the Son; and clearly revealing the gilded cloak in which she seemed to be covered, she opened it, and spreading it out before Dominic, his tearful servant, it was a garment of such capacity and immensity that it sweetly embraced and contained the whole heavenly fatherland. Under this covering of security, in this bosom of piety, that contemplator of high things and penetrating searcher of the Lord's secrets, Dominic, saw an innumerable multitude of brothers of his order. Thus mourning was turned into joy, and lamentation into jubilation.

units.la: Hæc Antonin*: Ridiculè, insulsè, & absurdè. Dicet fortasse quispiam, quis negat? Sed quemadmodum superius de nugis Bernardonicis diximus, cuicui-modi hæc sunt, tamen & Papatus auctoritate comprobata sunt, & ab Ecclesia Rom. recepta: ac proinde, cum indiuidua religio sit, (nam, ut ait Mª Tullius, aut undique religionem tolle, aut usquequaque conserua) ab iis omnibus qui ecclesiæ Rom. nomen dabunt, oraculorum loco ac numero habenda: graui sanctione adiecta, ut qui secus en-tiat, in hæreticorum & schismaticorum numero censeatur: quandoquidem his commentis à Papa comprobatis,Dominicus æque ac Francifcus in diuorum ecclesiæ R.numerum relatus est, eodem auctore Antonino,tit.23.§.17.f[?]. l.97. Ex quibus intelligitur,primum quot& quàm iustis causis adducti plerique Christiani Reges, Principes ac Magistratus Papatum impietatis,& confictæ religionis nomine damnarint.deinde,quantum aucto ritatis habere apud Parlameta Gallica debeat hæc execrata Sixti quinti nuper ex cucullati monachi Declaratio, qua supradicti serenissimi Principes non aliam ob causam hæretici pronuntiati sunt, quàm quòd istius generis commenta non eodem quo Scripturam sacram loco sibi habenda esse iudicarunt. Nam ut sæpenumero antehac profesi sunt, & hodie quàm maximè possunt, apud omnes omnium generum atque ordinum homines profitentur, palámque denuntiant, cùm ecclesia Rom.mixtam habeat & confusam cum istius generis commentis ac fabulis religionem, quæ ex puris Scripturæ sacræ fontibus hausta sunt,ea studiosissimè ampleftuntur: quæ ex istis monachalibus lacunis & colluuionibus in religionem inducta sunt,ea repudiant ac detestantur. Quæ tamen sola causa est,cur Papa Sixtus quintus utrumque illorum Principum nuper ita superbè ac ferociter est execratus.De quo Papa Sixto dicendum aliquid hoc loco videtur:ut & qualis & quibus ortus radicibus in tantam confidentiam venerit, tantòsque sibi spiritus sumpserit[?], ab omnibus intelligatur. Nomen igitur illi ab initio fuit: FELIX PERETVS. Natus est in pago tenui, proximo ciuitati Formanæ,cui nomen est Montalto: anno CIↃ IↃ
units.tr: These are the words of Antoninus: ridiculous, silly and absurd. Someone will perhaps say, "Who denies it?" But as we said above about Bernardine's trifles, whatever their character, these things have been approved by papal authority and received by the Roman Church. Therefore, since religion is indivisible (for, as Marcus Tullius says, either remove religion altogether or preserve it entire), all who give their name to the Roman Church must hold them as oracles and count them among their number, with a severe sanction attached: whoever thinks otherwise is to be counted among the heretics and schismatics. For with these inventions approved by the Pope, Dominic, no less than Francis, has been placed in the number of the saints of the Roman Church, on the authority of the same Antoninus, title 23, §17, f. l.97. From this it is understood, first, for how many and how just reasons many Christian kings, princes and magistrates have condemned the Papacy in the name of impiety and fabricated religion. Second, how much authority this accursed declaration of Sixtus V, lately issued by a hooded monk, ought to carry with the Parlements of France, by which the aforesaid most serene princes were pronounced heretics for no other reason than that they judged such inventions should not be held in the same place as Holy Scripture. For, as they have often professed before and as they now most strongly can, they declare openly before all men of every rank and order that, since the Roman Church has a religion mixed and confused with this kind of invention and fable, they embrace most eagerly what has been drawn from the pure fountains of Holy Scripture, and they reject and detest what has been introduced into religion from those monastic pools and sewers. Yet this is the only reason why Pope Sixtus V has so arrogantly and fiercely cursed both of those princes. Concerning this Pope Sixtus something seems to be said here, so that it may be understood by all both what sort of man he is, from what roots he sprang, and how he came to such confidence and took to himself such spirit. His name was at first Felix Peretus. He was born in a poor village near the city of Fermo, called Montalto, in the year 1521, on the thirteenth day of December.

units.la: xxi.die Decembris xiii. Parentem habuit olitorem pauperculum: apud quem, gradiusculus factus, primum hunc in patria honoris gradum est adeptus, vt custos caprarum Montaltitarum fieret. In hac procuratione forte accidit vt errantem e grege capram amitteret, tum patris iracundiam veritus, in proximum Franciscanorum monasterium profugit. Ibi comiter a monachis acceptus, sensim literis imbui legereque ac scribere a sene quodam edoctus est : tandemque mysteriis Franciscanicis initiatus cucullam esti ndutus. Vbi, & aetate & monachalium artium scientia ita procesit, vt monachis ad maiora negotia gerenda idoneus videretur, tandem ab inquisitoribus fidei Romanæ in ipsorum collegium cooptatus est, quo magisterio cùm aliquot ab hinc annis ita fungeretur, vt pauci truculentum ipsius ingenium ferre possent, forte tum accidit, vt nobilem quendā Venetum ad suum tribunal euocaret. Cum homine contumeliis audiendis insuetum ferocius accepisset, non ita multis interiectis diebus eidem Nobili forte obuiam factus est : quem vt primum Nobilis animaduertit, vni ex suis asseclis imperauit, vt fuste quam gestabat ferocia infelicis Pereti contunderet. Infelix illico Romam profectus, casum illum suum Papæ Pio quarto, qui tum Romæ imperabat, renuntiat. Indignatus Papa, rursus illum cum auctoritate ac potestate maiore Venetias remittit. Simul ac suam Senatui bullam exhibuit, sapientes viri, qui turbulentum hominis ingenium non ignorabant, eumque ultionis studio inflammatum esse animadvertebant, confestim cereum accendi iusserunt : eique seuere imperarunt, vt prius quàm cereus igne consumptus effet, maturè, si saperet,è suis finibus excederet. Infelix iterum Romam profectus suam Papæ querimoniam detulit. Papa cùm hominem ad suas rationes accommodatissimum fore iudicaret, primùm hoc illum honore affecit,vt sui eum palatij magistrum crearet.deinde cùm in Hispania Toledanus archie pifcopus ab inquisitione Hispanica,gentibus omnibus formidabili,in suspicionem hæresis vocatus effet,Papa eum,vt illi quæstioni ac iudicio interesset,in Hispaniam misit. Forte per id tempus accidit,vt qui tum Generalis, hoc est,antistes Franciscanorum erat(quæ summa apud illud hominū genus præfectura ac dignitas habetur) mortem obiret: quam hereditatem Papa Pereto Felici detulit: qui hoc modo Franciscanorum Archicucullus,siue Protocucullus,factus est: paucisque post annis etiā in Cardinalium ordinem ab eodem Papa cooptatus. Quo in magistratu dici non potest quàtopere se legatis Hispaniensibus, qui Romæ assidui esse solent, venditarit:quàm diligenter omnia Consistorij Papalis consilia & arcana eisdem enutiarit: quàm studiosè suam illis in omnibus Hispaniensibus negotiis procurandis operam navarit: quo labore atque assiduitate tandem assecutus est, vt præmia sibi permagna quotannis ex Hispania mitterentur, cùm interea tamen cibaria ex penu Pontificia quotidie,& eo amplius centenos ex eiusdem thesauro quotmensibus aureos nihilominus acciperet.Paupertatem enim & inopiam in illo Franciscanorum ludo & disciplina egregie didicerat: parcéque omnino, & sordidè victitabat. Verùm illa paupertatis simulatio non ita multò pòst patefacta facta est.primùm vbi Papæ Nicolai fui quondam popularis,& in Franciscanorum collegio sodalis mo-numentum vetustate collapsum instaurare, ma-gnisque sumptibus exornare instituit: tum verò postquam palatium sibi magnificum ac plane re-gium ædificare cœpit. Qua re Gregorius.XIII a-nimaduersa, vtrunque illud beneficium, siue(vt Feudistæ loquuntur)feudum ex cauea & camera tribui solitum ei ademit. Ad extremum hoc eodē Gregorio XIII.mortuo,noster Caprarius olitoris filius, Franciscano cucullo tectus, studiosissima eius commendatione & gratia, qui Romæ in his procurandis negotiis dominatur, & cui non obscu-rè suam in reliqua Nauarreni regni parte occupanda operam nauat,in demortui locum Felix in con-turbanda Gallia suffectus est. His gradibus atque incrementis qui aliquot ab hinc annis Cordigerulus despicatissimus monachus fenestratis calceis reptabat, nunc fulguritor[?], fulminator, Regum ac Principum proscriptor factus est:
units.tr: His father was a poor gardener. Having risen a little in his service, he first obtained in his homeland this step of honour, that he became keeper of the goats of Montalto. In this charge it happened by chance that he lost a goat that had strayed from the flock; then, fearing his father's anger, he fled to the nearby monastery of the Franciscans. There he was kindly received by the monks, gradually imbued with letters, and taught by an old man to read and write; and at last, initiated into the Franciscan mysteries, he put on the hood. Here, advancing in age and in knowledge of monastic arts, he came to seem fit to carry out greater business for the monks, and at last he was co-opted by the inquisitors of the Roman faith into their college. While he discharged this office for some years, so harshly that few could bear his savage temper, it happened that he summoned a certain Venetian nobleman before his tribunal. The man, unused to hearing insults, took it more fiercely, and not many days later he happened to meet the same nobleman. As soon as the nobleman saw him, he ordered one of his followers to beat the unhappy Peretus with the cudgel he carried. The unhappy man went straight to Rome and reported his mishap to Pope Pius IV, who was then reigning at Rome. The Pope, indignant, sent him back to Venice again with greater authority and power. As soon as he showed his bull to the Senate, the wise men, who did not ignore the restless character of the man and saw that he was inflamed with a desire for revenge, at once ordered a candle to be lit, and sternly commanded him that, unless he was wise, he should leave their territory before the candle burned down. The unhappy man went to Rome again and laid his complaint before the Pope. The Pope, judging that he would be most suitable for his purposes, first honoured him by making him master of the sacred palace. Then, when in Spain the Archbishop of Toledo was called under suspicion of heresy by the Spanish Inquisition, a body feared by all nations, the Pope sent him into Spain to take part in that inquiry and trial. At about that time it happened that the man who was then General, that is, head of the Franciscans (which is the highest office and dignity among that class of men), died; and the Pope conferred this inheritance on Felix Peretus. In this way he became Archhood, or Protohood, of the Franciscans, and a few years later he was co-opted by the same Pope into the order of Cardinals. In this office it cannot be said how greatly he ingratiated himself with the Spanish envoys, who are usually constantly at Rome; how diligently he revealed to them all the counsels and secrets of the papal consistory; how zealously he devoted his labour to them in all Spanish affairs. By such toil and constancy he at last achieved that very great rewards were sent to him every year from Spain, while meanwhile he nonetheless received daily food from the papal larder, and moreover, every month, more than a hundred gold pieces from the same treasury. For in that Franciscan school and discipline he had thoroughly learned to feign poverty and want, and he lived most sparingly and meanly. Yet that pretence of poverty was not revealed for long. First, when he undertook to restore, at great expense and with splendid decoration, a monument of his former fellow-countryman Pope Nicholas, a companion in the Franciscan college, which had collapsed with age; and then, indeed, when he began to build for himself a magnificent palace, truly royal. Gregory XIII, noticing this, took away from him that benefit, or (as the feudal lawyers say) the fief, which had been customarily granted to him from the cavea and the chamber. Finally, when this same Gregory XIII died, our Capraio, the goatherd's son, covered with the Franciscan hood, through the most diligent recommendation and favour of Gregory, who held sway at Rome in managing these affairs, and by whose not obscure labour he was also working to occupy the rest of the kingdom of Navarre, was put in the dead man's place as Felix for the disturbing of France. By these steps and advances, he who a few years ago crept about as a most contemptible cord-bearing monk in shoes full of holes, has now become a thunderer, a lightning-bearer, and a proscriber of kings and princes.

units.la: Ense potens gemino, cuius vestigia adorantCæsar, & aurato vestiti murice Reges:
units.tr: Powerful with the twin sword, whose footsteps Caesars adore, and kings clothed in purple dyed with gold.
So Mantuan sang of Julius II.
The crime of usurped tyranny in the Church

units.la: PRoximum est, vt ad secundum Papatus cri-men accedamus, quod in occupato in Eccle-siam Christianā dominatu & intoleranda po-tentia cōsistit. Nam scriptura sacra docet nos,solū Christū esse caput ecclesię, 1.Petr.2.& 5.Heb.5.& 7.& 9.4.Ephe.5. &16.ite in c.5.ite alio loco. Christū esse caput corporis ecclesię, 1.Col.18. Eadē scriptura soli Christo hoc nomē tribuit,vt sit ἀρχιποίμην[?], & ἀρχιερεὺς.1.Petr.2.& 5.Hebr.6.& 7.At Papa Rom. Cu-ncta,inquit,per mundum nouit ecclesia, quod sacrosancta Romana ecclesia fas de omnibus habeat iudicandi: neque cuiquam liceat de eius iudicare iudicio,&c. sequenti, Cuncta per mundum nouit Ecclesia, quoniam quorumlibet iudiciis ligata Pontificum sedes B.Petri ius habeat resoluendi,ut pote quae de omni ecclesia ius habeat iudicandi. Item Clement.pastoralis, de sent.& re iud. Pastoralis cura solicitudinis nobis diuinitus super cunctas Christiani populi nationes iniuncta. Item c.1. Extrauag.de empt.& vend. Regimini vniuersalis ecclesiae,disponente domino praesidentes. item.c.ad Regimen.extrauag.de praebend. Ad regimen ecclesiae generalis superna dispositione vocati. item.c.1. de treug. & pac. Ad vniuersalis ecclesiae regimen diuina disponente clementia vocati, item.ca.1. de consuet. Super gentes & regna Romanus Pontifex a Domino constitutus est. item.c.3.de elect. Sancta Romana ecclesia, quae disponente Domino super alias omnes obtinet principatum a Deo,vt pote mater vniuersorum fidelium & magistra. item, Ideo ecclesias omnes Romanae sedi subiectas esse,quia sedes Petri ab Antiochia Romam translata est. 24. q.1.c.rogamus, &c. sacrosancta. Item, Romanam sedem esse caput & cardinem omnium ecclesiarum: & sicut cardine ostium regitur,ita illius sedis auctoritate omnes ecclesias regi. d.c. sacrosancta. Sed quid illa vetera conquirimus? cum Franciscanus noster Caprarius Sixtus quintus Bullam hac suam ita sit exorsus: Auctoritatem sibi a Christo & B. Petro traditam supereminere,omnes omnium Regum & Principum potestates, & incumbere sibi ecclesiarum omnium,populorum,ac gentium solicitudinem. Hæc igitur Papa Romanus. Nunc quo iure, quáque auctoritate tantam sibi potestatem ac dominatum arroget, paulisper considerandum est. Duplicem enim videmus ab ipso & ipsius parasitastris titulum, causamque istius dominij ac principatus afferri: priorem, ex Christi decreto: Pasce oues meas, &c. Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram. Nam dicite domino, Pasce oues meas, inquit Papa, & generaliter, Meas, nō singulariter, Has vel illas, per hoc commisisse sibi intelligitur universas. c. unam sanctam, Extravag. de maiorit. & obed. Alteram causam Papa profert ex donatione Imp. Constantini, dist. 66. c. Constantinus, vbi Constantinus dicitur ei principatum tribuisse super omnes vniuersi terrarum orbis ecclesias. Sed videamus, ne Papa in illum errorem incurrerit, qui tolerari in iure ac iudiciis non solet, neque vero ferri vllo modo potest: ut actor intentionis suae causas alleget inter se contrarias. l. si quis, 7. D. de petit. haered. l. 1. C. de furt. l. Titius, 99. D. de cond. & demonstrat.
units.tr: Next we come to the second crime of the Papacy, which consists in the domination it has usurped over the Christian Church and its intolerable power. Holy Scripture teaches us that Christ alone is the head of the Church: 1 Peter 2 and 5; Hebrews 5, 7 and 9; Ephesians 4 and 5 and 16, likewise in chapter 5 and likewise in another place. Christ is the head of the body of the Church: 1 Colossians 18. The same Scripture gives this name to Christ alone, that he is the chief shepherd [ἀρχιποίμην?] and high priest [ἀρχιερεύς]: 1 Peter 2 and 5; Hebrews 6 and 7. But the Roman Pope says: The Church knows throughout the world that the most holy Roman Church has the right to judge all things, and that no one may pass judgment on its judgment, and so on. In the following words: The Church knows throughout the world that the See of Blessed Peter, bound by the judgments of no one, has the right to annul the decisions of Popes, since it has the right to judge the whole Church. Likewise the Clementine Pastoralis, On sentence and res judicata: The pastoral care of solicitude, enjoined upon us by God over all the nations of the Christian people. Likewise chapter 1 of the Extravagants, On buying and selling: Presiding over the government of the universal Church by the Lord's arrangement. Likewise the chapter Ad regimen of the Extravagants, On prebends: Called by heavenly disposition to the government of the general Church. Likewise chapter 1, On the Truce and Peace: Called by the divine clemency to the government of the universal Church. Likewise chapter 1, On customs: The Roman Pontiff has been appointed by the Lord over the nations and kingdoms. Likewise chapter 3, On elections: The holy Roman Church, which by God's disposition holds the primacy over all others from God, as mother and teacher of all the faithful. Likewise: Therefore all churches are subject to the Roman See, because the See of Peter was transferred from Antioch to Rome. 24 q. 1, chapter Rogamus, and so on, sacrosancta. Likewise: The Roman See is the head and hinge of all churches, and just as a door is governed by its hinge, so all churches are governed by the authority of that See. The same, chapter sacrosancta. But why do we search out those old texts, when our Franciscan Caprarian, Sixtus V, began his Bull in this way: That the authority handed down to him by Christ and Blessed Peter surpasses the powers of all kings and princes, and that the care of all churches, peoples and nations rests upon him. These, then, are the words of the Roman Pope. Now we must consider for a little while by what right and what authority he claims for himself so great a power and dominion. For we see that he and his parasitic hangers-on put forward a twofold title and cause for this lordship and principate: the first from Christ's decree: Feed my sheep, and so on, You are Peter, and upon this rock. For the Pope says: Say to the Lord, Feed my sheep, and generally, My sheep, not singly, these or those; by this it is understood that he has committed to him all of them. Chapter Unam sanctam, Extravagants, On the majority and obedience. The Pope brings forward a second cause from the donation of the Emperor Constantine, Distinction 96, chapter Constantinus, where Constantine is said to have granted him the primacy over all the churches of the whole world. But let us see that the Pope does not fall into that error which is not usually tolerated in law and in courts, and cannot in any way be allowed: that a plaintiff should allege reasons for his claim that contradict one another. Digest 47, si quis; Code, On theft; Digest 35, Titius, On condictio and demonstratio.

units.la: Repugnant autem inter se, Christum dedisse Papae principatum in omnes ecclesias, (quod apertissime supra scriptis locis affirmat) & eundem principatum eidem a Constantino donatum. quia quod suum cuiusque est, pluribus ac pręfertim contrariis ex causis suum esse non potest. l. & an eadem, 14. §. penult. D. de except. rei iud. l. non ut ex pluribus, 159. de reg. iur. Neque enim ferri commentum eorum poterit, qui disputant, principatum illum primum a Christo Papae Romano tributum fuisse: Constantinum autem illam Christi donationem confirmasse: & cum primus Imp. Christianus esset, Syl-vestro Papae vacuam illius possessionem tradidisse. Primum quia Pseudoconstantinus diserte scribit, se duarum maximarum rerum donationes ei conferre: Ecclesiastici principatus in omnes, qui in orbe Christiano sunt, sacerdotes, quem Papæ Spiritualem principatum appellant: & totius Occidentalis imperij dominatum, quem iidem Temporalem vocant. De priore, Pseudoconstantinus ita loquitur:Constantinus priuilegium Romanæ ecclesiæ Pontifici contulit, ut in toto orbe Romano sacerdotes ita hunc caput habeant, sicut iudices Regem. Et mox, Sancimus, ut principatum teneat, tam super quatuor sedes, Alexandriam, Antiochenam, Hierosolymitanam & Constantinopolitanam, quàm etiam super omnes in vniuerso orbe terrarum ecclesiás Dei. Quid dilucidius scribere potuit, ut ostenderet se nouum quoddam ius Papæ tribuere, quod antea nunquam habuerat? quis ignorat Priuilegium opponi Iuri communi? & si Constantinus priuilegium Papæ tribuit, Papa antea paris eiusdemque iuris fuisse, quo reliqui episcopi omnes eiusdem collegæ & socij utebantur? Quod si donare principatum vniuersalem Eccle-siasticum Constantinus potuit, certè pleno iure do-minum illius principatus eū fuisse oportet. neque enim plus iuris quisquam transferre in alterū po-test, quàm ipse habeat. At hoc esse absurdissimum, etiam Canonistę omnes fatentur, ut secularis Prin-ceps spiritualem principatum, id est, vniuersalem Episcopatum in omnes Ecclesias possideat, cùm ne vnius quidem Ecclesiæ quantumuis exiguæ sa-cerdotium, aut episcopatum habeat. Quod si nul-lum omnino Constantinus Episcopatum habuit, quomodo vniuersalem orbis terrarum episcopa-tum donare Syluestro potuit, cùm nemo (ut iam diximus) plus iuris transferre in alterum possit, quàm quantum ipse habeat. Et hoc argumentum videmus ante annos ducentos Papæ obiectum à Marsilio Patauino,in Defens. pacis cap. ii. ubi sic scribit: In decretis reperitur privilegium quoddam Imp. Constantini à Pontificibus approbatum, quo B. Sylvestro Romano Pontifici concessit iurisdictionem coactivam super omnes mundi Ecclesias, reliquosque presbyteros seu episcopos omnes. Cumque concessionem illam fuisse va-lidam fateatur Papa Romanus, & cum eo Presbyte-rorum seu Episcoporum reliquus coetus, consequenter ipsis concedendum est, eundem Constantinum hanc iurisdi-ctionem seu potestatem in eos penitus habuisse. Sed re-deamus ad dilemma propositum. Nam sive Papa se principatum illum à Deo adeptum esse contendit, ut in locis paulo ante prolatis profitetur: sive ex Constantini donatione: falsum esse utrumque pro-babimus. primùm ex illa repugnantia, quam modo exposuimus. deinde ex eo quod ipsemet suo se gla-dio iugulat. nam in Decreto locum hunc ex Chrysostomo producit: Quicunque desiderauerit primatum in terra, inueniet confusionem in cœlo, nec inter servos Christi computabitur, qui de primatu tractauerit. dist. 4. c.multi.§. quicunque. Item, Prima sedis Episcopus non appelletur princeps sacerdotum, vel summus sacerdos, aut aliquid eiusmodi, sed tantum Prima sedis Episcopus. Universalis autem nec etiam Rom. Pontifex appelletur. c. primæ sedis. dist.99. quod idem duobus cc. seqq. totidem prope verbis inculca-tur. Quod si ex iure civili disputandum est, ac demonstrandum, eum Christi successorem dici non posse, satis constat tria successorum esse genera. Nam alii sunt successores iuris, quales sunt heredes, qu successores vniuersales dicuntur : alij successores rei, veluti legatarij, emptores, donatarij : qui successores singulares appellantur. l. vlt. D. de except. rei. vend. l. 1. §. in locum, D. quod legat. l. 7. l. 8. de iurem-ran. Postremò alij sunt successores muneris personalis, qui functionis successanei appellantur in l. priuilegio, 27. C. de decur. lib. 10. Prioris generis successores ius & causam habent ab iis, quibus succedunt, siue vniuersales sint, siue singulares l. qui in ius, 177. D. de reg. iu. cum similib. Tertij verò non ab antecessoribus suum ius & causam habet, sed ab iis à quibus eliguntur, & in illorum locum sufficiuntur: quales sunt successores magistratuum, tutorum, curatorum. munus enim personale est, quod solicitudine animi ac vigilantia sustinetur. l. 1. §. 1. l. 6. §. vlt. l. vlt. D. de munerib. & hon. Itaque magistratu vel tutore mortuo, alter est hereditatis, alter muneris successor. l. 1. §. sciendum, l. 4. l. 6. D. de magist. conue. l. 6. §. vlt. D. de his qui not. infam. & quanuis quis testamento tutor detur, imo quanuis quis heres simul & tutor instituatur : tamen non tam à testatore, quàm à lege ius illud adipiscitur, l. 1. D. de testam. tut. l. saepe 53. D. de verb. signif. l. quo tutela, 73. §. 1. D. de reg. iur. His ita constitutis, cùm Papa contendit se Christi successorem esse, quaerere ex eo possumus, cuius se generis successorem esse profiteatur. Nam heres quidem & iuris vniuersi successor dici non potest, siue quia hereditas viuentis ne cogitari quidem potest. l. 1. D. de hered. vend. Christus autem morte extinctus non est, sed vitam viuit & beatam & sempiternam. siue potius, quoniam impia & intoleranda blasphemia est, hominem vllum esse Christi Dei heredem profiteri, cùm heres definitur vnivniuersi iuris successor, quod defunctus habuit. l. hereditas,62. D.de reg.iur.vt omittā, quod nullus heres est,nisive! teftameto, vel lege quorū neutrū: nisi impiè& scelerate ꝓnūtiari potest.Nihilomagis rei singularis successor dici potest:cū regnū Christi neque communionem recipiat,neque diuisionem, be[?] inter Angelos quidem.Heb.1.verf.5.quia Deus constituit illum, vt Paulus loquitur, longe supra omne imperium ac potestatem,& potentiam, & dominium, & omnia subiecit sub pedibus eius, eumque constituit caput super omnia ipsi Eccle- siæ. Ephef.1. 21.&22. Muneris autem sui vniuersi quo modo fucceffotem aut vicarium haberet, qui neque morte extinctus est,sed vitam viuit beatam & sempiternam: & cum perpetuo in Ecclesia sua præsens sit, semper summi pastoris ac sacerdotis munere fungitur?1.Pet.2.Marc.vlt.20.Pfal.110.Heb. 2.&4.&7.& 9. Quinetiam addere illud sine dubitatione possumus,nullum vnquam vel fuisse antea mortalem,vel posthac futurum esse, qui diuinū illud personale Christi Dei hominis munus sustinere posit: vt omnibus Christianis gentibus quę in orbe terrarum vbicunque versantur præsit, prouideat,| consulat. Eodem accedit quod nullus Episcopus,ne Petri quidem,aut alterius Apostoli, successor dici potest, quo modo Papa solet à Canonistis Petri successor appellari: præsertim apud Decium & Cagnollum,qui multos coaceruant,in l. qui per successionem, De regul. iur. vbi cùm Iurisconsulti dicere soleant, Heredem heredis testatoris, esse heredem testatoris, quanuis per successionem longissimam heres sit: Canonistæ ratiocinantur, quemlibet Papam esse successoré Petri, licet quāplurimi intercesserint. Neque enim causam habet vllus Episcopus a Petro,vel alio quouis Apostolo: sed ab electione, Christi auctoritate facta,seu potius ab ipso Christo:sicuti dicere solemus,electum iussu testatoris causa habere non ab eo qui elegit, sed ab ipso testatore.l.vnu,67.§.1.D.de legat.2. l.pater,22.D.de manum.vind.item in substitutionib' testamentariis substitutum non habere causam & ius ab eo cui substitutus est, sed ab ipso testatore. l.coheredi, 4.§.cum filius,D.de vulg.subst.l. vnu ex familia,67.& 1.D.de legat.2.eo accedit, quod succes- sionem non facit locus,aut sedes,siue cathedra,sed Christianæ doctrinæ continuatio: cum accepta a Christo religio continenter per singulos succes- fores,quasi per manus, populo Christiano traditur.Quare nihil nobis aduersantur nouæ quorundam assentatorum Papalium argutiq, qui spe sacerdotij alicuius adducti sic disputant: Papam Ro. non spirituale esse caput ecclesiæ Catholicæ, sed ministeriale:quia quemadmodum Christus particulares Ecclesias, (hoc est dioeceses singulas) per episcopos particulares vicarios suos regit, eodem modo idem Christus vniuersalem ecclesiam per vnum aliquem vniuersalem vicarium suum, Papa R.administrat:qui inferiores illos & particulares episcopos suæ iurisdictioni subiectos in officio contineat. Nam huic obiectioni triplex parata responsio est. Prima est quod hic Principatus non modo a Christo institutus non est, verum etiam contra perspicuum Christi institutum ambitione & libidine dominandi a pontificibus R. occupat*: Etenim Christus XII. apostolos ad prædicandū euangelium suum circumittens, non vni alicui singulare quoddam & præcipuum mandatum dedit:sed vnum idémque vniuersis: hoc modo, Itote in omnes terrarum oras,& prædicatote apud gentes ac nationes omnes euangelium. Itaque in Apocalipsi cœlestis Hierusalem non vnica & singulari,vel vna ex omnibus potissimum,sed simpliciter duodecim columnis fundata esse dicitur: & cum die Pentecostes spiritus sanctus in duodecim Apostolos effusus est, non in vnum aliquem ex ijs potissimum ac præcipue effusus dicitur,sed simpliciter effusus in cunctos. Apparuerunt (inquit Lucas) dispertitę linguæ, quasi linguæ ignitæ: quarū singulæ supra singulorum[?] caput constiterunt. Vbinam aut linguæ aut flammæ mentio fit, quæ præter cæteras lata & ampla supra Petri caput consederit? Denique cum Paulus pastorū Ecclesiæ procurationes ac munera describit, nemini vni principatum super alios tribuit, sed his illud disertis exponit verbis. Christus ascendit in altum, captiuam duxit captiuitatem,& dedit dona hominibus: nam alios dedit apostolos, alios prophetas, alios Euangelistas, alios pastores,& doctores ad instaurationem sanctorum, in opus administrationis ad edificationem corporis Christi.
units.tr: The principate that Christ gave to the Pope over all churches (which the passages cited above affirm most plainly) contradicts the principate that Constantine is said to have given him. What belongs to one person cannot belong to him on many contrary grounds. Dig. 14, §penult., de except. rei iud.; Dig. 159, de reg. iur. Nor can the claim of those be accepted who argue that the Roman Pope first received that principate from Christ, that Constantine then confirmed Christ's gift, and that, since he was the first Christian emperor, he handed over the empty possession of it to Pope Sylvester.
