The first reason is that the Pseudo-Constantine writes expressly that he is conferring on him the gifts of two very great things: the principate of ecclesiastical power over all the priests in the Christian world, which the Papists call the spiritual principate; and dominion over the whole Western empire, which they call the temporal one. On the former, the Pseudo-Constantine speaks thus: Constantine conferred on the Pontiff of the Roman Church a privilege, that throughout the Roman world the priests should have this man as their head, just as judges have the king. And soon after: We decree that he hold the principate not only over the four sees, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem and Constantinople, but also over all the churches of God in the whole world. What could he have written more clearly, if he wanted to show that he was giving the Pope a new right which he had never had before? Who does not know that a privilege is set against common law? And if Constantine conferred a privilege on the Pope, then the Pope was previously equal to all the other bishops, and enjoyed the same right that they, his colleagues and fellows, all enjoyed. But if Constantine could give over the universal ecclesiastical principate, then he must certainly have been its full owner, for no one can transfer to another more right than he himself has. Yet all the canonists agree that it is most absurd for a secular prince to possess the spiritual principate, that is, a universal episcopate over all churches, when he does not even have the priesthood or the episcopate of any single church, however small. And if Constantine had no episcopate at all, how could he give Sylvester the episcopate over the whole world, since, as we have said, no one can transfer to another more right than he himself has? We see that Marsilius of Padua, two hundred years ago, raised this argument against the Pope in his Defensor pacis, chapter 2, where he writes thus: In the decrees there is found a certain privilege of the Emperor Constantine, approved by the Pontiffs, by which he granted to blessed Sylvester, Roman Pontiff, coercive jurisdiction over all the churches of the world and over all the other presbyters or bishops. And since the Roman Pope admits that this grant was valid, and with him the rest of the company of presbyters or bishops, it follows that the same Constantine must have had this jurisdiction or power over them entirely. But let us return to the dilemma proposed. For whether the Pope contends that he obtained that principate from God, as he professes in the passages quoted a little earlier, or from the donation of Constantine, we shall prove that both claims are false. First, from that contradiction which we have just set out. Second, from the fact that he cuts his own throat with his own sword. For in the Decretum he cites from Chrysostom this passage: Whoever shall desire the primacy on earth will find confusion in heaven, and he who has discussed the primacy shall not be counted among the servants of Christ. Dist. 4, c. Multi, §. Quicunque. Likewise: let the Bishop of the first see not be called prince of the priests, or chief priest, or anything of that kind, but only Bishop of the first see. Nor let the Roman Pontiff be called universal. C. Primae sedis, dist. 99. The same thing is driven home in almost the same words in the two following chapters. But if we must argue from the civil law, and demonstrate that he cannot be called Christ's successor, it is well established that there are three kinds of successors. For some are successors in right, such as heirs, who are called universal successors; others are successors in a thing, such as legatees, buyers and donees, who are called singular successors. Dig. last, de except. rei vend.; Dig. 1, §in locum, quod legat.; Dig. 7 and 8, de iurejurando. Last of all, there are successors in a personal office, who are called successors in the function, as in Cod. 27, privilegio, de decurionibus, lib. 10. Successors of the first kind have their right and cause from those whom they succeed, whether they are universal or singular: Dig. 177, qui in ius, de reg. iur., with similar passages. But successors of the third kind have their right and cause not from their predecessors, but from those by whom they are chosen, and are put in their place: such as the successors of magistrates, guardians and curators. For an office is a personal matter, which is sustained by the care and vigilance of the mind. Dig. 1, §1; Dig. 6, §last; Dig. last, de muneribus et honoribus. Therefore, when a magistrate or guardian dies, one man succeeds to the inheritance and another to the office. Dig. 1, §sciendum; Dig. 4; Dig. 6, de magistratibus conveniendis; Dig. 6, §last, de his qui notantur infamia. And although someone is appointed guardian by a will, indeed even though someone is instituted both heir and guardian at once, nevertheless he obtains that right not so much from the testator as from the law. Dig. 1, de testamentaria tutela; Dig. 53, saepe, de verborum significatione; Dig. 73, §1, quo tutela, de reg. iur. With these points settled, when the Pope contends that he is Christ's successor, we can ask him which kind of successor he professes to be. For an heir cannot be called successor to the whole right either, since the inheritance of a living man cannot even be conceived of: Dig. 1, de hered. vend. But Christ, who is not extinguished by death, lives a life that is blessed and everlasting. Or rather, since it is an impious and intolerable blasphemy for any man to profess himself heir of Christ God, when an heir is defined as the successor to the whole right which the deceased had (Dig. 62, hereditas, de reg. iur.), to pass over the fact that no one is an heir except by will or by law, neither of which applies here, it can be pronounced only impiously and wickedly. Nor can he be called the successor to a single thing either, since Christ's kingdom admits neither sharing nor division, not even among the angels. Heb. 1.5. For God, as Paul says, has set Christ far above every principality and power and might and dominion, and has put all things under his feet, and made him head over all things to the Church itself. Eph. 1.21, 22. But how could he have a successor or vicar in his universal office, he who was not extinguished by death, but lives a life that is blessed and everlasting, and who, being always present in his Church, always discharges the office of the supreme Shepherd and Priest? 1 Pet. 2; Mark 16.20; Ps. 110; Heb. 2, 4, 7, 9. Indeed we may add without doubt that no one has ever yet existed, or will exist hereafter, who could sustain that divine personal office of Christ, God and man, so as to preside over, provide for and counsel all Christian nations that live anywhere in the world. To this is added that no bishop, not even Peter's or that of any other apostle, can be called a successor, as the Pope is customarily called Peter's successor by the canonists; especially Decius and Cagnolus, who heap up many examples on Dig. qui per successionem, de reg. iur., where, although the jurists are accustomed to say that the heir of the testator's heir is the testator's heir, even though he is heir by a very long succession, the canonists reason that any Pope is a successor of Peter, however many have intervened. For no bishop derives his cause from Peter or from any other apostle, but from election made by Christ's authority, or rather from Christ himself; just as we are accustomed to say that one who is chosen by the command of a testator has his cause not from the one who chose him, but from the testator himself. Dig. 67, §1, unus, de legatis 2; Dig. 22, pater, de manumissione vindicta. Likewise, in testamentary substitutions, the substitute has his cause and right not from the one for whom he is substituted, but from the testator himself. Dig. 4, §cum filius, de vulgari substitutione; Dig. 67 and 1, unus ex familia, de legatis 2. Moreover, succession is not made by a place, or a seat, or a chair, but by the continuation of Christian doctrine, since the religion received from Christ is handed on to the Christian people continuously through the individual successors, as if by hand. Wherefore those new arguments of certain Papal flatterers do us no harm, who, led by hope of some priesthood, argue thus: the Roman Pope is not the spiritual head of the Catholic Church, but a ministerial one, because just as Christ rules the particular churches (that is, the individual dioceses) through his particular vicar bishops, in the same way the same Christ administers the universal Church through one universal vicar of his, the Roman Pope, who keeps those lesser and particular bishops in obedience to his jurisdiction. For there is a threefold ready answer to this objection. The first is that this principate was not only not instituted by Christ, but is actually seized by the Roman Pontiffs in ambition and lust for domination, against the plain institution of Christ. For when Christ sent the twelve apostles around to preach his gospel, he gave not some single and special command to one of them, but one and the same command to all: "Go into all the corners of the earth, and preach the gospel among all peoples and nations." So in the Apocalypse the heavenly Jerusalem is said to be founded not on one single column, or one chief column above all the others, but simply on twelve columns. And when the Holy Spirit was poured out on the twelve apostles on the day of Pentecost, it is not said to have been poured out on one of them in particular and above all, but simply poured out on all of them. Luke says: "There appeared divided tongues, as of fire, and one sat upon each of them." Where is there any mention of a tongue or a flame which, larger and wider than the rest, sat above Peter's head? Finally, when Paul describes the duties and offices of the ministers of the Church, he gives the principate over the others to no single man, but sets it out in these plain words: Christ ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and he gave gifts to men: for he gave some apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, some pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ.

units.la: Altera responsio est,quòd si Christus, aut Petrus principatum aliquem & vnum ministeriale caput in Ecclesia instituisset,non dubiū est,quin Ecclesia primitiva,tā recenti memoria,institutum illud tenuisset. At ex contrario videmus antiquissimas synodos vniuersales. Nicæna nepe, Costātinopoli-tana,Ephesina & Calcedonē[?] instituisse[?],vt singulis ciuitatibus singuli præficerentur Episcopi. tum singulis prouinciis, singuli Archiepiscopi,siue Pa-
units.tr: The second answer is this: if Christ or Peter had instituted some principal authority and a single ministerial head in the Church, there is no doubt that the primitive Church, so recent in memory, would have kept that institution. But on the contrary we see that the most ancient universal synods, namely those of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon, established that single bishops should be set over single cities, and then single archbishops, or patriarchs, over single provinces,

units.la: d. ij. triarchæ,pari omnes eadémque dignitate, auctoritate,iurisdictione,potestate, gradu: extra quàm, quòd Archiepiscopo Rom. propter vrbis antiquitatem & amplitudinem honos delatus est,vt in synodis & comitiis,primus,ante omnes,non tamen superiore loco,sederet:tum proxime ipfu Archie-pifcopus Constantinopolitanus assideret,propter caussam illius simillimam,quia nouę Romæ Imperatoriæ vrbis antistes erat:cùm, fi antiquioris Ecclesiæ habita ratio fuisset, aut primus, aut certè fecudus ille loc' Antiochino Episcopo deberetur:tu[?] deinde Alexandrinus,Hierosolimitanus,postea tres Archiepiscopi Iuftinianici, pp leuissimas caussas ab Imp.Iustiniano creati,locū in paribus fellis caperet:quas caussas posterius sub Crimine falsi,demonstrabimus:vbi falsitates,impofturas,& corruptelas à Papa R. ad hanc explendam ambitionem suā institutas commemorabimus. Tertia refpofio est, quòd cùm Christus instituerit Apostolos, vt effent nuntij & prædicones mandatorum suorum, per varias orbis terrarum oras concursantes, nullum aliquem ab eo legimus institutum Archinuntium aut Archipræconem: præsertim mutum & quiescentem, qui Romæ deses & ignauus, quæ à cæteris vbicunque terrarum gesta essent, auditione acciperet:suaeque interea ambitioni otiosus, & nihil agens seruiret.Episcopi enim nihil aliud sut, nisi Christi nuntij, & prædicones mandatorum ipsius, in singulis ciuitatibus instituti: sicut olim mandata Procofulibus & Præsidibus,qui in varias imperii prouincias mittebantur ab Imperatoribus Rom. dari folebant, vt inter omnes Iuris & antiquitatu Rom.studiosos constat. Itaque, qui vel natura, vel voluntate mutus est,hoc est, qui tacet qui silet,qui ut in comoediis mutam personā sustinet, & neque nutii neque praeconis officio fungitur, nec Euange[?]lium praedicat, is non modò iure, sed ne nomine quidem Episcopi, aut Archiepiscopi dignus est.
units.tr: d. ij. all equal in the same dignity, authority, jurisdiction, power and rank. The only exception was that the Archbishop of Rome, because of the antiquity and size of his city, was given the honour of sitting first in the synods and assemblies, before all the others, though not in a higher place. Next to him the Archbishop of Constantinople would sit, because he was bishop of New Rome, the imperial city, for a reason very like the first. Yet if the claim of the more ancient Church had been taken into account, that second place would have been owed to the bishop of Antioch. Then the Alexandrian and the Jerusalemite would take their place among equals, and afterwards three Justinianic archbishops, created by the Emperor Justinian for the very slightest reasons. These reasons we will set out later under the charge of forgery, where we will recall the falsehoods, impostures and corruptions which the Roman Pope devised to satisfy this ambition of his. The third answer is that, since Christ appointed the Apostles to be messengers and heralds of his commands, running about through the various shores of the earth, we read of no one appointed by him as chief messenger or chief herald. Least of all do we read of a mute and quiet one who, sitting idle and lazy at Rome, would learn by hearsay what was done elsewhere in the world, and meanwhile, idle in his ambition, would serve and do nothing. For bishops are nothing other than the messengers of Christ and the heralds of his commands, appointed in individual cities, just as commands were once usually given to proconsuls and governors whom the Roman emperors sent into the various provinces of the empire, as all students of Roman law and antiquity agree. Therefore whoever is mute by nature or by choice, that is, whoever keeps silent and quiet, who, as in comedies, takes on the mute role and performs neither the office of messenger nor of herald, nor preaches the Gospel, such a one is worthy not only in law but not even in name of the title of bishop or archbishop.

units.la: Ex quibus cum singulis tum universis sine ulla dubitatione concludimus, temporis & successionis antiquitatem nihil Papae. R. ad suam tuendam tyrannidem prodesse: quando quidem diutina possessio(ut Imp.loquuntur) tantum iure successionis sine iusto titulo obtenta prodesse ad praescriptionem longi temporis non potest.l.4.C. de praescripti long.temp. Sed quoniam Papae in suis Decre-talibus tertio quoque versu cantilenam illam inculcant. Quia Petro dictum est, Pasce oues meas, & Super hanc petram: operae pretium est, veram ac germanam illorum locorum interpretatione subiicere. Nam August. tract.124.in Ioan. Quando, inquit, dictum est Petro, Tibi dabo claves regni coelorum, & Quodcunque ligaveris super terram: vniuersam significabat Ecclesiam, quae fundata est super petram. Vnde & Petrus nomen accepit. Non enim a Petro, sed a petra Petrus: sicut non Christus a Christianis, sed a Christo Christianus vocatur. Ideo quippe ait Dominus, Super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam, quia dixerat Petrus, Tu es Christus filius Dei viui. Super hanc ergo, inquit, petram, quam confessus es, aedificabo Ecclesiam meam. Petra enim erat Christus, super quod fundamentum etiam ipse aedificatus est Petrus. Fundamentum quippe aliud nemo potest ponere, praeter id quod positum est, quod est Iesus. Ecclesia ergo quae fundatur in Christo, claves ab eo regni & coelorum accepit in Petro, id est, potestatem ligandi soluendique peccata. Quod e-nim est per proprietatem Christus in ecclesia, hoc per significationem est Petrus in petra: qua significatione intelligitur Christus petra, Petrus Ecclesia. Haec Augustus. quod idem inculcat in lib.contra Iud.paga. Itemque in Ioan.tractat.decimo. & de verbo Domini, serm.20. qua in sententia Cyrillus in dialogis de trinit.lib.4. Petram, inquit, per agnominatione aliud nihil quam inconcussam ac firmissimam discipuli fidem vocauit, in qua Ecclesia Christi fundata est. Et hoc idē confirmant A[?] b.in Epist.ad Ephe.cap.2. Chryso-stomus in homilia in Mat.55. quinetiam Canoni-stæ inc.quodcunque.24.q.1. hanc Augustini sententiam proferunt. Quoniam in persona Petri Ecclesia ipsa claues accepit. quod idem inculcatur ex Hieronymo in c.omnib.ead.q. Bernardus autem acriter in illam Paparum arrogantiam inuehes, tandē in Epist.230.in haec verba prorumpit: Et olim quidem, eratis contra Apostolum Petrum, dominantes in Clerum: imo & contra coapostolum eius Paulum dominabamini fidei totius orbis. At nunc nouum aliquid addidistis, vsurpantes amplius & in ipsam religionem. quid restat, nisi vt adiuciatis & ipsi Angelis sanctis dominari? Gregorius autē cognomento magnus Epi.30.ad Mauricium Imp.li.16. Ego fidenter dico, quod quisquis se vniuersale sacerdotem vocat, vel vocari desiderat, in elatione sua Antichristi praecurrit, quia superbiendo se cateris praeponit, quorum similia multis locis videre licet apud eundem & ad eundē Mauricium li.6.Epi.188.& epi.194. item li.7.epist.3.& 74.& 79.& 80. Atque haec quidem hactenus de priore dilemmatis superioris parte. Nunc de altera, hoc est, de Constantini donatione videamus, quanquam idoneior de illa differendi locus fore videatur: vbi de falsi crimine exponemus, commodius est in praesentia vno hoc verbo totā illam disputationem perstringere: Totum videlicet illud donationis instrumentum, quod a Papa profertur, falsum, fictum, spurium, suppositum, & adulterinum esse, atque ex eadem officina prose-ctum, unde superius ostendimus Conformitatum Franciscanarum volumen prodiisse: cuius rei quia posterius suo loco argumenta xxv. certisima proferentur, nunc secundo huic crimini fine imponemus. Tatum coronidis loco quaestione huic monacho nostro Franciscano proponemus, haud sanè (ut videtur) explicatu facilem. Sixtus noster est Papa, & simul Franciscanus. quatenus est Papa, dignitate habet (ut superius demonstravimus) non modo summam in terris, verum etiam magnā in cœlo, purgatorio, & inferis. quatenus est Franciscanus, nō dubiū est, quin pro sua erga patronum suū pietate fateatur B. Franciscū Supercherubinicā dignitate obtinere. Non dicimus inter cherubin (ait Antoninus Florentinus) sed super Cherubin, & certum est secundum doctores, quod super Cherubin, sunt Seraphin. hac Anto. lib. hist. 3.Tit.23.c.cap.1. Quaeritur ergo, cum hic Papa e vita excedens a suo Francisco excipietur, utrum super Cherubin, an super Seraphin sedem sit habiturus? nam sub stola B. Virginis solis fratribus Dominicanis locum esse demonstravimus. Ambigui causa permagna est: quoniā Papa (ut Augustinus Steuchus ostendit) Deus est: ut Canonistę disputat, semideus. At Franciscus (ut superius ex Diaboli testimonio dictum est) nihil nisi monachus sto-machofus. Ex altera parte Franciscus appellatur ab hoc nostro monacho, Iesus typicus: quasi quis di-xerit, Alter Iesus, vel cum priore Iesu conforma-tus. Si Franciscum super Papam collocaremus,super Deum suum aut semideum illum collo-caremus:quod esset absurdissimum.Si infra Papam ei locum attribueremus, nihilominus absurdè alterum Iesum Papæ subiiceremus:neque id fortas-se Iesuitę propter eximiam nominis sui dignitatem ferre possent. Quid igitur dicemus? Bartolus in arduis quæstionibus monere auditores solebat, vt cogitarent. Nos sine præiudicio veritatis atque vt pragmatici loquuntur, per modum prouisionis in-terea locum huic Papæ relinquemus eum ipsum, quem ei Gregorius Magnus attribuit: qui qualis sit, aliquanto posterius vbi de Luciferi apud inferos aduentu mentio fiet,describemus.
units.tr: From these points, both individually and taken together, we conclude without any doubt that the antiquity of time and of succession does nothing to help the Roman Pope in defending his tyranny. For long possession, as the emperors put it, obtained merely by right of succession without a just title, cannot help towards prescription of long time (Code 4, on prescription of long time). But since the Popes in their Decretals hammer home that refrain in every third line, Because it was said to Peter, Feed my sheep, and Upon this rock, it is worth setting out the true and genuine interpretation of those passages. For Augustine, tractate 124 on John: "When it was said to Peter, I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and, Whatever you bind upon earth, he signified the whole Church, which is founded upon the rock. Whence Peter also took his name. For Peter is not from petra, but petra from Peter, just as Christ is not called Christian from the Christians, but Christians are called from Christ. Indeed the Lord said, Upon this rock I will build my Church, because Peter had said, You are Christ, the Son of the living God. Upon this rock, then, he says, which you have confessed, I will build my Church. For the rock was Christ, upon which foundation Peter himself was also built. For no one can lay another foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus. The Church, then, which is founded in Christ, received from him the keys of the kingdom of heaven in Peter, that is, the power of binding and loosing sins. For what Christ is in the Church by proper meaning, that Peter is in the rock by signification; by which signification Christ is understood as the rock, and Peter as the Church." So Augustine. He repeats the same in his book against the Jews and pagans, and in tractate ten on John, and in sermon 20 on the words of the Lord. In the same sense Cyril, in the Dialogues on the Trinity, book 4: "By the figure of a name he called the rock nothing other than the disciple's unshaken and most firm faith, on which the Church of Christ is founded." The same is confirmed by Ambrose on Ephesians chapter 2, and by Chrysostom in homily 55 on Matthew. Moreover the canonists, in the chapter Quodcunque, 24 q. 1, cite this saying of Augustine: "Because in the person of Peter the Church itself received the keys." The same is repeated from Jerome in the chapter Omnibus, in the same question. Bernard, moreover, attacking fiercely that arrogance of the Popes, at last breaks out in Epistle 230 in these words: "And formerly indeed you were lording it over the clergy against the Apostle Peter; nay, even against his fellow apostle Paul you lorded it over the faith of the whole world. But now you have added something new, usurping even over religion itself. What remains, except that you should also lord it over the holy Angels?" Gregory, surnamed the Great, in Epistle 30 to the Emperor Maurice, book 16: "I confidently say that whoever calls himself, or desires to be called, universal priest, in his pride runs before Antichrist, because by his arrogance he puts himself above the others." Similar things can be seen in many places in the same Gregory and to the same Maurice: book 6, epistles 188 and 194; likewise book 7, epistles 3, 74, 79 and 80. And so much for now concerning the first part of the above dilemma. Now let us look at the other part, that is, the donation of Constantine. Although a more suitable place for discussing it would be where we treat the charge of forgery, it is more convenient for the present to sum up that whole disputation in one word: namely, that the whole instrument of donation which the Pope produces is false, fabricated, spurious, supposititious and counterfeit, and came from the same workshop from which we showed above that the volume of the Franciscan Conformities issued. Since twenty-five very certain arguments for this will be set out later in their proper place, we will now put an end to this second charge. As a crown to the whole, we will put a question to this Franciscan monk of ours, one not easy (as it seems) to explain. Our Sixtus is Pope and at the same time a Franciscan. As Pope he holds dignity (as we showed above) not only supreme on earth but also great in heaven, purgatory and hell. As Franciscan, there is no doubt that out of his devotion to his patron he confesses that Blessed Francis holds a dignity above the Cherubim. "We do not say among the Cherubim," says Antoninus of Florence, "but above the Cherubim, and it is certain according to the doctors that above the Cherubim are the Seraphim" (so Antoninus, History book 3, title 23, chapter 1). The question therefore arises: when this Pope departs this life and is received by his Francis, will he have his seat above the Cherubim or above the Seraphim? For we showed that under the mantle of the Blessed Virgin there is room only for the Dominican brothers. The doubt is very great, since the Pope (as Augustinus Steuchus shows) is God, and (as the canonists dispute) a demigod. But Francis (as was said above from the devil's testimony) is nothing but a surly monk. On the other hand, Francis is called by this monk of ours Jesus typicus, as if one had said "another Jesus", or one conformed to the earlier Jesus. If we placed Francis above the Pope, we would place him above his God or demigod, which would be most absurd. If we gave him a place below the Pope, we would still absurdly set another Jesus beneath the Pope, and perhaps the Jesuits could not bear that, because of the exceptional dignity of their name. What then shall we say? Bartolus used to advise his hearers in difficult questions to think it over. We, without prejudice to the truth, and as the practical men say, by way of provisional measure, will meanwhile leave to this Pope the place which Gregory the Great assigned to him. What sort of place that is, we will describe a little later, when mention is made of Lucifer's coming among the dead.
THE CRIME OF CORRUPTED RELIGION.

units.la: HActenus de secundo Papatus crimine summatim pro instituti nostri ratione dictum videtur satis. Proximum est, vt de crimine corruptæ religionis differamus[?]. Nam cum Papa summum illum dominatum sibi in Christianā religionem sumpsisset, tum quasi pro suo iure noua-re,interpolare,ac transformare illam arbitratu suo instituit. Cuius rei primum hoc documentum est. Scriptura sacra docet nos,vnicam esse religionis & colendi Dei formam,eam quæ Prophetarum & Apostolorum literis consignata est: sic, vt ei nihil vel addere, vel detrahere, ne per Angelum quidem cœlestem, liceat. Ioann.14.2. Timoth.3. Itaque Christus, Frustrà, inquit, me colunt docentes doctrinas, quæ sunt mandata hominum. Matth.15. Marc.7. Item, Non addetis ad verbum quod vobis loquor,nec auferetis ex eo.Deut.4. Item,Non de-clinabis neque ad dextram,neque ad sinistram: sed per viam quam praecepit Dominus Deus vester ambulabitis. Deut.5.& 6. Quinetiā Irenaeus Lug-dunensis Episcopus auctor antiquissimus: scripsit enim circiter annum Christi 198. Postquam,inquit, surrexit dominus noster a mortuis, & imbuti sunt Apostoli spiritu sancto superveniente virtute ex alto, de omnibus adimpleti sunt, & habuerunt perfectam cognitionem salutis. Item cap.4. Non oportet apud alios quaerere Veritatem: cum Apostoli plenissime in ecclesia contulerunt omnia, quae sunt veritatis: ut omnis quicunque velit sumat ex ea potum vitae. Item Athanasius in pr. lib.2.adversus gentes. Sancta,inquit, & divinitus inspirata scriptura sola ad omnem veritatis instructionem abunde sufficit. Haec ille. Audiamus nunc quid Papa & Papae assentatores Iesuastri de Scriptura sacra statuant: Scriptura sacra est doctrina imperfecta, mutila,manca: quae non continet omnia quę ad salutem,fidem & mores pie vivendi pertinet: sed ille sanctae scripturae defectus sarciendus est assumento traditionum. Haec Iesuastri in censura Colonienși sol.220.item in Catechismo Canisij sol.126.160.161. 162. Et in eandem sententiam liber Concilij Tridentini Sess.4.cap.1.disciplinam ecclesiae, praeter Sanctam scripturam, contineri in traditionibus maiorū, quae quasi per manus traditae ad nos usque pervenerunt, tanquam vel ore tenus a Christo, vel a spiritu sancto dicta-tis. Videamus nunc cuiusmodi traditiones per manus a maioribus traditae nobis observandae sint. Atq; imprimis illa proferatur. Papa solet certo & stato die imagunculas quasdā effingere in formam agni, ex alba cera oleo delibuta. Has affirmat de collo suspensas, peccata hominum æque purgare, ut Christi sanguis purgat: easdem affirmat fulgura depellere, parturientibus opem ferre, & homines ex incendio ac naufragio seruare. Quid sceleratius dici aut cogitari potest? Atqui maiorum hæ traditiones appellantur, huic Papæ à superioribus per manus traditæ. Nam in lib. Ceremon. Pontific. 1. sect. 7. scriptum ita est,
units.tr: So far, I think, enough has been said, in the summary way suited to my plan, about the second crime of the Papacy. Next we must take up the crime of corrupted religion. For once the Pope had claimed for himself supreme lordship over the Christian religion, he set about renewing, interpolating and transforming it at his own pleasure, as if it were his right. The first proof of this is as follows. Holy Scripture teaches us that there is one form of religion and of worshipping God, the one recorded in the writings of the Prophets and Apostles, and that nothing may be added to it or taken from it, not even by a heavenly angel. John 14.2. Timothy 3. So Christ says: "In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines that are the commandments of men." Matt. 15. Mark 7. Likewise: "You shall not add to the word that I speak to you, nor take anything from it." Deut. 4. Likewise: "You shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left, but shall walk in the way which the Lord your God has commanded you." Deut. 5 and 6. Moreover, Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, a very ancient author, wrote about the year of Christ 198: "After our Lord rose from the dead, and the Apostles were filled with the Holy Spirit coming upon them from on high with power, they were fulfilled in all things and had perfect knowledge of salvation." Likewise, chapter 4: "It is not right to seek the truth among others, since the Apostles most fully deposited in the Church everything that belongs to the truth, so that whoever wishes may draw from it the drink of life." Likewise Athanasius, in the preface to book 2 Against the Gentiles: "Holy and divinely inspired Scripture alone is abundantly sufficient for instruction in all truth." So he says. Let us now hear what the Pope and his flattering Jesuits lay down about Holy Scripture: Scripture is an imperfect, maimed and lame doctrine, which does not contain everything that pertains to salvation, faith and the pious conduct of life, and this defect of Holy Scripture must be patched with the addition of traditions. So the Jesuits in the Cologne censure, p. 220, and likewise in Canisius's Catechism, pp. 126, 160, 161, 162. To the same effect, the decree of the Council of Trent, session 4, chapter 1, says that the discipline of the Church is contained, besides Holy Scripture, in the traditions of our ancestors, which, handed down as if from hand to hand, have come down even to us, as dictated either by word of mouth by Christ or by the Holy Spirit. Let us now see what kind of traditions, handed down from our ancestors by hand, we are bound to observe. And first let this one be brought forward. The Pope is accustomed, on a fixed and set day, to fashion little images in the form of a lamb from white wax anointed with oil. These he declares, when hung from the neck, cleanse men's sins just as the blood of Christ cleanses them; he declares that the same images drive off lightning, bring help to women in labour, and save men from fire and shipwreck. What more wicked thing can be said or imagined? Yet these are called traditions of our ancestors, handed down by hand to this Pope from his predecessors. For in the Ceremonial of the Pontiffs, book 1, section 7, it is written thus:

units.la: Balsamus & cera munda, cum Chrismatis unda Conficiunt agnum: quod munus do tibi magnum Fonte velut natum per mystica sanctificatum, Fulgura desursum depellit, omne malignum Peccatum frangit, ut CHRISTI SANGVIS & angit.
units.tr: Balsam and pure wax, with the chrism's anointing, they make a lamb: a great gift that I give to you, as if born of the font and consecrated by mystic rites. It drives down the lightning from on high, breaks every evil sin, so that the BLOOD OF CHRIST may crush it.

units.la: Prægnans seruatur, simul & partus liberatur. Dona refert dignis, virtutes destruet ignis. Portatus munde de fluctibus eripit unda.
units.tr: The pregnant woman is kept safe, and at the same time the birth is freed. It gives gifts to the worthy; it destroys the powers of fire. Carried clean, it snatches from the waves.

units.la: Ex eodē genere illud est carmē impiū ac plane ne-farium quod nō multis ante annis Biturigę in summo Episcopali templo in tabula lapidea incisum, & ad caput trunci siue tigilli pauperum affixum e-rat: sed Francisci Duareni admonitu, qui tum in illa Academia ius ciuile profitebatur exemptum ac disturbatum est.
units.tr: Of the same kind is that impious and utterly nefarious verse, which not many years ago was cut into a stone tablet in the main episcopal church at Bourges and fixed to the head of a trunk or box for the poor. It was removed and disturbed only at the urging of Francis Duaren, who then taught civil law in that university.

units.la: Hic des deuote cælestibus associo te,[?] Mentes ægrotæ per munera sunt ibi lotæ. Ergo venite gentes à sorde remotæ. Qui datis, estote certi de diuite dote. Te precor, accelera, spargas hic dum potes æra: Et sic reuera secure calica spera.
units.tr: Here give devoutly; I join you to the heavenly ones. Sick minds are washed here by gifts. Therefore come, you nations, removed from filth. You who give, be certain of a rich dowry. I pray you, hurry, and scatter money here while you can; and so, truly, with confidence hope for the cup.

units.la: O si tu scires quantum data prosit ibi res, Tu iuxta vires donares quod dare quires.
units.tr: Oh, if only you knew how much the gift profits there, you would give what you are able to give, according to your means.

units.la: Te miser àpœna, dum tempus habes, aliena.Huc dare te pœna, veniæ fit aperta crumena.Co fors cœlestis fabricæ, qui porrigit est is.Ex hoc sum testis, hic vos mundare potestis.
units.tr: Wretch, while you have time, free yourself from another's punishment. Give yourself here to punishment; the purse is opened for pardon. He who holds out the box is one of the heavenly builders. Of this I am a witness: here you may be cleansed.

units.la: Fratres haurite de trunco pocula vitæ:Hic aliquid finite, veri velut Israelitæ.Crede mihi, crede, cœli dominaberis æde.Nam pro mercede Christo dices, Mihi cede.
units.tr: Brothers, drink the cups of life from the trunk. Here, like true Israelites, make some offering. Believe me, believe: you will rule in the house of heaven. For as your reward you will say to Christ, "Give way to me."

units.la: Hic datur exponi paradisus venditioni.Currant ergo boni rapientes culmina throni.Vis retinere forum? mihi tradas pauca bonorum,Pro summa quorum reserabitur aula polorum.
units.tr: Here paradise is put up for sale. Let the good hurry, snatching at the heights of the throne. Do you want to keep your place? Hand over a few of your goods, for the price of which the hall of heaven will be unlocked.

units.la: Hic si large des, in cœlo sit tua sedes:Qui fert hic parce, parce comprendet in arce.Cur tardus tantum? nummi mihi des aliquantum.Pro solo nummo gaudebis in æthere summo.
units.tr: Here, if you give generously, let your seat be in heaven. Whoever gives little here will be received sparingly in the citadel. Why so slow? Give me some money. For a single coin you will rejoice in the highest heaven.

units.la: Denos sume quater, unum semel, hæc sacra materAnnos condonat, sanctus pater ista coronat.Tot quadragenas dat & abluit hic tibi pœnas.Mil missis decies socius, si des ibi, fies.
units.tr: Take ten four times and one once: this sacred mother remits years, and the holy father crowns these. She gives so many forties and here washes away your penalties. Sent ten times over, you become a partner, if you give there.

units.la: Est igitur hæc prima Paparum traditio, quæ nobis pari eadémque qua Scriptura sacra, auctoritate traditur. Sequitur altera: Scriptura sacra docet nos, sacramentum Baptismi esse aspersionem sanguinis Iesu Christi, in remissionem peccatorum, & iustitiæ ipsius imputationem. Act. 22. Rom. 6.1. Corinth. 6.15. At Papæ traditiones tribuunt Baptismum Campanis: tatóque sacramento sacerdotes Papatus passim ita scelerate ac nefarie abutuntur, ut Imp. Maximilianus primus que-relam ea de re conscripserit, quae inter ipsius gra-uamina, his extat verbis: Item suffraganei excogitaue-runt, ut solum ipsi, & nullus alius sacerdos, Campanas baptizaret. Credunt deinde simpliciores, ita affirmanti-bus suffraganeis, tales campanas baptizatas, daemones & tempestates pellere. quapropter innumeri interdum ad-hibentur compatres, praecipue vero qui fortuna pollent, exorantur, quo baptizationis tempore funem, quo campana ligata est tangunt, ac suffraganeo praecinente (que-admodum in infantium baptizatione fieri solet) omnes pariter respondent, ac campanae nomen ingeminant, vestesque nova (quemadmodum & Christianis fieri solet) induunt. Et mox: Res igitur tam nefanda & illicita merito aboleri debet. Praeclare Maximilianus, ac luculenter. Sed ut sues coeno, ita Papae corruptelis ac sordibus istis delectantur. Et de ista turpissima sacramenti polluendi consuetudine videatur Martin. de Arles, in tracta. de superstit. num. 3. num. 9. nu. 14.
units.tr: This, then, is the first tradition of the Popes, which is handed down to us with the same equal authority as Holy Scripture. Another follows: Scripture teaches us that the sacrament of Baptism is the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ, for the remission of sins and the imputation of his righteousness. Acts 22. Rom. 6. 1 Cor. 6. But the Papal traditions ascribe Baptism to bells, and the priests of the Papacy everywhere abuse so sacred a sacrament so wickedly and impiously that the Emperor Maximilian I drew up a complaint on this matter, which stands among his grievances in these words: Likewise, the suffragans have devised that only they, and no other priest, may baptize the bells. Then the simpler folk believe, since the suffragans so assert, that bells so baptized drive away demons and storms. Therefore countless godparents are sometimes called in, especially those who are powerful by fortune, and they are entreated so that at the time of the baptism they touch the rope to which the bell is tied, and when the suffragan intones (as is usually done at the baptism of infants) they all respond alike and repeat the name of the bell, and dress it in new clothes, as is customarily done for Christians. And soon after: Such an unspeakable and illicit thing ought therefore rightly to be abolished. Admirably and clearly said, Maximilian! But as swine delight in mire, so the Papists delight in these corruptions and filth. And concerning this most shameful custom of polluting the sacrament, see Martin de Arles, in his treatise on superstitions, nn. 3, 9, 14.

units.la: Age porro: & aliquot insuper religionis corruptelas persequamur. Scriptura docet nos, unicum esse Mediatorem Dei & hominum, Iesum Christum. 1. Timoth. 2. & rursus 1. Ioann. 2. & Rom. 8. Heb. 7.
units.tr: Come, let us pursue yet some further corruptions of religion. Scripture teaches us that there is one Mediator between God and men, Jesus Christ. 1 Tim. 2. And again 1 John 2, Rom. 8, Heb. 7.

units.la: Itaque Ambrosius in eandem epistolam: Solent, in-quit, misera uti excusatione, dicentes per iustos posse iri ad Deum, sicut per Comites perveniretur ad Regem. Age, numquid tam demens est aliquis, & salutis suae immemor, ut honorificentiam Regis vindicet Comiti, cum hac de re si qui etiam tractare fuerint inventi, iure ut rei damnentur maiestatis. Et isti non putabunt reos qui honorem nominis Dei deferunt creaturae, & relicto domino conservos adorant: quasi sit aliquid plus, quod seruitur Deo.
units.tr: Accordingly Ambrose, on the same epistle: People, he says, are wont to use a wretched excuse, saying that one can come to God through righteous men, just as one would come to the king through the counts. Come now, is anyone so foolish, and so forgetful of his own salvation, as to claim for a count the honour due to the king? And if any were found even discussing this matter, they would rightly be condemned as guilty of treason. And those men will not think guilty those who transfer the honour of God's name to a creature, and, leaving the Lord, worship their fellow-servants, as if there were something more in serving God.

units.la: Nam & ideo ad Regem per tribunos & Comites itur, quin quia homo utique Rex:& nescit quibus debeat Remp. committere. Ad Deum autem,quem utique nihil latet (omnium enim merita nouit) promerendum ,suffragatore non est opus:sed mente deuota.Ubicunque enim talis locutus fuerit,nihil respondebit.Hęc Ambros.Quid? Papatus quàm religiosè hoc Scripturæ sacræ & Ecclesiæ veteris institutum seruat? Negat ullum unquam ex hac vita sanctum excessisse, & in beatorum sedes receptum esse, qui non Mediatoris, ac deprecatoris officio fungatur. Tantùmne? imò verò quoscunque Papæ vita defunctos ganeones, quoscunque Franciscos, Dominicos & eiusdem generis planos,agyrtas,impostores,præstigiatores in diuorum numerum referre voluerunt, eosdem mediatores ac suffragatores nobis induxerunt. Scriptura docet nos,duo tantùm esse loca mortuorum animis post hanc vitam constituta, beatis quidem coelos,maledictis autem inferos, Ioan.5.Mat.25.Itaque Augusti.libro hypognost. Primum, inquit,fides Catholicorum diuina auctoritate regnum esse credit coelorum:secundum,gehennam,vbi omnis Apostata vel à Christi fide alienus supplicia experitur. Tertium penitus ignoramus: nec esse in Scripturis sanctis reperimus. Hæc ille: At Papatus locum fingit esse tertium, vbi quorundam animæ leuiusculis & (vt loquuntur) venialibus peccatis obnoxiæ, priusquam in coelum ascendant,purgantur:quem iccirco Purgatorium ignem appellant: quasi præter Christi sanguinem, qui nostri purgandi causa effusus est, aut illis agnorum imagunculis, aut hoc imaginario igne fit opus:cùm tamen dilucidè nos Scriptura doceat, animos nostros solo Christi sanguine purgari, eorumque labes hoc solo medicamento dilui. 1. Ioann. 1. Sanguis eius purgat nos ab omni peccato.& Matth. 26. Sanguis meus pro multis effundetur in remissionem peccatorum. Deniq; [?]e verba Tridentini concil. sess. 25. haec sunt. Purgatorium esse, animasque ibi detentas fidelium suffragiis, potissimum vero acceptabili altaris sacrificio, iuuari. Item sess. 6. ca. 30. Sessione 22. cap. 2. & c. 3. Videmus, quantas in Christianam religionem Papatus corruptelas inuexerit. Sed aliae praeterea recenseri solent innumerabiles. Scriptura docet nos, duo tantum esse sacramenta: nempe baptismum, & coenam : quorum illud institutū est Math. 28. Marc. 16. hoc vero Matth. 26. Marc. 14. Luc. 22. & 1. Corint. 11. 23. Itaque Augusti. epist. 218. ad Ianuarium: Christus, inquit, sacramentis numero paucissimis, obseruatione facillimis, significatione praestantissimis, societatem noui populi colligauit, sicut baptismus trinitatis consecratus, & communicatio corporis & sanguinis ipsius. Item, lib. 3. de doctrin. Christia. cap. 9. Pauca signa Dominus & Apostolica tradidit disciplina: sicut est baptismi sacramentū, & celebratio corporis & sanguinis Domini. Ac pari numero Ambrosius in li. de sacram. duo tantum agnoscit, baptismum & eucharistiam. At Papatus quinque insuper adiungit: Ordinem, Confirmationem Vnctionem, Poenitentiam, & Matrimonium. Trid… dent. concil. sess. 6. c. 14. sess. 14. c. 1. & sequ. Scriptura sacra docet nos, coniugium non modò esse hominibus omnibus decorum atque honorabile, verum etiam ad scortationes vitandas pene necessarium. Heb. 13. & 1. Corinth. 7. Itaque Petrum Apostolum vxorem habuisse legimus, Marc. 1. & Matth. 8. ubi de Petri socru mentio fit. de aliis testimonium est cap. Act. 1. v. 13. & 14. ubi Lucas, enumeratis apoapostolis, subiungit eos perquandiu in eodem loco mansisse cum uxoribus, & Maria matre Iesu, cum omnes coniunctis animis Deum precaretur. Quin etiam Chrysostomus ad Tit. homil. 1. Apostolus, inquit, obturat os haereticis, qui calumniantur nuptias: ostendens quod non sit res detestanda, sed tam honorabilis, ut cum ea possint etiam in Sanctum thronum, Episcopalem scilicet, ascendere. Quid multa? Papa ipse in Decret. dist. 28. Si quis docuerit, inquit, sacerdotem sub obtentu religionis propriam uxorem contemnere, anathema sit. item dist. 31. Quoniam cautum est, ne foveretur coelibatus, & ut a communione fidelium arceretur, qui propter ecclesiasticos ordines ab uxore sua se separat. item dist. 3. c. si quis nuptias. Et apud Iustinianum patet antiquo iure licuisse sacerdotibus legitimas & iustas uxores habere. l. eum qui, 19, cum aliis similib. C. de epis. & cler. At Papa in concilio Tridentino usque adeo clericis & monialibus suis coniugio interdicit, ut etiam sacris suis initiatos ad iusiurandum adigat, se in perpetuo coelibatu victuros: quam esse certam Antichristi notam, Paulus demonstrat 1. Tim. 4. Tit. 3. Scriptura docet soli misericordiae Dei accepto ferendam esse salutem & iustificationem nostram per Iesum Christum. Isaiae. 43. Ego, ego sum, inquit dominus, qui deleo iniquitates vestras. Item Matth. 9. Ut sciatis filium hominis habere potestatem in terra remittendi peccata, dico Paralytico, Surge, tolle lectulum tuum & abi domum. At Papa sic loquitur apud Bernardin. Rosetum, sermon. 20. Nos operibus possumus vitam aeternam promereri. Ergo debemus praesumere, & pro certo tenere, quod post hac vitam sine dubio habebimus vitam aeternam, pro remuneratione bonorum operum.Item in compendio de grat. sa-ctific.Opera bona sunt meritoria trium, scilicet vitæ æternæ, augmenti gratiæ, remissionis pœnæ. Quasi vero vel tanta esse carnis nostræ castitas & sanctimo-nia possit, ut non semper servi inutiles iudicemur, vel eas operas Domino ac patrono nostro præter debitas præstare, ut mereri aliquid possimus. Sed cętera videamus, Scriptura docet nos, in Cœna do-minica æque vinum ut panem accedentibus præ-bendum esse. Matth.26.Marc.14. 1. Cor.11. At Papa non nisi panem præberi populo permittit: sum-ptione calicis & vini interdicit. Concil. Constan-tiens. sess.13.[?] quod interdictum eo magis mirari licet, quod Papa in Decret.de consecrat.dist.2.c.co-perimus, ita scriptu reliquit. Comperimus quod quidam sumpta tantummodo corporis sacri portione, à calice sacri cruoris abstinent: qui procul dubio aut integra sacramenta percipiant, aut ab integris arceantur: quia dignitio[?] unius eiusdemque mysterii sine grandi sacrilegio non potest pervenire. Eadem scriptura iubet omnes accipere, comedere, & bibere. At in Papatu soli sacer-dotes accipiunt, comedunt, & bibunt. quod tamen diserte prohibitum est in eod.decret.de consecrat.dist.L.c.Peracta: his verbis: Peracta consecratione omnes communicent, qui noluerint ecclesiasticis carere (arceri)liminibus. sic enim & apostoli statuerunt, & sancta Romana tenet ecclesia. Eadem Scriptura sacra statuit, ut in ecclesia & piorum conventu pronuntientur omnia vulgari lingua, ut quid a quoque dicatur, facile a multitudine intelligatur: & rationem subiungit, quia si quid alieno & ignoto sermone pronuntiaretur, assensum præbere multitudo non posset, & respondere. Amen. At in Papatu non tantum a sacerdotibus, verum etiam a multitudine & mulierculis certas precationum formulas admur-murantibus omnia Latina lingua pronuntiantur.
units.tr: For this is why one goes to the King through tribunes and counts, because a king is only a man, and does not know to whom he ought to entrust the commonwealth. But to God, from whom nothing is hidden (for he knows the merits of all), no advocate is needed in order to earn his favour, only a devout mind. For wherever such a man has spoken, he will give no answer. Thus Ambrose. What then? How scrupulously does the Papacy keep this institution of holy Scripture and of the old Church? It denies that any saint has ever departed from this life and been received into the seats of the blessed without performing the office of Mediator and intercessor. Is that all? Indeed, whatever debauched men, whatever Franciscans, Dominicans, and their like, planners, mountebanks, impostors and jugglers, the Popes have wished to enrol among the saints after their death, they have introduced as our mediators and advocates. Scripture teaches us that only two places have been set up for the souls of the dead after this life: heaven for the blessed, and hell for the cursed (John 5; Matt. 25). Therefore Augustine in the Hypognosticon: First, he says, the faith of Catholics believes on divine authority that there is a kingdom of heaven; second, Gehenna, where every apostate, or one alien to the faith of Christ, undergoes punishment. The third we altogether do not know, and we find no trace of it in the holy Scriptures. So he. But the Papacy invents a third place, where the souls of certain people, liable to rather slight and (as they say) venial sins, are purged before they ascend into heaven; and for that reason they call it the purgatorial fire. As if, besides the blood of Christ, which was poured out for our cleansing, there were need of those little images of lambs or of this imaginary fire! Whereas Scripture plainly teaches us that our souls are cleansed by the blood of Christ alone, and that their stains are washed away by this one remedy. 1 John 1: His blood cleanses us from all sin. And Matt. 26: My blood shall be poured out for many for the remission of sins. Finally, the words of the Council of Trent, session 25, are these: That there is a purgatory, and that the souls detained there are helped by the suffrages of the faithful, but especially by the acceptable sacrifice of the altar. Likewise session 6, chapter 30; session 22, chapters 2 and 3. We see how many corruptions the Papacy has introduced into the Christian religion. But innumerable others besides these are usually listed. Scripture teaches us that there are only two sacraments, namely baptism and the Supper. The former was instituted in Matt. 28 and Mark 16, the latter in Matt. 26, Mark 14, Luke 22, and 1 Cor. 11:23. Therefore Augustine, in letter 218 to Januarius: Christ, he says, with the fewest sacraments, the easiest to observe, and the most excellent in meaning, has bound together the fellowship of the new people, such as the baptism consecrated in the Trinity, and the communion of his body and blood. Likewise, in On Christian Doctrine book 3, chapter 9: The Lord and the apostolic discipline have handed down few signs, such as the sacrament of baptism and the celebration of the body and blood of the Lord. And Ambrose in his book On the Sacraments likewise acknowledges only two, baptism and the eucharist. But the Papacy adds five more: Orders, Confirmation, Unction, Penance and Marriage. Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 14; session 14, chapter 1 and following. Holy Scripture teaches us that marriage is not only decent and honourable for all men, but even almost necessary for avoiding fornication (Heb. 13; 1 Cor. 7). Therefore we read that the apostle Peter had a wife (Mark 1; Matt. 8, where mention is made of Peter's mother-in-law). Concerning the others there is testimony in Acts 1:13–14, where Luke, after listing the apostles, adds that they remained in the same place with their wives and Mary the mother of Jesus, all praying to God with one accord. Indeed Chrysostom on Titus, homily 1: The apostle, he says, stops the mouths of heretics who slander marriage, showing that it is not a thing to be detested, but so honourable that with it one may even ascend to the holy throne, namely the episcopal. What more is there to say? The Pope himself, in the Decretum, distinction 28: If anyone shall teach, he says, that a priest should despise his own wife under pretext of religion, let him be anathema. Likewise distinction 31: Since it has been provided that celibacy should not be fostered, and that he who separates himself from his wife on account of ecclesiastical orders should be kept from the communion of the faithful. Likewise distinction 3, the chapter Si quis nuptias. And in Justinian it is clear that under ancient law priests were permitted to have lawful and just wives (the law Eum qui, 19, with other similar laws, Code, on bishops and clergy). But the Pope at the Council of Trent so forbids marriage to his clergy and nuns, that he even compels those initiated into his sacred orders to swear an oath that they will live in perpetual celibacy. Paul demonstrates that this is a certain mark of Antichrist (1 Tim. 4; Titus 3). Scripture teaches that our salvation and justification are to be ascribed to the mercy of God alone, through Jesus Christ. Isaiah 43: I, I am he, says the Lord, who blots out your iniquities. Likewise Matt. 9: That you may know that the Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins, I say to the paralytic, Arise, take up your bed and go home. But the Pope speaks thus in Bernardinus Rosetus, sermon 20: We can merit eternal life by our works. Therefore we ought to presume, and to hold for certain, that after this life we shall without doubt have eternal life, as the reward of good works. Likewise in the Compendium on sanctifying grace: Good works are meritorious of three things, namely of eternal life, of increase of grace, and of remission of punishment. As if indeed our flesh could be so chaste and holy that we are not always judged unprofitable servants, or could perform those works for our Lord and patron beyond what is owed, so as to merit anything! But let us look at the rest. Scripture teaches us that in the Lord's Supper wine is to be given to those who come, as well as bread (Matt. 26; Mark 14; 1 Cor. 11). But the Pope permits only bread to be given to the people, and forbids the taking of the cup and the wine (Council of Constance, session 13). This prohibition is the more remarkable, since the Pope, in the Decretum, De consecratione, distinction 2, the chapter Comperimus, wrote thus: We have learned that certain people, having taken only a portion of the sacred body, abstain from the cup of the sacred blood. Without doubt they either receive the sacraments entire, or are kept from entire ones, because the partaking of one and the same mystery cannot take place without great sacrilege. The same Scripture bids all to receive, eat and drink. But in the Papacy only priests receive, eat and drink. Yet this is expressly forbidden in the same Decretum, under the chapter Peracta, in these words: Peracta: after the consecration let all communicate, who do not wish to be kept from the doors of the church. For so the apostles decreed, and the holy Roman Church holds. The same holy Scripture decrees that in the church and the assembly of the godly everything should be pronounced in the vernacular, so that what is said by each may be easily understood by the multitude; and it adds the reason: if anything were pronounced in a foreign and unknown language, the multitude could not give assent or respond, Amen. But in the Papacy, not only by priests but also by the multitude and by little women murmuring fixed formulas of prayer, everything is pronounced in the Latin tongue.

units.la: Scriptura docet nos Christum esse solum Pontificem & sacerdotem, qui suum corpus semel pro genere humano sacrificauit. 1.Timoth. 2.Ephes.5. & Hebr.9.Christus semel oblatus vt multorum peccata tolleret. Et c.10.Sanctificati sumus per oblationem corporis Christi semel faclam. Item,Vna oblatione consecrauit in perpetuum eos qui sanctificantur. At Papa innumerabiles creauit sacerdotes, quibus mandauit, vt quoties missificarent, toties Christi corpus & pro viuis,& pro mortuis sacrificarent. vnde illa Canonis formula in Missa;Petimus vt accepta habeas,& benedicas haec dona, haec munera, haec sancta sa-crificia, quae tibi offerimus pro ecclesia tua. Item, die Pasch. in secret. missae:Suscipe preces populi tui, cum oblationibus hostiarum. Item, ex missa pro defunctis:Hostias quas tibi pro animabus famulorum famularumque tuarum offerimus. Item,Hostias tibi, domine, pro anima famuli tui offerimus. Item, in lib. Coformitatum sol.65.Frater Ioannes missam celebrans, & corpus Domini leuando cum ipsum pro animabus defunctorum Deo Patri offerret, vidit infinitas animas de purgatorio egredi, quasi multitudinem scintillarum de ignita fornace, & ad coelestia volantes ob merita Christi, qui quotidie in sacratissima hostia offertur pro viuis; & mortuis. Ve-rum haec quidem de corrupta, inquinata, contaminata, conspurcata religione haetenus, exempli tantum causa, dicta sint. Nam cum hoc Papatus crimē multis magnisque voluminibus per annos amplius quinquaginta continuos, a Theologis Germanis, Heluetiis, Gallis, Anglis; & aliis copiosisfimè fit expositum ac tractatum, commodiùs videtur ad quartum eiusdem Papatus crimen accidere.
units.tr: Scripture teaches us that Christ alone is the High Priest and priest, who once offered his body for the human race (1 Tim. 2; Eph. 5; Heb. 9): Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many. And chapter 10: We have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Christ made once. Likewise: By one offering he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified. But the Pope has created innumerable priests, to whom he has commanded that as often as they say mass, so often they should offer the body of Christ, both for the living and for the dead. Hence that formula of the Canon in the Mass: We ask that you accept and bless these gifts, these offerings, these holy sacrifices, which we offer to you for your church. Likewise, on Easter Day, in the Secret of the Mass: Receive the prayers of your people, with the offerings of victims. Likewise, from the Mass for the dead: The victims which we offer to you for the souls of your menservants and maidservants. Likewise: We offer victims to you, Lord, for the soul of your servant. Likewise, in the book Conformities, sermon 65: Brother John, celebrating mass, and lifting up the body of the Lord while offering it to God the Father for the souls of the dead, saw infinite souls coming out of purgatory, like a multitude of sparks from a fiery furnace, and flying up to heaven because of the merits of Christ, who every day is offered in the most sacred victim for the living and the dead. But these things concerning the corrupted, polluted, contaminated and defiled religion have so far been said merely by way of example. For since this crime of the Papacy has been set out and treated in many great volumes over more than fifty continuous years, by German, Swiss, French and English theologians, and by many others, it seems more convenient to pass to the fourth crime of the same Papacy.
THE CRIME OF SACRILEGE.

units.la: Hactenus de tertio Papatus crimine dictum est. Deinceps ordo postulat, vt de sacrilegio differamus, & eo scelere quod vulgus Simoniam, à Simone mago appellat. Nam Romæ duas à Papa, Simoniacas nundinationes exerceri cõstat, earum rerum, quas spirituales vocant. Vna est, in qua sacerdotia palàm, sine vlla dissimulatione, veneunt, eáque longè quæstuosissima. Altera non ita quæstuosa, sed nihilominus turpis, ac detestanda: quæ Taxa pœnitentiariæ apostolicæ appellatur: cū peccatorum & scelerum omnium impunitas certo cuique imposito pretio ita palàm atque aperte di-uenditur, vt etiam nonnulli Canonistæ insatiabile illam auaritiam & rapacitatem detestentur. Velut apud glo.in.c.fundamenta de elect. in vj. vbi Ioannes Monachus ait, Romam à prædonibus fundatam, adhuc de suis primordiis retinere. Et profecto ita est, vt Romam quotânis innumerabile pondus au-ri ex opulentissimi cuiusque regni gazis exportetur, quod postea Papæ, Cardinales, cæterique ordinis eiusdem Epicurei in profundissimum libidi-num suarum gurgitem, summa cum Christiani nominis infamia, profundunt. Prioris nomina & ti-tuli sunt innumerabiles: sed ex tanta copia hi ferè præcipui nominantur: Tributum ex Annatis, siue vacantiis: quo verbo primi anni reditus appellan-tur, quos ærario suo Pontifices asciscunt: sed ij ple-rumque duplicantur, ac triplicantur. Ite, tributum ex praeuentionibus,resignationibus in fauore,com mendationibus,dispensationibus ætatis,ordinis,ir regularitatis, vitij corporalis. Ite, ex gratiis expecta tiuis,ex deuolutionibus,ex beneficiis vacaturis, ex priuilegiis,exeptionibus nō visitandi, vel per pro-curatorem visitandi,homologationibus concorda-torum, transactionibus sub beneplacito Papæ fa-ctis,permutationibus beneficiorum cum dispensa-tione,mandatis Episcopalibus, expeditionibus in forma ratione congrui,creandis protonotariis, & notariis Apostolicis:cum coadiutoribus,literis ma-ioris aut minoris iustitiæ,dignitatibus secularibus ecclesiasticis,nouis fundationibus,vel immutatio-ne antiquarum, vel reductione regularium mona-steriorum in secularem statum, vel restitutione in integrum,pro fructibus percipiendis in absentia,pro legitimationibus, altaribus portatilibus, pro non obstantiis,pro indultis clericorum secularium,pro reuocationibus,& reductionibus,pro Toleramus, siue tolerantiis concubinarum,& pro rescriptis ad lites. Dies nos deficeret, si singulas ærufcationū,ac potius latrociniorum istorum species enumerare conaremur.Neque vero necesse est. Nam extat his de rebus ac nundinationibus liber Pōtificius, hoc titulo, Taxæ cancellariæ Apostolicæ cum notabi-libus,iuxta stylum hodiernum curię Romanæ.quo in libro memorabilis extat quodam loco sententia his expressa verbis: ET NOTA diligenter,quod eiusmodi gratia & dispensationes non concedūtur pauperribus: quia non sunt: ideo non possunt consolari. Quis tam securus numinis diuini contemptor, quis tam nulla conscientia inter Regios consiliarios reperiri poterit, quem hæc latrociniorum, sacrilegiorum,simoniarum portenta nō moueant? Quis tam ferreus, ac patriæ inimicus, qui Gallicarum opum direptione, & miseræ plebis depopulatione, cuius ex medullis ac viscéribus illæ pecuniæ diripiùtur, quas profundæ Papārum, & Cardinalium libidines deuorarūt, non magnopere commoueatur? Incredibile videbitur quod iam dicturi sumus, sed tamè certum & exploratum est. Stante quondam Roma-no Imperio tanta ex omnibus orbis terrarum partibus opum ac diuitiarum copia, tanta auri, argentíque, vis ex gentium populorumque penè omnium tributis ac vectigalibus imperatis Romam quotannis importabatur, vt ciuitas illa dici voca-bulo Græco solcret. Epitome orbis terrarum: (Athenæus lib. 1. Ἐπιτομὴ τῆς οἰκουμένης[?].) Quid si iam doceamus Papam Romanum, suis artibus, technis, præstigiis, ex sola Europa (quæ pars orbis tertia numeratur) non minus auri argentíque Romam quotannis elicere, quàm quantum Imperatores Romani tot legionibus præsidio vbique impositis ex omni-bus terrarum oris exigebant? Audiamus Flauij Blondi, hominis Itali, & summi Papārū[?] assentato-ris testimonium, ex ipsius libro Romæ instauratæ
units.tr: So far I have spoken of the third crime of the Papacy. Now the order of the argument requires that we take up sacrilege, and that wickedness which the common people call Simony, after Simon the magician. For it is well established that at Rome the Pope conducts two Simoniacal markets in the things they call spiritual. The first is the one in which benefices are openly sold, without any pretence, and it is by far the more profitable. The second is less profitable but no less shameful and detestable. It is called the Taxa of the Apostolic Penitentiary, and in it the impunity of all sins and crimes is openly and plainly sold to anyone at a fixed price. Even some canonists denounce that insatiable greed and rapacity. So John the Monk says in the gloss on glo.in.c.fundamenta de elect. in vj., that Rome, founded by robbers, still keeps something of its beginnings. And indeed it is so: an countless weight of gold is carried to Rome every year from the treasuries of the wealthiest kingdoms, and the Popes, Cardinals and the rest of that Epicurean order then pour it into the bottomless whirlpool of their lusts, to the great disgrace of the Christian name. The names and titles of the first kind are innumerable, but from so great a number these are the chief ones: the tribute from annates or vacancies, a term by which the first year's revenues of benefices are called, which the Pontiffs claim for their treasury, though these are very often doubled or tripled. Then the tribute from advance provisions, resignations in favour, recommendations, dispensations for age, for order, for irregularity, for bodily defect. Then from expectative graces, from devolutions, from benefices about to fall vacant, from privileges, from exemptions from visitation or from visitation by proxy, from ratifications of concordats, from transactions made under the Pope's pleasure, from exchanges of benefices with dispensation, from episcopal mandates, from expeditions in the form of congrua, from the creation of protonotaries and apostolic notaries, with coadjutors, with letters of greater or lesser justice, from secular and ecclesiastical dignities, from new foundations, or the alteration of old ones, or the reduction of regular monasteries into the secular state, or restitution in integrum, for the enjoyment of fruits while absent, for legitimations, for portable altars, for non obstantes, for indults for secular clerks, for revocations and reductions, for Toleramus, or tolerances of concubines, and for rescripts concerning lawsuits. The day would fail us if we tried to list each species of these extortions, or rather robberies. Nor is there any need. For there is a Papist book on these matters and these markets, under this title: Taxae cancellariae Apostolicae cum notabilibus, iuxta stylum hodiernum curiae Romanae. In that book there is a memorable sentence in these words: ET NOTA diligenter, quod eiusmodi gratiae et dispensationes non conceduntur pauperibus: quia non sunt: ideo non possunt consolari. Who is so careless a despiser of the divine majesty, who can be found among the King's counsellors with so little conscience, that these monstrosities of robbery, sacrilege and simony do not move him? Who is so hard-hearted and so hostile to his country that he is not deeply stirred by the plundering of French wealth and the laying waste of the wretched common people, from whose very marrow and vitals those sums are torn which the bottomless lusts of Popes and Cardinals have devoured? What we are about to say will seem incredible, yet it is certain and proven. When the Roman Empire stood, so great was the abundance of wealth and riches from every part of the world, and so great a quantity of gold and silver was brought to Rome every year from the tributes and taxes imposed on almost all nations and peoples, that the city was accustomed to be called by the Greek word, Epitome of the inhabited world [Ἐπιτομὴ τῆς οἰκουμένης] (Athenaeus, book 1). What if I now show that the Roman Pope, by his own arts, tricks and deceits, draws out of Europe alone (which is counted as one third of the world) no less gold and silver to Rome every year than the Roman Emperors, with so many legions posted everywhere as a guard, exacted from every shore of the world? Let us hear the testimony of Flavius Blondus, an Italian and a great flatterer of the Popes, from his book Roma instaurata:

units.la: III. Nunc, inquit, principes orbis terrarum Dictatorem perpetuum non Cæsaris, sed piscatoris Petri successorem, & Imperatoris prædicti vicarium, Pontificem summum ADORANT, & colunt. Nunc orbis terrarum Cardina-lium senatum in urbe Roma, post Pontificem veneratur.
units.tr: III. Now, he says, the princes of the world worship and honour as their perpetual Dictator not Caesar but the successor of the fisherman Peter, the vicar of the aforesaid Emperor, the Supreme Pontiff. Now the senate of Cardinals of the whole world reveres the city of Rome after the Pontiff.

units.la: Quid? quod maiora, vel certè paria prisc orum temporum vectigalibus Europa penè omnis tributa Romam mittit, dum singulæ ciuitates à Romano Pontifice beneficia sacerdotalia accipiunt? hæc Blondus. Sed huius imma-nis sacrilegij ratio paulò diligentius coficienda est. Nam Suetonius in vita Julij Cęsaris, ita scribit, Om-nem Galliam, in provincia formam redegit, eique in sin-gulos annos quadringenties sestertium stipendii nomine imposuit. Hoc idem Eutropius libro Breviarij sexto totidem prope verbis scriptum reliquit. Hunc se-stertium numerum, si Guillielmi Budæi rationem sequamur, reperiemus respōdere[?] nostrati pecuniæ ad decies centena aureorum coronatorum millia: sive (ut vulgus loquitur) unum millionem: ut Ger-mani usurpant, decem tonnas auri. Ingens hoc fuit Galliæ tributum: quod (ut dixi) quotannis ita Cæ-saribus pensitabat, ut tamen ex eo stipendium præ-sidiariis aliquot legionibus persolveretur. Quid si jam doceamus Papam Romanum non minorem quotannis summam, sine ullo impendio, Romam suis præstigiis atque artibus elicere? Incredibile fortassis alicui videbitur, ac plane monstri simile: ut ante diximus, sed tamen esse verissimum, certis-simo testimonio convincemus. Ecquis igitur istius tam immanis latrocinij, vel potius sacrilegij testis est? Senatus ipse Parisiensis, qui in Gallia dominatur, qui circiter centum ab hinc annis Regi Ludovico XI. postulata quędam pro Gallicis Ecclesiis detulit his verbis, quæ Franciscus Duarenus Jurifcon. La-tinè convertit, & edidit, cum privilegio Regis, bis Lutetiæ, & iterū bis Lugduni: sub fine libri de Be-neficiis. Nam sub illorum postulatorum articulo LXXII. ita scriptū est: Ut speciatim ac sigillatim de-mostremus, quatopere hoc triennio pecunia regnu exhau-stu sit, animadvertedum est, Pii Pontificis tempore vacasse in hoc regno plusqua[?] viginti Archiepiscopatus & Epis-copatus. nec dubiu est, quin tam pro annuo illo vestigali, (quod Annatam vacamus) quam pro reliquo sumptu accessorio & extraordinario in singulas Bullas sena aureorum millia depensa, numeratáque sint: qua summa est centum & viginti millium aureorum. Sequitur articulus LXVIII. Abbatia ab sexaginta eo amplius vacauerunt in hoc regno: quarum singulae duobus millibus aureorum minimum constiterunt. Summa ergo est centum & viginti millium aureorum. LXXIIII. Eode tempore Prioratus, Decanatus, praepositurae, praeceptoriae, & aliae dignitates, quae lituo [?] insignita non sunt, plus quam ducenta vacauerunt: ac in singula huiusmodi beneficia aurei numerati sunt quingenti. Summa igitur est centum millium aureorum.
units.tr: What? That almost all Europe sends to Rome tributes greater than, or at least equal to, the revenues of earlier times, while each city receives its priestly benefices from the Roman Pontiff? So Blondus. But the reckoning of this monstrous sacrilege must be made rather more carefully. For Suetonius, in the life of Julius Caesar, writes thus: He reduced all Gaul into the form of a province, and imposed upon it, in the name of tribute, four hundred thousand sesterces every year. Eutropius, in the sixth book of his Breviarium, left the same thing written in almost the same words. If we follow the reckoning of Guillaume Budé, we shall find that this number of sesterces corresponds to our money as a thousand thousand times ten hundred gold crowns, or (as the common people say) one million, which the Germans call ten tons of gold. This was a huge tribute from Gaul, which, as I said, was paid to the Caesars every year, though part of it was used to pay the garrison of several legions. What if I now show that the Roman Pope draws to Rome, by his tricks and arts, no smaller sum every year, without any expense? It will perhaps seem incredible to someone, and quite like a monster, as I said before, but I will prove it by the most certain testimony that it is entirely true. Who then is a witness to this so monstrous robbery, or rather sacrilege? The Parisian Senate itself, which rules in Gaul, which about a hundred years ago brought certain demands on behalf of the French churches before King Louis XI in these words, which Francis Duaren, the jurist, translated into Latin and published, with the King's privilege, twice at Paris and again twice at Lyon, at the end of his book De Beneficiis. For under article LXXII of those demands it is written thus: To demonstrate in particular and one by one how greatly the kingdom has been drained of money in these three years, it must be noted that in the time of the pious Pope there were more than twenty archbishoprics and bishoprics vacant in this kingdom. Nor is it doubtful that for each of those bulls there were paid and counted out six thousand gold pieces, both for that yearly tax which we call annates and for the rest of the accessory and extraordinary expense; and that sum is one hundred and twenty thousand gold pieces. Then follows article LXVIII. More than sixty abbeys were vacant in this kingdom, each of which cost at least two thousand gold pieces. The sum therefore is one hundred and twenty thousand gold pieces. LXXIIII. At the same time more than two hundred priories, deaneries, provostships, preceptories and other dignities, which are not marked with the crozier, were vacant; and for each such benefice five hundred gold pieces were paid. The sum therefore is one hundred thousand gold pieces.

units.la: LXXV. Constat in hoc regno vt minimum centum millia parœciarum esse, quæ inhabitentur & incolantur. Nec vlla est, in qua eo tempore gratiam expectatiua aliquis non impetrauerit: in quarum singulas vigintiquinque aurei impensi sunt, tam pro itineris sumptu, quam bullarum confectione: pro non obstantiis, prærogatiuis, annullationibus, & aliis specialibus clausulis, quæ gratiis expectatiuis adscribi consueuerunt. Itē pro exsecutorio processu super eisdem gratiis facto. Summa hæc est vicies quinquies centena millia aureorum. Hęc Senatus Parisiensis. Colligatur nunc illarum summarum summa. Reperietur ad nouies centena sex & quadraginta millia sexcentos sex & sexaginta coronatos, & insuper unius coronati bessem [?]: quæ tertia pars est eius summæ, quam Senatus Parisiensis demonstrat illo triennio Romam esse delatam: nempe duodetricies centenum & quadragenum millium coronatorum: siue (vt vernaculo sermone vtamur) trium auri millionum, minus centum sexaginta millibus: siue (vt Germani loquuntur) ad octo fere & viginti auri tonas. Quinetiam compertum est, taxam, vacantiarum descri-pta in libris Camerae de Ecclesiis cathedralibus & Abbatiis Gallicarum, taxatis tātum sexto quoque anno cōficere summam sexentorum nonaginta se-ptem millium septingētarum quinquaginta libra-rum Gallicarum extra prælaturas non taxatas: & a-lia beneficia, quorū exactiones ferè illam summam exæquant. Et erit quisquâ in regiis Parlamētis Gal-licis, qui hanc siue voraginē, siue gurgitem, siue potiùs Scyllā ac Charybdim, æquo se animo ferre fa-tebitur? ac non potiùs vbi tantarū summarum ia-cturam audierit, non illam immanem ac tetram belluam precibus omnibus detestabitur? Neque ta-men vnum hoc testimonium proferemus. Ecce nobis aliud ex libello, cui titulus est, Sylua locorum communium, sub exitum Concilij Basiliēsis edito, vbi ratio cōfecta eius pecuniæ, quæ sub Papæ Mar-tini quinti Pontificatu ex sola Gallia Romā expor-tata est, excurrisse dicitur ad nonagies centena au-reorum coronatorum millia. Et miramur eundem illum Parisiēsem Senatum, in iisdem postulatis, ar-tic. LXXI. grauiter & acerbè questum esse, tantā au-ri argentiqué Gallici copiam quotannis Romā ex-portari, vt interdū ad vsum plebis Gallicæ pecuniā æream pro argentea cudi oportuerit? Sed audiamus articulum eorundem postulatorum LXII. Antehac (inquit Senatus Parisiēsis) populares regni huius certatim concurrebant Romam, quorū alii Cardinalibus & aulicis inseruiebant: alii nullius hominis familiæ mancipati, sed aliquâ spe vana illecti, suam parentúmque suorum substantiam absumebant: alii, & hi quidem plurimi, eo consilio Romam migrabant, vt cæteris hic manentibus molestiam exhiberent, & Ecclesias, beneficiā-que ab eis, quo iure quâque iniuria extorquerent. Nam experimento compertum est, maxima eorum partem, qui hinc Romam proficiscebatur, siue ob itineris periculu & molestia, siue ob peste, qua Romae crebro grassatur, morte statim oppetere solitos fuisse: qui vero ex his periculis incolumes euadebant, negotium facessebant senibus, valetudinariis, & aliis eiusmodi, qui in Ecclesiis & beneficiis suis erant assidui. Ac saepenumero contingebat, vt miseri homines in curiam Romanam citati, cum aduersus istos calumniatores se defendere nequirent, prae tædio & mœrore vitam finire cogerentur. LXII. Plerique beneficiorū captatores parentum & amicorum loculos exhaurie-bant omnino, tandemque ad summam inopiam, atque adeo mendicitatem redigebantur. Nec vero vlla spe[?] alia tātas perferebant miserias, nisi vt plumbum forte pro auro domum aliquando referrent accidebatque interdum, vt eorum inhians deluderetur, vtque plumbū auro emptum nihil plane aliud quàm plumbum esset. Cùm enim bullis suis plumbeis cōsiderent, interueniebat alius, qui annul-lationem aliquam ex insperato afferret: ac interdum de-cem aut duodecim ad idem beneficium anhelantes & acceptantes existebant. Orta vero lite inter eos Romam denuò redeundum erat litigandi causa[?]. sic omnibus passim Romam confluentibus, regnum popularibus ac subditis miserabiliter destituebatur. Atque hæc quidem Senatus Parisiensis querela fuit de insatiabili Paparum auaritia, & inexplebili rapacitate annis ab hinc amplius cētum, Regi Ludouico delata, neque tamen ex nouis & recentibus Paparum latrociniis nata. Extat enim eius Ludouici regis, qui Beatus dictus est, ex anno MCCXXIIX[?]. constitutio, quę quanta iam tum in Galliæ regno Paparum auaritia grassaretur, non obscure ostendit: sub titul. de Ta-liis: Exactiones, inquit, & onera grauia pecuniarum per curiam Romanam Ecclesiis regni nostri imposita, quibus regnum miserabiliter depauperatum extitit, seu etiam imponenda leuari & colligi nullatenus volumus, nisi duntaxat pro rationabili, pia, & urgentissima, vel ineui-tabili necessitate, ac de expresso & spontaneo consensu nostro, & ipsius Ecclesiæ regni nostri. Iuuat etiam huius eiusdem memorabilis Senatus illius auctoritatis testimonium proferre ex Chronic. Britanniæ Armoricæ lib. 4. annal. CIↄ Iↄ LXVII. impressis & editis Lutetiæ anno 1531. Fuit, inquit, per id tempus regius fisci procurator Iohannes Santromanus: cui Senatus Parisiensis bullam pontificis legendam & cognoscendam dedit. Is ea perlecta & cognita demonstrauit Senatui, summam rerum omnium confusionem ex illius comprobatione nasciturum. Nā illius auctoritate populares regni superioribus te-poribus magno numero patria deseruisse, seseque Romā contulisse: quorum alij sese Cardinalium famulatui & clientelis dicabat, alij liberius viuentes patrimonia sua otiose consumebat: alij vel in itinere, vel in ipsa urbe propter aeris intemperiem & frequentem pestilentiam interibant. Ita Gallia ciui-bus ac praesertim literatis exhauriebatur.
