Demonstrauit praeterea copiam ingentem archiepiscopatuum, episcopatuum & abbatiarum, itemque paroeciarum, quarum numerus esse dicitur adiectum millia: cum tamen vnaquaeque ciuitas pro vna pecuria numeretur. Innumerabilem igitur pecuniā Romam exportari pro vacantiis & gratiis expectatiuis: quarum tanta est copia, ut interdum decem aut duodecim Bullæ unius sacerdotij nomine diuendantur. Itaque neminem in posterum mediocribus facultatibus praeditum fore, quin Romam mittat, ut sacerdotium aliquod vel filio vel propinquo impetrare possit. Cuius rei argumentum hoc esse. Triennio vno vacasse in regno Galliæ archiepiscopatus xxii. quorum nomine Romam exportata fuerant centum & vrgenti scutatorum millia. Vacasse item Lxi. abbatias quarum nomine par summa Romam exportata fuerat. Vacasse insuper opimos prioratus, decanatus, prępofituras, commendas, & alias dignitates electiuas, litui expertes: quarum nomine Romam exportata fuerant centum scutatorum millia. Nullum esse in Gallia parochum quipro gratia expectatiua non soluerit ad minimum scutatos xxv. quinetiam pro aliis expectatiuis & priuilegiis tantas summas exhauriri, vt facile excurrant ad duos scutatorum milliones. pro aliis item euacuationibus exhausta esse illo triennio ad duos milliones, supra scutatorum octingenta millia. Et secundum ea Rector vna cum proceribus Academiæ Parisiensis multis verbis contra supradictam Papæ bullam protestatus est, atque ab illius iniquitate ad futurum concilium appellauit.
units.tr: LXXV. It is established that in this kingdom there are at least a hundred thousand parishes that are inhabited and occupied. There is not one of them in which, at that time, someone has not obtained an expectative grace. Each of these cost twenty-five gold crowns, spent both on the cost of the journey and on the making of the bulls, for the non obstantes, prerogatives, annulments, and other special clauses that are customarily attached to expectative graces, and likewise for the executory process carried out on those same graces. The sum of this is two and a half million gold crowns. So far the Parisian Senate. Let us now add up these sums. We shall find about nine hundred and forty-six thousand six hundred and sixty-six crowns, and in addition a fraction of one crown. This is a third part of the sum which the Parisian Senate shows was carried to Rome in that three-year period, namely two million eight hundred and forty thousand crowns: or (to use the vernacular) three million gold, less one hundred and sixty thousand; or (as the Germans put it) nearly twenty-eight tons of gold. Indeed it has been found that the tax on vacancies recorded in the Camera's books for the cathedral churches and abbeys of Gaul, taxed only once every sixth year, amounts to six hundred and ninety-seven thousand seven hundred and fifty pounds of Gallic money, leaving aside the untaxed prelacies, and other benefices whose exactions nearly equal that sum. Will anyone in the royal Parlements of Gaul admit that he can bear this whirlpool, this gulf, or rather this Scylla and Charybdis with equanimity? Will he not rather, on hearing of the loss of such great sums, curse that monstrous and foul beast with every prayer? Nor shall we bring forward this one testimony alone. Behold another, from a little book entitled the Sylva locorum communium, published towards the end of the Council of Basel, where the reckoning of that money which was exported from Gaul alone to Rome under Pope Martin V is said to have amounted to nine million gold crowns. And we marvel that the same Parisian Senate, in the same petitions, article LXXI, complained bitterly and severely that such a great quantity of Gallic gold and silver was exported to Rome every year, so that sometimes copper money had to be coined in place of silver for the use of the Gallic common people. But let us hear article LXII of the same petitions. Formerly (says the Parisian Senate) the commoners of this kingdom ran eagerly to Rome: some of them served Cardinals and courtiers; others, bound to no man's household but lured by some vain hope, squandered their own and their parents' substance; others, and these very many, went to Rome with the intention of harassing those who remained here, and of wresting churches and benefices from them by whatever right or wrong they could. For experience has shown that most of those who set out from here for Rome were accustomed to meet death at once, either from the dangers and hardships of the journey or from the plague, which is constantly raging in Rome; and those who escaped these dangers unharmed gave trouble to old men, invalids, and others of that kind, who were resident in their churches and benefices. And very often it happened that wretched men, summoned to the Roman curia, when they could not defend themselves against these slanderers, were forced to end their lives out of weariness and sorrow. LXII. Most of the seekers of benefices drained their parents' and friends' purses completely, and were at last reduced to utter poverty and even beggary. Nor did they endure such great miseries for any other hope than that they might perhaps bring home lead in place of gold. And sometimes it happened that, while they gaped after it, they were cheated, and the lead bought as gold was nothing else but lead. For while they were relying on their leaden bulls, someone else would come along and unexpectedly produce some annulment; and sometimes ten or twelve men were found gasping for and accepting the same benefice. When a dispute arose between them, they had to return to Rome again for the sake of litigation. Thus, with everyone flocking to Rome on all sides, the kingdom was wretchedly abandoned by its common people and its subjects. This was the complaint of the Parisian Senate about the insatiable avarice and unquenchable rapacity of the Popes, laid before King Louis more than a hundred years ago, and yet it did not arise from the new and recent robberies of the Popes. For there exists a decree of that King Louis, who was called Blessed, dated 1228, which clearly shows how great the avarice of the Popes was already raging in the kingdom of France at that time, under the title De Taliis: Exactions, it says, and heavy burdens of money imposed by the Roman curia upon the churches of our kingdom, by which the kingdom has been miserably impoverished, or even those to be imposed, we are in no way willing to be lifted or collected, except only for a reasonable, pious, and most urgent or unavoidable necessity, and with the express and voluntary consent both of ourselves and of the Church of our kingdom. It is also helpful to bring forward the testimony of the authority of this same memorable Senate from the Chronicle of Armorican Brittany, book 4, year 1467, printed and published at Paris in 1531. At that time, it says, the royal procurator of the treasury was Jean Santromanus, to whom the Parisian Senate gave the papal bull to read and examine. He, having read and examined it, showed the Senate that a total confusion of all things would arise from its confirmation. For by its authority many of the commoners of the kingdom in former times had left their country in great numbers and gone to Rome; some of them devoted themselves to the service and clientage of Cardinals, others, living more freely, idly consumed their patrimonies; others died, either on the journey or in the city itself, from the unhealthy air and frequent pestilence. Thus France was drained of its citizens, and especially of its learned men. He showed, moreover, the vast number of archbishoprics, bishoprics and abbeys, and likewise of parishes, whose number is said to be more than a thousand, although each city is counted as one parish. Therefore an innumerable sum of money is exported to Rome for vacancies and expectative graces, and these are so abundant that sometimes ten or twelve bulls are sold under the name of one priesthood. And so in future no one of moderate means will fail to send to Rome, so that he may obtain some priesthood for his son or kinsman. The proof of this is the following. In one triennium, twenty-two archbishoprics fell vacant in the kingdom of France, in whose name one hundred and twenty thousand scudi were exported to Rome. Likewise sixty-one abbeys fell vacant, for which an equal sum was exported to Rome. Moreover, rich priories, deaneries, provostships, commendams and other elective dignities, which are free from the lituus, fell vacant, for which one hundred thousand scudi were exported to Rome. There is no parish priest in France who has not paid, for an expectative grace, at least twenty-five scudi; and indeed such great sums are drained for other expectatives and privileges, that they easily run up to two million scudi. For other vacancies, too, about two million and eight hundred thousand scudi were drained in that same triennium. And accordingly the Rector, together with the nobles of the University of Paris, protested at length against the aforesaid bull of the Pope, and appealed from its iniquity to a future council.

units.la: Hæc auctor illius Chronici. Neque vero silentio prætereundum hoc loco videtur illud præclarum Abbatis Vrspergensis epiphonema ex vita Philip. Imp. pa. 321. vnde intelligatur, quam vetus querela hæc fuerit de Papatus R. sacrilegiis, quæ Sixtus v. pro sua tyrannide fortiter tueri instituit. Vix remafit, inquit, aliquis Episcopatus, sive dignitas ecclesiastica, vel etiam parochialis ecclesia, quæ non fieret litigiosa, & Romam deduceretur ipsa caussa: sed non manu vacua. Gaude mater nostra Roma, quoniam aperiuntur cataractae thesaurorum in terra, vt confluant vini & aggeres nummorum in magna copia. Latare super iniquitates filiorum hominum: quoniam in recom-penfatione tantorum malorum datur tibi pretium, iocundare super adiutrice discordia: quia erupit de puteo infernalis abyssi, ut accumulentur tibi multa pecuniarum praemia. habes quod semper sitisti.decanta canticum, quia per malitiam hominum, non per tuam religionem orbem vicisti. Adte trahit homines non ipsorum deuotio, aut pura conscientia, sed scelerum multiplicium perpetratio, & litium decisio pretio comparata. Audiamus praeterea Theodori Nihemij non dissimilem in hoc genere querimoniam ex Tract. 6.cap.37. ut Regis Galliae consiliarij cognoscant, quàm liberè complures boni viri iampridem hæc Papatus R.sacrilegia detestati sint: & per ea tempora dereftati, quibus ecclesia Christiana crudelissimo eiusdem Papatus dominatu premebatur. Camera Apostolica, inquit, assimilatur mari in quod intrant omnia flumina, & non exundat. Sic enim in-stam [?] portantur ex diuersis mundi partibus auri pondo millia: attamen non impletur: in qua est generatio, quae pro dentibus gladios commutat: ut comedat inopes de terra, & pauperes ex hominibus: in qua sunt multa sanguisugae dicentes, AFFER, AFFER. cuius quidem camerae officiales Gentes camerae nuncupantur. Bene quidem. Gentes enim sunt barbarae nationes, habentes ritus extraneos a moribus hominum. O iustissimae gentes, recte cum infernalibus furiis seu Harpiis, & Tantalo sortem sitibundi posituri, qui nunquam satiantur. Quinetiam Canonistarum quorundam extant versiculi, perditam Paparum auaritiam execrantium: in his Ioannis Monachi, eius quem paulò ante memorauimus, cuius ex præclaris monumentis hæc celebrantur.
units.tr: These are the words of the author of that Chronicle. Nor does it seem right to pass over in silence at this point that famous exclamation of the Abbot of Ursperg from the life of Philip the Emperor, page 321, from which it may be understood how old this complaint is about the sacrileges of the Roman papacy, which Sixtus V has set himself to defend vigorously in his tyranny. Scarcely any bishopric, it says, or ecclesiastical dignity, or even parish church, has remained which has not become a matter of litigation, and the case brought to Rome: yet not empty-handed. Rejoice, our mother Rome, since the floodgates of the treasures of the earth are opened, so that rivers of wine and heaps of money flow together in great abundance. Exult over the iniquities of the sons of men, since in recompense for so many evils a price is given to you; rejoice over the helping discord, because it has burst forth from the pit of the infernal abyss, so that many rewards of money may be heaped upon you. You have what you have always thirsted for. Sing a song, for you have conquered the world not by your religion but by the malice of men. Men are drawn to you not by their devotion or a pure conscience, but by the perpetration of manifold crimes and the settlement of lawsuits bought at a price. Let us hear, besides, a complaint of Theodoric of Niem, not unlike this in kind, from Tract 6, chapter 37, so that the counsellors of the King of France may know how freely many good men have long since detested these sacrileges of the Roman papacy, and cursed them in those times when the Christian Church was oppressed by the most cruel dominion of that same papacy. The Apostolic Camera, it says, is likened to a sea into which all rivers flow, and it does not overflow. For thus thousands of pounds of gold are carried in from the various parts of the world, yet it is never filled. In it there is a generation which exchanges swords for teeth, so that it may devour the poor of the earth and the needy from among men; in it there are many bloodsuckers saying, GIVE, GIVE. The officials of this Camera are commonly called the Gentiles of the Camera. Rightly so! For the Gentiles are barbarous nations, having customs foreign to the morals of men. O most just Gentiles, rightly to be given the lot of the infernal Furies or Harpies, and of Tantalus, thirsting forever, who are never satisfied. Moreover, there exist some verses of certain canonists cursing the ruinous avarice of the Popes; among them those of John the Monk, whom we mentioned a little earlier, from whose famous monuments these lines are celebrated.

units.la: Roma manus rodit, quas rodere non valet, odit. Dantes exaudit, non dantibus ostia claudit, Curia curarum genitrix, nutrixque malorum, Ignotos notis, inhonestos æquat honestis.
units.tr: Rome gnaws the hands it cannot gnaw, and so it hates them. It listens to those who give and shuts its doors on those who do not. Curia, mother of cares and nurse of evils, makes the unknown equal to the known and the dishonourable equal to the honourable.
Likewise in another place.

units.la: Curia vult marcas, bursas exhaurit & arcas. Si bursæ parcas, fuge Papas & Patriarchas: Si dederis marcas, & eis impleueris arcas, Culpa solueris, quaque ligatus eris. Intus quis? tu quis? ego sum: quid quæris? ut intrem. Fers aliquid? non, esto foris: fero, quid? satis, intra.
units.tr: The Curia wants marks; it drains purses and coffers. If you spare your purse, flee the Popes and the Patriarchs. If you give marks and fill their coffers, you will be absolved of your guilt, and whatever binds you. Who is within? Who are you? I am I. What do you seek? To enter. Do you bring anything? No, then stay outside. I bring? What? Enough: come in.

units.la: Adhuc de prodigiosis Paparum latroniciis, & priore sacrilegiorum ac simoniacorum criminum genere dictum est. Nunc consequens est, ut de altero dicamus, quod Penitentiaria taxa vulgo no-minatur, si prius unum illud addiderimus quod Franciscus Petrarcha, homo Italus, de Papa Ioane XXII. scriptum reliquit: reperta in eius mortui æ-rario[?], ab ipsius heredibus fuisse non minus vicies quinquies millena aureorum millia. quam summam Galli sic exprimunt, viginti quinque milliones au-ri. Germani vero, ducentas quinquaginta auri ton-nas. Quin ne illud quidem alterum præterire pos-sumus, quod Thom. V Valsinghamius Anglicus hi-storicus de Papa Bonifacio octauo commemorat:[?] Cum iussu Regis Philippi Pulchri Anagniæ captus a Gallis militibus fuisset, mox, inquit Historicus, despoliatus est, eiusque camera & thesauraria dire-pta, vestimentaque exportata cum ornamentis & auro atque argento, aliisque rebus omnibus ibidē inuentis. Et reuera creditur, quod OMNES RE-GES MVNDI non possent tantum de thesauro reddere infra unum annum, quantum fuit de Pa-pali palatio asportatum. Hæc ille, ex quib* [?] de alijs Paparum & consimilium prædonum sacrilegiis, ac latrociniis cujuis existimandi copia est. Extat igitur liber editus Lutetiæ anno 1520. cum privilegio Parlamenti Parisiensis, ex die Junij 6. eod. anno, cui titulus est, Taxæ Cācellariæ apostolicæ, & Ta-xe sacræ pœnitentiariæ itidem apostolicæ: ubi folio 36. videre hæc absolutionum pretia, & nundinationes apostolicas licebit. Absolutio pro monacho portante sotulares rostratos, & tunicas nodatas, grossi septem. Absolutio pro presbytero, qui conjunctos in gradu prohibito matrimonialiter copulavit, & coram eis celebravit, grossi septem. Pro eo qui in Ecclesia cognovit mulierem, & alia mala commisit, grossi sex. Pro presbytero, qui nonnullas personas clandestine matrimoniavit, & clandestinis matrimoniis interfuit, grossi septem. Pro laico qui res sacras de loco sacro cepit. g.7. Absolutio pro eo qui matrem, sororem, aut aliam consanguineam, vel affinem suam aut commatrem carnaliter cognovit, grossi quinque, pro eo qui virginem defloravit, g. 6. pro periuro, g.6. Pro laico, qui Abbatem, aut alium presbyterum minorem Episcopo, monachum vel clericum juterfecit, grossi septem, 8. vel 9. Absolutio super homicidio laicali pro laico, g.5. Pro presbytero, decano, aut clerico, quando signatur supplicatio per Fiat, g. 18. vel 16. Absolutio pro eo qui interfecit patrem, matrem, fratrem, sororem, uxorem, aut alium consanguineum laicum: quia si esset aliquis eorum clericus, teneretur interfector visitare sedem apostolicam. g.5. vel 7. pro marito, qui uxorem suã percussit, de qua peperit abortivum & ante tempus, gr. 6. Pro muliere, qua bibit aliquem potum, ac alium actum fecit, per quem destruxit fœtum in utero vivificatum. gr. 5. Annon misera ac deplorada getium Christianarū conditio est, quarū ex sanguine & visceribus, tanti pecuniarum acervi, Romam exportantur; quæ mox in lustris, ganeis, & helluationibus Parum, Cardinalium, & eiusdem generis Epicureorum consumantur. qui (vt inter omnes cœtat) regio cultu & victu ætatem agunt? Annon funestū ac luctuosum plebis Galliæ spectaculum videtur, cum his temporibus, toties instauratis ac renouatis Ecclesiarum reformatarum persecutionibus, innumerabiles familias intuemur, fame & inopia enectas, vicatim, miseria perditas ac deploratas, mendicare? Romanos autem Epicureos opimos, & pingues ciuium nostrorum sanguine saginari? Gallos indigenas antiquissimis ortos familiis, patriis sedibus expulsos, per exteras regiones vagari egetes, cumconiugibus & liberis: Romanos Ganeones à Sixto v. in illorum locum summissos benigne & liberaliter ab iis qui rerum potiuntur, excipi? O nationem Gallorum, cæteris gentibus omnibus ridiculam, quæ tandiu tyrannicum istum Papatus dominatum ferre potest! O IesuChriste, crucifixe pro nobis, & resuscitare, & ad Dei Patris dextram collocate, ecquem ostendis exitum nobis, aut quem das finem Rex magne laborum?
units.tr: So far we have spoken of the monstrous robberies of the Popes and of the earlier kind of sacrilege and simony. It now follows that we speak of the other kind, commonly called the Penitentiary tax, but first let us add that one thing which Francesco Petrarca, an Italian, left written about Pope John XXII: that when he died, his heirs found in his treasury no less than twenty-five times a thousand thousand gold pieces. The French express this sum as twenty-five million gold; the Germans, however, as two hundred and fifty tons of gold. Nor can we pass over that other thing which Thomas Walsingham, the English historian, records about Pope Boniface VIII: when, by the order of King Philip the Fair, he had been seized at Anagni by French soldiers, he was at once stripped, the historian says, and his chamber and treasury were plundered, and his vestments carried off with their ornaments, and the gold and silver and all other things found there. And indeed it is believed that ALL THE KINGS OF THE WORLD could not restore from their treasuries within a year as much as was carried off from the papal palace. So he writes. From these things one may gather an abundance of examples of the sacrileges and robberies of other Popes and of similar pirates. There is therefore a book published at Paris in 1520, with the privilege of the Parlement of Paris dated 6 June of the same year, entitled The Taxes of the Apostolic Chancery and likewise the Taxes of the Apostolic Sacred Penitentiary. On folio 36 of it one may see these prices of absolutions and apostolic bargains. Absolution for a monk who wears pointed shoes and knotted tunics, seven groats. Absolution for a priest who married persons related within a forbidden degree and celebrated the marriage before them, seven groats. For one who knew a woman in a church and committed other evils, six groats. For a priest who secretly married some persons and was present at clandestine marriages, seven groats. For a layman who took sacred things from a holy place, seven groats. Absolution for one who carnally knew his mother, sister, or another blood relation, or his relation by marriage, or his godmother, five groats; for one who deflowered a virgin, six groats; for a perjurer, six groats. For a layman who killed an abbot or another priest below a bishop, or a monk or clerk, seven, eight or nine groats. Absolution for lay homicide, for a layman, five groats. For a priest, dean or clerk, when the supplication is signed by Fiat, eighteen or sixteen groats. Absolution for one who killed his father, mother, brother, sister, wife, or another lay blood relation, because if any of them had been a clerk, the killer would have been bound to visit the apostolic see: five or seven groats. For a husband who struck his wife, from whom she bore an aborted child before its time, six groats. For a woman who drank some potion and did another act by which she destroyed a foetus quickened in the womb, five groats. Is not the condition of the Christian peoples wretched and deplorable, whose viscera and blood are exported to Rome in such heaps of money, which are soon consumed in brothels, taverns and the debauches of Popes, Cardinals and that kind of Epicureans, who (as everyone knows) live in royal style and luxury? Does it not seem a mournful and sorrowful sight for the people of France, when in these times, with the persecutions of the Reformed Churches so often begun and renewed, we see countless families, killed by hunger and want, going begging from village to village, ruined and wretched? And the rich and fat Roman Epicureans fattened on the blood of our citizens? French natives, sprung from the most ancient families, expelled from their ancestral homes, wander as beggars through foreign lands with their wives and children, while the Roman revellers sent in by Sixtus V in their place are received kindly and generously by those who hold power? O the French nation, ridiculous to all other peoples, which can bear this tyrannical dominion of the Papacy for so long! O Jesus Christ, crucified for us and raised, and set at the right hand of God the Father, what way out do you show us, or what end do you give to our labours, O great King?

units.la: Atque vt clarissimi Parlamentorum Senatores Iurisperiti intelligant, fuisse iampridem eiusdem ordinis eruditos viros, qui crudelem istam ac barbaram tyrannidem aperte detecтati sunt, deinceps aliquot ex ipsorum libris testimonia proferemus, quorum illud primum est ex doctore Alberico in l. bene à Zenone. nu. 18. C. de quadr. præscrib. Præsidentes Ecclesiæ Romanæ, inquit, eorum asluta & sagaci prudentia secundum temporū varietatem sua variauerunt statuta. modo imperiū sublimando, modo pau-latim deprimendo de tempore in tempus. Sed ad quid? nisi vt sensim omnia & coelestia & terrena, & spiritua-lia & temporalia (vt vocant) pedibus suis, vt palam gloriantur, subiicerent? Secundus auctor prodeat Ioa. Petrus Ferrariensis, cuius in Practica forensi, quam ante annos amplius cētum quinquaginta scripsit, verba haec sunt, in Formul. act. confess. In tantum excreuit hic appetitus, quod nedum laici, sed etiam sū-mi sacerdotes & clerici, sunt tali modo & vitio penitus infecti. Vides enim quod ipse qui deberet, tanquam verus vicarius, vestigia sequi Iesu Christi, possidere, & manu armata nituntur detinere iurisdictionem in terris, ciuitatibus, & villis, & locis, quae sunt naturaliter & a mundi creatione, & Christi ordinatione imperii Roma-ni. iuxta illud. Quod est Dei, reddatur Deo: & quod est Caesaris, Caesari. Imo ipse Papa in ipsum Imperatorem nituntur superioritatem habere, quod ridiculum est dicere, atque abominabile audire. Item in forma re-sponsi. rei conuen. num. 10. Nota, quo modo & quos modis isti clerici illaqueent laicos, & suam iurisdictionem amplient. Sed heu miseri Imperatores & Principes seculares, qui hoc & alia sustinetis: & vos seruos Pontificum facitis, & mundum per eos infinitis modis usurpari videtis, nec de remedio cogitatis: quia prudentia & scientia non intenditis. Ideo attendite, & memoria commendate, quid dicat Hieronymus: Veteres scrutans hystorias, inuenire non possum scidisse ecclesia, & de domo Domini populos seduxisse, praeter eos qui sacerdotes Deo positi fuerunt. Haec ille Pragmaticus, ante annos, vt diximus, cētū & quinquaginta, liberè, fortiter, & animosè cū tñ [?] ꝑ id tēp⁹ Ecclesia Christiana tyrannico Paparum dominatu, vel maxime premeretur. Quid est igitur, quod quisquam hoc tempore miretur, si Sixti quinti impietate in confictis Francisci sui religionibus tuendis, crudelitatem in Galliae regno toties lacerando, impotetiam in Regum maiestate conculcanda, rapacitatem & sacrilegia in bonis ecclesiasticis diripiendis tantopere detestemur? Audiamus alteram ciusdem Pragmatici sententiam in formula rei conuent. §. Praescriptionis, vbi sic loquitur: Nunqua quiescet Italia, donec ipsa Ecclesia non possideat omnes civitates vel castra, & donatio eidem facta per Constantinum fuerit per aliquem probum & potentem Imperatorem penitus revocata: cum non bene conueniat psalterium cum cithara: nec datum sit a Christo, nec B. Petro, quod possidere debeant talia: sed quod est Caesaris, reddatur Caesari, & quod est Dei, Deo. Item, in form. Sent. definit, §. Sed ad quemcunque. Ad Papam, inquit, quocunque omisso medio appellare licet. Quod ideo prouiderunt, ut lites ad curiam suam traherent, & suam auaritiam satiaret: quod tamen nunquam faciunt, quia clericorum animus & appetitus & enixus prae caeteris, in pecuniis cumulandis, contra honestatem communem, & fidem Dei promissam non attendentes, nec studentes bonis moribus, nec scripturis diuinis. Item, in forma libel. quo agitur ex substitut. §. ex suo corpore. Scire debes tu, ignare lai-ce, quod imperium aliquando habuit utrumque gladium: temporalem scilicet & spiritualem: adeoque quod tum Imperatores conferebant omnia beneficia Ecclesiastica per vniuersum orbem, & amplius eligebant Papam, ut habetur in c. Adrianus, 13. distinct. & notat Innocent. in c. 2. de maiorit. & obedien. Imperatores concesserunt privilegium, ut bona ingredientium monasteria applica-rentur rentur ipsis monasteriis:propter quod privilegium multiplicata sunt, & fundata monasteria infinita per v-niversum orbem: olim causa devotionis, licet hodie causa rapinæ & avaritiæ: in tantum, quod destruxe-runt hodie mundum & annihilaverunt statum imperii, & omnium laicorum. Possunt ergo dici merito illa loca facta vel facienda, Retia contexta ad capienda laicorum bona. Surgat ergo bonus Imperator, & dicat omnes, Fiat pax in virtute tua, & abundantia in turribus tuis.
units.tr: And so that the most distinguished Senators of the Parlements, learned in law, may understand that there were long ago learned men of the same order who openly exposed this cruel and barbarous tyranny, we will presently bring forward some testimonies from their books. The first is from Doctor Albericus on l. bene a Zenone, n. 18, C. de quadriennii praescriptione: The presidents of the Roman Church, he says, by their subtle and shrewd prudence have varied their statutes according to the variety of the times, now raising up their power, now gradually lowering it, from time to time. But to what end? Unless that they might gradually bring all things, both heavenly and earthly, both spiritual and temporal (as they call them), under their feet, as they openly boast? Let the second author come forward: Giovanni Pietro Ferrariense, whose words in his Practica forensis, which he wrote more than a hundred and fifty years ago, in Formula actionis confessoriae, are these: This appetite has grown so much that not only laymen but even the highest priests and clerics are wholly infected with this kind of vice. For you see that those who ought, as true vicars, to follow the footsteps of Jesus Christ, strive to possess, and with armed hand to hold, jurisdiction over lands, cities, villages and places which belong naturally, from the creation of the world and by the ordinance of Christ, to the Roman empire, according to that saying: What is God's is to be rendered to God, and what is Caesar's to Caesar. Indeed the Pope himself strives to have superiority over the Emperor himself, which is ridiculous to say and abominable to hear. Likewise in the form of response, rei conventae, n. 10: Note how and by what means these clerics ensnare laymen and enlarge their jurisdiction. But alas, wretched Emperors and secular Princes, who endure this and other things, and make yourselves slaves of the Pontiffs, and see the world usurped by them in infinite ways, and do not think of a remedy, because you do not apply your prudence and knowledge. Therefore pay attention, and commit to memory, what Jerome says: searching the ancient histories, I cannot find that the Church was ever split, and that peoples were led away from the house of the Lord, except by those who were set up as priests of God. So spoke that Pragmaticus, more than a hundred and fifty years ago, as we said, freely, bravely and boldly, although at that time the Christian Church was especially oppressed by the tyrannical dominion of the Popes. What is there, then, for anyone to wonder at in these times, if we so greatly detest the impiety of Sixtus V in defending his Franciscan superstitions, his cruelty in repeatedly tearing the kingdom of France to pieces, his impotence in trampling on the majesty of kings, and his rapacity and sacrilege in plundering ecclesiastical goods? Let us hear another opinion of the same Pragmaticus, in the formula rei conventae, §. Praescriptionis, where he speaks thus: Italy will never be at rest until the Church itself possesses all the cities and castles, and the donation made to it by Constantine is wholly revoked by some worthy and powerful Emperor: since the psaltery does not agree well with the harp; nor was it given by Christ, nor to Blessed Peter, that they should possess such things; but what is Caesar's is to be rendered to Caesar, and what is God's to God. Likewise, in the form Sententia definitiva, §. Sed ad quemcunque: It is permitted, he says, to appeal to the Pope by passing over any intermediate step. They provided this so that they might draw lawsuits to their court and satisfy their avarice; which nevertheless they never do, because the mind, appetite and eagerness of the clergy, above all others, for piling up money, does not heed common honesty or the faith promised by God, and strives neither for good morals nor for the divine Scriptures. Likewise, in the form of a libel, quo agitur ex substitutione, §. ex suo corpore: You ought to know, ignorant layman, that the empire once held both swords, the temporal namely and the spiritual; so much so that the Emperors then conferred all ecclesiastical benefices throughout the whole world, and moreover elected the Pope, as is held in c. Adrianus, dist. 13, and Innocent notes it on c. 2, de maioritate et obedientia. The Emperors granted the privilege that the goods of those entering monasteries should be applied to the monasteries themselves. On account of this privilege monasteries have multiplied, and infinitely many have been founded throughout the whole world, formerly for the sake of devotion, although today for the sake of rapine and avarice: so much so that they have today destroyed the world and annihilated the state of the empire and of all laymen. Those places which have been made, or are to be made, may therefore rightly be called nets woven to catch the goods of laymen. Let therefore a good Emperor arise, and say to them all: Let there be peace in your strength, and abundance in your towers.
THE CRIME OF MAJESTY

units.la: PRoximum est, ut ad crimen conculcatæ maiestatis accedamus. quid enim Læsæ dicemus, aut Imminutæ? cum Papatus his prope quadringentis annis, ita superbè, & Imperatores & Reges, ac Potentatus Europæ omnes contempserit, ut eos non tantum pro vassalis ac feudatariis suis, sed etiam pro vilissimis mancipiis habuerit. Cuius furiosæ atque intolerādæ superbiæ testimonia hæc sunt certissima: primum in c. unam sanctam, Extra-vag.de maior. & obed. De necessitate salutis credendum est, Papæ Romano creaturam omnem subesse. Item illud, Super Gentes & regna Romanus Pontifex constitutus est. c.1. Extravag.de consuetud. Papa superiora-tum habet in Imperium, & vacante Imperio Imperatori succedit. Clement. Pastoralis, de reiudic. Papa potest transferre imperium de Gente in gentem. c.venerabilem, de elect. Papa potest Imperatorem deponere. c.2. de re iud. Papa Romanus habet utriusque potestatis temporalis, & spiritualis monarchiam: Habet sacerdotii principatum, & est Christianæ religionis caput. c. fundamenta, de elect. in vj. Quanto sol supe-rat lunam, tanto Papa superat Imperatorem. c. solit. ext.de maior.& obed. Omnes homines, cuiuscunque sint dignitatis,& præeminentiæ, vt primum in conspe-ctum Papæ veniunt,distantibus spatiis, ter debent ante illum genua flectere, & eius pedes osculari. lib.1. ce-rem.pontific.sect.3.c.3. Quando Papa per scalam ascendit equum,maior princeps qui præsens adest,etiam si Rex esset aut Imperator, stapham equi Papalis tenere debet,& deinde ducere equum per frænum aliquantum. Si Imperator aut Rex soli essent, id est, non esset alius Rex,soli equum ducerent cum dextra manu. Sin vero esset alius Rex,dignior a dextra, alius a sinistra frænum tenerent: si vero Pontifex non equo, sed sella vehere-tur, etiamsi Imperator aut Rex adesset, sellam ipsam cum Pontifice humeris suis portare aliquantulum de-bent.Item sectio.12.cap.5. Princeps ciuitatis quam Papa intrabit, etiam si esset Rex, ducet equum Pontificis fræno: vel si Pontifex vehitur sella, subit sellam cum suis proceribus dignioribus per aliquot passus: deinde iubente Pontifice, Rex ascendit equum,& equitat suo ordine,d.lib.1.tit.2.Quod si ita placeat Papæ,vt non equo,sed sella vehatur,tunc Imperator vel Rex, si quis adsit, debet ipsam sellam suis humeris sustinere. tit.2. Imperator in conuiuio aquam Papæ manibus ad lotionem præbere debet. tit.2. In Papali conuiuio Imperator vel Rex Romanorum debet portare primum ferculum,eod.tit.2. Imperator tenetur præstare Papæ iuramentum fidelitatis,& obedientiæ, cuius formula extat in c.1.de iureiur. & c.tibi domino, dist. 63. Satíne perspicuè Paparum intoleranda audacia his testimoniis conuicta est? Sanè sic videtur, apud eos quidem iudices ac parlamentorum senatores, quibus aliquis conscientiæ & diuini numinis metus supererit. præsertim cum etiam Doctores Ca-noninonistæ hoc ipsum fateantur. Nam Cardinal.Za-barella, qui tractatum scripsit de schismate circa annum Christi MCCCCVI. in illo tractatu ita scribit: Considerandum est de honorificentia facienda Papæ, ne in ea excedatur modus, vt videatur non magis honorari Papa, quàm Deus. Ita enim honorandus est, vt non [?]adoretur. quod de se fieri passus non fuit B. Petrus: de quo legitur Act. 10. quod Cornelius procidens ante pedes eius adorauit eum. Petrus vero eleuauit eum dicens, Surge: Ego ipse homo sum, sicut & tu. Hæc Za-barell. quibus consentaneum est illud Ioh.Fabri in præfat.institut. Papa, inquit, in verbis se dicit seruum seruorum: de facto tamen se adorari permittit. quod Angelus in Apocalypsi refugit. Hæc Faber. Papæ autem huius tantæ superbiæ titulum atque auctoritatem proferunt ex Imperatoris Constantini Magni beneficio, cuius instrumentum extat primum Latinè in dist.96. c. Constantinus. deinde Græcè apud Augustum Steuchum Papæ Bibliothecarium in lib. de donat. Constant. impresso Lugduni anno MDXLVII. in hanc sententiam: Ut totius Occidentis, hoc est, Italiæ, Siciliæ, Sardiniæ, Galliæ, Hispaniæ, Angliæ, Germaniæ, imperium sit penes Papam Romanum: eóque nomine pari or-natu, parique, atque adeò maie-state, imperio & potestate præditussit, atque ipse Constantinus fuerat: comitatum etiam equitum consimilem habeat: vsque eò vt ei in equo seden-ti Imperator aliquatisper pedisequi operam præ-stet, & ipsius equi frænum tenens aliquandiu eum assectetur. Qua de re idem Steuchus libro secun-do capitulo sexagesimofexto, pagina 134. ita scri-bit. Illa quoque edicti pars, qua magnus Imperator prædicat se frænum equi S.Syluestri Papæ Romani tenuisse, equúmque duxisse (in quo noscitur pedum deosculatio) probatur vera esse, quod successores Imperatores, non multo post tempore similia fecerunt. Nam ingrediente Pontifice Romano Constantinopolim, Iustinianus cum regno in capite sese prostrauit, & pedes osculatus est Pontificis. Item cum Stephanus Pontifex proficisceretur ad Francorum Regem Pipinum, audies idem Rex eiusdem aduentum, nimis festinanter in eius aduenit occursum, vna cum coniuge, & filiis, & primatibus, & fere ad centum milliaria filium suum Carolum ei misit, cum aliquibus optimatibus. Ipse quoque in Palatio, quod dicitur Ponticone fere ad trium milliarium spatium descendens de equo suo, cum magna humilitate, terræ prostratus, vna cum coniuge & filiis, & optimatibus eundem suscepit Pontificem, cui & vice stratoris vsque in aliquantulum locum iuxta eius sellam properauit, & cum gloria ad palatium duxit. Hæc ad verbum protuli ex Iuone Carnotensi: ille (ut reor) ex Anastasio bibliothecario. Hactenus Steuchus:quorum similia, Platina in vita Stephani II. de Pipino & Carolo commemorat. Conferamus iam cum istis Thrasonicis ac phaleratis Papæ Romani verbis Christi modestiam, & præcepta, cuius se Papa vicarium & successore esse contendit. Scitis, inquit, principes gentium in eas dominari, & qui magni sunt, potestatem in illas exercere. Verum, non ita erit inter vos: sed quicunque voluerit inter vos magnus fieri, sit vester minister: & quicunque voluerit inter vos primus esse, sit vester minister: sicut filius hominis non venit ut sibi ministraretur, sed ut ministraret. Matth.20. Ego sum in medio vestrum, ut qui ministrat. Luc.22. Itaque quoties Apostolis mandatum aut negotium aliquod dedit, nusquā vnum aliquem cæteris anteposuit: sed omnes pari eodemque loco habuit: vt pote negotij eiusdem collegas ac socios. veluti cùm eos obire iussit terrarum orbem, & euangelium prædicare, ac miraculis eam prædicationem confirmare. Math.10.7.& 8.Luc.10.9. aut cùm ijsdem prædicit fore, vt XII.tribus Israel iudicent, nullum ex iis aliquem in tribunali, reliquos in subselliis sessuros dicit. Math.19.30. sicuti Pseudoconstantinus scribit, Concedo Ecclesiæ Romanæ Pontifici, vt sacerdotes ita eum caput habeant, sicut iudices Regem. c.Constantinus, 96.dist. Cùm in Apostolos congregatos Spiritus sanctus immissus est: cùm iis ligandi & soluendi ius datum est, cùm ad prædicandum euangelium missi sunt, cui tandem illorum aliquam iuris prærogatiuam, aut priuilegium Christus attribuit? Ioh.20. Mat.28. Act.1. Ac magna quidem illa sunt Papalis insolentiæ, superbiæ, & contumaciæ exempla: sed illud aliquanto maius ac mirabilius, quod de Imperat. Friderico Ahenobarbo historici complures memoriæ prodiderunt: in his Helmodus Chronic. Scl. cap.8. Naucler.generat.39. Barnus de vit.Pontific. Cùm inter ipsum & Papam Adrianum conuenisset, vt ipse Papæ quantam maximam posset reuerentiam, quasi B. Petri successori, exhiberet: denique vt ei ex equo descendenti strepam teneret, Imperatorem ad latus dextrum extitisse, strepamque dextram contigisse. quo facto Papam indignatum. Imperatorem increpuisse: sed hunc illi respondisse, factum id tenendarum strepamum insciëntia, quòd eo primum tempore tenendæ strepę munus obiisset. Quæ cùm ita sint, ac tantum sibi Papa dominatum in summos quosque orbis terrarum Prin[?] cipes sumserit, tamen suaue auditu est, quod pro-tocucullus noster Sixtus V. dominatum illum FA-MULATUS nomine appellat. Nam initio suae contra Regem Nauarrum Declarationis, his utitur verbis: Ideo se[?] Nauarrum Regem & Condaeum Principem excommunicare, ut Sui[?] FAMULATUS tempore sublatis haereticis, pace & otio fruatur. Quod, malum, istuc Famulatus genus est, quod in occupando orbis terrarum imperio, in conculcada Regum & Imperatorum maiestate consumitur? Ex eodem Famulatus genere illud est, quod idem Adrianus Papa eidem Friderico his scripsit verbis: Super prudentia tua non mediocriter miramur, quod B. Petro, & S.Rom.Ecclesiae non quantam deberes, exhibere reverentiam videris. In literis enim ad nos missis, nomen tuum nostro praeponis. in quo insolentia, ne dicam arrogantia, notam incurris. Qua de re idem Naucle-rus Genef.39. testatur. Sed iam ad summum ac praecipuum Papalis superbiae, & conculcatae Regum Maiestatis testimonium veniendum est. Nam cum illius Adriani successor Alexander supradictum imperatorem Fridericum in illis terris Ecclesiae Christianae nubibus, ac tenebris, usitata excomunicatione terruisset, Fridericus autem, temporum illorum superstitione imbutus, absolui se ab illa postulasset, diem ei Papa praestituit, qua se Venetiis in summo templo sisteret. Ubi eo ventum est, adstante magna Cardinalium & Episcoporum copia, tum Papa negauit se gratiam ei suae proscriptionis facturu, nisi prius ad ipsius pedes proastratus ac supplex veniam ab ipso deprecaretur. Quod ubi factu est, tum Papa pede altero sublato, & collo prostrati Imperatoris imposito, carmen illud ex Psalmis Dauidis à suis sacerdotibus cani iussit.Super aspidem & Basiliscū ambulabis, & conculcabis Leone & Dra-conem. cuius Cyclopicę immanitatis testimonia luculeta extat apud eundē Nauclerum Gen.40. Barnum de vit.Pōtific.[?]& Funccium,in Chron. Ecquis est ex tanto Regis Galliæ senatorum & Consiliariorū numero,quid[?] maius aliquod aut certius conculcatę maiestatis testimoniū requirat? Quaquam dixerit fortasse quispiam,Cur tam angusto animo tantus Imperator,& tam potēs Monarcha? Nimirum hæc fatalis temporū illorum superstitio fuit, quæ mentes hominum in illa caligine occupabat. quo de genere scitum est illud T.Liuij,de Bacchanalibus scribentis:Nihil est in speciem fallacius quàm praua religio,quum Deorum numē præteditur[?] sceleribus. Subit enim animos timor,ne fraudibus humanis vindicandis diuini iuris aliquid immixtum violetur.Hęc ille.Sed iam alia quædā Papalis Famulatus testimonia ex cōculcata Regū nostrorum maiestate proferenda sunt,quò facilius intelligatur,quàm admirāda nō sit in hoc Papa Sixto tanta illa vetustate corroborata audacia,cūm sereniss.regem Nauarræ & Illustriss.Principem Condęum hoc verborum honore afficere est ausus, ut eos IRAE FILIOS appellaret: Superbientis Luciferi ministros: Hæresum & Hæreticorum patronos: in luto ac cœno peruolutatos: seditiosorum capita, Duces, & propugnatores hæreticorum ,exterorum acerrimos fautores: concitatores armorum contra suum Regem , & aduersus ipsum , & omnes Catholicos: Religiosorum hominum trucidatores: Condæum autem separatim Hæreticis parentibus genitum, Patris fui impiissimi Ecclesiæ Catholicæ persecu-toris vestigiis insistentem: bellorum ciuilium, & seditionum auctorem, omne feritatis & sæuitiæ genus exercentem. Utrumque autem prolem detestabilem, ac degenerem: læsæ maiestatis diuinæ reos: Orthodoxæ fidei Christianæ hostes. Malam verò tibi pestem, Antichriste natum quantum est hominum quantumque nascetur sacrilegissime, qui hæc incesto ore contra tales ac tantos Principes eructare, & istuc acerbitatis tuæ virus euomere ausus es. Sed quid miremur, ut iam dixi, tantam Papæ in hos duos Principes serenis.insolentiam? cum etiam in potentissimum quondam Galliæ Regem PhilippumPulchrum nihilo minore audacia fit u-sus? Nam anno MCCXCVI. Bonifacius octa-vus tanta fuisse superbia narratur, ut eum imperio ac potestati suæ subiectum esse contenderet, non tantum in spiritualibus, verum etiam in temporalibus. Tantúmne? Imò verò schismaticum, & hæreticum illum pronuntiauit, dirìsque omnibus devotum excommunicavit. At rex imprimis magna-nimus, huic tantæ illius audaciæ cedendū sibi nō putauit: imò verò, ut fortem Principem decuit, eam ferociam atque amentiam contrivit, ac contudit. Nam & de nefariis ipsius sceleribus cognitionem iudiciùmque instituit, & vbi manifestis eū testimoniis conuictum esse comperit, tum illum Anagniæ comprehendendum, & in carcerem compingendum curauit: qua in custodia, (ut Baldi & Platinæ verba usurpemus) qui tàquam Leo regnarat, tanquam canis interiit: cuius historiæ præter Platinam auctores sunt plerique Gallicorum Annalium scriptores. Huiusmodi quondam fuit Regum nostrorū magnanimitas in aspernāda & reprimenda Paparū impudentia, vt eos ad despera- tionem ac rabiem adigeret. Nam ecquis tota Gal- lia vel nobilis, vel plebeius, vel cum imperio, magi- stratu, potestate, vel etiam priuatus, bene erga Regiam maiestatem animatus existimabitur, cui non ista tanta Romani tyranni superbia stomachum moueat? Et miramur, Sixtum nostrum ista Sathanae disciplina institutum, ista ferociae vetusta- te corroboratum, ausum esse in hac sua DECLA- RATIONE pronuntiare se Henricum Nauarre Re- gem, & Henricum Condaum Principem, eorumque om- nes posteros, regno, principatibus, Ducatibus, domi- niis, ciuitatibus, & locis feudisque priuare: itemque dignitatibus, honoribus, & officiis etiam Regis: Haec enim illius verba sunt. Item, eosdem Incapaces de- clarare, & inhabiles ad succedendum in quibuscunque ducatibus, principatibus, dominiis, & regnis, ac specialiter in regno Francia. Proh Dei, hominumque fide? quaenam ista Tragica & Thyestea execratio est, & furiosa.Antichristi,ac monachi impudentis superbia? Cuius vnquam molosi aut Cerberi latratus rabiosior auditus est?
units.tr: Next we come to the crime of trampled majesty. For what shall we call it, injured or diminished? For the Papacy, for nearly four hundred years, has so arrogantly looked down on emperors, kings and all the potentates of Europe that it has regarded them not merely as its vassals and feudatories but even as the most abject slaves. The following are the most certain proofs of this mad and intolerable arrogance. First, in the chapter Unam sanctam, Extravagants on majority and obedience: It must be believed for the necessity of salvation that every creature is subject to the Roman Pontiff. Likewise that: The Roman Pontiff has been set over the nations and kingdoms. c.1, Extravagants on custom. The Pope has superiority over the Empire, and when the Empire is vacant he succeeds the Emperor. Clement, Pastoralis, on judgments. The Pope can transfer the empire from nation to nation. c. venerabilem, on elections. The Pope can depose the Emperor. c.2, on judgments. The Roman Pope holds the monarchy of both temporal and spiritual power: he holds the principate of the priesthood and is the head of the Christian religion. c. fundamenta, on elections, in the Sixth Book. As far as the sun surpasses the moon, so far does the Pope surpass the Emperor. c. solit., Extra, on majority and obedience. All men, whatever their dignity and eminence, as soon as they come into the presence of the Pope, must kneel three times before him at a distance and kiss his feet. Book 1, Ceremonial of the Pontiffs, sect. 3, c.3. When the Pope mounts his horse by the ladder, the greater prince who is present, even if he were a King or Emperor, must hold the stirrup of the papal horse and then lead the horse a little way by the bridle. If the Emperor or King were alone, that is, if there were no other King, they alone would lead the horse with the right hand. But if there were another King, the more worthy would hold the bridle on the right, the other on the left. But if the Pontiff were carried not on a horse but in a litter, then even if the Emperor or King were present, they ought to carry the litter itself with the Pontiff on their shoulders for a little distance. Likewise section 12, c.5. The prince of the city which the Pope enters, even if he were a King, shall lead the Pontiff's horse by the bridle; or if the Pontiff is carried in a litter, he shall put his shoulder under the litter with his more distinguished nobles for some steps; then, at the Pontiff's command, the King mounts his horse and rides in his proper order. d. Book 1, title 2. But if it so pleases the Pope that he be carried not on a horse but in a litter, then the Emperor or King, if any is present, must bear that litter on his shoulders. title 2. At a banquet the Emperor must offer water to the Pope for washing his hands. title 2. At a papal banquet the Emperor or King of the Romans must carry the first course. same title 2. The Emperor is bound to render the Pope an oath of fidelity and obedience, whose formula is found in c.1 de iureiur. and c.tibi domino, dist. 63. Is not the intolerable audacity of the Popes plainly convicted by these testimonies? Surely it seems so, to those judges and senators of parliaments in whom some fear of conscience and of the divine power remains, especially since even the canonist doctors themselves confess this. For Cardinal Zabarella, who wrote a treatise on the schism around the year of Christ 1406, writes thus in that treatise: One must consider how much honour is to be paid to the Pope, lest the measure be exceeded, so that the Pope seems to be honoured no less than God. For he is to be honoured in such a way that he is not adored. This St Peter did not allow to be done to himself: of him we read in Acts 10 that Cornelius, falling down at his feet, adored him. But Peter raised him up, saying: Stand up; I am a man, as you are. These are Zabarella's words, and to them agrees that of John Faber in the preface to the Institutes: The Pope, he says, calls himself in words the servant of servants; yet in fact he allows himself to be adored, which the angel in the Apocalypse refused. Thus Faber. Now they derive this title and authority of such pride from the benefit of the Emperor Constantine the Great, whose instrument is found first in Latin in dist. 96, c. Constantinus, and then in Greek in Augustinus Steuchus, the Pope's librarian, in his book on the Donation of Constantine, printed at Lyon in 1547, to this effect: that the empire of the whole West, that is of Italy, Sicily, Sardinia, Gaul, Spain, England and Germany, be in the power of the Roman Pope; and that under that name he be endowed with equal honour, equal and indeed greater majesty, empire and power than Constantine himself had; and that he have a similar retinue of horsemen, to such a degree that when he sits on a horse the Emperor for some time performs the office of attendant, and holding the bridle of his horse follows him for a while. Concerning this same matter Steuchus, in book two, chapter sixty-six, page 134, writes thus: That part of the edict also, in which the great Emperor declares that he held the bridle of the horse of St Sylvester, the Roman Pope, and led the horse (in which the kissing of feet is known), is proved to be true, since the successor emperors did similar things not long after. For when the Roman Pontiff entered Constantinople, Justinian with his crown prostrated himself and kissed the Pontiff's feet. Likewise, when Pope Stephen set out to visit the Frankish King Pepin, the same King, hearing of his arrival, hastened too eagerly to meet him, together with his wife, sons, chief men, and almost a hundred miles away sent his son Charles to him with some of the nobles. He himself, too, in the palace called Ponticum, descending from his horse about a three-mile distance, with great humility prostrated himself on the ground, together with his wife, sons and nobles, and received the Pontiff, and in place of a groom hurried with him to a little place near his chair, and with honour led him to the palace. I have related these words verbatim from Ivo of Chartres, who (I think) took them from the librarian Anastasius. So far Steuchus; and Platina, in the life of Stephen II, recounts similar things about Pepin and Charles. Let us now compare with those boastful and gilded words of the Roman Pope the modesty and precepts of Christ, whose vicar and successor the Pope claims to be. You know, he said, that the princes of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who are great exercise power over them. But it shall not be so among you: whoever wishes to become great among you, let him be your minister; and whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be your servant; just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve. Matt. 20. I am among you as one who serves. Luke 22. Therefore, whenever he gave the Apostles a commission or some task, he never set one of them above the others, but held them all in the same place and equal rank, as colleagues and partners in the same business: as when he ordered them to go through the whole world and preach the gospel and confirm that preaching by miracles, Matt. 10.7 and 8, Luke 10.9; or when he foretold that they would judge the twelve tribes of Israel, he did not say that one of them would sit on the tribunal and the rest on benches, Matt. 19.30. As the Pseudo-Constantine writes: I grant to the Roman Pontiff of the Church that, as judges have the King as their head, so priests have him as their head. c. Constantinus, dist. 96. When the Holy Spirit was poured out on the Apostles gathered together; when the right of binding and loosing was given to them; when they were sent to preach the gospel: to which of them did Christ at last assign any prerogative or privilege of right? John 20, Matt. 28, Acts 1. These are indeed great examples of papal insolence, pride and obstinacy; but this is somewhat greater and more wonderful, which several historians have recorded in memory concerning the Emperor Frederick Barbarossa: among them Helmold, Chronicle, chap. 8; Naucler, generation 39; Barnus, on the lives of the Popes. When it had been agreed between him and Pope Adrian that he should show the Pope the greatest possible reverence, as to the successor of St Peter, and finally that he should hold the stirrup for him as he dismounted from his horse, the Emperor stood at his right side and touched the stirrup with his right hand. At this the Pope was indignant and rebuked the Emperor; but Frederick replied that this was done from ignorance of how to hold a stirrup, since it was the first time he had performed the duty of holding a stirrup. Since these things are so, and the Pope has claimed such dominion over the highest princes of the world, it is nonetheless sweet to hear that our protocucullus Sixtus V calls that dominion by the name SERVICE (FAMULATUS). For at the start of his Declaration against the King of Navarre he uses these words: Therefore I excommunicate the King of Navarre and the Prince of Condé, so that in the time of his SERVICE, with the heretics removed, he may enjoy peace and leisure. What, pray, is this kind of service, which is spent in seizing dominion over the world and in trampling the majesty of kings and emperors? From the same kind of service is that which Pope Adrian wrote to the same Frederick in these words: We are not a little surprised at your prudence, that you seem not to show to the blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church the reverence that you owe. For in the letters you sent to us you put your name before ours, in which you incur the mark of insolence, not to say arrogance. Naucler testifies to this same matter, Gen. 39. But now we must come to the chief and principal testimony of papal pride and of the trampled majesty of kings. For when Alexander, successor of that Adrian, had frightened the aforesaid Emperor Frederick, in those clouds and darkness of the Christian Church, with the usual excommunication, Frederick, steeped in the superstition of those times, asked to be absolved from it. The Pope fixed a day on which he should present himself at Venice in the great church. When he arrived there, with a great company of Cardinals and bishops standing by, the Pope then declared that he would not grant him the favour of lifting his proscription unless first he came prostrate at his feet and begged pardon from him. When this was done, the Pope, raising one foot and placing it on the neck of the prostrate Emperor, ordered that song from the Psalms of David to be sung by his priests: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon. Clear evidence of this Cyclopean monstrosity is found in the same Naucler, Gen. 40, in Barnus on the lives of the Popes, and in Funck's Chronicle. Is there anyone among the great number of the senators and councillors of the King of France who would seek a greater or surer testimony of trampled majesty? Although someone may perhaps say: why such a narrow mind in so great an emperor and so powerful a monarch? Surely this was the fatal superstition of those times, which occupied men's minds in that darkness. On this kind of thing the saying of Titus Livy about the Bacchanalia is apt: Nothing is more deceptive in appearance than a perverse religion, when the power of the gods is put forward as cover for crimes. For fear creeps into men's minds lest, in avenging human frauds, something of divine law be violated. So he. But now other testimonies of papal service, drawn from the trampling of the majesty of our kings, must be brought forward, so that it may more easily be understood how little this audacity of Pope Sixtus, so strengthened by antiquity, is to be wondered at, since he has dared to honour the most serene King of Navarre and the most illustrious Prince Condé with such terms of abuse, calling them SONS OF WRATH: ministers of proud Lucifer; patrons of heresies and heretics; wallowing in mire and filth; heads of seditious men, leaders and champions of heretics, most fierce supporters of foreigners; stirrers-up of arms against their King, against him and against all Catholics; butchers of religious men. And Condé, born of heretical parents, treading in the footsteps of his most impious father, the persecutor of the Catholic Church, the author of civil wars and seditions, exercising every kind of savagery and cruelty. Both are a detestable and degenerate offspring, guilty of injured divine majesty, enemies of the orthodox Christian faith. But you, a deadly pestilence, son of Antichrist, how many men you are, and how many will be born, most sacrilegious, who have dared to belch these things from an incestuous mouth against such great princes and to vomit out the poison of your bitterness! But why should we wonder, as I have said, at such great insolence of the Pope against these two most serene princes, since he has used the same audacity against the once most powerful King of France, Philip the Fair? For in the year 1296 Boniface VIII is said to have been of such pride that he contended that the King was subject to his rule and power, not only in spiritual but also in temporal matters. So much? Indeed he pronounced that King schismatic and heretical, and devoted him to all curses and excommunicated him. But the King, most magnanimous, did not think he should yield to such great audacity; rather, as a brave prince should, he crushed and broke that ferocity and madness. For he both instituted an inquiry and judgment into his wicked crimes, and when he found him convicted by clear evidence, he had him seized at Anagni and thrown into prison; in that custody (to use the words of Baldus and Platina) he who had reigned like a lion died like a dog. The authors of this story, besides Platina, are most of the writers of the French annals. Such once was the magnanimity of our kings in scorning and checking papal impudence, that it drove the Popes to despair and rage. For who in all France, noble or commoner, whether holding office, magistracy or power, or even as a private person, well disposed toward the royal majesty, would not be stirred in his stomach by the pride of this Roman tyrant? And are we to wonder that our Sixtus, trained in this Satanic school and strengthened by this ancient ferocity, has dared to pronounce in this his DECLARATION that he deprives Henry, King of Navarre, and Henry, Prince of Condé, and all their posterity, of kingdom, principalities, duchies, dominions, cities, places and fiefs, and likewise of dignities, honours and offices, even of the King's. For these are his words. Likewise he declares the same men incapable and unfit to succeed in any duchies, principalities, dominions and kingdoms, and especially in the kingdom of France. Good God, and good faith of men! What tragic and Thyestean curse is this, and frenzied, the arrogance of Antichrist and of a shameless monk? Has ever the howl of any mastiff or Cerberus been heard more raging?

units.la: Sed non magnopere admiranda, vt dixi, haec Papae aduersus Regem Nauarreum audacia est, cum tam effraenatus eiusdem furor in potentissimū Gal- liae Regem extiterit. Quare alia potius paris eiusdem superbiae testimonia audiamus: neque enim maledictis cum Sathana certare, humanum est: satisque fuerit illam Michaelis Angeli imprecationem vsurpare, Increpet te Dominus. Iud.i.cap.9. Ergo, vt ad institutum redeamus, ne illud quidem eiusdem Papalis famulatus testimonium praeter- eundum est, quod de eodem Bonifacio memoriae est proditum, qui anno CIↃ CCC. magno populorum concursu ad urbem Romam propter Iu-bilæum facto. primo solenni die, Pontificalibus infulis ornatus, sese multitudini spectandum præbuit: postero vero die Imperatorio paludamento insignis, nudatum ante se gladium deferri iussit, magna voce clamitans: Ego sum Pontifex, & Imperator, terrestréque ac cœleste imperium habeo. paucisque post diebus Albertum Imperatorem a Germanis electoribus creatum, & confirmationem ab ipso postulantem superbe repudiavit, ne-gans electionem sine sua auctoritate factam, ra-tam haberi oportere: quippe cum solus utriusque gladij potestatem haberet. Aliquam multis post diebus ea conditione illum confirmavit, ut quam primum Regi Galliæ bellum inferret, cuius regnum in prædam & victoriæ præmium condonabat. Quarum rerum testes sunt Cuspinianus in vita Alberti, Paralip. Vrspergens. [?] & Gallicorum Annalium scriptores. Sed quid hæc levia & minuta persequimur? Superius demonstratum est, Papam Rom. totius Occidentis Imperium sibi ex Imperatoris Constantini donatione vindicare. Nuda hæc verba sunt. Quare rem ipsam videamus. Negamus enim ullum esse in Occidente Regem, Gal-lum dico, Hispanum, Arragonicum, Portugalli-cum, Hungaricum, Bohemicum, Anglicum, Scoti-cum, Danicum, Suecicum, Ruscianicum, Croati-cum, Dalmaticum, quem non Papatus Rom. suum sibi vassallum & feudatarium asciscat: quasi qui ab ipso regnum suum feudi ac beneficij loco accepe-rit, eoque nomine fidelitatem, atque hominium ei præstare debeat. Magnum est quod dicimus, ac dictu prope incredibile. Sed prolatis instrumentis, adhibitisque testimoniis veritas illustrabitur. Nā regna singula literarum ordine persequemur, si prius à nouissimo semiregis creati instrumēto exordium ceperimus, quod Aldus Manutius in vita Cosmi Medicis nuper edidit:vbi Papa nomine Pius anno Christi 1569. cum illum Cosmum Magnum Etruriæ ducē crearet, scribit se id superiorum Paparum exemplo facere, qui Portugaliæ, & Bulgarorū & Blachorū, & Hiberniæ, & Bohemiæ Reges crearant. Ex certa scientia, inquit, maturaque deliberatione nostris ac de suprema nostra apostolica potestatis plenitudine, tam dictorum praedecessorum, quam etiam Alexandri III, & Innocetii pariter III. ac Pauli IV, similiter praedecessorum nostrorum, qui Portugalliæ & Bulgarorum ac Blachorum, necnon Hybernie Reges, & vt tunc dux Bohemiæ Rex in suis literis nominari pof-sit, respectiue crearunt, constituerunt, & concesserunt, &c. & aliquanto post: Eundem Cosmum Ducem eiusque successores magnos duces & Principes Etruriæ creamus: Deinceps igitur regnorum omnium Christianorum nomina literarum (vt diximus) ordine exequamur. DE ANGLICO. Aug. Steuchus Papæ Bibliothecarius in lib.de donat. Constant. 2.pag. 138. testatur, in illa Papæ bibliotheca extare Regi-strum Papæ Alexandri tertij, in quo hæc ad Guillielmum Anglorum Rege Epistola reperitur. Nā vt ex illo Steuchi Bibliothecarij libro intelligitur, singulorum Paparum acta omnia singulis quibus-que registris attributis consignata sunt: quibus quemadmodū fides habenda sit, regula iuris ostendit, qua dicitur: Priuatæ scripturæ fidem haberi, sed aduersus ipsum scriptorem tantum. Ergo Ale-xandri epistola hæc fuit. Nouit prouidentia tua Anglorum Regnum, ex quo nomen Christi ibi glorificatum est, sub Apostolorum principis manu & tutela extitisse. Nam, ut bene nosti, Anglifideles erant & pia deuotio-nis respectu ac cognitione Religionis, annalem pensionem Apostolicæ sedi exhibebant: ex qua, pars Romano Pontifici, pars Ecclesiæ S.Mariæ, quæ vocatur schola Anglorum, in usum fratrum deferebatur.Hæc ex Steucho. sed præter Steuchum aliis locis hæc testimonia reperio. Flau.Blondus lib.6.Decad.2.Tunc, inquit, Ioannes Anglorum Rex vires suas Regi Francorum impares fore veritus, ad Innocentii tertii Pontificis Rom. misericordiam confugit. nam Angliam, Hybernïamque Romanæ Ecclesiæ feudatarias ex fœdere constituens, centum auri marcas pro utraque infula quotannis soluere est pollicitus. Anton. Florent. Histor. part.3. tit. 19.§.quinto. Anno 1223. Ioannes Rex Anglorum sponte de consilio suorum Principum obtulit ac liberè concessit Deo & Apostolis eius sanctissimis, Petro & Paulo, & S.Romanæ Ecclesiæ, & D.Papæ Innocetio 3.totum Angliæ Regnum & Hyberniæ pariter, cum omnibus iuribus & pertinentiis suis: & fecit ac iurauit homagium pro dictis Regnis, dicto Innocentio Papæ, ut illa de catero, ut feudatarius, ab ipso Papa & successoribus eius tenere. Quod idem Polydorus Virgilius lib. 15. commemorat. Hoc Papæ instrumento, si fides priuatæ, ut dixi, scripturæ habenda est, regnum Angliæ Papæ feudatarium est. Age, reliqua videamus.
units.tr: But, as I said, this audacity of the Pope against the King of Navarre is not greatly to be wondered at, since his unbridled rage has been just as fierce against the most powerful King of France. Let us rather hear other testimonies to the same arrogance. For it is not becoming for a man to contend with Satan in insults; it is enough to use that imprecation of the archangel Michael: The Lord rebuke thee. Jud. i. cap. 9. So, to return to our purpose, we must not pass over this further testimony of the same Papal servitude, which is recorded about the same Boniface, who in the year 1300, when a great crowd of people had come to the city of Rome for the Jubilee, appeared on the first solemn day adorned with the Pontifical mitres and let himself be seen by the multitude. On the following day, however, wearing the imperial mantle, he ordered a naked sword to be carried before him, crying out loudly: "I am the Pontiff and the Emperor, and I have both the earthly and the heavenly empire." A few days later he proudly rejected Albert, who had been elected Emperor by the German electors and asked him for confirmation, denying that an election made without his authority ought to be held valid, since he alone possessed the power of both swords. Many days afterwards he confirmed him on condition that he would make war on the King of France as soon as possible, granting him that kingdom as booty and as the reward of victory. Cuspinianus in the life of Albert, the Paralipomena of Urspergensis, [?] and the writers of the French annals are witnesses to these things. But why do we pursue these light and trivial matters? It has been shown above that the Roman Pope claims for himself the empire of the whole West by the donation of the Emperor Constantine. These are his very words. Let us therefore look at the thing itself. For we deny that there is any King in the West, I mean the French, Spanish, Aragonese, Portuguese, Hungarian, Bohemian, English, Scottish, Danish, Swedish, Russian, Croatian, or Dalmatian, whom the Roman Papacy does not claim as its vassal and feudatory, as though he had received his kingdom from it as a fief and benefice and therefore owed it fealty and homage. What we say is great, and almost incredible to speak of. But once the documents are produced and the testimonies adduced, the truth will be made clear. For we will go through the kingdoms one by one in alphabetical order, beginning with the most recent instrument by which a semi-king was created, which Aldus Manutius lately published in the life of Cosimo de' Medici. There Pope Pius, in the year of Christ 1569, when he was creating that Cosimo the Great Duke of Etruria, writes that he does this after the example of his predecessors, who created the Kings of Portugal, of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, of Ireland, and of Bohemia. From certain knowledge, he says, and mature deliberation, and from the fullness of our supreme apostolic power, we have created, constituted and granted, respectively, both by our said predecessors and also by Alexander III, and likewise by Innocent III, and by Paul IV, our predecessors, who created, constituted and granted the Kings of Portugal and of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, and also of Ireland, and the Duke of Bohemia, who could then be named King in their letters, &c. And a little later: We create the same Duke Cosimo and his successors great dukes and princes of Etruria. From here on, therefore, let us go through the names of all the Christian kingdoms in alphabetical order, as I said. CONCERNING THE ENGLISH. Augustinus Steuchus, Librarian of the Pope, in his book on the Donation of Constantine, book 2, page 138, testifies that in that Papal library there is a register of Pope Alexander III, in which this letter to William, King of the English, is found. For, as is understood from that book of Steuchus the librarian, all the acts of each Pope were recorded and assigned to their individual registers. The rule of law shows how much faith is to be placed in them, which says: "Private writing is to be believed, but only against its own author." So the letter of Alexander was this: Your foresight knows that the kingdom of the English, since the name of Christ was glorified there, has existed under the hand and protection of the chief of the Apostles. For, as you well know, the English were faithful, and in respect of their pious devotion and knowledge of religion they paid an annual pension to the Apostolic See, part of which was carried to the Roman Pontiff and part to the Church of St. Mary, which is called the school of the English, for the use of the brothers. So far from Steuchus; but apart from Steuchus I find these testimonies in other places. Flavius Blondus, book 6, Decade 2: "Then," he says, "John, King of the English, fearing that his forces were unequal to the King of the French, fled for mercy to Pope Innocent III of Rome. For, establishing England and Ireland as fiefs of the Roman Church by treaty, he promised to pay a hundred gold marks yearly for each island." Antoninus Florentinus, Histories, part 3, title 19, § fifth: "In the year 1223, John, King of the English, of his own accord and with the counsel of his princes, offered and freely granted to God and to his most holy Apostles, Peter and Paul, and to the Holy Roman Church and to the lord Pope Innocent III, the whole Kingdom of England and likewise of Ireland, with all their rights and appurtenances; and he did and swore homage for the said kingdoms to the said Pope Innocent, to hold them henceforth from the Pope himself and his successors as a feudatory." Polydore Vergil also records the same, book 15. By this instrument of the Pope, if the faith due to private writing is to be given, as I said, the kingdom of England is a feudatory of the Pope. Come now, let us see the rest.
CONCERNING THE KINGDOM OF ARAGON.

units.la: Steuchus eodem lib. pag. 193. Petrus Rex Arragoniæ, anno tertio Domini Innocentii tertii Papæ venit Roma ad eundem Innocentium, ab eoque militiam solenniter, ac honorificè accepit: obtulitque sponte totum regnum B.Petro, & sacrosanctæ Rom. Ecclesiæ: ibique accepit[?] in feudum, prædictum regnum. Itémque pro regno Sardinia, certam pecuniæ summam constituit se daturum.
units.tr: Steuchus, in the same book, page 193: Peter, King of Aragon, in the third year of Pope Innocent III, came to Rome to the same Innocent, and received knighthood from him solemnly and with honour. He freely offered the whole kingdom to St Peter and the most holy Roman Church, and received the aforesaid kingdom back from it as a fief. Likewise, for the kingdom of Sardinia, he agreed to give a certain sum of money.
CONCERNING THE KINGDOM OF CROATIA AND DALMATIA.

units.la: Steuchus eodem libro, pag.191. in registro Gregorij VII. ita legitur. In nomine Dom. S. & individuæ Trinitatis, anno Dominicæ incarnationis millesimo septuagesimo sexto: indictione quarta decima mensis Octobr. Ego Demetrius, qui & Suinumir nuncupor, Dei gratia Croatiæ Dalmatiæque Dux, à te D. Gebizo, ex apostolicæ sedis legatione, Domini Papæ Gregorii potestatem obtinente, in Salontana Basilica S. Petri, Synodali & concordi totius cleri & populi electione, & Croatiorum Dalmaticorúmque regni regimine per vexillum, ensem, sceptrum, & coronam investitus atque constitutus Rex, tibi devoveo & polliceor me incommutabiliter completurum omnia, quæ mihi tua reverenda iniunget sanctitas, ut in omnibus & per omnia Apostolicæ sedi fidem servem, & quicquid in hoc regno tam Apostolica sedes quàm legati sui sanxerunt vel sanxerint irreuocabiliter custodiam: Iustitiam excolam, Ecclesiam defendam, ducentorum quoque Bizantiorum[?] tributum, meorum omnium consultuum, primatuum, S. Petro per singulos annos in resurrectione Domini, de mihi concesso regno persoluendo statuo. Praterea cum Deo servire regnare sit, vice B. Petri ac domini nostri Papæ Gregorii, atque post se successorum in Apostolica sede, me tuis manibus comitto, & comittendo, hanc fidelitatem iuramento stabilio, Ego, inquâ, Demetrius, qui & Suinumir, Dei gratia & Apostolicæ sedis dono, Rex ab hac die in antea S. Petro & domino meo Papæ Gregorio & suis successoribus canonicè intrantibus, ero fidelis. Regnū autem quod mihi per manū tuā, domine Gebize[?], traditur, fideliter retinebo, & illū suúque ius Apostolicæ sedi aliquo
units.tr: Steuchus, in the same book, page 191, reads as follows in the register of Gregory VII: In the name of the Lord, the holy and undivided Trinity, in the year of the Lord's incarnation 1076, in the fourteenth indiction, in the month of October. I, Demetrius, who am also called Suinumir, Duke of Croatia and Dalmatia by the grace of God, having been invested and installed as king, by you, Lord Gebizo, holding the authority of the apostolic see as legate of Pope Gregory, in the basilica of St Peter at Salona, by the synodal and unanimous election of the whole clergy and people, and by the rule of the kingdom of the Croats and Dalmatians, through a banner, a sword, a sceptre and a crown, I vow to you and promise that I will unchangeably carry out all that your reverend holiness shall enjoin upon me, so that I keep faith with the apostolic see in all things and in every respect, and that I will irrevocably observe whatever both the apostolic see and its legates have decreed or shall decree in this kingdom. I will cultivate justice, defend the Church, and I resolve to pay to St Peter each year, at the resurrection of the Lord, a tribute of two hundred Byzantine coins, from all my own consuls and nobles, from the kingdom conferred on me. Moreover, since to serve God is to reign, I commit myself into your hands in place of St Peter and of our lord Pope Gregory, and of his successors in the apostolic see; and by committing myself I confirm this fidelity by oath. I, I say, Demetrius, who am also called Suinumir, by the grace of God and the gift of the apostolic see, will be faithful from this day forward to St Peter, to my lord Pope Gregory, and to his successors who enter canonically. The kingdom which is handed over to me by your hand, Lord Gebizo, I will faithfully hold, and I will never at any time by any device withdraw it or its right from the apostolic see.

units.la: ingenio aliquando non subtraham: Dominum meum Papam Gregorium, & suos successores atque legatos, si in meam potestatem venerint, honorifice suscipiam, & honeste tractabo, & remittam, & undequaque me inuitauerint, prout potero simpliciter eis seruiam. Haec Steuchus. Ex quibus cognosci licet, quam scitos & literatos scribas habere Papae soleant, qui non modo Francisci & Dominici res gestas & admiranda facinora literis mandare possint, verum etiam inuestitutarum feudalium instrumenta & breuia testata conscribere.
units.tr: I will honourably receive my lord Pope Gregory and his successors and legates, should they come into my power, and I will treat and send them on honourably; and wherever they invite me, I will serve them simply, as far as I am able. Thus Steuchus. From these words it may be seen how learned and literate the scribes are whom the Pope usually keeps, who can not only commit to writing the deeds and marvellous crimes of Francis and Dominic, but can also draw up the instruments and attested letters of feudal investitures.
CONCERNING THE KINGDOM OF DENMARK.

units.la: Steuchus eodem libro 2. pag. 189. Regnum Danorum, inquit, est peculium & vectigal sacrosanctae Rom. Ecclesiae: quod eadem Pontificum vera monimenta testantur. Alexander Episcopus S.S.D. dilecto filio Sueum, Regi Danorum salut. & Apostolic. benedict. Prudentiam tuam monemus, ut censum regni tui, quem antecessores tui sanctae Apostolicae Ecclesiae persoluere soliti sunt nobis & successoribus nostris transmittere studeas: ita tamen ut non sicut oblatio super altare ponatur, sed tanquam nobis, quam successoribus nostris, ut certius approbetur, praesentialiter offeratur.
units.tr: Steuchus, in the same book 2, page 189: The kingdom of the Danes, he says, is the private property and tribute of the most holy Roman Church, as the true records of the Pontiffs attest. Alexander, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Sueno, King of the Danes, greeting and apostolic blessing. We advise your prudence to take care to send on to us and to our successors the tax of your kingdom, which your predecessors were accustomed to pay to the holy apostolic Church; yet not in such a way that it is placed upon the altar as an offering, but rather that it be presented in person to us, and to our successors, so that it may be more certainly acknowledged.
CONCERNING THE KINGDOM OF FRANCE.

units.la: Extat apud Nicolaum Gilliu Gal. Annal. scriptore, insignis Papae Bonifacij VIII. epistola, qua subscribem. Bonifacius seruus seruorum Dei Philippo Francorum Regi: Deutime & madata eius obserua. Scire te volumus, quod in spiritualibus & TEMPORALIBVS nobis subes: Beneficiorum atque praebendarum ad te collatio nulla spectat: & si aliquarum vacatiu custodia habeas, usufructum eorum successoribus reserua: & si quas contulisti, collatione haberi irrita decernimus. aliud credentes Fatuos reputamus. Datu Laterani, IIII. Non. Deceb. Pontificatus nostri anno sexto. Hoc Papae Bonifacij instrumenstrumentum est à Bibliothecariis, sine dubio in i-psius registro ex consuetudine reconditum: sed audiamus quid pars adversaria respondeat. Nam ex Regis responso quantum fidei atque auctoritatis istis registris tribui oportet, cognoscemus. Neq; enim dubitadū est, quin cæteri Reges pleriq; pari libertate in impudentiam illius retuderint.
