Philippus Dei gratia Francorum Rex, Bonifacio se gerēti pro summo Pontifice, salutem modicam, sine nullam. Sciat tua maxima FATVITAS in temporalibus nos alicui non subesse. Aliquarum Ecclesiarum & prabedarum vacātium collatione ad nos iure Regio pertinere, & percipere fructus earum contra omnes possessores. utiliter nos tueri: secum autem credentes, fatuos reputamus atque dementes. Hæc ex Chroni.Brit.Armori.libr.4.cap.14 Nicol. Gillio in Chroni. Gallis. ex quibus facilis coniectura est, ut maxime concedamus furiales illas literas superiores à Papis ad Reges missas fuisse, tamē eos acriter ac vehementer illorum audacia ac temeritatem compressisse. Et tamen idem Steuchus, Papæ, ut diximus, Bibliothecarius illo suo registro fretus, in eode suo libro, pag. 198. ita scribere est ausus: & Lugduni ededu curare. Bonifacius VII. contra Philippum Gallorū regē, quod contra Ecclesia sese extolleret, cum ei Pontifex vetera monimenta explicasset, quibus doceret, quod Romana Ecclesia & in sacris, ET IN PROFANIS Gallia subesset, quo necesse esset Pontificem UTI DOMINUM REGNI SUI eum venerari, & colere, cū ille despiceret, eum excōicauit. DE GERMANICO IMPERIO. Apud eūde Steuchū de hoc imperio fūnū siletiū, propter sumā (ut credi par est) Imperatoris Caroli v. potentia, que offendere Steuchus metuebat. sed aliundè permulta testimonia suppetunt. Primum apud Canonistas in c. tibi domino, distin.63 .vbi Imperatoris Othonis iusiurandum continetur, Papæ præstitum, quod Papa Clemens contendit esse iusiurandum fidelitatis, quod vassalli feudo accepto, suis patronis præstant in c. de iureiuran. in Clem. Unde Canonistæ fortissimè disputant, ac ratiocinantur Imperatorem esse Papæ vassallum, & imperium ab eodem feudi nomine teneri: sed & Papa Innocentius III in c. venerabilem, extra. de elect. scribit, ius eligendi Imperatoris ad Principes Germaniæ ab Apostolica sede peruenisse, &c. 2. de re iudic. in vj. Imperatorem posse à Papa deponi: & in c. 1. Extr. De sed. vacan. Papam vacante imperio Imperatorem esse. Atque hinc illa Papæ Innocentij II. nata confidentia est, vt Romæ in Lateranensi Basilica Lotharium Imperatorem pingeret, quasi vassallum ad pedes ipsius prostratum, & Imperij coronam ab eo accipiente atque hos illi pictvræ versus adscri-beret:
units.tr: There survives, among the annals of Nicolas Gilles, a notable letter of Pope Boniface VIII, to which the following is subscribed: Boniface, servant of the servants of God, to Philip, King of the Franks: Let your mind be well advised, and observe his commands. We wish you to know that in spiritual and TEMPORAL matters you are subject to us. The conferring of benefices and prebends on you does not belong to you at all; and if you hold the custody of any vacant benefices, you shall reserve their usufruct for our successors; and if you have conferred any, we decree that the conferment is void. Those who think otherwise we count as fools. Given at the Lateran, the fourth of the Nones of December, in the sixth year of our pontificate. This instrument of Pope Boniface is kept by the librarians, undoubtedly stored away in his own register as is customary; but let us hear what the opposing side replies. For from the King's reply we shall learn how much faith and authority ought to be given to these registers. Nor is it to be doubted that many other kings, with equal freedom, have repulsed the impudence of that man. Philip, by the grace of God King of the Franks, to Boniface, who conducts himself as the supreme Pontiff, a modest greeting, or rather none at all. Let your greatest FOOLISHNESS know that we are not subject to anyone in temporal matters. The conferment of vacant churches and prebends belongs to us by royal right, and we are entitled to receive their fruits against all possessors. Those who think otherwise we count as fools and madmen. These things are from the Chronicle of Brittany and Armorica, book 4, chapter 14, and from Nicolas Gilles in his Chronicle of the French. From these a ready inference follows: even if we grant that those furious letters were sent by the Popes to the kings, nevertheless the kings sharply and vehemently suppressed their audacity and temerity. Yet the same Steuchus, as we have said, a librarian of the Pope, trusting in that register of his, dared to write in the same book, page 198, and to have it printed at Lyon: Boniface VII, against Philip, King of the French, because he exalted himself against the Church, when the Pontiff had set out to him the ancient records, by which he might teach that the Roman Church, both in sacred matters AND IN PROFANE ones, had authority over France, so that the Pontiff had to revere and honour him as LORD OF HIS KINGDOM, but since he despised this, excommunicated him.

units.la: Rex venit ante fores, iurans prius vrbis honores. Post homo fit Papæ: sumit, quo dante, coronam.
units.tr: The king comes before the gates, first swearing the honours of the city. Afterwards he becomes the Pope's man, and takes the crown at his giving.

units.la: Cuius rei memoria extat in Chro. Hirsaug. in vit. Abbatis Hartuingi, & apud Radeuic. lib. 1. num. 9. & 10. Et cum ea die Imperator Fridericus eum Adriani Papæ legatis expostulasset, Radeuicus sic eos respondisse scribit, A quo ergo habet, si à Domino Papa non habet imperium? Quinetiam extat apud Ioannem Auentinum lib. 6. pagina 636. Adriani Papæ Epistola ad Archiepiscopos Treuirensem, Mogun-tinum, & Colonienfem, his verbis: Romanum imperium à Græcis translatum est ad Alemannos: vt Rex Theutonicorum non antequam ab Apostolo coronare-tur, tur, Imperator vocaretur. Ante consecrationem, Rex: post, Imperator. Vnde igitur habet imperium nisi a nobis? Ex electione principum suorum habet nomen Regis, ex consecratione nostra habet nomen Imperatoris & Augusti, & Cæsaris. Ergo per nos imperat: Roma nostra sedes est: Imperatoris est Aquis, in Arduenna, quæ est sylua Gallia. Imperator, quod habet, totum habet a nobis. Sicut Zacharias transtulit imperium a Græcis ad Theutonicos, ita nos possumus ab Alemannis transferre ad Græcos. Ecce in potestate nostra est, vt demus illud cui volumus: propterea constitutus a Deo super gentes & regna, vt destruamus, & euellamus, ædificemus, & plantemus. Hæc Papa de Germanico imperio: satis, vt videtur, confidenter: cum illum Aquisgranum, & in syluam Arduennam, quasi pastorem ac bubulcum quendam, vel caprarium, sui similem relegat. Ecquis erit ex illustribus inuictissimi Imperatoris consiliariis, qui tam immanem atque importunam illius Tyranni vocem æquo animo ferre possit? Sed alia audiamus. DE REGNO HISPANICO. Steuchus eod. lib. 2. pag. 133. Gregorius VII. inquit; scribens Regibus ac Principibus Hispaniæ, ita dicit, Vos scitis, quod antiquitus Regnum Hispaniæ est Romanæ Ecclesiæ. Et paulò post, ex registro epistolarum eiusdem Papæ, quod in sua bibliotheca religiosè asseruari affirmat, hanc epistolam profert. Gregorius Episcopus seruus seruorum Dei, Regibus, Comitibus, caterisque Principibus Hispaniæ salutem. Notum fieri vobis volumus, regnum Hispaniæ, ex antiquis constitutionibus B. Petro & S. Romanæ Ecclesiæ in ius & proprietatem traditum esse, & quæ sequuntur. DE REGNO HVNGARIAE testimonium eiusdem generis extat apud eundem Bibliothecarium pag. 186.
units.tr: A memorial of this matter survives in the Chronicle of Hirsau, in the life of Abbot Hartwig, and in Radevicus, book 1, sections 9 and 10: And when on that day the Emperor Frederick expostulated with the legates of Pope Adrian, Radevicus writes that they answered thus: From whom then does he have the empire, if not from the Lord Pope? Moreover, there is also in John Aventinus, book 6, page 636, a letter of Pope Adrian to the Archbishops of Trier, Mainz and Cologne, in these words: The Roman empire was transferred from the Greeks to the Germans, so that the King of the Teutons, before he was crowned by the Apostle, should not be called Emperor. Before consecration he is king; after it, emperor. Whence, then, does he have the empire, if not from us? He has the name of king from the election of his princes; from our consecration he has the name of Emperor, and of Augustus, and of Caesar. Therefore he rules through us. Rome is our seat; the Emperor's is at Aachen, in the Ardennes, which is a forest of Gaul. Whatever the Emperor has, he has entirely from us. Just as Zachary transferred the empire from the Greeks to the Teutons, so we can transfer it from the Germans to the Greeks. Behold, it is in our power to give it to whom we will, since we are set by God over nations and kingdoms, to pull down and root out, to build and to plant. Thus the Pope on the German empire, quite confidently, as it seems, since he relegates it to Aachen and to the forest of the Ardennes, as if it were some shepherd or cowherd or goatherd, like himself. Who among the illustrious counsellors of the most unconquered Emperor could bear with an even mind the voice of so monstrous and insolent a tyrant? But let us hear other matters. CONCERNING THE KINGDOM OF SPAIN. Steuchus, in the same book 2, page 133: Gregory VII, he says, writing to the kings and princes of Spain, speaks thus: You know that from of old the kingdom of Spain belongs to the Roman Church. And a little later, from the register of letters of the same Pope, which he affirms is kept devoutly in his library, he produces this letter: Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the kings, counts and other princes of Spain, greeting. We wish you to know that the kingdom of Spain, by ancient constitutions, has been handed over to St Peter and the holy Roman Church, in right and as property, and what follows. CONCERNING THE KINGDOM OF HUNGARY, testimony of the same kind is found in the same librarian, page 186.

units.la: Gregorius Episcopus S.S.D. dilecto filio Salomoni, Regi Hungariae salutem. Sicut a maioribus patria tua cognoscere potes, regnum Hungariae sacrosanctae Romanae Ecclesiae proprium est, a rege Stephano olim B. Petro, cum omni iure ac potestate sua, oblatum, & devote traditum. Et mox. Idem Gregorius ad Gensum[?] Hungariae Regem: Notum tibi esse credimus, Regnum Hungariae, sicut & alia nobilissima Regna in propria libertatis statu debere esse, & nulli Regi alterius Regni subiici, nisi Sanctae & universali matri, Ecclesiae Romanae. De regno Polonico. Albertus Krantz in VVandal. lib. 8. capit.2. Lakoldus hac tempestate dux erat Cracoviae, & qui per omnem Poloniam facile principaretur. hic a Iohanne Pontifice Romano suscepit coronam: quod Ludovicum (quia eum exsecrabatur & excommunicabat Papa) non duceret legitimum Imperatorem. iam enim Pontifices in eam venerant maiestatem (quam principes seculares dicunt Praesumptionem) ut Reges crearent: citantes verbum primi post Christum Pontificis: Ecce, inquit Petrus, duo gladii hic. Contra quod principes ipsi verbum aeterni Pontificis, Mitte gladium tuum in vaginam, de gladio carnali humano & seculari interpretantur: quasi non liceat summo Pontifici in eo pugnare. Lakoldus autem a Pontifice Rex nominatus & consecratus omne regnum fecit B. Petro tributarium, ut per singula quotannis capita solueretur nummus unus: qui appellatur S. Petri. De regno Rusciae. Steuchus eodem lib. pag.109. Regnum item Rusciae iuris ac districtionis est Romanae Ecclesiae, quod eadem prisca monimenta pro se ferunt, Gregorius VII. Regi & Reginae Rusciae scribens: Dilectis, inquit, filiis Demetrio Regi Ruscorum: & regina uxori eius salutem, & Apostolicam benedictionem. Filius vester, limina Apostolorum visitans ad nos venit, & quod regnum illud dono Sancti Petri per manus nostras vellet obtinere, eidem beato Petro Apostolo, debita fidelitate exhibita, devotis precibus postulavit: indubitanter asserens, illam suam petitionem nostro consensu ratam fore ac stabilem, si Apostolicæ au-ctoritatis[?] gratia ac munimine donaretur. Cuius petitioni-bus assensum præbuimus: & regni nostri gubernacula ex parte B. Petri illi tradidimus, ea videlicet intentione charitatis, ut B. Petrus vos & Regnum vestrum sua apud Deum intercessione defendat. DE REGNO SICI-LIAE. Papa Clemes V.in cle.pastoralis, de sentet. & re iudic. Rursus non est silentio relinquendum, quod ipse Rex Siciliæ noster & Ecclesiæ Romanæ ratione regni prædicti notorie subditus, homoque ligius, & vassallus in eodem regno continuum habet domicilium. Plenius autē Baldus in l.cū in antiquioribus,19.c.de iur.de lib. Constat namque quod dominus Clemens quartus, quarto kale.Iunij pontif. sui anno primo anno domini, MCCCLXV. concessit perpetuo regnū Siciliæ domino Carolo comiti Andegauensi filio fe-licis memorię domini Ludovici octavi regis Fra-corum, fratris sancti Ludovici noni regis Franco-rum, & heredibus ipsius domini Caroli ex eo de-scendentibus, & investivit eum pro se & suis here-dibus autoritate Apostolica de dicto regno cum certis pactis modis & conditionibus, & inter ali-quod semper primogenitus dicti domini Caroli vel descendentium ex eo ad quos deveniat dictum regnum, succedat in dicto regno, & quod descen-dentes ex domino Carolo, & eius heredibus Siciliæ regibus mares, & feminæ in eodem regno succedant: sic tamen de duobus maribus in eadem linea con-curretibꝰ primogenitꝰ & de duabꝰ feminis primogenita & de mare:de feminina in eodem gradu similiter concurretur masculus aliis omnibus praeferatur.
units.tr: Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Solomon, king of Hungary, greeting. As you can learn from your forefathers, the kingdom of Hungary is the own property of the holy Roman Church, offered long ago to St Peter, with all its right and power, by King Stephen, and devoutly handed over. And soon after: The same Gregory to Gensus [?], king of Hungary: We believe you know that the kingdom of Hungary, like the other most noble kingdoms, ought to be in the state of its own liberty, and to be subject to no king of another kingdom, except to the holy and universal mother, the Roman Church. Concerning the kingdom of Poland, Albert Krantz in the Wandalia, book 8, chapter 2: Lackold was at that time duke of Krakow, and was able easily to rule over all Poland. He received the crown from Pope John, because (since the Pope cursed and excommunicated Louis) he would not be regarded as a lawful emperor. For the popes had already come to such majesty (which secular princes call presumption) as to create kings, citing the word of the first pontiff after Christ: "Behold," said Peter, "here are two swords." Against this, the princes themselves interpret the word of the eternal Pontiff, "Put your sword into its sheath," as referring to the carnal, human and secular sword, as if it were not lawful for the supreme Pontiff to fight with that. Lackold, however, named and consecrated king by the Pope, made the whole kingdom tributary to St Peter, so that one penny, called St Peter's penny, was paid yearly for each head. Concerning the kingdom of Russia, Steuchus, in the same book, page 109: The kingdom of Russia also is under the jurisdiction and control of the Roman Church, as those same ancient records bear witness for it, Gregory VII writing to the King and Queen of Russia: "To our beloved sons, Demetrius, king of the Russians, and his wife the queen, greeting and apostolic blessing. Your son, coming to us while visiting the thresholds of the Apostles, asked with devout prayers that he might obtain that kingdom as a gift of St Peter through our hands, from the same blessed Peter the Apostle, having first shown due fealty, affirming without doubt that his petition would be ratified and established with our consent, if it were granted by the favour and protection of apostolic authority. To his petitions we gave assent, and on behalf of St Peter we handed over to him the governance of our kingdom, with this intention of charity: that St Peter, by his intercession before God, may defend you and your kingdom." CONCERNING THE KINGDOM OF SICILY. Pope Clement V, in the decretal Pastoralis, On sentences and judgments: Again, it must not be passed over in silence that the same King of Sicily, our vassal, notoriously subject to the Roman Church by reason of the aforesaid kingdom, and a liege man and vassal, has a continual dwelling in that kingdom. Baldus, more fully, on the law Cum in antiquioribus: It is established that Lord Clement IV, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June in the first year of his pontificate, in the year of the Lord 1365 [sic], granted the kingdom of Sicily in perpetuity to Lord Charles, count of Anjou, son of Lord Louis VIII, king of the Franks of happy memory, brother of St Louis IX, king of the Franks, and to the heirs of Lord Charles descended from him, and by apostolic authority invested him with the said kingdom for himself and his heirs, under certain pacts, modes and conditions; and that the firstborn of Lord Charles, or of his descendants to whom the said kingdom comes, shall always succeed in the kingdom; and that the descendants of Lord Charles and his heirs, as kings of Sicily, males and females, succeed in the same kingdom; yet so that, of two males concurring in the same line, the firstborn, and of two females the firstborn, and of a male and a female in the same degree, the male is likewise preferred to all others.

units.la: De Regno Scotico. Polydorus Virgil. lib. 17. ita scribit:
units.tr: On the Kingdom of Scotland. Polydore Vergil, book 17, writes thus:

units.la: Bonifacius interea Pontifex a Scotis precibus fatigatus, interdixit Edouardo Regi, ne amplius posthac Scotos bello vexaret: quod id regnum antea in Romani Pontificis fidem & potestatem a Scotis ipsis permissum fuisset. Et ideo asseuerabat sibi soli integrum esse cuicunque liberet, dare aut auferre.
units.tr: Meanwhile Pope Boniface, worn out by the entreaties of the Scots, forbade King Edward to harass the Scots with war any more hereafter, because that kingdom had formerly been placed by the Scots themselves under the faith and power of the Roman Pontiff. And therefore he asserted that it lay wholly with himself alone to give or take away that kingdom from whomever he pleased.

units.la: Hactenus regna Christianorum R gu omnia enumerauimus, quae Papa feudi ac beneficij ab se accepti loco tenere ac possideri contendit. Ex quibus singulis atque vniuersis diiudicandum cordatis viris relinquimus, vtrum ne haec modesti Ecclesiae pastoris humilitas esse videatur, tantopere a Christo commendata, an potius immanis atque intolerandi Cyclopis confidentia. simul ab iisdem cogitari cupimus, an non tanta ista Paparum superbiloquentia ex eodem spiritu profecta sit, unde illa Tyranni Neronis oratio a Seneca libro de Clementia primo posteritati tradita. Ego ex omnibus mortalibus placui, electúsque sum, qui in terris deorum vice fungerer. Ego vitae necisque gentibus arbiter. Qualem quisque fortEstatúmque habeat, in manu mea positum est. Quid cuique mortalium fortuna datum velit, meo ore pronuntiat. Ex nostro responso laetitiae causas populi, urbésque cocipiunt. Nulla pars vsquam, nisi volente propitióque me, floret. haec tot millia gladiatorum, quae potestas mea comprimit, ad nutum meum stringetur. Quas nationes funditus exscindi, quas transportari, quibus libertatem dari, quibus eripi, quos reges macipia fieri, quorúmque capiti regium circundari decus oporteat, quae ruant urbes, quae oriantur, mea iurisdictio est.
units.tr: Thus far we have enumerated all the kingdoms of Christians, which the Pope contends he holds as a fief and benefice received from himself. Upon each and all of these we leave it to thoughtful men to judge whether this seems to be the modest humility of the Church's pastor, so commended by Christ, or rather the arrogance of a huge and intolerable Cyclops. At the same time we wish them to consider whether this so great boastfulness of the Popes did not proceed from the same spirit as that speech of the tyrant Nero, handed down to posterity by Seneca in the first book On Clemency: I have been chosen above all mortals and selected to act in the place of the gods on earth. I am the arbiter of life and death for the nations. Whatever fortune and standing each man has is placed in my hand. What fortune wishes to be given to each mortal, it announces through my mouth. From my answer people and cities take the causes of their joy. No part of anywhere flourishes unless I am willing and favourable. These many thousands of gladiators, whom my power restrains, will be drawn at my nod. Which nations are to be utterly uprooted, which transported, to which liberty is to be given, from which it is to be snatched, which kings are to be made slaves, and whose head ought to be encircled with royal dignity, which cities fall and which arise: this is my jurisdiction.
THE CRIME OF PERDUELLION.

units.la: SEquitur sextum crimen, cuius Papam Romanum iampridé à maxima Christianitatis parte non modò acc fatum, verum etiam cõ ictum & condemnatum esse diximus. Nos Perduelliona-tum illud appellamus, hoc est factiones hostili animo ad evertendum omnium Rerumpublicarum statum, quæ in orbe Christiano sunt, comparatas. qua eadem mente sortilegi[?] humani generis hostes appellantur. l. etsi, 7. C. de mal. item hostes communis salutis. l. vlt. C. eod. communes omniu hostes, cum quibus non fides esse debet, ait M. Tullius nec jusjurandum commune. Sed quoniam Galliæ nostræ causa potissimum hæc à nobis instituta disputatio est, in præsentia satis futurum videtur, si ex ea sola, atque adeò ex recenti factionum illarum memoria, hius criminis testimonia proferamus. Annus jam abiit tertius & vicesimus, ex quo Gallia nostra continuis prope bellis civilibus miserandum in modum vexatur. Bellis dico? Imo verò lanienis & cruentis ac furialibus carnificinis. Qui eorum, quos illa bella sustulerunt, numerum diligentius inierunt, non minus reperiunt duodecies centenis Gallorum indigenarum millibus. Ecquis est in Gallicis Parlamentis, vel Præses, vel Senator, qui ex animi sui sententia deierare audeat, Papam Romanum non tantis malis Alastorem, non præcipuam tantorum incendiorum facem extitisse? non assiduè Cardinales aut Episcopos, & alios ex suo comitatu emissarios ad aulam Gallicam misisse qui Regum animos tanquam malingenij, ad hæc funesta[?], & internecina bella, ad carnificinas, ad vastitatem terræ Galliæ inferendam inflammarent? Cùm interea quasi lanista sanguinarius, commissis inter se gladiatoribus, cruentos istos ludos ex sua Santangeli mole spectaret: aut, tanquam alter Nero, incensam ab se urbem, è sua turri despiceret, suosque oculos istis funestis spectaculis pasceret, crudelemque animum exsaturare cuperet? Quod si quæ patrum memoria in hoc regno contige-runt recordari volumus, primum hoc reperiemus: Ludovicum xii.(ut[?], quem Regem? qui Patris patriæ nomen summo bonorum omnium consensu adeptus est) urbes aliquot Italiæ bello captas, Papæ Iulij secundi ditioni adiunxisse. Papam intermissis aliquot mensibus hac Regi pro accepto beneficio gratiam retulisse, ut non modo eum schismaticum & hæreticum pronuntiaret, proscriberet, diris suarum excommunicationum fulminibus in-sectaretur: verum etiam Gallos omnes hostilem in modum cruciandos, interficiendosque curaret: præ-mium etiam percussoribus polliceretur, peccatorum omnium veniam, & impunitatem, si quis vel unicum Gallum quoquo modo trucidaret. Quid est Perduellem esse, communem humani generis hostem esse, aut vero perduelles omni scelere & crudelitate superare, si hoc non est? Sed operæpre-tium est, aliquato planius totam illam tragœdiam exponere. Erat is Papa ingenio truculento, atque ita diro, immani, turbulento, ut ne sui quidem la-trocinij sociis, Episcopis & Cardinalibus Romanis ferendus, Regibus vero & Principibus plane into-lerandus videretur. Itaque summo Regū & princi-pum omnium consensu, Concilium in urbem Ita-liæ, Pisas indictum fuit, ut communi consilio imPendentibus ab ipso Ecclesię Christianę malis ob-uiam iretur. Quàm prudenter autem, & legitimè ac solenniter Concilium illud conuocatum fuerit, patet ex Philippi Decij Iurisconsulti per ea tempora celeberrimi Consilio CLI. quod Mediolani aduersus illum Papam & scripsit, & edidit. Eum conuentum furibundus Papa confestim bello & armis deturbauit. Quapropter Regis nostri auctoritate Mediolanum primum, tum deinde Lugdunum translatum est: vbi re cognita, & deliberata, Iulius à suo Papatu suspensus fuit: hoc est ad tempus Papatus administratione circumscriptus.
units.tr: Next follows the sixth crime, of which we have said that the Roman Pope has long since been not only accused but also convicted and condemned by the greater part of Christendom. We call it perduellion, that is, the plotting of factions with hostile intent to overthrow the condition of all the commonwealths that exist in the Christian world. With the same meaning, sorcerers are called enemies of the human race: l. etsi, 7. C. de mal. Likewise they are called enemies of the common safety: l. vlt. C. eod. Marcus Tullius says that there ought to be no good faith, nor any common oath, with common enemies of all. But since this discussion has been undertaken by us chiefly on account of our own France, for the present it will seem enough if, from that alone, and indeed from the recent memory of those factions, we bring forward the evidence of this crime. Now the thirty-third year has passed since our France has been vexed, almost without respite, by civil wars, in a pitiable manner. Wars, do I say? Nay rather butcheries, bloody and frenzied slaughters. Those who have carefully reckoned the number of those whom those wars have carried off find not fewer than twelve hundred thousand native Frenchmen. Is there anyone in the French Parlements, whether president or senator, who dares to swear from his heart that the Roman Pope was not the Alastor of such great evils, not the chief torch of such great fires? Has he not constantly sent Cardinals, or bishops, or other emissaries from his retinue to the French court, who would inflame the minds of kings, like the minds of madmen, to these deadly and murderous wars, to the butcheries, and to the devastation of the land of France? Meanwhile, like a bloodthirsty gladiator-master, he watched those bloody games from his fortress of Sant'Angelo, with his gladiators set against one another; or, like another Nero, he gazed down from his tower at the city he had set on fire, feeding his eyes on those deadly spectacles and wishing to glut his cruel spirit. If we wish to recall what has happened in this kingdom within the memory of our fathers, we shall first find this: that Louis XII (who, by the universal consent of all good men, obtained the name of Father of his Country) annexed to the dominion of Pope Julius II several cities of Italy taken in war. After a few months the Pope repaid the king for that favour with this return: he not only pronounced him schismatic and heretic, proscribed him, and assailed him with the dreadful thunderbolts of his excommunications, but also took care that all Frenchmen should be tormented and killed in a hostile manner; he even offered a reward to murderers, and pardon for all sins and impunity, if anyone should slay even a single Frenchman by whatever means. What is it to be a perduellio, to be the common enemy of the human race, or indeed to surpass perduellions in every crime and cruelty, if this is not so? But it is worth while to set out that whole tragedy a little more clearly. That Pope was of such a savage, dire, monstrous and turbulent disposition that he seemed not even bearable to his fellow-robbers, the Roman bishops and Cardinals, and altogether intolerable to kings and princes. Therefore, by the common consent of all kings and princes, a council was called to the Italian city of Pisa, so that by common counsel the evils hanging over the Christian Church from him might be met. How prudently and lawfully and solemnly that council was convened is clear from the Consilium 151 of Philip Decius, the most celebrated jurist of that time, which he both wrote and published at Milan against that Pope. The raging Pope at once drove that assembly away by war and arms. For this reason, by the authority of our king, it was transferred first to Milan and then to Lyons; there, the matter having been examined and deliberated, Julius was suspended from his Papacy, that is, for a time he was restricted in the administration of the Papacy.

units.la: Quo nuntio Iulius accepto, tanto dolore atque iracundia exarsit, vt non modò Gallis omnibus aqua & igni interdiceret, verumetiam obuium quemque mactari, trucidarique imperaret: praemiis e-tiam, vt dixi, sicarios ac percussores inuitaret.
units.tr: When Julius received this news, he blazed up with such grief and anger that he not only forbade all Frenchmen water and fire, but also ordered that whoever he met should be slaughtered and butchered; he even, as I said, invited assassins and murderers with rewards.

units.la: Quam ipsius insaniam, ac potius rabiem, quoniam Gulielmus Budæus, Parifiensis, vir non minus patriæ amans quàm doctus & literatus, in suis de Asse libris, acriter atque animose persecutus est, commodissimum videtur, totam illam cordati viri ac ciuis boni querimoniam non modò Parlamentorum nostrorum Senatoribus, verumetiam omnibus omnium generum atque ordinum hominibus legendam proponere: præsertim cum historici ad vnum omnes in eadem querela exponenda mirificè cum eo consentiant.
units.tr: Since William Budé of Paris, a man no less a lover of his country than learned and literate, has pursued fiercely and spiritedly that madness of his, or rather rage, in his books On the As, it seems most fitting to set before the senators of our Parlements, and indeed before all men of every kind and rank, that whole complaint of a wise man and good citizen; especially since all the historians, with one voice, agree wonderfully with him in setting forth this same complaint.

units.la: Nam is est Iulius se-cundus, de quo & Arnaldus Ferronus, vir inprimis doctus, & Galliæ nostrę historicus, & Burdegalesis quondam Parlamenti Senator, itemque alij com-plures memoriæ prodiderunt: quod cum exercitu comparato Roma in Galliam, infesto in Regem nostrum animo, contenderet, suasque armatas copias ipse loricatus ex urbe per Tiberis pontem educeret: multis hominum millibus audientibus haec pronuntiauit: Quando nobis claues Petri nihil prosunt, age, gladium Pauli distringamus: simul claues, quas secum attulerat, in Tiberim proiecit gladiumque vagina eduxit. qua de re notum illud vetus carmen est:
units.tr: For Julius II is the one of whom Arnaud Ferron, a man most learned and historian of our France, and once a senator of the Parlement of Bordeaux, as well as several others, have left record: when, with an army assembled, he was marching from Rome into France with hostility toward our king, he himself, in armour, led his armed forces out of the city across the bridge over the Tiber. Before many thousands of men who heard him, he declared: "Since the keys of Peter are of no use to us, come, let us draw the sword of Paul." At the same time he threw into the Tiber the keys he had brought with him and drew his sword from its scabbard. Concerning this there is that old verse:

units.la: In Gallum, vt fama est, bellum gesturus acerbum Armatam educit Iulius urbe manum.
units.tr: Girded with his sword, as the story goes, he is about to wage a bitter war against the Gauls;

units.la: Accinctus gladio, claues in Tibridis amnem Proiicit, & saevus talia verba facit:
units.tr: Julius leads out an armed band from the city. Then, with his sword, he throws the keys into the river Tiber, and in his savagery speaks these words:

units.la: Cum Petri nihil efficiant ad prælia claues, Auxilio Pauli forsitan, ensis erit.
units.tr: "Since the keys of Peter achieve nothing for battles, perhaps the sword will be of help, with the aid of Paul."

units.la: Sed iam ad Budæi querimoniam accedamus: quam in libro de Asse quinto, his luculentis exponit verbis: Cleri magister sanguinarius, effractis timoris diuini repagulis, feras nationes in Domini populum immittebat, & Gallorum partes, eorumque fautores diris execrationibus denouens scelere plusquâ Tragico totum pene orbem religione solutâ in deuotos cocitabat. Item, lib.4. An eius temporis in mentem nô venit, cum Diuus Petrus Paulúsque & eorum sequaces, Ecclesiæ Architecti, non armorum splendentium fiducia infecti ad prælia grassabantur, sed cruce, sed innocentia freti, cætera inermes, ad castra Christi tuenda in tumultu flagrantissimæ charitatis classico ciebantur? Nunc inania tantum ipsi nomina tanto interuallo facti, etsi eorum demum maiestate apud populos sacrosancti sacerdotum ordines primarii fastus suos obumbrant. O duram portentosamque vecordiam sacrosanctæ potestatis! Quis enim vnquam tantum animo cocepit nefas, vt SACERDOTVM CULMEN, ut cleri magister, ut sacrorum summus opifex manus inauguratrices, ab altaris operatu adhuc calentes, in familiam Domini armare sustineret! ut animo plusquam gladiatorio grassaretur ad Christiani nominis culmen, nempe Regem Christianissimum mundo stupente delendum! & nunc mysticum illum ensem casim [?] punctimque irato, ut credimus, proposito vibraret: nunc à Marte sanguinariam frameam mutuaretur, & consternatos diris execrationibus, quæ fortasse in cum ipse verterunt, ad internecionem quoque conniteretur? En quos pedes, quas manus lubens exosculere, unde vel os cruentum, atque pollutum referres. Miserum verò te tum, IULI, atque intemperiùs actum, qui usque adeò iræ cæcæ indulgendum putaris, tute, ut transuersus, vesana animi cæcitate raperere? & nec te, nec decorum maiestatis beatissimæ præ odio respicere, sed ordinem amplissimum, sed senatum illum purpuratum, præcipua veneratione insignem, sed Libani gloriam tecum rapiens invitum bona ex parte, & mussitantem arcis Ecclesiæ ruina nos obruere, teque adeò ipsum cuperes? orbem etiam penè totum immutares, fulminibus ciendis, intorquendisque collabefactum, ut nos odio & invidia flagrantes, igneque deinde ardentes toruis istis oculis inspiceres, nec jam recusares, quin in rogum nostrũ flammantem voti compos insilires? Proh superi immortales! tantúmne de summo sanctuarii vertice licuit malesuadæ noxæ, ut ostro vindicta plus quam Atreiæ percitum, per fas agere, nefasque præcipitem, ut vel corpus animúmque in busto inimicorum properaret ire perditum. Nō fuit iræ efferatissimæ satis retrò nos in fines fulmine perterrefactos egisse, Italiæ perditè nobis adamatæ possessione cedentes cum fremitu gemituque, nisi de aris insuper & foris dimicare extremáque deinde exempla timere coegisset? Cum interim sub ipso lanista sanguinario totus propemodum hic orbis nobiscum pariter digladiaretur animo infestissimo. Ubinam erat igitur ille zelus domini, quae est ira iusta laesa[?] aut imminuta vindex diuinae maiestatis? hoc enim demum signifero in aciem prodire sacris cohortibus fas est, si quando prodire fas est. Num tandem igitur ex illa arce charitatis aut fidei sacello auxilia prompserat, & signa cruciata? Ecquid igitur eum pudebat SERVUM SERVORUM Dei se vocare, cum Franciam Christianorum decus semper, & Pontificum aedem religionisque asylum bustis ipse Gallicis insignire gestiret? Cum sacerdos septuagenarius, Christi, pacis conditoris & parentis, legatus Bellonae sacris operaretur: cui cum generis humani luculento dispendio litare contendebat. Idq; tum cum profanum vulgus ad delubra pacis & concordiae miserabili specie supplicationes inibat. Enimuero visendum spectaculum. Patrem non modo sanctissimum, sed etiam senio & canitie spectabile, quasi ad tumultum Gallicum Bellonae fana suos evocatos cientem: non trabea, non augustis insignibus venerandum, non Pontificis gestaminibus sacrosanctum, sed paludamento & cultu barbarico conspicuum, sed furiali, ut ita dicam, confidentia succinctum, fulminibus illis brutis & inanibus lucidum, eminete in truci vultu cultuque spirituum atrocitate. Profecto nos vidimus in paucis annis multa, quae prorsus maiora fide posteris videbuntur. Hoc turbine, hac procella luxata Ecclesiasticae auctoritatis ac disciplinae compage, quonam modo fides recta, nisi clauis trabalibus & aeternis fixa, sacrisque monimentis semel affirmata constabilitaque fuisset? Hactenus Budaeus: vir, ut ante dixi, patriae amans, & omni laude dignus. qui etsi nondum plane cognorat, quantum inter Christum & Antichristum interesset, tamè patriæ charitate impulsus non potuit, non illam Papæ crudelitatem ac barbaram immanitatem litoris ad sempiternam Papatus ignominiam commendare: ut omnis posteritas intelligeret, quàm hostili ac perduelli animo Alastores nostri in Gallia, Budæi ætate grassati essent. Age: alterum haud paulò ve-tustius eiusdem in Galliæ Reges perduellionatus testimonium audiamus. Nemo ignorat, partem Galliæ regni propè dimidiam per annos amplius trecentos ab Anglorum regibus quondam occu-patam fuisse. Eam regionem tum Rex Galliæ Phi-lippus (cui posterius Augusti cognomen fuit) bello recuperare conaretur, dici non potest, quàm su-perbè ac ferociter Papa Innocentius III. ei sit ad-versatus. Neminem paulò humaniorem esse ar-bitramur, qui nesciat, Romanorum quondam hanc artem ad subigendas gentes exteras fuisse, ut si quam inter vicinos aut Reges aut populos conten-tionem exortam animadvertissent, eam studiosè alerent, partique alteri amicitiam ac societatem honorificetissimis senatusconsultis deferrent: simul ei auxilium adversus alterum pollicerentur. His ar-tibus altera superata & subacta parte, postea breui tempore interiecto, perfacilè alterius opprimendæ occasionem reperiebant. Noster populus, (ait M. Tullius in lib. de Rep.) focis defendendis terrarum iam omnium potitus est. Hanc eandem maiorum suo-rum, hoc est (ut Ioannes monachus, Canonista no-bilis, interpretatur) prædonum ac latronum viam ac vestigia secuti Papæ, ut primum aliquid inter vicinos Reges aut Principes discordiæ subortum esse cognouerant, eam per emissarios quosdam Cardinales augere atque alere incipiebant: simul pactiones cum alterutro facere, vt li sua opera regno aduersarij potiri possent, tum sedem Romanam tanti beneficij auctorem agnoscerent: eíque de nouo adepto regno fidem, hominium, ac proinde tributum annuum praestarent. Hac pactione & coniuratione facta, illico Princeps aduersarius à Papa schismaticus & haereticus pronuntiabatur: Regnumque ipsius primo occupanti adiudicabatur, quibus artibus dici non poterat, quot incendia Papae in omnibus Christiani orbis partibus quadringentis hisce annis excitarint: quàm multos sibi suaeque stercorariae sedi Reges ac Principes, vassallos, feudatarios, stipendiarios redegerint. Qua de re quia paulò ante copiosè dictum est, satis erit de duobus illis Galliae & Angliae Regibus exponere. Exorta igitur inter illos contentione, Papa Innocentius III. primùm ex suo consistorio duos legatos in Galliam misit, qui & Regem excecrationum minis terrerent, & regni populares adversus ipsum Regem concitarent, & arcana cum Episcopis Gallis caeterisque sacerdotibus consilia & consensus inirent. Tum deinde Imperatorem Othonem IIII., itemque Ferdinandum Flandriae comitum aliosque complures exteros Principes ad arma contra Regem Gallorum ita celeriter, atque acriter concitauit, vt nisi Rex forti magnoque animo Papae illius minas & bruta fulgura, contempsisset, non tantum illas regni sui regiones, verumetiam breui tempore reliquas omnes amisisset. Cuius rei memoria extat, non modò in Gallicis nostris Annalibus, verumetiam apud Canonistas in c. nouit, 13. extr. de iudic. Nā illa Decretalis semsempiternum erit Papalis erga Reges ac patriam nostram odij, ac perduellis animi, monimentum. Ex his igitur & aliis quæ superius demonstrauimus,perspicuum omnibus esse arbitramur, quantum auctoritatis huic Papę Sixti DECLARATIO-NI tribui ab ordinibus & Regni Galliæ consiliariis oportéat. q é apertissimis testimoniis docuimus, multis atrocissimis criminibus à maxima Christianitatis parte nō modò accusatum,verùm-etiam conuictum,& condemnatum fuisse. Quòd si qui forte sint,qui disputér, quemadmodum ex eo, quod duæ partes è tribus Europæ partibus.Papam exauctorarunt, nulla ei auctoritas à reliqua parte tertia tribuenda est:ita eum duæ partes è tribus Galliæ partibus suam illi auctoritatem conserua-tam velint,æquum esse,vt suū ei ius in Gallia con-ferue-tur: duplex nobis in promptu responsio est. Prior,quoniam ex illo Gallorum numero qui Pa-parum partibus student, omnes Cardinales, Ar-chiepiscopi, Episcopi, Sacerdotes, monachorum phalanges innumerabiles, & clerici, cæteríque generis eiusdem scarabæi,Papæ beneficiarij, canes denique omnes,qui Papæ tribunal lambunt primo loco eximendi sunt: propter regulam iuris, qua dicimus,Quo in negotio res alicuius agitur, (quoniam ipsius aliqua ex parte interest) eum in eo negotio testem idoneum non esse.§. sed neque, Inst.de testam.ordi.l.nullus,10. D. de testib.l. omnibus, 9.C.eod.li.§.in propria, D. quand.appell.sit. Secunda est, quòd illis omnibus è numero exemptis non exigua pars cæterorum qui inueteratam in Gallia religionis consuetudinem sequuntur, non iudicio & sponte id faciunt,sed terrore & minis compulsi ut nihilo magis inter Papatus clientes numerandi sint, quàm (ut Iurisconsulti dicunt) testes aut tutores vi & metu in aliquo negotio retenti, inter idoneos testes & auctores numerantur. de quibus eleganter Ulpianus scribit, eos qui inviti negotio & actui alicui praesentes adsunt, non magis adesse videri, quàm si somno vel morbo comitiali occupati in eo loco fuissent. l. 1 §. vltim. D. de tutel. l. qui testamenta, 20 §. vltim. D. qui testamen fac. l. nouissime, 7. §. 1. quod falsi tutor. auctor. l. 2. D. de iudic.
units.tr: But let us now come to Budaeus's complaint, which he sets out in these striking words in the fifth book of De Asse: The bloody master of the clergy, having broken down the barriers of the fear of God, sent savage nations against the people of the Lord, and with dire curses he doomed the party of the French and their supporters, and stirred up almost the whole world against the condemned, with a crime more than tragic, religion cast aside. Likewise in book 4: Did it not come to mind in that age, when the divine Peter and Paul and their followers, the architects of the Church, were not seized by confidence in gleaming arms, but went out to battle relying on the cross and on innocence, and were called to the defence of Christ's camp, unarmed in all else, amid the tumult of a most burning charity? Now they are only empty names, separated from us by so great an interval, although by their majesty the holy orders of the priests, the chief men, overshadow their own pride among the peoples. O hard and monstrous madness of a holy power! For who ever conceived such a wicked thought, that the summit of the priesthood, as master of the clergy, as the chief craftsman of the sacred rites, while his hands which consecrate were still warm from the altar's work, should dare to arm himself against the household of the Lord? That he should rage with a mind more than gladiatorial against the summit of the Christian name, namely the Most Christian King, to be destroyed while the world stood amazed! And now he brandished that mystical sword, as we believe, with an angry purpose, now he borrowed a bloody blade from Mars, and strove to destroy by slaughter those whom he had struck with dire curses, which perhaps have turned back upon himself! Behold what feet, what hands you would gladly kiss, from which you might bring back a mouth bloody and defiled. Wretched indeed were you then, Julius, and too intemperately driven, who thought you must indulge blind anger to such a degree, that you were swept along, perverse and wild in the blindness of your mind? And not regarding yourself, nor the dignity of the most blessed majesty, out of hatred, but dragging with you, against its will in large part, the most ample order, that senate clad in purple, distinguished by the highest veneration, and the glory of Lebanon, and wishing to overwhelm us with the collapse of the citadel of the Church, murmuring, and wishing even yourself to perish? You would also almost wholly change the world, by stirring up and hurling thunderbolts, so that, inflamed with hatred and envy, you might look upon us with those savage eyes, burning then with fire, and would not hesitate to leap, with your wish fulfilled, into our flaming pyre? O immortal gods! Was so much permitted from the highest summit of the sanctuary to a counselling of harm, that vengeance, roused more than that of Atreus by purple, should be carried out in defiance of right, and wrong headlong, so that body and soul should hasten to ruin in the tomb of enemies? Was it not enough for the most savage wrath to have driven us back to the borders, terrified by the thunderbolt, yielding possession of Italy, so dearly loved and lost to us, with roaring and groaning, unless it also forced us to fight at the altars and outside them, and then to fear the most extreme examples? Meanwhile, under that very bloody gladiator-master, almost this whole world was fighting alongside us with a most hostile mind. Where then was that zeal of the Lord, what is the just wrath, the avenger of the divine majesty, wounded or diminished? For it is lawful to come forth into battle with the standard-bearing sacred cohorts in this manner, if ever it is lawful to come forth at all. Did he at last draw aid and crucified standards from that citadel of charity or chapel of faith? Was he not ashamed to call himself servant of the servants of God, when he himself was eager to mark France, the ever glory of Christians and the shrine of the Pontiffs and refuge of religion, with French tombs? When a priest of seventy years, the legate of Bellona, was performing sacred rites for Christ, the author and parent of peace, and strove to sacrifice to her at the great cost of the human race? And that at a time when the profane crowd, in the wretched guise of supplication, went to the shrines of peace and concord. Truly a sight to be seen: a father not only most holy, but also made notable by old age and white hair, as though calling together the shrines of Bellona to the French tumult; not revered by the trabea, not distinguished by the august insignia, not made sacred by the pontifical ornaments, but conspicuous in a military cloak and barbarian dress, girded, so to speak, with a frenzied confidence, shining with those brute and empty thunderbolts, standing out in the savage look and dress of a fierce spirit. Indeed we have seen many things in a few years which will seem to posterity wholly greater than belief. With this whirlwind, this storm, the framework of ecclesiastical authority and discipline dislocated, how could the sound faith have been established and confirmed, unless it had been fixed with iron nails that never loosen, and once affirmed by sacred monuments? Thus far Budaeus: a man, as I said before, a lover of his country, and worthy of all praise, who, although he had not yet fully recognised how much lies between Christ and Antichrist, nevertheless, impelled by love of his country, could not help commending that cruelty and barbarous savagery of the Pope to everlasting shame for Papacy, so that all posterity might understand with how hostile and treasonous a mind our Alastors rampaged in Gaul in Budaeus's age. Come, let us hear another, rather older, testimony of the same man to the treason against the Kings of France. No one is ignorant that for more than three hundred years almost half of the kingdom of France was once occupied by the kings of the English. How bitterly and fiercely Pope Innocent III opposed King Philip of France (who was later called Augustus) when that king tried to recover the region by war, cannot be told. We think there is no one of even moderate culture who does not know that this was once the art of the Romans for subduing foreign nations: when they noticed any strife arising between neighbouring kings or peoples, they fostered it eagerly, and offered friendship and alliance to one party by most honourable decrees of the Senate, promising at the same time aid against the other. By these arts, when one party had been overcome and subdued, they soon found, after a short interval, an easy occasion for crushing the other. Our people, says Marcus Tullius in his book on the Republic, has now gained possession of all lands, by defending their hearths. Following this same path and footsteps of their ancestors, that is (as John the monk, the noble canonist, explains) of robbers and brigands, the Popes, as soon as they knew that some discord had arisen between neighbouring kings or princes, began to increase and feed it through certain emissary cardinals. At the same time they made pacts with one of the parties, so that by their work he might gain possession of the enemy's kingdom, and thus acknowledge the Roman see as the author of so great a benefit, and so that they might render to it, for the kingdom newly obtained, fealty, homage, and consequently an annual tribute. Once this compact and conspiracy had been made, the opposing prince was at once pronounced by the Pope a schismatic and heretic, and his kingdom was adjudged to whoever first seized it. By what arts, it could not be told, how many fires the Pope had kindled in all parts of the Christian world in these four hundred years, how many kings and princes, vassals, feudatories, and mercenaries he had reduced to his dung-heap of a see. Since this has been said at length a little earlier, it will suffice to set out concerning those two kings of France and England. So, when a dispute arose between them, Pope Innocent III first sent two legates from his consistory into France, who were to terrify the king with threats of curses, and to stir up the people of the kingdom against the king himself, and to enter into secret counsels and agreements with the bishops of France and the other clergy. Then he stirred up so swiftly and so fiercely the Emperor Otto IV, likewise Ferdinand, count of Flanders, and many other foreign princes, to arms against the King of the French, that, had the king not with a brave and great spirit despised the threats and brute thunderbolts of that Pope, he would have lost not only those regions of his kingdom, but in a short time all the rest. The memory of this matter survives not only in our French annals, but also among the canonists, in c. Nouit, 13, extra de iudiciis. For that decretal will be an everlasting monument of the Papal hatred and treasonous mind towards kings and our country. From these things, therefore, and from others which we have demonstrated above, we think it is clear to all how much authority ought to be attributed to this declaration of Pope Sixtus by the orders and counsellors of the Kingdom of France. We have shown by most manifest testimonies that he has not only been accused by the greatest part of Christendom of many most atrocious crimes, but has also been convicted and condemned. But if there are any who argue that, just as he was deposed by two parts of the three parts of Europe, no authority is to be attributed to him by the remaining third part, then it is fair, if two parts of the three parts of France wish his authority to be preserved for him, that his right in France should be preserved for him as well: we have a twofold answer ready. The first is that, out of that number of the French who favour the Papists' side, all cardinals, archbishops, bishops, priests, the countless battalions of monks, and clerics, and other beetles of the same kind, the Pope's beneficiaries, indeed all the dogs who lick the Pope's tribunal, must first be removed from consideration, on account of the rule of law by which we say that in a matter in which something of someone's is at stake (since it is in some way of his interest) he is not a suitable witness in that matter. § sed neque, Inst. de testamentis ordinandis; l. nullus, 10, D. de testibus; l. omnibus, 9, C. eodem; l. in propria, D. quando appellandum sit. The second is that, with all those removed from the number, no small part of the others who follow the long-established custom of religion in France do not do so by judgment and of their own accord, but are compelled by terror and threats, so that they are no more to be counted among the clients of Papacy than (as the jurists say) witnesses or guardians who are held in some matter by force and fear are counted among suitable witnesses and authors. Of these Ulpian writes elegantly, that those who are present unwillingly at some transaction or act are seen to be present no more than if they had been in that place occupied by sleep or the falling sickness. l. 1 §. ultim., D. de tutelis; l. qui testamenta, 20 §. ultim., D. qui testamenta facere possunt; l. nouissime, 7 §. 1, quod falsi tutor. auctor.; l. 2, D. de iudiciis.

units.la: Denique constat inter omnes, sive par Gallis hominibus utriusque colendae exercendaeque religionis libertas sive optio permitteretur, vix quartam popularium regni partem in sedis Romanae religione permansuram. Quo loco iuvat nos vetus illud Bartholi commemorare, qui in praefat. Digest. num. 14. ubi de donatione Constantini disputans, & aliorum Doctorum sententias enumerans, cùm ad suam ventum est, ita loquitur: Videte nos sumus in terris ecclesiae. (nam Bononiae docebat) & ideo dico, quod illa donatio valuit. Ubi tamen multa contra illam donationem non obscurè subiungit. Ac pari modo cùm Canonistae disputarent, non licere Imperatori quemquam perduellionis crimine damnare, qui Pontificiam factionem sequeretur, Bartholus de Imp. Henrici sententia, qua Robertum Siciliae regem perduellionis damnarat, & contraria Papae Clementis V. sententia, qua eundem Robertum absoluerat, commemorans: Papae quidem se adversari non audere ostendit. Imperatoris utem[?] sententiam probare non dissimulat. Canonistis Bartholo idcirco vehementer indignanti-bus, qui de Papa & Caesare versum illum usurpant, Papam suum Iouem appellantes,
units.tr: Finally, everyone agrees that if the French were allowed a free choice, or an option, of worshipping and practising either religion, scarcely a quarter of the people of the kingdom would remain in the religion of the Roman See. Here it is worth recalling that old remark of Bartolus, who in his preface to the Digest, no. 14, discussing the donation of Constantine and listing the opinions of other doctors, comes at last to his own and says: "See, we are on earth the Church's" (for he was teaching at Bologna), "and so I say that donation was valid." Yet he there adds many things against that donation, not obscurely. Likewise, when the canonists argued that the Emperor could not condemn for treason anyone who followed the Papist faction, Bartolus, recalling the Emperor Henry's sentence by which Robert, king of Sicily, had been condemned for treason, and the contrary sentence of Pope Clement V by which the same Robert had been absolved, shows that he does not dare to oppose the Pope. But he does not hide that he approves the Emperor's sentence. The canonists were greatly angered at Bartolus for this, since they use that verse about the Pope and the Caesar, calling their Pope Jove:
"Caesar holds the empire divided with Jove."

units.la: Quinetiam eodem loco Bartholus disputat, tantum abfuisse, vt Robertus Papæ vafallus effet, quemadmodum Papa contra Imperatorem contendebat: vt testetur, mortuo Roberto Aloyfium ipsius heredem Imperatori fidelitatem Siciliæ nomine iuraffe, in ciuitate Pifarum, fe præfente. Qua de re videnda Henrici constitutio Ad reprimendâ, Qui dicant rebell. & contraria Papæ constitutio, illam abrogans & contumeliosè rescindens, In Clemet. Pastoralis, de Iudic.
units.tr: Moreover, in the same place Bartolus argues that Robert was so far from being a vassal of the Pope, as the Pope contended against the Emperor, that after Robert's death his heir Aloysius swore fealty to the Emperor for the kingdom of Sicily, in the city of Pisa, in my presence, as he attests. For this matter, see Henry's constitution Ad reprimendam, "Qui dicant rebellionis," and the contrary constitution of the Pope, which annuls it and rescinds it with insults, in the Clementines, Pastoralis, "De iudiciis."

units.la: Quod fi de Perduellionatu Paparum Ecclesiastico dicendum aliquid videtur, non alienum erit proferre testimonium Senatoris quondam Parifiensis celeberrimi, nomine Cosmæ Guymerij: qui in Præfationem Prægmaticæ sanctionis Biturigæ auctore Rege Carolo vii. conscriptæ, nonnulla commemorat magnopere ad cognoscendam Alaftorum Romanorū insaniā pertinetia. Circa annū Domini, inquit, CIↃ CCCXXC. mortuo Gregorio XI. Cardinales debetes procedere ad electionē successo-ris, fuerunt à Romanis cōminati, quōd occiderētur, si non eligerent Italicū aliqnē. Elegerunt ergo Archiepiscopum Barensē, qui tunc erat Romæ, exprimentes ei, quōd eum eligebant ad vitandum periculum seu fingebant eligere: sed postea data opportunitate aliū eligere libere intendebant. Electio igitur illo, qui Vrbanus vi. dictus est, ille dixit, quōd si volebant eum eligere, quōd eum eligerent, quia intendebat Papa esse. Illi tamen Cardinales post aliquod tempus recesserunt ab eo, & fugientes ad ciuitatem Fundansem, elegerunt alium, qui dictus est Clemens vi. qui transtulit curiam suam in Auenionem, illūmque venerata est pro Papa Francia Hispania, Catalonia. Alteri vero scilicet Urbano, adhæsit obedics Italia, Alemannia, & Hūgaria. & du-raunt hoc pessimum schisma vltra xxx. annos. Duran-te hoc schismate, post Urbanum successit ex illa parte Bonifacius ix, Bonifacio successit Innocentius vi. Inno-centio Gregorius xii. Ex alia parte Clementi successit Benedictus xiii. qui dicebatur Petrus de Luna, sub quibus fuit factum concilium Pisis: anno MCCCCX. in quo, ipsis depositis fuit eleƈtus Alexander, qui dicebatur Petrus de Candia, cui successit Ioannes xxiii. propter quod generatum fuit aliud schisma. Tande con-cilio congregato Constantiæ, per Imperatorem Sigismu-dū.consentientibus diƈtis Ioanne xxiii. & Gregorio xii. & Cardinalibus D. Benedicti ibidem accedentibus, i-bidem cessit Gregorius xii. & alii duo depositi fuerunt propter contumaciam, & ad sedandum schisma. Hæc Guimerius. Nunc alterum eiusdem testimonium audiamus ex eodem libro, folio 5. col. 2.
units.tr: But if something must be said about the treason of the Ecclesiastical Popes, it will not be out of place to bring forward the testimony of Cosmas Guimerius, once a most celebrated senator of Paris, who, in the preface to the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges, written under King Charles VII, mentions several things very relevant to understanding the madness of the Roman Alastors. "About the year of the Lord 1378," he says, "when Pope Gregory XI died, the cardinals, who were to proceed to elect a successor, were threatened by the Romans that they would be killed if they did not choose some Italian. They therefore elected the Archbishop of Bari, who was then at Rome, telling him that they were electing him to avoid danger, or pretending to elect him, but intending afterwards, when the opportunity came, to choose another freely. So at that election the man who was called Urban VI said that if they wanted to elect him, they should elect him, because he intended to be Pope. Yet those cardinals withdrew from him after some time, and fleeing to the town of Fondi, they elected another, who was called Clement VII. He moved his court to Avignon, and France, Spain and Catalonia revered him as Pope. But Italy, Germany and Hungary adhered to the other, Urban. And this most wicked schism lasted more than thirty years. During this schism, after Urban, Boniface IX succeeded on that side; Boniface was succeeded by Innocent VII, Innocent by Gregory XII. On the other side, Clement was succeeded by Benedict XIII, who was called Peter de Luna; under them the council was held at Pisa in 1409, in which, when they were deposed, Alexander V was elected, who was called Peter of Candia, and John XXIII succeeded him, on account of which another schism arose. Finally, a council was assembled at Constance, by the Emperor Sigismund, with John XXIII and Gregory XII consenting, and the cardinals of Benedict coming there too; there Gregory XII resigned, and the other two were deposed for their obstinacy, and so the schism was ended." Thus Guimerius. Now let us hear another testimony of the same man from the same book, folio 5, column 2.

units.la: Martinus, inquit, fuit eleƈtus in Papam per concil-ium Constantiense, depositis aliis contendentibus, qui diu schisma habuerunt. Et concilium iussit congre-gari in Basilea, cui morte præuentus non interfuit. ibi-dem tamen misit Iulianum, tunc legatum suum, tituli Sancti angeli, anno xiv. fui Pontificatus Calend. Fe-bruar. pro celebratione concilii & ei successit Eugenius iv. qui licet approbasset concilium Basiliense, & Basilea misisset diƈtum legatum pridie Calen. Maii, Pontifica-tus sui anno primo, ac etiam dissolutionem diƈti concilii per ipsum attetatam anno MCCCCXXXIII. & sui Pontificatus anno tertio renocasset in publica sua cessio-ne Romæ celebrata apud S. Petrum xvii. Calend. Ian-uar. eodem anno, & per suas bullas patentes promisisset de cætero dicto concilio obedire, confitendo ipsum conci-tium semper fuisse vere continuatum.noluit tamē postea decreta concilii Constantiensis seruare, nec obedire concilio Basiliensi, asserens magis ū[?] contra debere fieri, & illud iterato dissoluit. & transtulit Ferrariam, propter reductionem Græcorum, & inde Florentiam, propter superuenientem ibi pestem. unde orta est grandis altercatio scribentium de hac materia. nam una pars dicebat Papam esse supra concilium, alia concilium esse supra Papam. Propterea a concilio Basiliensi fuit citatus, pridie Calen. Augusti anno MCCCCXXXVII. suspen-sus ab administratione Papatus xi. Calend. Februar. anno MCCCCXXXIIX, & etiam depositus vii. Calen. Iulii, anno MCCCCXXXIX. in locum cuius fuit electus a concilio Basiliensi Amedeus, Dux Sabaudiæ, postea dictus Felix v. sed non curauit Eugenius propter quod fuit schisma, quod duravit annis nouem, & usque ad mortem Eugenii, cuius in locum fuit electus in urbe Nicolaus v. cui cessit Felix, in fauorem vnionis Ecclesiæ. Papa Pius ii. antè dictus Aeneas Syluius, qui interfuit concilio Basiliensi, fecit tractatum pro auctoritate concilii Basiliensis: sed factus Papa eum retractauit.
units.tr: "Martin," he says, "was elected Pope by the Council of Constance, the other contenders having been deposed, who had long maintained the schism. And the council ordered a meeting at Basel, to which he, prevented by death, did not come. Yet he sent there Julian, then his legate, cardinal of St Angelo, in the fourteenth year of his pontificate, on 1 February, to conduct the council. And Eugenius IV succeeded him. Although he approved the Council of Basel, and sent the said legate there on 30 April in the first year of his pontificate, and although he also, in the year 1433 and the third year of his pontificate, by his own public act celebrated at Rome at St Peter's on 16 December of that year, revoked the dissolution of the said council, which he had himself attempted, and by his open bulls promised henceforth to obey the said council, confessing that the council had always truly continued, nevertheless afterwards he would not keep the decrees of the Council of Constance, nor obey the Council of Basel, asserting that the opposite ought rather to be done, and he dissolved it again. And he transferred it to Ferrara, for the reconciliation of the Greeks, and thence to Florence, because of a plague that came upon them there. Hence arose a great dispute among writers on this matter: for one party said the Pope is above the council, the other that the council is above the Pope. On this account he was summoned by the Council of Basel on 31 July 1437, suspended from the administration of the papacy on 22 January 1438, and also deposed on 25 June 1439; in his place the Council of Basel elected Amadeus, Duke of Savoy, afterwards called Felix V. But Eugenius did not heed this, on account of which there was a schism, which lasted nine years, until the death of Eugenius; in his place Nicholas V was elected in the city, and Felix yielded to him, for the sake of the union of the Church. Pope Pius II, formerly called Aeneas Sylvius, who attended the Council of Basel, wrote a treatise in support of the authority of the Council of Basel; but once he became Pope he retracted it." Thus Guimerius, a senator of Paris, as we have said, once.

units.la: Hæc Guimerius: Parisiensis, vt diximus, quondam Senator: quo attentius huius ætatis Senatores intelligant, quanta ambitione, contentione, insania Romani Alastores Perduellionatum in Ecclesia exercuerint, & quàm fureter inter se bacchati sint, quótque incendia in omnibus Europæ partibus, vt ambitioni suæ seruiret, passim excitarint. Quin-etiam quàm antiqua & inueterata hæc sit illorum insania, cognosci licet ex historia Ammiani Mar-cel. Christianæ religionis expertis, lib. xxvii. cuius haec verba sunt : Damasus & Vrsicinus supra humanum modum ad rapiendam Episcopalem sedem ardentes, sciscitabantur asperrime confluctabantur ad usque mortis vulnerumque discrimina, adiumentis utriusque progressis: quae nec corrigere sufficiens Viuentius urbis praefectus, nec mollire, ut magna coactus successit in sub-urbanum, & in concertatione superauerat Damasus, parte quae ei fauebat instate[?]. Constatque in Basilica Seruini, vbi ritus Christiani est conuenticulum, vno die centum triginta septem reperta cadauera peremptorum: efferatamque diu plebem agre postea delinitam. Neque ego abnuo, ostentationem rerum considerans Vrbanarum, huius rei cupidos ob impetrandum quod appetunt, omni contentione laterum iurgari debere: cum id adepti, futuri sint ita securi, ut ditentur oblationibus matronarum, procedantque vehiculis insidentes circumspecte vestiti, epulas curantes profusas, adeo ut eorum conuiuia regales superent mensas, qui esse poterant Beati revera, si magnitudine urbis despecta, quam vitiis opponunt, ad imitationem Antistitum quorundam Provincialium viverent: quos tenuitas edendi potandique parcissime, vilitas etiam indumentorum & supercilia humum spectantia, perpetuo numini verisque eius cultoribus, ut duros commendant & verecundos. Haec Ammianus: ex quibus perspicuum est, quam vetus haec fuerit Paparum Romanorum ambitio, ac libido domi-nandi, feritate & crudelitate coniuncta. Sed ut ve-tera omittamus, & ad ea quę nos nostramque Galliam propius attingunt, veniamus: ecquis est ex tanto Regiorum Senatorum numero, qui nesciat, quot bella Papae Romani inter Christianos Principes his quinquaginta annis potentiae suae vel tuendae vel amplificandae caussa in Europa excitarint? primum mum fuit Helveticum, quo pacatissimas ciuitates, nec tam fœderis arctissimi necessitudine, quàm charitate mutua, communísque patriæ coseruandæ studio coniunctas crudelissimè inter se commiserunt. Secutum est bellum Germanicū, inde Anglic. & Scotic. quod etiam nunc ijdems Alastores per e-missarios suos Jesuastros, certissimo orbis Christiani incendiarios renouare conātur. Quid de nostris Gallicis ciuilibus & funestis bellis dicemus? Nam primùm omnium Papæ Romani à Francisco primo effl agitarunt, ut si qui reformatam religionem ampléctérentur, viui, præsecta lingua, subiectis ignibus, cremarentur. Extant inter regias constitutiones Gallicas, edicta illius Regis, edita anno MDXXXIV, itémque anno XL, & rursus anno XLII. quorum auctoritate Senatores parlamentorum tantum Christiani sanguinis profuderunt, & tamen tanta cum martyrum pietate & constantia, ut vix apud posteros fidem habitura videatur. Quid hæc Alastoribus illis crudelitas, profuerit, operæpretiū est ex eius testimonio cognoscere, quo nemo locupletior hoc in genere produci testis poterit. Is est Rex Henricus secundus, horū recentiorum Regum pater, Princeps, (ut plerique meminisse possunt) belli domíque clarissimus. Extat enim eius edictum mense Junio anni MDLI Castrobrianti scriptum: cuius hæc verba sunt: Videre ante-hac omnibus licuit, quanto studio, quantaque cotentione parens noster (quem Deus absoluat) Rex Franciscus, ut pote princeps Christianissimus & maxime catholicus, per universum vitæ suæ tempus conatus sit hæreses, & falsas doctrinas, quæ in suo regno contra nostram sanctam fidem & religionem catholicam pullulabant, extirpare: & quàm multas leges & constitutiones idem Rex eodem animo & consilio promulgarit: prout varietas & necessitas temporum ferebat. Verumtamen illud tantum studium tantaque contentio non magnopere profuit. Nam ille morbus ita per nobilissimas quasque regni nostri civitates peruasit, ut omnium generum, atque ordinum familias, quasi contagio quadam infecerit. Hæc ille in-edicto, cuius sex & quadraginta sunt articuli, omnes ad cohibendum illius religionis cursum, acerrimè & seuerissimè conscripti. Quinetiam aliquanto post, id est anno MDLVII. aliud eiusdē Regis edictum promulgatum, quo nominatim multis verbis profitetur, palamque denuntiat, se nullum in illa opprimenda religione laborem, nullum studium, nullam diligentiam prætermisisse. Tantumne? immo vero, inquit, quato studiosius ac laboriosius in eam curam incubuimus, tanto magis magisque doctrina illa inualuit. De studio certè & conatu, vel ex eo fieri coniectura potest, quòd inter omnes constat, magnum omnis generis hominum numerum illo misero & acerbo supplicij genere interijsse.
units.tr: I have cited these things so that the senators of our age may understand more attentively with how much ambition, contention and madness the Roman Alastors have exercised their treason within the Church, and how furiously they have raged among themselves, and how many fires they have everywhere kindled throughout the parts of Europe, to serve their ambition. Moreover, one may know how ancient and inveterate this madness of theirs is from the history of Ammianus Marcellinus, who was acquainted with the Christian religion, book 27, whose words are these: "Damasus and Ursinus, burning beyond human measure to snatch the episcopal see, contended most bitterly, and they fought to the point of deadly danger and wounds, with the support of both sides advancing; the city prefect Viventius, being unable either to correct or soften it, was compelled to withdraw to the suburbs, and Damasus, the party favouring him being urgent, had the upper hand in the struggle. And it is established that in the basilica of Sicinius, where the Christian rite has its little assembly, on one day one hundred and thirty-seven corpses of the slain were found; and the people, long enraged, were afterwards with difficulty pacified. Nor do I deny that, considering the display of urban affairs, those who covet this office, to obtain what they seek, ought to be contending with every effort of their sides: since, once they have obtained it, they will be so secure that they are enriched by the offerings of matrons, they go about riding in carriages, dressed in fine clothes, providing lavish feasts, so that their banquets surpass royal tables. They could truly be blessed if, despising the greatness of the city, which they object to as a vice, they lived in imitation of certain provincial bishops, whom the scantiness of eating and drinking, the cheapness of clothing, and eyes fixed on the ground commend to the eternal Divinity and its true worshippers as austere and modest." Thus Ammianus. From these words it is plain how ancient is this ambition of the Roman Popes, and their lust to dominate, joined with savagery and cruelty. But to pass over antiquity and come to those things which touch us and our France more closely: who among so great a number of royal senators does not know how many wars the Roman Pope has stirred up among Christian princes in Europe in these fifty years, to defend or extend his power? The first was the Swiss war, in which they most cruelly set against each other the most peaceful cities, joined not so much by the strictest bond of covenant as by mutual charity and the zeal to preserve their common fatherland. Next came the German war, then the English and Scottish, which these same Alastors, through their emissaries, the Jesuits, the most certain incendiaries of the Christian world, now try to renew. What shall we say of our French civil and deadly wars? For first of all the Roman Popes urged Francis I to act so that whoever embraced the reformed religion would be burned alive, with the tongue cut out and fires lit beneath them. Among the royal French constitutions there survive the edicts of that king, issued in 1534, likewise in 1540 and again in 1542, by whose authority the senators of the parliaments shed so much Christian blood; and yet with such piety and constancy of the martyrs that it will scarcely seem credible to posterity. What benefit these cruelties brought to those Alastors is worth learning from the testimony of one whom no one could better produce as a witness in this matter. This is King Henry II, father of these more recent kings, a prince (as most can remember) most distinguished in war and at home. For there is his edict, written at Châteaubriant in June 1551; its words are these: "It has been possible for everyone to see hitherto with what zeal and what effort our father (whom God absolve), King Francis, as a most Christian and most Catholic prince, throughout the whole time of his life tried to root out the heresies and false doctrines which were sprouting in his kingdom against our holy faith and the Catholic religion; and how many laws and constitutions the same king promulgated with the same spirit and purpose, as the variety and necessity of the times required. Yet that so great zeal and so great effort did not greatly profit. For that disease has so spread through all the most noble cities of our kingdom that it has infected the families of every kind and rank, as with a kind of contagion." Thus he says in the edict, which has forty-six articles, all written most fiercely and severely to check the course of that religion. Moreover, a little later, that is in 1557, another edict of the same king was promulgated, in which he openly professes and declares in many words that he had left no labour, no zeal, no diligence untried in suppressing that religion. "How much?" "Indeed," he says, "the more zealously and laboriously we have applied ourselves to that care, the more and more that doctrine has grown strong." Certainly, one may conjecture about his zeal and effort from this, that everyone agrees a great number of men of every kind perished by that wretched and bitter kind of punishment.

units.la: Successit illis Regibus, auo nepe & patri, Rex Francifcus fecudus. Eius edicta videre licet numero sex acerrima & vehementissima, præter innumera diplomata & patentes literas, quas assiduè per singulas Regni sui prouincias missitabat, tato animi ardore ac stomacho, ut homines amplius trecenti, vix trium mensium spatio, Parisiensis præsertim & Tholosani senatus decretis, cruciati, ustulati, cremati, (atque ut perscribi in Senatusconsultis, solebat) in cineres redacti sint. Satiare fortasse hæc tata profusi sanguinis copia vel immanisimos tyrannos potuit: quales antiquis tęporib* fuisse memorantur rantur Cyclops,Bufiris, Siron, Phalaris, Tython» Gyges.At Papam Romanum, quem verè generis humani perduellem appellare possumus, explere tāta crudelitas non potuit. His enim cunctis spectaculis & carnificinis delectatur, his pascitur,his perfruitur.Quid ꝑfecerit,audire est operæpretiu. Extat enim cōstitutio ciusdē Regis Fracifci secūdi edita Ambofiæ,mense Martio,āni MDLIX. his verbis,quæ perattente legi à consiliariis Regiis optamus,momentoque suo ponderari. Nos,vt ossi-cio & functioni nostræ Regiæ satisfaceremus, coacti fui-mus variis vti supplicioru & poenarum generibus,prout rerum status & tempora postulabant.
units.tr: He was succeeded by those kings, his grandfather and father, namely King Francis the Second. His edicts, six in number, are very fierce and violent, and there are countless decrees and open letters which he kept sending through every province of his kingdom. With such fervour and rage, within barely three months, more than three hundred men were tortured, burned and reduced to ashes, especially under the decrees of the Parliament of Paris and of Toulouse, and (as was customary to write in the decrees of the Senate) they were consigned to the flames. Perhaps such a great outpouring of blood could have satisfied even the most savage tyrants, such as are recorded in ancient times: Cyclops, Busiris, Sciron, Phalaris, Tython and Gyges. But the Roman Pope, whom we may truly call the enemy of the human race, could not be sated by such cruelty. He delights in all these spectacles and butcheries, feeds on them and takes his pleasure in them. What he did is worth hearing. There exists a constitution of the same King Francis the Second, issued at Amboise in March 1559, in these words, which we wish the king's counsellors read very attentively and weighed in their minds: We, in order to satisfy our royal office and duty, were compelled to use various kinds of punishment and penalties, as the state of affairs and the times demanded.

units.la: Sed ex caussarum criminalium instrumentis cognitum & patefactum est, ingentem numerum virorum,mulierum,ætatum ,generu & ordinum omnium interfuisse illicitis & clandestinis concionibus,cœnis,baptismis, per eos administratis,quibus id facere non licebat.
units.tr: But from the records of the criminal cases it has become known and plainly shown that an immense number of men, women, persons of every age, rank and order, took part in illicit and secret sermons, suppers and baptisms administered by them, which it was not lawful for them to hold.

units.la: Quod si de vnoquoque illorū suppliciu sumeretur,prout iuris & Legū nostrarum rigor postulat,admirabile sanguinis effusione fieri oporteret,virorū,mulierū,virginū,adolescentū florescētis adhuc ætatis,quorū alii inducti & subornati,alii simplicitate quadā & ignorantia persuasi, alii curiositate quadā potius quàm malitia illecti, in istiusmodi errores & incomoda inciderūt.Quod si fieret,magno & perpetuo animi dolore afficeremur:neque id vel naturæ nostræ,vel ætati satis coueniret:quarum vtraq; nos ad clementia & mansuetudinem ac misericordiam hoc in genere exercendam inuitat. Itaque notum omnibus esse volumus , cum hac tota de re , mature à consiliariis nostris coram nobis deliberatum fuisset, non esse nobis in animo primum regni nostri annum memorabilem posteritati relinquere,tanquam cruentum, sanguinarium, & cadibus miserorum nostrorum ciuium plenum : etiam si hoc maxime meriti fuissent: imo ad exemplum Patris cælestis statuimus parcere sanguini nostrorum populariū, & subiectos nostros ad viam salutis reducere, eorumque vitam conseruare: sperantes per Dei misericordiam fore, vt per viam mansuetudinis & clementiæ plus quam per supplicium rigore proficiamus. Itaque de supradictorum no-strorū consiliariorum sententia, dicimus, statuimus, ordinamus, ne posthac propter causam criminum præteritorum fidei & religionem concernentium, per iudices nostros molestia exhibeatur nostris subditis, cuiuscunque sint generis & conditionis, neque in iudicio neque extra iudicium. Declaramus insuper nos talium criminum, fidem & religionem concernentium, gratiam, remissionem & abolitionem generalem omnibus nostris subditis condonasse. Et paulo infrà. Ex auctoritate regis qui huic consilio præfuit, & de sententia dominorum Cardinalium de Bourbon, de Lorraine, de Chastillon, les Ducs de Montpensier, de Guise, de Niuernois, & d'Aumale, Hac-tenus Rex Francifcus secundus: perspicuè, vt appareret, declarans ac testificans, superiorum temporum cruciatus & supplicia nihil omnino ad hanc extinguendam religionem valuisse.
