units.tr: If punishment were to be exacted from each of them, as the strictness of our law and of our statutes demands, there would necessarily be a dreadful effusion of blood: of men, women, virgins and young people in the flower of their age, some of whom were led on and induced, others persuaded by a certain simplicity and ignorance, others drawn into such errors and troubles by a certain curiosity rather than by malice. If this were done, we would be afflicted with great and lasting grief of spirit, and this would not suit either our nature or our age, both of which invite us to exercise clemency, gentleness and mercy in this matter. Therefore we wish it to be known to all that, when this whole matter had been maturely deliberated before us by our counsellors, it was not our intention to leave the first year of our reign to posterity as memorable, as bloody, sanguinary and full of the slaughter of our wretched citizens, even though they had deserved this most. Rather, after the example of the heavenly Father, we have decided to spare the blood of our people, to lead our subjects back to the way of salvation and to preserve their lives, hoping, by the mercy of God, that we shall make more progress by the way of gentleness and clemency than by the rigour of punishment. Therefore, by the opinion of our aforesaid counsellors, we declare, decree and ordain that henceforth, on account of past crimes concerning faith and religion, no trouble shall be caused to our subjects through our judges, of whatever kind or condition they are, either in court or outside court. We further declare that we have granted to all our subjects grace, remission and a general abolition of such crimes concerning faith and religion. And a little below: By the authority of the king who presided over this council, and by the opinion of the lords Cardinals de Bourbon, de Lorraine, de Châtillon, the Dukes of Montpensier, de Guise, de Nivernais and d'Aumale, Thus far King Francis the Second, clearly, so that it might appear that he declared and testified that the torments and punishments of former times had altogether no effect in extinguishing this religion.

units.la: Quid tum Alastores, ac perduelles humani generis, Papæ Romani, quid egerunt? Vbi senserunt aliquot eiusdem regni proceres, aliquot præterea regij sanguinis Principes religionem illam degustasse & Bernardonicas ac Dominicanas fraudes atque imposturas repudiasse, vbi præuiderunt fore, vt Gal-lia paulatim ac pedetentim è Papatus seruitute sese in Christianam libertatem vindicaret, vbi denique tam opimam prædam è suis faucibus ere-ptum iri senserunt, tum verò nouas bellorum ciui-lium faces passim per vniuersam Galliâ immittere cœpecoeperunt. deinde cùm nec hac quidem illis via fuc cederet, furiales carnificinas & lanienas cum sempiterna Gallici nominis ignominia instituerunt, ad extremum, vbi nec hoc quidem modo profici quicquam posse animaduerterunt, exortus est monachus Bernardonicus, Sixtus noster quintus, qui meretricia & monachali impudentia fretus, Serenissimos principes nostros proscriberet, potetisi-mumque[?] Galliae regem iuberet, vt eos vi, armis, castris insectaretur, miserumque suum regnum denuò caedibus, rapinis, incendiis compleret. Sed de furiali Alastorum Romanorum perduellionatu satis iam videtur dictum.
units.tr: What then did those avengers and enemies of the human race, the Roman Popes, do? When some of the nobles of that kingdom, and some princes of royal blood besides, perceived that this religion had been tasted and that the Bernardine and Dominican frauds and impostures had been rejected; when they foresaw that France would gradually and step by step free herself from the servitude of Papacy into Christian liberty; when at last they felt that such a rich prey would be snatched from their jaws, then at length they began to kindle everywhere through the whole of France the new torches of civil wars. Then, since not even this way succeeded for them, they set up furious butcheries and slaughters, to the everlasting disgrace of the French name. Finally, when they perceived that nothing could be achieved even in this manner, there arose our Sixtus the Fifth, a Bernardine monk, who, relying on harlot-like and monkish impudence, proscribed our most serene princes and ordered the most powerful king of France to pursue them by force, arms and camps, and to fill his wretched kingdom again with slaughter, plunder and burning. But enough seems to have been said about the furious avengers of the Roman Pope.
THE CRIME OF FORGERY.

units.la: REstat, vt de crimine quod in postremum locum reiecimus, quàm breuissimè fieri poterit, differamus: nempe falsi, siue subiectarum aut corruptarum tabularum. Cùm autè huius sceleris permulta nobis vndecunque testimonia suppetunt, tum praecipuè ex pontificali decreto Gratiani, quod huius generis corruptelis & falsitatibus redundat. Ex quibus paucas quasdam quasi exempli loco, delibabimus, atque imprimis instrumentum illud donationis Constatini, quo Papa donata sibi ab illo Imperatore vrbem Romam, itemque Italiam, Siciliam, Sardiniam, Hispaniam, Germaniam, & Britanniam contendit, dist.96.c. Constantinus. & plenius apud Bartholomaeum Picernum, & Augustinum Steuchum, qui instrumentum illud Romae in Bibliotheca Papae, Graeca lingua scriptum repertum esse affirmarunt, latinéque ab se conuersum ediderūt. Nam eius haec summa est: Imperator Constantinus, Christianorum hostis, lepræ morbo affectus, in somnis à Petro & Paulo apostolis admonitus, ut se Syluestro Papæ Romano purgadum traderet, confestim ab illo baptizatus atque sanatus, tanti beneficij remunerandi causa donauit eidem Syluestro, eiusque successoribus urbem Romam, totumque Occidentis imperium: simul coronam suam auream, & sceptrum, & reliqua impe-ratoria insignia, ut maiorem dignitatem Papa Romanus haberet quàm ipse Imperator. Simul imprecatur suis successoribus usque ad finem mundi, concremationem in inferno inferiore, cum Diabolo & impiis, nisi eam donationem ratā habeant, & obseruent. Datum Romæ 3.Kal.April.Constantino A. quater & Gallicano Coss. Hoc igitur instrumentum, quo solo Paparum dominatus sustinetur, falsum, fictum, ementitum, atque à Papa ne-scio quo, perinde ut librum Conformitatum, sub-iectū fuisse, quamplurimis argumentis euincemus. quorum illud primum est. 1 Quòd cùm tot extent historici qui res Constantini literis mandarunt, nullus tamen auctor locuples reperitur, qui tam immensæ, tam effusæ ac tàm inofficiosæ prodigalitatis metionem faciat. in his Eusebius, qui libros quinque de ipsius vita conscripsit. Item Socrates, Theodoritus, Euagrius, Rufinus, Eutropius, Paulus Diaconus, Orosius, Beda, Zonaras, Nicephorus: quos non est verisimile, si vera illa donatio fuisset, tantam rem, tanto silentio prætermisturos fuisse. Quinetiā Papæ ipsi Romani, qui sæpe multumque de sua potentia & amplitudine cum aliis Episcopis contenderunt, tamen in suo iure persequendo, & instrumentorum suorum editione, nullū unquam de illo instrumento fecisse verbum leguntur. II. Quòd coplures Papalis dominatus patroni & defensores testificatur, totum illud caput ab antiquis Gratianici Decreti codicibus abesse: in his Antoninus Florent. Episcop. primæ partis historialis tit. 8. c. 1. & Volaterranus vbi de Constantino commemorat. Caput illud, inquit Antoninus, non habetur in antiquis Decretis. Quid ergo & quantum Constantinus donauit, non est bene certum. Nicolaus autem Cusanus lib. de concor. Cathol. 3. Absque dubio, inquit, si non fuisset illud dictamen apocryphum, Gratianus in veteribus codicibus, & canonum collectionibus inuenisset. & quia non inuenit, non posuit. Quinetiã Æneas Syluius (is qui postea Papatum adeptus, dictus est Papa Pius) in dialogo quodam, quem adhuc Cardinalis scripsit, aperte instrumentum istud falsitatis arguit: & stolidos Legistas appellat, qui tantopere sudarint in disputando an ea donatio valeat, quæ nunquam facta fuit. III. Quòd Eusebius lib. de vita Constant. 4. memoriæ prodidit, eum perexiguo ante obitum tempore hanc Imperij sui diuisionem inter suos filios fecisse, vt natu maximo Occidente, secundo Orientem, tertio interiectam regionem assignaret. Sed & Socrat. hist. Ecclesiast. 3. c. vlt. Cùm tres, inquit, filios haberet, singulos eorum Imperii sui participes esse constituit. Primum quidem filium, sui nominis Constantinum, Occidentalium partium. Secundum, aui nomine, Constantium, in Oriente constituit. Iuniorem vero Constantem in media regione ordinauit. Itè Sext. Aurel. Victor. Ad tres, inquit, orbis Romani dominatio redacta est, Constantinum, Constantium, & Constantem filios Constantini. Hi singuli has partes regedas habuerunt. Itè Zosimus lib. hist. pr. 2. Eius liberi, inquit, successionem in Imperio nacti nationes inter se partiti sunt. Et Constantinus quidem natu maximus cum mini-mo natu Constante omnia transalpes sita, & Italiam, & Illyricum sortitus est. Nunc posteriorum temporum historiam consideremus. Nam, ut inter omnes Chronographos constat, non tantum Italiae, verumetiam Romae urbis imperium penes Constantini successores per annos centum & quadraginta permansit, usque ad annum Christi CCCCI. quo tempore imperii illud Occidentis vexari coeptum a Gottis, Francis, Alanis, Burgundis, Vandalis: semper tamen in iure Imperatorum Romanorum mansit, usque ad Imperatorem Augustulum, quem Odo Gottorum rex Italia expulit, urbe Roma potitus, anno CCCCLXXVI. quo tempore Romanum Imperium in Occidente defecit, Barbaris & Romae & in Italia regnatibus. Nam regium Romanorum nomen, penes Odoacri posteros ac successores per annos CCCXXV. permansit. Itaque videre licet quamplurimas apud Cassiodorū Theodorici regis literas, partim ad Senatum urbis Romae, partim ad populum Romanum regio nomine atque auctoritate scriptas: ut nemini dubium esse possit, quin & Italia, & urbs ipsa Roma sub Gottorū regū ditio-ne, nō sub ullius Papae dominatu permaserit: usque dum Gottis ab Imperatore Constantinopolitano Italia exactis, praesides in illam provinciam mitti coeperunt, Exarchorum nomine: qui etsi Rauenę domicilium habebat, tamen in Italia per annos complures dominati sunt. Rursus Logobardi, quorum regnum exortū est anno DLXVIII. universam Italiam, praeter urbem Romam, per annos CCVI. hoc est usque ad annū DCCXLI, v.tenuerūt. quę omnia ex Procopij,Iornădis,Marcellini,Pauli Diaconi,& aliorū scriptis intelligūtur:ut perspicuū cuiuis esse possit, falsum esse quod Papæ contendunt, maio-res suos vel in Italia, vel in urbe Roma dominatum ex Constantini donatione obtinuisse: cum is dominatus anno demum Christianæ salutis o-ctingentesimo initium habuerit, ex Pipini & Caroli magni liberalitate, qui Exarchatu Lögobardis ereptū una cum urbe Roma Papę Stephano secundo donarūt:ut Platina, Volaterranus,& alij omnes te-statur.sed præsertim Sabellicus Ennead.8.libr.8.ubi præter cæteros adscribit, Constantinum quartum Orientis Imp. legatos ad Pipinum in Italiam mi-sisse,qui ab eo peterēt,ut Rauennā & cętera Exar-chatus loca suo Imperatori restituēda curaret.quip-pe,quæ Imperii essent(sic loquitur Sabellicus)nō aut Pōtificis.Neque se Pipinus Costantino aut cuiquā homi-nū prætērquā Ecclesiæ Romanæ militare, eōque cōsilio se arma indūisse,ut Apostolicā sedem ab omniū mortalium iniuria vindicaret:utque Rauennam & quicquid Longobardi vi & armis subegissent, Romanæ subiiceret Ecclesiæ. Ita Græci oratores re infecta domum redierunt. Hæc Sabellicus. Platina autē Exarchatu Astulpho Longobardo ereptum,& Papę Stephano traditum subiungit, anno DCCLVI. simulque Imperatoris nomen Carolo magno Pipini filio tribuisse, quod Imperatores Orientis ægrè per ea tepora tuebātur, hoc est,anno DCCCI[?].qua de re Albert° Krantzius in Saxon.lib.2.c.1.sic scribit: Tribuunt nonnulli Constātino Magno donationem illā Italiæ,& Germaniæ & nescio quarum provinciarum Ecclesiæ Romanæ factam:de qua ipsi viderint.Carolus erat,qui ex victoria Lögobardorum Romanam Ecclesiam ditauit, cum pridem aliquanta & Gotti per sua tempora, & deinde Longobardi reges nonnulla contulissent. iv. Quod Papæ ipsi inter se de hac donatione pugnantia loquuntur, & valde discrepantia. Nam cum hoc loco(id est,in d.c.Constantinus.dist.96.)regnum Romanum atque Italiæ & Occidentis totius Constantino acceptum referant, ex anno Christi cccxxxiix. tamen alio loco sui huius beneficij auctorem laudant Ludouicum Pium, Caroli magni filium, ex anno Christi io cccxxxv. Cuius mendacij ac falsitatis impudentia quo dilucidius appareat, bina huius posterioris donationis instrumenta, quæ Papæ & Canonistæ nobis ediderunt, inter se comparabimus. Nam Volaterranus lib.Geor.3.sic loquitur, De pietate ipsius Ludouici Pii in Romanos Pontifices multa Bibliothecarius refert, ciuitates quas eis dedit enumerans. Ego quoque ex Antigrapho vetusti libri, quod in Bibliotheca Vaticana hodie cotinetur, ubi eius enarratur donatio, Apographum excerpsi.
units.tr: It remains that I deal, as briefly as possible, with the crime which we have placed last, namely forgery, that is, the falsifying or corrupting of documents. Since very many proofs of this crime are available to us from every quarter, especially from the papal decree of Gratian, which abounds in corruptions and falsifications of this kind, we shall pick out a few from these, as examples. First and foremost, there is that instrument of the donation of Constantine, by which the Pope claims that the city of Rome was given to him by that Emperor, and likewise Italy, Sicily, Sardinia, Spain, Germany and Britain (Dist. 96, c. Constantinus); and this is more fully set out by Bartholomaeus Platina and Augustinus Steuchus, who affirmed that this instrument was found at Rome in the Pope's library, written in Greek, and who published it translated into Latin. For its substance is this: the Emperor Constantine, enemy of the Christians, afflicted with leprosy, admonished in a dream by the apostles Peter and Paul to surrender himself to Pope Sylvester of Rome to be cleansed, was at once baptised by him and healed; and in order to repay so great a benefit, he gave to the same Sylvester and his successors the city of Rome and the whole Western empire, together with his golden crown, his sceptre and his other imperial insignia, so that the Roman Pope might have a greater dignity than the Emperor himself. At the same time he invokes upon his successors, to the end of the world, burning in the lower hell with the Devil and the impious, unless they hold and observe that donation. Given at Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the fourth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the consulship of Gallicanus. We shall prove by very many arguments that this instrument, on which alone the dominion of the Popes rests, is false, feigned, fabricated and falsely attributed, and was subjected by some Pope or other, just as the book of the Conformities was. The first of these arguments is this. (1) Although so many historians exist who committed the deeds of Constantine to writing, yet no trustworthy author is found who makes mention of such an immense, lavish and so unbecoming a prodigality. Among these is Eusebius, who wrote five books on his life; likewise Socrates, Theodoret, Evagrius, Rufinus, Eutropius, Paulus Diaconus, Orosius, Bede, Zonaras and Nicephorus; it is not probable that they would have passed over so great a matter in such silence, if that donation had been true. Moreover, the Roman Popes themselves, who often and greatly contended with other bishops about their power and greatness, are nowhere read to have said a single word about that instrument, either in pursuing their rights or in publishing their documents. (2) Several patrons and defenders of papal dominion testify that the whole chapter is absent from the ancient codices of Gratian's Decretum; among them Antoninus, Bishop of Florence, in the first part of his Historiale, title 8, chapter 1, and Volaterranus, where he speaks of Constantine. That chapter, says Antoninus, is not found in the ancient Decrees. Therefore what and how much Constantine gave is not quite certain. Nicolaus Cusanus, however, in his book On the Concord of the Catholics, book 3: Without doubt, he says, if that dictum were not apocryphal, Gratian would have found it in the old codices and in the collections of canons; and because he did not find it, he did not insert it. Moreover Aeneas Sylvius (he who afterwards obtained the papacy and was called Pope Pius), in a certain dialogue which he wrote while still a cardinal, clearly proves that this instrument is false, and calls stupid lawyers those who have laboured so hard in disputing whether that donation is valid, which was never made. (3) Eusebius, in book 4 of his Life of Constantine, records that a very short time before his death he made this division of his empire among his sons: to the eldest he assigned the West, to the second the East, and to the third the region lying between. Socrates too, in his Ecclesiastical History, book 3, last chapter: When he had three sons, he says, he established each of them as sharer in his empire. The first son, named after himself, Constantine, he set over the Western parts. The second, named after his grandfather, Constantius, he established in the East. The youngest, Constans, he appointed in the middle region. Likewise Sextus Aurelius Victor: The rule of the Roman world was reduced to three, Constantine, Constantius and Constans, the sons of Constantine. Each of them had these parts to rule. Likewise Zosimus, in book 2 of his history: His children, he says, having obtained succession in the empire, divided the nations among themselves. And Constantine, the eldest, with Constans the youngest, received all the lands beyond the Alps, and Italy and Illyricum by lot. Now let us consider the history of later times. For, as is agreed among all chroniclers, not only Italy but also the city of Rome remained under the rule of Constantine's successors for one hundred and forty years, until the year of Christ 401, at which time the Western empire began to be harassed by the Goths, Franks, Alans, Burgundians and Vandals; yet it always remained under the right of the Roman Emperors, until the Emperor Augustulus, whom Odoacer, king of the Goths, expelled from Italy, seizing the city of Rome in the year 476, at which time the Roman empire in the West failed, with barbarians reigning both in Rome and in Italy. For the title of Roman king remained with the descendants and successors of Odoacer for three hundred and twenty-five years. Thus one may see very many letters of King Theodoric, preserved in Cassiodorus, written partly to the Senate of the city of Rome and partly to the Roman people in the king's name and authority; so that no one can doubt that both Italy and the city of Rome itself remained under the dominion of the Gothic kings, and not under the dominion of any Pope, until the Goths were driven out of Italy by the Emperor of Constantinople, and governors began to be sent into that province under the name of Exarchs, who, although they had their residence at Ravenna, nevertheless ruled in Italy for many years. Again, the Lombards, whose kingdom arose in the year 568, held the whole of Italy, except the city of Rome, for two hundred and six years, that is, until the year 774. All these things are understood from the writings of Procopius, Jornandes, Marcellinus, Paulus Diaconus and others, so that it may be clear to anyone that what the Popes contend is false: that their predecessors obtained dominion either in Italy or in the city of Rome from the donation of Constantine, since that dominion began only in the eight hundredth year of Christian salvation, from the generosity of Pepin and Charles the Great, who, having taken the Exarchate from the Lombards, gave it together with the city of Rome to Pope Stephen the Second, as Platina, Volaterranus and all the others testify. But above all Sabellicus, Ennead 8, book 8, where, among other things, he writes that Constantine IV, Emperor of the East, sent envoys to Pepin in Italy, who asked of him that he see to it that Ravenna and the other places of the Exarchate be restored to their Emperor, for they were of the Empire (so Sabellicus speaks), not of the Pontiff. Pepin, however, replied that he was serving neither Constantine nor any man except the Roman Church, and that he had taken up arms for this purpose, to defend the Apostolic See from the injury of all mortals, and that he would subject Ravenna and whatever the Lombards had conquered by force and arms to the Roman Church. Thus the Greek envoys returned home with their business undone. So Sabellicus. Platina, however, adds that the Exarchate was taken from the Lombard Astulf and handed over to Pope Stephen, in the year 756, and at the same time that the title of Emperor was granted to Charles the Great, son of Pepin, because the Emperors of the East could hardly defend it in those times, that is, in the year 801. Concerning this matter Albert Krantz, in Saxonia, book 2, chapter 1, writes thus: Some attribute to Constantine the Great that donation of Italy and Germany and I know not what provinces made to the Roman Church: let them see to it themselves. It was Charles who, from the victory over the Lombards, enriched the Roman Church, although earlier the Goths had also given some things in their time, and afterwards the Lombard kings had contributed some others. (4) That the Popes themselves speak among themselves about this donation in contradictory and very discordant ways. For in this passage (that is, in the chapter Constantinus, Dist. 96) they attribute to Constantine the kingdom of Rome and of Italy and of the whole West, in the year of Christ 339; yet in another place they praise as the author of their benefit Louis the Pious, son of Charles the Great, in the year of Christ 835. So that the shamelessness of this lie and falsehood may appear more clearly, we shall compare with each other the two instruments of this later donation which the Popes and the canonists have published for us. For Volaterranus, in book 3 of his Geography, speaks thus: The librarian relates many things about the piety of Louis the Pious towards the Roman Pontiffs, enumerating the cities which he gave them. I too have excerpted a copy from an antigraph of an old book, which is kept today in the Vatican Library, where his donation is narrated.
THE INSTRUMENT, VOLATERRAN EDITION.

units.la: Ego Ludouicus Imp.concedo tibi beato Petro Principi Apo-stolorum, & per te vicario tuo Domino Paschali summo Pon-tifici, successoribusq;eius in per-petuum, ciuitatem Romanam, cum sua iurisdictione, omnibúsque circa terris, ciuitatibus, por-tubus, ac maritimis locis Etru-riæ: In ea denique mediterranca[?]
units.tr: I, Emperor Louis, grant to you, blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, and through you to your vicar, Lord Paschal, the supreme Pontiff, and to his successors forever, the city of Rome with its jurisdiction, and all the lands, cities, harbours and maritime places around it in Etruria; and finally the inland [?] region.
THE INSTRUMENT, DECRETAL EDITION.

units.la: Ego Ludouicus Imp.Romanus Augustus statuo & concedo per hoc pactum confirmationis nostrae B.Petro principi Apostolo-rum, & per te vicario tuo Domino Paschali summo Pontifici, vrbem veterem Balneoregium, Viterbium , Saonam , Populoniam, Rofellas, Perufium , Mathuranum, Sutrium , Nepe versus Campaniam , Ananiam, Signiam , Ferentinum, Alanum, Patricum, Frufinonum, cum omnibus circa oppidis & vicis: nec non exarchatum Rauennæ integrum, sicut piæ recordationis Carolus pater,& item Pipinus auus noster (notet Lector mirum de Constantino silentium) Beato Petro dudum concessere. Videlicet Rauennam, Bonicum,Acmiliam,ForumPopuli , Forum Iulij, Fauentiam, Imolam,Romaniam,Ferrariam Comadum, Adriam , Seruiam, In marchia Pisaurum , Fanum. Senogalliam, Anconam , Oximum , Numanam, Esium, Forum Sempronij,Feretrum, Vrbinum , territorium Valnense, Callių[?], Luceolos, Eugubiu, In Campania Sorum , Aquinum Arpinum, Thranum,Capuam, patrimoniaquoque ad nostram pertinentia ditionem , Beneuentanum , Salernitanum,Calabriæ inferioris ac superioris, ac Neapolitanū ducatū:insuper Spoletinū,Tuderotreculū,Haruiā,reliquáque eius ditionis:In& successoribus e- ius in perpetuum, sicut à prædecesso- ribus nostris vsque nunc in vestra po- testate & ditione tenuistis,& dispo- suistis, Romanam ciuitatem cum du- catu suo & subur- banis,atque villi- culis omnibus, & territoriis eius mo- tanis,& maritimis litoribus,& portu- bus,ceu cunctisci- uitatibus,Castellis oppidis,ac villisin Tofcaniæ partibus.
units.tr: I, Emperor Louis, Roman Augustus, establish and grant by this pact of our confirmation to blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, and through you to your vicar, Lord Paschal, the supreme Pontiff, the old city of Balneoregium, Viterbo, Savona, Populonia, Rosellae, Perugia, Matturanum, Sutri, Nepi towards Campania, Anagni, Segni, Ferentino, Alatri, Patrica, Frosinone, with all the towns and villages round about; and likewise the whole exarchate of Ravenna, just as Charles of pious memory, our father, and likewise Pepin our grandfather, granted to blessed Peter long ago (let the reader note the remarkable silence about Constantine). Namely Ravenna, Bononia, Aemilia, Forum Popilii, Forum Iulii, Faenza, Imola, Romagna, Ferrara, Comacchio, Adria, Servia; in the March, Pesaro, Fano, Senigallia, Ancona, Osimo, Numana, Iesi, Forum Sempronii, Fossombrone, Urbino, the territory of Gubbio [?], Cagli [?], Luceoli, Gubbio; in Campania, Sora, Aquino, Arpino, Terracina, Capua, and the patrimonies also pertaining to our dominion; Benevento, Salerno, Lower and Upper Calabria, and the Duchy of Naples; moreover Spoleto, Todi, Orte, Narni, and the rest of its dominion: and to its successors forever, just as you have held and disposed of them in your power and dominion from our predecessors until now; and the city of Rome with its duchy and suburbs, and all its small villages and territories, and its maritime shores and harbours, as well as all cities, castles, towns and villages in the parts of Tuscany.

units.la: Item quādo diui- na vocatione hu- ius sacratissimæ sedis pontifex de hoc seculo migra- uerit,nullus ex re- gno nostro aut Fra- cus, aut Logobar- dus dequalibetpar te homo sub nostra potestate costitutus licetiā habeat co- tra Romanos aut publicè aut priua- tim coneniedi, aut sulasquoque inferi maris, Corsi-cam, Sardiniam, Siciliam, quae omnia piae memoriae Pipinus avus, deinde Carolus Imperator genitor noster, per Atheniu[?] & Mainardum Abbates, ad hoc sponte missos, B. Petro eiusque successoribus scripto concesserunt, nos item probamus atque concedimus. Praeterea summi Pontificis deligendi Romano consilio potestatem esse volumus, modo sine discordia fiat, ac post consecrationem legati ad nos successoresque nostros Reges Francorum conciliandae charitatis & amicitiae causa mittantur: sicuti temporibus Dom. Caroli atavi, & Pipini avi, & postremo Caroli genitoris nostri mos fuit. Hanc igitur voluntatem nostram scripto ac iurejurando firmamus, & per legatum S.R.E. Theodorum domino Paschali misimus, manuque propria me subscripsi, EGO LU-DOVICUS. subscripsere quoque tres filii eius, Episcopi decem, Abbates octo, Comites quindecim, Bibliothecarius, Masionarius, Ostiariusque unus. nume-rabatur annus ab incarnatione Domini DCCCXXXV.
units.tr: Likewise, when the pontiff of this most sacred see shall have departed this life by divine calling, let no one of our kingdom, whether Frank or Lombard, nor any man placed under our power from any part, have licence to assemble against the Romans, either publicly or privately, or to islands also of the deep sea: Corsica, Sardinia, Sicily, all of which Pepin of pious memory, our grandfather, and then Charles the Emperor, our father, granted in writing to blessed Peter and his successors through the abbots Atheniu [?] and Mainard, sent for this purpose of their own accord; we likewise approve and grant these. Moreover we wish that the power of choosing the supreme pontiff rest with the Roman counsel, provided it be done without discord, and that after the consecration legates be sent to us and our successors, the Kings of the Franks, to arrange charity and friendship; just as in the times of Lord Charles our ancestor, and Pepin our grandfather, and lastly Charles our father, was the custom. We confirm this our will by writing and by oath, and have sent it to Lord Paschal through Theodore, legate of the Holy Roman Church; and I subscribed with my own hand, I, LOUIS. His three sons also subscribed, ten bishops, eight abbots, fifteen counts, one librarian, one sacristan and one doorkeeper. The year was counted from the incarnation of the Lord, 835.

units.la: electione faciendi, nullusque in civitatibus aut territoriis ad ecclesiae B. Petri Apostoli potestate pertinentibus aliquod malum praeterea facere praesumat: sed liceat Romanis cum omnivene-ratione & sine qua-libert perturbatione honorifica suo pontifici exhibere sepulturæ: & eu quę divina inspiratione, & Beati Petri intercessione omnes Romani uno cōsilio atq; una cōcordia, sine aliqua promissione, ad pontificatus ordine elegerint, sine aliqua ambiguitate atq; contradictione more canonico consecrare:& dū cōsecratus fuerit, legati ad nos, vel ad nostros successores Reges Francorum dirigatur, qui inter nos & illum amicitiam, charitatem & pacem concilient. Ex hac comparatione perspicuū est, quibus fraudibus, & quàm malis artibus Papatus ad consequendum summum illum Italiæ dominatum sit vsus. Nam, vt vetus Imp. Constantinus apud Iustinianū loquitur, Scripturæ diuersæ & fidem sibi[?] inuicem derogantes, nihil habere firmitatis possunt. l. scripturæ, 14. c. de fid. instrum. quippe cùm duæ orationes pugnantia continentes veræ esse non possint, l. si is qui. 13. §. vtrum, D. de reb. dub. l. vbi pugnantia, 188. D. de reg. iur. Itaque quoties plura eiusdem actus instrumenta conficiuntur, oportet ea inter se totidem verbis congruere: tametsi error in aliqua notula sit tolerabilis, veluti si L. pro C. scripta sit l. Sepronius, 47. D. de leg. 2. Sed aliud est error in nota numeri, aliud diuersitas in rebus ipsis, velut hoc loco, vbi in vno instrumento sola Romæ suburbana quædam nominantur: in altero, præter maximam Italiæ partem, etiam Sicilia, Sardinia, & Corcyra: quo casu quia diuersæ donationes sunt, diuersa instrumenta requirebantur. l. sancimus, 34 §. si quis autem, C. de donat. l. quingenta, 12. D. de probat. Denique si Constantinus tanto ante Occidentis Imperium Papatui donarat, ecquod ius nouum adipisci Papa ex hac noua Ludouici donatione potuit? cum, vt vulgò traditur, rei suæ acquisitio nulla sit. l. 4. C. de cōtrah. emp. V.
units.tr: to make an election, and let no one in the cities or territories pertaining to the power of the church of blessed Peter the Apostle presume to do any other harm; but let the Romans be allowed to bury their pontiff with all honour and without any disturbance; and let him whom all the Romans, by divine inspiration and the intercession of blessed Peter, with one counsel and one accord and without any promise, shall have chosen to the order of the pontificate, be consecrated in the canonical manner without any ambiguity or objection; and when he has been consecrated, let legates be sent to us or to our successors, the Kings of the Franks, who shall arrange love, charity and peace between us and him. From this comparison it is plain by what frauds and how wicked arts the Papacy has used to attain that supreme dominion over Italy. For, as the old Emperor Constantine speaks in Justinian, diverse writings which mutually contradict one another and their credit cannot have any firmness. Law "Scripturae", 14, C. de fide instrumentorum. Indeed, since two statements containing contrary things cannot both be true (law "Si is qui", 13, §. "Utrum", D. de rebus dubiis; law "Ubi pugnantia", 188, D. de regulis iuris). Therefore whenever several instruments of the same act are drawn up, they ought to agree with one another word for word, although an error in some small mark is tolerable, as if L. were written for C. (law "Sempronius", 47, D. de legatis 2). But it is one thing to have an error in a numeral sign, another to have a difference in the things themselves; as here, where in one instrument only certain suburbs of Rome are named, while in the other, besides the greater part of Italy, Sicily, Sardinia and Corcyra are also named. In such a case, since the donations are different, different instruments were required (law "Sancimus", 34, §. "Si quis autem", C. de donationibus; law "Quingenta", 12, D. de probationibus). Finally, if Constantine had given the Papacy so great a donation long before the empire of the West, what new right could the Pope acquire from this new donation of Louis? Since, as is commonly taught, there is no acquisition of what is already one's own (law 4, C. de contrahenda emptione, V).

units.la: Quod alio etiam loco Papæ pugnantia inter se de hac eadem donatione locuti sunt, extat enim in eodem Gratiani decreto, 12. q. 1. c. futuram, Melchiadis Papæ testimonium, qui ante Syluęstrum Papalem sedem obtinuit, vbi iam tum ante Syluęstri, inquâ, Papatū huius donationis à Constantino etiam ante suū Papatum factæ mentione his verbis facit, Donaria immensa cotulit, & fabricam templi prima sedis B. Petri instituit: adeo ut sedem Imperialem relinqueret, & B. Petro successoribusque suis profuturam concederet. Nam si ante Melchiadis tempora Constantinus illam donationem fecit, quid argumenti habere hæc Sylvestri fabula potuerit, affirmantis & baptizatum à se Constantinum, & se ab illo tanto imperio donatum fuisse? vi. Sed iam propiùs ad ipsum donationis instrumentum, & historici verba veniendum est. Nam cum verisimile videbitur, somnium divinitùs oblatum fuisse homini, non tantùm ethnico, & idolorum cultori, verùmetiam acerrimo religionis Christianæ infectatori? aut si oblatum fuisset, quis credat Deum non id potiùs per angelum aliquem, ex vetere (ut scriptura testatur) ac perpetua consuetudine, quàm per Apostolos mortuos id facturum fuisse? denique temerarium est quicquam de somnijs, præter Scripturæ sacræ auctoritatem credere. Quare dubium nemini esse debet, quin hoc de Petri & Pauli visione commentum ex eadem officina prodierit, unde alia eiusmodi innumerabilia Papatus figmenta, & mendacia nata sunt, quale illud est apud Antoninum, part. 3. tit. 24. §. 3. Cum Dominicus effet Roma, & in basilica S. Petri orationem suam pro conservatione & dilatatione ordinis sui effunderet, facta manu Domini super eum, gloriosos principes Petrum & Paulum ad se subito venientes aspexit: quorum Petrus baculum, Paulus vero librum tradere videbatur: addebantque dicentes: Vade, prædica: quoniam a Deo ad hoc ministerium electus es: aut illud alterum Papæ Stephani secundi, apud Reginonem in Chronic. anni DCCLIII, ubi Stephanus Papa, cui Pipinus exarchatu Italiæ (ut pau-lo anIo[?] ante dicebamus)donauit, scribit se cùm in mona-sterio S. Dionysii apud pagum Parisiacum (haec illius verba sunt) subter campanis dormiret, vidisse ante altare D. Petrum, & magistrum Gentium Paulum, quos de illorum succaris cognouit, B. Dionysium subtilem & longiorem: dixisseque Dominum Petrum, Hic frater noster postulat sanitatem, & D. Paulum respondisse, Modò sanabitur. & appropinquantem misisse manum suam ad pectus Domini Dionysii amicabiliter, & dixisse D. Petrum ad Do. Dionysium hilariter: Tua gratia est sanitas eius. Et statim Dom. Dionysium thuribulum incensi, & palmam in manu tenentem, presbytero & Diacono dixisse praelibato Stephano Papae, Pax tecum frater: Noli timere surge sanus. Et mox, inquit, factus sum sanus: & volebam implere quod mihi praeceptum erat: & dicebat qui ibi aderant, quod dementabam. & caetera, quae adeo stolida, atque insulsa sunt, ut Papa Stephanus illo commento risum captasse videatur. Sed laudā-dus Deus, quòd tantam improbitatem non nisi in homines stultos ac stolidos incidere passus est.
units.tr: That the Popes also spoke in contradictory terms about this same donation in another place is shown by the testimony of Pope Melchiades, who held the apostolic see before Sylvester, found in the same decree of Gratian, 12, q. 1, c. "Futuram". There, already before Sylvester's time, he mentions this donation made by Constantine even before his own papacy, in these words: He bestowed immense gifts and founded the building of the church of the first see of blessed Peter, so much so that he left the imperial seat and granted it to be of benefit to blessed Peter and his successors. For if Constantine made that donation before the time of Melchiades, what argument could this fable of Sylvester have, which asserts both that Constantine was baptised by him and that he was endowed by him with so great an empire? But now we must come nearer to the instrument of donation itself and to the words of the historian. For when will it seem likely that a dream was divinely offered to a man, not only a heathen and worshipper of idols, but even a most bitter persecutor of the Christian religion? Or, if it were offered, who would believe that God would have done this through some angel, according to the ancient (as Scripture testifies) and perpetual custom, rather than through the dead Apostles? Finally, it is rash to believe anything about dreams apart from the authority of holy Scripture. Hence no one ought to doubt that this fiction about the vision of Peter and Paul came from the same workshop from which the countless other such figments and lies of the Papacy were born, such as that in Antoninus, part 3, title 24, §. 3: When Dominic was at Rome, and in the basilica of St Peter poured out his prayer for the preservation and spreading of his order, the hand of the Lord being laid upon him, he suddenly saw the glorious princes Peter and Paul coming towards him; of whom Peter seemed to hand him a staff, and Paul a book; and they added, saying: Go, preach, for you have been chosen by God for this ministry. Or that other story of Pope Stephen II, in Regino's Chronicle, year 753, where Pope Stephen, to whom Pepin gave the exarchate of Italy (as we said a little earlier), writes that when he was sleeping under the bells in the monastery of St Denis near the village of Paris (these are his words) he saw before the altar Peter the Apostle and Paul the teacher of the Gentiles, and recognised from their appearance blessed Dionysius, slender and taller; and Lord Peter said: This our brother asks for health; and Lord Paul replied: He shall now be healed. And approaching, he put his hand kindly on the breast of Lord Dionysius, and Lord Peter said cheerfully to Lord Dionysius: Your grace is his health. And at once Lord Dionysius, holding a censer of incense and a palm in his hand, said to the presbyter and deacon who were present, to the aforesaid Pope Stephen: Peace be with you, brother; do not fear, rise, you are whole. And soon, he says, I was made whole, and I wished to fulfil what had been commanded me; and those who were present said that I was raving. And the rest, which is so foolish and insipid that Pope Stephen seems to have sought laughter by that invention. But God is to be praised, that he has allowed such wickedness to fall only upon foolish and stupid men.

units.la: Quin ne illud quidem de visis in somnio Petro & Paulo apostolis praetermittendum est, (semper enim eosdem illos Apostolos inculcant, cęterorum mē-tionem faciunt nullam) quod in libro Conformi-tatum legitur, sol. 51. B. Franciscus Romam perges fuit à sanctis apostolis Petro & Paulo dulciter amplexatus ibidem Petrus & Paulus à Francisco rogati impetrarunt à Christo regulæ Minorum confirmationem. VII. Quòd verisimile non est, Constantinum magnum illo lepræ morbo laborasse: quandoquidem neque Eu-sebius, qui vitam eius accuratè quinque, ut dixi, li-bris complexus est, neque Zosimus, qui religionis odio Constantinū quibus potest contumeliis exagitat,neque Paulus Diaconus,neque alius quisquā vllam illius morbi mentionem facit:vt omittā Baptistæ Mantuani argumentum ex lib.de Patient.1. cap.30.vbi cum ex Plinij lib.21.cap.1.docuisset,genus illud morbi iampridem in Italia restinctum fuisse,sic infert:Si ergo tempore Plinii, qui sub V espasiano floruit, erat iam restinctus hic morbus in Italia, verisimile non est, Constantinum eo laborasse, qui post longum tempus imperauit. viii. Quod etiam impium commentum illo loco subiicitur,& quod Christianorum aures animisque respuunt, Costantinum,dum in lauacro à Papa baptizabatur,vidisse manum Dei de cęlo in suum corpus demissam,quę illum lepra purgauit. In sinu lauacri positus, inquit, manum tangentem me à cœlo propriis oculis aspexi, sub qua mundatum me à lepra cognoui.Nam quis non videt figmentum hoc eiusdem esse generis, cuius illa sunt,quæ passim in libro Conformitatum Francifcanarum,aut in vita Dominici leguntur? ix.Quod neque verisimile est tam inconsultum Syluestrum Papam & Diaconos ipsius fuisse, vt Constantino Christianorum ,ac præsertim Ecclesiæ Romanæ hosti infestissimo tam repente, pōst suum illis narratum somnium ,baptismū conferre vellent: ac nō prius ei Christianæ religionis mysteria, Catechumenorum instituto,traderent.Quinetiam Zosimus Christianæ,vt dixi,religionis inimicus narrat eum ab Hispano quodam eam Religionem edoctum, didicisse, quanta vis illius esset in delendis hominum peccatis: ac tum demum ariolos & flamines ceterosque Romanarum superstitionum sacerdotes ab aula sua remouisse. x. Quod summi auctores atque historici testantur,Constantinum nō n si paulo ante mortem,& anno demum ætatis LXV. baptizatum fuisse,neque id Romæ, vel à Sylvestro Papa,qui quinq; prope ante annis vita excesserat, sed Nicomediæ,ab Eusebio Nicomediensi,magna Episcoporum frequentiss.Hæc Eusb.in libr.de vit. 4.Hieronym.in Chron. Ruffinus lib.1. cap.11. Socrates lib.1.cap.39. Theodor.lib.1.cap.31. Ambrosius lib.de obitu Theodos.Neque enim Nicephoro fides habenda est,qui libro 7.cap.35.cùm Romę illum baptizatum scribit,simul adiungit,se Romanam Ecclesiam in ea re auctorem sequi.Præsertim cùm Vincentius lib. histor.24. non dubitarit scribere,secúdum S.Hieronymum, Constantinū uxorem Faustam,& filium Crispum crudeliter occidisse, & in extremo vitæ ab Eusebio Nicomediæ Episcopo baptizatum fuisse. xi. Quòd nec verisimile est, si Constantinus calido puerorum infantium sanguine suum morbum curare instituisset, vel eum voluisse pueros illos palam à Capitolij sacerdotibus iugulari,vel tanta sanguinis copia opus fuisse,ut eo cisterna tota impleretur. xii. Nihilomagis credibile est, Constantinū tandiu Christianam religionem oppugnasse, quin aliquid de Petro & Paulo,celeberrimis Christi Apostolis, auditione accepisset:neque adeo rerum Christianarum imperitum fuisse,ut somno illo excitatus ex Sylvestro quæreret,quinam essent illi Dij, qui Petrus & Paulus appellabantur.nam ut nihil omnino præter diuinam visionem didicisset,tamen non est verisimile Petrum & Paulũ eise [?] pro diis vèditasse [?].xiii. Quòd impium fuisset,beneficium recuperatę valetudinis referre potiùs acceptum Apostolo Petro, Dei internuntio, quàm ipsi Deo, à quo Petrus ad eum missus fuerat. Deinde soli Petro potius, quàm coniunctim Petro & Paulo. His enim verbis vtitur, Et beneficentius ipsius Petri sanitatem corporis redeuntem integerrime sensi. xiv. Absurdius est etiam quod subijcitur, Constantinum, qui quinque liberos habebat, tamen de sententia omnium Satrapa-rum suorum (quod verbum in legibus & monumentis Impp. Romanorum plane nouum, insolens, atque inusitatum est) & vniuersi senatus & optimatium, & cuncti populi, qui Romano imperio subiacebat, dimidiam imperii sui partem pauperculo sacerdoti donasse: cum inter omnes constet, senatum Rom. non illo tantum tempore, verum etiam vsque ad Valentiniani imperium Gentilitias suas superstitiones retinuisse: quod vel ex Symmachi epistola intelligitur, ad Impp. Valentin. Theodos. & Arcadium scripta, lib.10. Epistol.54. vbi senatus Romani nomine, ab illis petit, vt superstitio & idolorum cultus in vrbe Roma restituatur: cui B. Ambrosius duabus Epistolis ad eundem Imp. Valentinianum scriptis, Aurelius autem Prudentius piis & elegantissimis versibus respondet. xv. aeque absurdum est, & Christiano Episcopo plane indignum, quod subiicitur, Constantinum non tatum parem Imperiali suo potestatem Syluestro Papae tribuere, verumetiam maiorem potestatis principatum, quàm nostra, inquit, Serenitas Regia ab omnibus habere dignoscitur. & mox: Tradentes ipsi potestatem & gloriae dignitatem, vigorem & efficaciam, & honorificentiam Imperialem. Qua de re ac Paparum ambitione operaepretium est Bernardi abbati Clareuallensis iudicium audire, scriptum Eugenio Papae, lib. de consideratione. Disce, inquit, exemplo prophetarum, præsidere non tàm ad imperitandum, quàm ad facilitandum[?] quod tempus requirit. Disce sarculo tibi opus esse, non sceptro, vt opus facias prophetæ. Item, Esto, vt alia quæcunque ratione hac tibi vindices, sed non apostolico iure. Nec tibi Petrus dare potuit quod non habuit: quod habuit, hoc dedit, sollicitudinem super Ecclesias. Nunquid dominationem? audi ipsum. Non dominantes, inquit, in clero, sed forma facti gregis. Et ne dictum sola humilitate putes, non etiam veritate, vox domini est in Euangelio: Reges gentium dominantur eorum, vos autem non sic. Planum est, Apostolis interdicitur dominatus. I ergo tu: & tibi vsurpare auide aut dominans Apostolatum, aut Apostolicus dominatum: plane ab vtroque prohiberis: si vtrumque simul habere voles, perdes vtrumque. xvi. Nihilo tolerabilius est quod subiicit, se Papæ Romano tribuere principatum super quatuor præcipuas sedes, Antiochiæ, Alexandriæ, Constantinopolis, & Hierosolymorum. In quo non modò manifesta, verùmetiam ridicula falsitas deprehenditur. Primùm quia ne Constantinopolis quidem adhuc vlla extabat: quippe quæ, anno demùm Imperij Constantini decimo ædificari coepta est, vt testatur Nicephorus lib. 8. cap. 4. & ciues plerique omnes idolorum cultui per id tempus erant dediti. Tantum abest, vt vlla ibi vel Ecclesia, vel Ecclesiarum metropolis, aut prærogatiua fuerit. xvii. Minus etiam ferri potest, quod subiicitur, Papam Romanum constitui super omnes in vniuerso terrarum orbe Ecclesias. Mitto enim quod alio loco demonstrauimus, verissimam & certissimam hanc esse Antichristi notam, cùm sibi quis principatum in omnes Ecclesias arrogat. Sed insignis hoc loco Paparum amentia perspicitur, quam etiam alio loco perstrinximus, cùm ex hoc instrumento contendant se principatum illum ex Constantini beneficio habuisse, quem tamen aliis locis innumeris gloriantur se immediate ab ipso Christo accepisse. nam, ut inter omnes constat, quod suum cuiusque est, id pluribus ex causis eius esse non potest, quandoquidem dominiu non ex pluribus causis, sed una tantum contingit. l.3 §. ex pluribus, D. de acq. poss. l. si res aliena, 52. D. ad trebell. xiix[?].
units.tr: Nor should we pass over what is read in the book of Conformities, fol. 51, about the visions of the apostles Peter and Paul in a dream (for they always keep harping on those same apostles and make no mention of the rest): Blessed Francis, when he went to Rome, was lovingly embraced by the holy apostles Peter and Paul; there Peter and Paul, at Francis's request, obtained from Christ the confirmation of the Rule of the Friars Minor. VII. It is not likely that Constantine the Great suffered from that leprosy. For neither Eusebius, who related his life in detail in the five books I mentioned, nor Zosimus, who, out of hatred for the religion, assails Constantine with every insult he can, nor Paulus Diaconus, nor anyone else makes any mention of that disease. I say nothing of the argument of Baptista Mantuanus from book 1 of De patientia, chapter 30, where, having shown from Pliny, book 21, chapter 1, that that kind of disease had long since died out in Italy, he infers: If, then, in the time of Pliny, who flourished under Vespasian, this disease had already died out in Italy, it is not likely that Constantine, who reigned a long time afterwards, suffered from it. VIII. The impious fiction that is appended in the same place, which Christian ears and minds reject, is that Constantine, while he was being baptized in the bath by the Pope, saw a hand of God let down from heaven onto his body, which cleansed him of leprosy. Placed in the bath, he says, I saw with my own eyes a hand touching me from heaven, under which I knew I had been cleansed of leprosy. For who does not see that this fiction is of the same kind as those that are read everywhere in the book of the Franciscan Conformities, or in the life of Dominic? IX. It is not likely that Pope Sylvester and his deacons were so ill-advised as to wish to confer baptism at once on Constantine, the most bitter enemy of Christians and especially of the Roman Church, right after his dream was told to them, and not first to teach him the mysteries of the Christian religion according to the custom of catechumens. Moreover, Zosimus, as I said, an enemy of the Christian religion, relates that Constantine learned from a certain Spaniard about that religion, and how great its power was in blotting out men's sins; and only then did he remove from his court the soothsayers and priests and the other priests of Roman superstitions. X. The chief authors and historians testify that Constantine was not baptized until shortly before his death, and only in the sixty-fifth year of his age; and that this happened not at Rome, nor by Pope Sylvester, who had died almost five years earlier, but at Nicomedia, by Eusebius of Nicomedia, with a large and very numerous gathering of bishops. So Eusebius in the book On his life, book 4; Jerome in the Chronicle; Rufinus, book 1, chapter 11; Socrates, book 1, chapter 39; Theodoret, book 1, chapter 31; Ambrose in the book On the death of Theodosius. Nor is Nicephorus to be believed, who, in book 7, chapter 35, writes that he was baptized at Rome, and at the same time adds that in this matter he follows the Roman Church as his authority. Especially since Vincent, in the Historical Mirror, book 24, did not hesitate to write, following St Jerome, that Constantine cruelly killed his wife Fausta and his son Crispus, and that at the end of his life he was baptized by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia. XI. Nor is it likely that, if Constantine had resolved to cure his disease with the warm blood of young children, he would have wanted those boys to be openly slaughtered by the priests of the Capitol, or that so great a quantity of blood would have been needed that an entire cistern would be filled with it. XII. It is no more credible that Constantine opposed the Christian religion for so long without having heard something about Peter and Paul, the most famous apostles of Christ; nor was he so ignorant of Christian matters that, roused from that sleep, he would ask Sylvester who those gods were who were called Peter and Paul. For even if he had learned nothing at all beyond the divine vision, it is still not likely that Peter and Paul were sold off as gods. XIII. It would be impious to attribute the benefit of his recovered health to the apostle Peter, the messenger of God, rather than to God himself, by whom Peter had been sent to him. Moreover, it is to Peter alone, rather than jointly to Peter and Paul, that the credit is given. For they use these words: And I most fully perceived the health of his body returning through the blessing of Peter himself. XIV. What is added is even more absurd: that Constantine, who had five children, nevertheless, by the judgment of all his satraps (a word quite new, unusual and unheard of in the laws and monuments of the Roman emperors), and of the whole senate and the nobles, and of all the people who were subject to the Roman empire, gave half of his empire to a poor priest. Yet it is agreed by all that the Roman senate kept its heathen superstitions not only at that time, but even down to the reign of Valentinian. This is clear from the letter of Symmachus written to the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius and Arcadius, book 10, letter 54, where in the name of the Roman senate he asks them that superstition and the worship of idols be restored in the city of Rome. St Ambrose answered him in two letters written to the same emperor Valentinian, and Aurelius Prudentius answered in pious and most elegant verses. XV. Equally absurd, and wholly unworthy of a Christian bishop, is what is added: that Constantine gave to Pope Sylvester power equal to his own imperial power, and even a greater princely authority than our royal Serenity is known to have among all men. And soon after: Handing over to him power and the dignity of glory, the vigour and efficacy, and imperial honour. On this matter, and on the ambition of the popes, it is worth hearing the judgment of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, written to Pope Eugenius in the book On consideration. Learn, he says, from the example of the prophets to preside not so much to rule as to make things easier, as the time requires. Learn that you need a hoe, not a sceptre, to do the work of a prophet. Again: Grant that you may defend this by some other reason, but not by apostolic right. Peter could not give you what he did not have. What he had, he gave: care over the churches. Do you suppose lordship? Hear him: Not lording it over the clergy, he says, but being examples to the flock. And lest you think this was said from humility alone and not also from truth, the Lord's own word is in the Gospel: The kings of the nations lord it over them, but you shall not be so. It is plain that lordship is forbidden to the apostles. So go, you who greedily claim for yourself either the apostolate as lordship or lordship as apostolic: you are clearly forbidden both; if you want to have both at once, you will lose both. XVI. What follows is no more tolerable: that he grants to the Roman Pope princely authority over the four chief sees, Antioch, Alexandria, Constantinople and Jerusalem. In this not only a manifest but even a ridiculous falsehood is detected. First, because Constantinople did not yet exist at all, since it was only begun to be built in the tenth year of Constantine's reign, as Nicephorus testifies, book 8, chapter 4; and at that time almost all its citizens were given over to the worship of idols. So far was there any church there, or a metropolis of churches, or any precedence. XVII. Even less can be tolerated what follows: that the Roman Pope is appointed over all the churches in the whole world. For I pass over what I have shown elsewhere, that this is a most true and certain mark of Antichrist, when anyone arrogates to himself primacy over all churches. But here the great madness of the popes is plainly seen, which I have also censured elsewhere: that, while they contend from this document that they had that primacy from the benefaction of Constantine, they boast in countless other places that they received it immediately from Christ himself. For, as is agreed by all, what belongs to each person cannot belong to him on several grounds, since ownership arises not from several grounds but from one alone. Dig. 3, §. ex pluribus, De acquirenda possessione; l. si res aliena, 52, D. ad Trebellianum. xiix[?]

units.la: Ridiculum autem illud est, quod Constantinum inducunt hæc de se prædicantem, In ædificando Romano templo duodecim se terræ cophinos suis propriis humeris extulisse, æquales, inquit, numero XII. Apostolis. Nam cùm toties uni Petro plus honoris tribuat, quàm coniunctim reliquis XI. omnibus, nunquid proportionis ratio postulabat, ut plures in illius unius honorem terræ cophinos exportaret, quàm in omnium reliquorum?xix.
units.tr: It is also absurd that they introduce Constantine declaring this about himself: In building the Roman temple I carried twelve baskets of earth on my own shoulders, equal in number to the twelve Apostles. For since the Papist writers always grant Peter alone more honour than all the other eleven together, was it not proportionate that more baskets of earth should be carried for the honour of that one man than for all the rest? xix.

units.la: Neque verò minus ridiculum est, quod subiungit, se pro continuatione luminarium, quæ in illo templo ardebant, non modò possessiones & agros contulisse, verum etiam in Oriente, Occidete, Septentrionali & Meridionali climate, in Iudæa videlicet, Asia, Thracia, Græcia, Africa, Italia & in diuersis insulis suam illi libertatem, id est, ius ac potestatem concessisse: ut per manus Beatiss. patris Sylvestri, & omnium eius successorum disponantur. Hæc Papa totidem verbis & syllabis. Ex quibus intelligi potest, mirificam fuisse cereorum ac luminarium illorum caritatem: quibus tuendis cùm universi terrarum orbis, tùm speciatim quatuor ipsius partium vectigalia & annuos proventus attribui oportuit. Neque verò id solum: sed quia Quæstorum fides interdum in hoc genere genere suspecta est, Constantinus statuisse memoratur, ut illorum proventuum administratio ac dispensatio ipsis Papis committatur. Ut non facile diiudicari posse videatur, utrum maior Paparum impudentia fuerit, conantium nobis istas aniles fabulas pro divinis oraculis tradere, an eorum hominum stupiditas, si qui unquam adeo stolidæ atque anili fabulæ fidem habuerunt. quanquam ubi Scripturæ sacræ lumen extinctum est, perfacile est Sathanæ, miseris mortalibus illudere, ut nō sine causa Christus Ioan.8. dixerit: Ego sum lux mundi: qui sequitur me, non ambulabit in tenebris, sed habebit lumen vitæ. xx. Æquè porrò ridiculum atque fabulosum est, quod sequitur, de decem muneribus, quibus Papa se à Constantino donatum scribit. 1. palatio Lateranensi. 2. diademate aureo. 3. mitra. 4. collari Imperatorio. 5. purpurea chlamyde. 6. coccinea tunica. 7. indumentis Imperatoriis. 8. popa præcedentium equitum. 9. Imperiali sceptro. 10. cunctis signis, bannis & vexillis. Fuerit ergo Petrus Apostolus olim squalidus, obsoletus, sordida penula, piscatoris modo, amictus: nunc vicarius ipsius auratis vestibꝰ, ornatu ac vestitu Regio insignis, equitū peditūmque comitatu cinctus, agmine quadrato, pōpa & apparatu magnifico, triumphans per orbem terrarum vagabitur. Quantò vicarij principis Apostolorum, quàm ipsius principis melior conditio est? O summe Deus, quanta tua est clementia, mansuetudo, patientia, qui tandiu propudium, ac prostibulum istud tā impunè Christo tuo illudere pateris? O miseri Reges ac Principes, qui tandiu spurca, & fœda meretricis istius menstrua lambitis! O bone Iesu, quantum inter tuam illam speciem ac figuram, atque inter istius tetri; crudelisque tyranni fastum, ac superbiam interfuit! Nulla fuit, inquit Esa. 53. in Christo forma, nullus decor. Ubi cum aspeximus, oculos aspectumque nostrum auertimus. Abiectus, & ab hominibus contemptus, doloribus conse-ctus, continentibus morbis affectus, abscondens vultum à nobis. Adeò despectus, ut pro nihilo habeatur. Et quisquam mirabitur Papam gloriari esse ausum, se à Constantino Deum esse appellatum? Nam in hac ipsa dist. 96. c. satis, ita scribit: Satis ostenditur, à secu-lari potestate nec ligari prorsus, nec solui posse Pontificem, quem constat à pio Principe Constantino Deum appellatum, cum nec Deum posse ab hominibus iudicari manifestum sit. Sed operæpretium est Doctoris Ber-nardi de hoc toto pomparum genere iudicium au-dire, qui lib. de considerat. 4. ad Papam Eugenium his scribit verbis: Petrus nescitur processisse aliquando vel gemmis ornatus, vel sericis: non tectus auro, non vectus equo albo, nec stipatus milite, nec circumstrepenti-bus septus ministris. Absque his & credidit satis posse impleri salutare mandatum: Si amas me, pasce oues meas. Item alio loco: Consideres ante omnia S. Ecclesiam Rom, cui Deo auctore præes, Ecclesiarum matrem esse, non dominam: te vero non dominum Episcoporum, sed unum ex ipsis. Hæc Bernard. verum quid de subse-quente huius instrumenti clausula dicemus, vbi Constantinus post illam Regiam Papæ Syluestri inuestituram subiungit, „se frænum equi Papalis manu tenuisse, pro reuerentia B. Petri, & statoris ei officium exhibuisse? Væ, væ meretrici venefica, cu-ius obscœna menstrua tanti principes tandiu li-guriunt. Nam hunc eundem honorem sibi Papa Stephanus II. à Pipino Rege proximè Lutetiam PariParisiorum tribui passus est. Eundem sibi Ale-xander tertius ab Imper. Friderico haberi voluit, ut non immerito B.Hieronymus in prolog.de Spi-rit.sanct.nominatim Roma appellet Babylonem, & purpuratam illam Meretricem, quae in Apocalypsi describitur. Sed hoc de genere toto, iterum supradicti Bernardi iudicium audiamus, qui in Cant.cant.serm.33.his scribit verbis: Honorati incedunt de bonis domini, cui domino honorem non deferunt. Inde is quem quotidie vides meretricius nitor, histrionicus habitus, Regius apparatus, inde aurum in frenis, sellis & calcaribus, & plus calcaria quam altaria fulgent. Inde splendidae mensae, & cibi, & scyphi. Inde comessationes & ebrietates. Inde cythara & lyra & tibia. Inde redundantia torcularia, & promptuaria plena, eructantia[?] ex hoc in illud. Inde dolia pigmentaria. Inde referta marsupia. Proh! huiusmodi volunt esse & sunt Ecclesiarum Praepositi, Decani, Archidecani, Episcopi, Archiepiscopi. Necenim haec cedunt negotio illi quod perambulat in tenebris: & mox, IPSE ENIM EST ANTICHRISTVS. Ecquid unquam vel Marsilius Patauinus, vel Petrarcha, vel Lutherus, vel alij cō-similes Papatus infectatores planius aut vehementius ad Papam Romanum antichristianismi crimine accusandum protulerunt?Sed pergamus porro.
units.tr: Nor is what follows any less absurd: that for the upkeep of the lights that burned in that temple he had given not only possessions and fields, but also, in the East, West, North and South climates, namely in Judea, Asia, Thrace, Greece, Africa, Italy and various islands, his freedom, that is, his right and power, so that these might be disposed through the hands of the most blessed father Sylvester and all his successors. The Pope says this in just these words and syllables. From this it can be understood that there was a remarkable fondness for those candles and lamps, for whose upkeep the revenues and yearly incomes not only of the whole orb of the earth but especially of the four quarters of it had to be assigned. And that is not all: because the good faith of the treasurers is sometimes suspect in such matters, Constantine is recorded to have decreed that the administration and disbursement of those revenues be entrusted to the Popes themselves. So it hardly seems possible to decide whether the impudence of the Popes is greater, in trying to pass off these old wives' fables to us as divine oracles, or the stupidity of those men, if any ever gave credence to so foolish and doddering a tale. Yet where the light of holy Scripture has been put out, it is very easy for Satan to mock wretched mortals; not without reason did Christ say in John 8: I am the light of the world; he who follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life. xx. Equally ridiculous and fabulous is what follows about the ten gifts with which the Pope writes that Constantine endowed him: (1) the Lateran palace; (2) a golden diadem; (3) a mitre; (4) the imperial collar; (5) a purple cloak; (6) a scarlet tunic; (7) imperial garments; (8) the escort of the horsemen going before him; (9) the imperial sceptre; (10) all the standards, banners and flags. So Peter the Apostle was once squalid, shabby, clothed in a dirty cloak like a fisherman; now his vicar, distinguished by golden robes, royal ornament and dress, surrounded by a retinue of horse and foot, in a square formation, with magnificent pomp and display, goes wandering triumphantly through the world. Is the condition of the vicar of the Prince of the Apostles better than that of the Prince himself? O highest God, how great is your clemency, meekness and patience, that you have so long allowed this harlot and whore to mock your Christ with such impunity! O wretched kings and princes, who have so long licked the foul and filthy menstruation of that whore! O good Jesus, how great was the difference between that form and figure of yours and the pride and arrogance of that foul and cruel tyrant! There was no form in Christ, says Isaiah 53, no comeliness. When we saw him, we turned our eyes and our gaze away. Despised and rejected by men, afflicted with sorrows, stricken with continual sickness, hiding his face from us. So despised that he was counted as nothing. And will anyone wonder that the Pope dared to boast that he was called God by Constantine? For in this same Dist. 96, c. satis, he writes thus: It is shown sufficiently that the Pontiff cannot be bound or loosed by secular power, since it is agreed that he was called God by the pious Prince Constantine, when it is clear that God cannot be judged by men. But it is worth hearing the judgement of Doctor Bernard on this whole kind of pomp, who in his book On Consideration, book 4, writes to Pope Eugenius in these words: Peter is not known ever to have gone forth adorned with jewels or silks, not covered with gold, not carried on a white horse, nor attended by soldiers, nor surrounded by noisy servants. Without these things he believed that the saving command could be fully carried out: If you love me, feed my sheep. Likewise in another place: Consider above all that the holy Roman Church, over which by God's ordering you preside, is the mother of the churches, not their mistress; and you are not the lord of the bishops, but one of them. These are Bernard's words. But what shall we say about the closing clause of this document that follows, where, after that royal investiture of Pope Sylvester, Constantine adds that he held the bridle of the Papal horse for reverence to blessed Peter and performed the office of groom? Woe, woe to the poisonous harlot, whose obscene menstruation so many princes have long been licking. For Pope Stephen II allowed the same honour to be paid to himself by King Pepin, shortly before at Lutetia, that is Paris. Alexander III wished the same to be held by himself from the Emperor Frederick; so it is not without reason that blessed Jerome, in his prologue on the Holy Spirit, names Rome by name Babylon, and that purple-clad harlot described in the Apocalypse. But on this whole kind of thing let us hear once more the judgement of the Bernard just mentioned, who in his sermon 33 on the Song of Songs writes these words: They go about honoured with the goods of the lord, yet do not render honour to that lord. Hence that harlot-like sheen you see every day, the actor's dress, the royal display; hence gold on bridles, saddles and spurs, and the spurs shine more than the altars. Hence splendid tables, and foods, and cups. Hence revelries and drunkenness. Hence the cithara and lyre and flute. Hence overflowing winepresses and full storerooms, belching from this to that. Hence jars of spices. Hence purses stuffed full. Alas! Such men want to be and are the provosts, deans, archdeacons, bishops and archbishops of the churches. For these things do not fit with that man who walks in darkness. And soon after, for he himself is the Antichrist. Did Marsilius of Padua, or Petrarch, or Luther, or others like them who attacked the Papacy, ever bring forward more plainly or more vehemently the charge of Antichristianism against the Roman Pope? But let us go on.

units.la: XXI. Neque enim satis hoc purpuratae meretrici visum est. nam in sequenti versu Constantinum ita loquentem facit: Clericis Ecclesiae Rom. servientibus eandem gloriam & potentiam & praeexcellentiam tribuimus, quam amplissimus Senatus noster habet: & sicut Imperialem exercitum, sic & clerum Ecclesiae Rom. adorari decernimus. Hac igitur libertate freti Cardinales, & ceteri clerici, deinceps laicis[?], galeis[?], scutis, gladiis, aliisque telis instructi ac parati vel ad prædicandum Euangelium, vel ad missi-ficationes obeundas accedent. Tantúmne? imò, inquit, quemadmodum Imperialis potentia diuersis officiis cubicularium[?], hostiariorum & excubitorum decoratur, ita & S. Ecclesiam Romanam decorari volumus, & vt candidissimo colore decoratos equos equiter, & si-cut Senatus noster calciamentis vtitur cum vlonibus, ita candidissimo linteamine illustrentur. Ecquis est ex tanto Senatorum Gallæ Regis numero, qui cum humilitatem, & modestiam Christi & ipsius Apostolorum recordatur, non istum Paparum fastum, ac superbiam precibus omnibus detestetur? xxii.
units.tr: XXI. Nor did this seem enough to the purple-clad harlot. For in the next passage he makes Constantine speak thus: To the clergy of the Roman Church, who serve, we grant the same glory, power and pre-eminence that our most distinguished Senate has; and just as we decree that the imperial army be honoured, so also we decree that the clergy of the Roman Church be honoured. Relying on this liberty, then, the Cardinals and other clerics, armed and ready with helmets, shields, swords and other weapons, will henceforth come either to preach the Gospel or to carry out missions. Is that all? Indeed, he says, just as imperial power is adorned with various offices of chamberlains, doorkeepers and guards, so we wish the Holy Roman Church to be adorned, and that its horses be ridden with white trappings, and just as our Senate uses shoes with buckles, so let them be decorated with white linen. Is there anyone, among so many senators of the King of Gaul, who, when he recalls the humility and modesty of Christ and of his Apostles, does not detest this pride and arrogance of the Papists with every prayer? xxii.

units.la: Quinetiam illud subiungit, vt si Papa velit aliquē è Constantini Senatoribus in clericorum ordinem ascisc ere, ne per superbiam illum honore recusent. Quis tyrannicā istā barbarie ferat, vt alicui collegio clericorum liceat vnum aliquem è Regiorum Senatorum ordine arbitrio suo deligere, quem etiam inuitum, clericum aut monachum fieri compellant? xxiii. Pergit porrò: atque vt Iurisconsulti meminerint, geminatæ orationis vim esse maiorem, iterum pronuntiat, se, & suum palatium, & vrbem Romam, & totius Italiæ & Occidentalium regionum prouincias, loca, ciuitates, Papis omnibus Romanis vsque ad mundi finem donare. Quinetiā cessionis & traditionis formulam adiungit, vt sese deinceps, relicto in Papæ possessione Occidentis imperio, ad Orientales regiones transferat, & in prouincia Byzantia sedem Imperii sui constituat, addita insuper causa valde idonea, quoniam, inquit, iniquum est, regem terrenum in ea regione potestatem habere, vbi Christiana religionis caput & sacerdotum principatus a cœlesti rege constitutus est. Præclarè se huiusce sententiæ initium dedit. nā Constantini ætate, hoc est ducentis ante Iustinianum annis, ad donationem perficiendā tradi-tionem vacuę possessionis opus erat. sed alia multa fuit quæ conturbent. Primùm quòd si Constantinus vacuam illius regionis possessione Syluestro tradidit, non potuit candè postea in suo testamento filio Constantio relinquere: cùm alienatio rei alicuius inter viuos facta, nullum de ea testamenti factioni locum relinquat. l. 6. C. de test. l. sequés. 52. D. de leg. 2. sinaauten donatio post illam inter filios partitio-nē facta est, perspicuè fuit lusoria: quia patris partitio inter liberos, testamenti, ac proinde vltimæ voluntatis vim obtinet. l. pen. & l. vlt. C. fam. ercisc. cum similib. Secundò, qua pietate potuit Constan-tinus, qui tres filios & duas filias habebat, tantam suis liberis iniuriâ facere, vt illos dimidia heredita-tis suæ parte priuaret, càmque in extraneũ aliquē, præsertim homunculum abiectum & vilem, trans-ferret? Nam scitum est illud Augustini: Quicunque vult exheredato filio Ecclesiam heredem facere, quærat alterum qui suscipiat, quàm Augustinum. 17.q.vl.c.vlt. vbi etiā laudatur eius Episcopi factū, qui testatori cuidam, à quo liberos non habente bona sua Ecclesiæ relicta fuerant, postea quàm liberos præter spem & opinionem susceperat, omnia restitue-rat. quod idem traditur 13. q. 2. c. si quis irascitur. Sed nihil æque ridiculum est, ac illa, quam Pseudoconstantinus subiicit, consilij sui ratio: In-quum esse, qua in ciuitate summus sacerdos præsi-det, in eadem ciuitate Imperatorem Imperii sui se-dem collocare. Vç tuo capiti, carnifex facerrime. Nā quid de Solomone, de Aza.de Iosia, & aliis piis Regibus Israelitis dicemus, qui fui domicilij ac regni sede Hierosolymis collocarunt? Quid de Theodosio, qui Mediolani? Sed ne longius exempla petantur, quid de Constantio Constantini filio, qui ex patris testamento Romae non tantum summum Imperium & iurisdictionem exercuit, verum etiam Papam Liberium propter susceptum Anastasij, Episcopi cuiusdam Magi ac sortilegi patrocinium, & Papatu suo exauctorauit, & urbe Roma exterminauit? quemadmodum Theodoricus, Sozomenus, & Amm. Marcellin.libr.15. scriptum reliquerunt.
units.tr: Moreover he adds this, that if the Pope wishes to admit any one of Constantine's senators into the order of clergy, they must not refuse the honour out of pride. Who could bear this tyrannical barbarity, that a college of clerics should be permitted, at its own will, to choose one from the order of royal senators and compel him, even against his will, to become a cleric or monk? xxiii. He goes on further: and so that the jurists may remember that the force of a repeated utterance is greater, he again declares that he gives to the Pope and his palace, and to the city of Rome, and to the provinces, places and cities of all Italy and the Western regions, to all the Roman Popes until the end of the world. He adds, moreover, a formula of cession and transfer, so that he himself, leaving the western empire in the Pope's possession, may move to the Eastern regions and establish the seat of his empire in the province of Byzantium, adding besides a very suitable reason: since, he says, it is unjust for an earthly king to have power in that region where the head of the Christian religion and the principate of priests has been established by the heavenly King. He made a fine start on this decision. For in Constantine's time, that is two hundred years before Justinian, a handing over of empty possession was needed to complete the donation. But there are many other things that disturb it. First, if Constantine handed over the empty possession of that region to Sylvester, he could not afterwards leave it in his will to his son Constantius, since an alienation of a thing made between living persons leaves no place for it in a testamentary disposition (C. de test.; D. de leg. 2, sequens). But if the donation was made after that, by a division among the sons, it was plainly a sham, because a father's division among his children has the force of a will, and so of a last wish (C. fam. ercisc., and the similar laws). Second, with what piety could Constantine, who had three sons and two daughters, do such an injury to his children as to deprive them of half his inheritance and transfer it to some stranger, especially a worthless and abject little man? For that saying of Augustine is well known: Whoever wishes to make the Church heir while disinheriting a son, let him seek another to accept it rather than Augustine. (17 q. ult. c. ult.), where also is praised the action of that bishop who, when a childless testator had left his goods to the Church, after the man unexpectedly and contrary to all hope had children, restored everything. The same is related at 13 q. 2 c. si quis irascitur. But nothing is as ridiculous as the reason for his plan that the pseudo-Constantine adds: I judge that in the city where the high priest presides, there the Emperor should establish the seat of his empire. Woe to your head, most wicked executioner! For what shall we say of Solomon, of Asa, of Josiah, and other pious Israelite kings, who established the seat of their residence and kingdom at Jerusalem? What of Theodosius, who did so at Milan? But, not to seek examples further, what of Constantius, son of Constantine, who by his father's will not only exercised supreme empire and jurisdiction at Rome, but also deposed Pope Liberius from his papacy, and drove him out of the city of Rome, because he had taken up the protection of Anastasius, a certain bishop, a magician and sorcerer? As Theodoret, Sozomen and Ammianus Marcellinus, book 15, have left written.

units.la: XXIV. Sed iam ad institutum reuertamur. Nam ad extremum, sanctio subiicitur horribilis: Siquis, inquiens, ex nostris successoribus temerator aut contemptor extiterit, aeterna damnationi subiaceat innodatus, & in inferno inferiore concrematus cum Diabolo & omnibus impiis deficiat. At ista execratione primus se ipse Constantinus induit, qui, ut modo dicebamus, in suo testamento imperium Occidentis filio suo maximo attribuit: eadem denique execratione, quicunque vel Occidentem, vel Occidentis partem aliquam vel Regio, vel Ducali, vel quouis alio nomine pro suo possedit, obligatus fuit. Neque ista ratione, quisquam antehac vel Galliae, vel Hispaniae Rex fuit, qui non in inferno inferiore vna cum Diabolo & impiis omnibus concremetur.
units.tr: XXIV. But let us now return to our subject. At the very end comes a dreadful sanction: "If anyone of our successors shall prove a violator or despiser, let him be bound and subject to eternal damnation, and let him perish burned in the lowest hell together with the Devil and all the impious." But Constantine himself first bound himself to this curse, for, as we have just said, in his will he assigned the empire of the West to his eldest son. By the same curse, whoever has held the West, or any part of it, whether as king, duke or under any other title, has been bound. Nor, for this reason, has anyone who was king of France or Spain before now escaped being burned in the lowest hell together with the Devil and all the impious.

units.la: xxv.Iam vero ecquis tam imperitus linguae Latinae reperietur, qui non videat, genus dicendi, quo illius instrumenti scriptor est vsus, longissimè ab illius seculi consuetudine abhorrere? quam reprehensionis partem, Platina in illo Sylvestro non praetermisit. Sed fusius persecutus est vir acerrimo in hoc genere iudicio Lauren.Valla.cui utum[?] hoc subiungemus: si quis genus dicedi consideret,quo Constantini leges in Theodosiano & Iustinianica codice scriptæ sunt,eū nullo negotio animaduer-surū, instrumentum hoc ex eadem officina prodi-isse,unde superius Fracifcanicas Coformitates, & Dominicanas fabulas prodijsse demonstrauimus. Neque verò silentio prætereunda est altera nescio cuius fabulatoris improbitas, ac nescio quo tem-pore apud Græcos nata. Nam hoc donationis in-strumentum Græca lingua relatum videmus à Balsamone Photij Nomocanonis scholiastæ,in tit. 8.vbi operæpretium est Græcorum vanitate,simul etiam Italicorum Paparum artes & calliditatem animaduertere,Sic enim Balsamon. Nota, inquit, quod ex præsenti edicto Constantini ius habet Papa Romanus Imperatoriis priuilegiis fruendi, præter solam coronam. & ideo in omnibus,quæ vbique fiunt, processionibus,& diuinis eorum misteriis,regio loco caput eius tegatur:induitur autem etiā veris instrumentis,& more Imperatoris equitat. Eosque qui ei subsunt Imperatoris dignitatibus honorat.Quia autem sancta synodus dedit Archiepiscopo Constantinopolitano omnia Papæ R. priuilegia,conati sunt nonnulli Patriarchæ,vt ille Cerulas,& dominus Michael,& alii, eadem sibi priuilegia arrogare,sed eis non recte cessit. Hæc ad verbū Balsamon ex interpretatione Heruet,Lutetiæ impressa & edita anno 1561. Ex quibus non modo Græcorum leuitatem(vt dixi)& in regali fastu affectando vanitatem licet perspicere: verum etiam Romanorum Paparum astutiam & calliditatem,qui quanto Italiæ artes Græcorum leuitatibus præstent,vel hoc vno in genere ostenderunt.
