Nam hoc falsum instrumentum etiam Græcè convertendum, & per Græciam pro vero & authentico[?] disseminandū curarunt: cùm tamē Cōstātini leges omnes in su-pra dictis Codicibus Theodosiano, & Iustiniani-co, Latina lingua conscriptæ extent: quamuis & Constantinopoli, & Græca vrbe, & apud Græcos ederentur. præterea Eusebius lib. de vita Const. 3. memoriæ prodidit, eū in Synodo Nicæna Latinè verba fecisse. Et lib. 2. testatur, se illius Epistolas & decreta Latinè scripta in Græcum sermonem cō-uertisse. Sed iam de falsitate & impio Paparum de Constantini donatione commento satis videtur dictum: vt perspicuum omnibus esse possit, totum Papatum, qui hoc solo fundamento nitebatur, sub-ruto fundamento, stare diutius non posse.
units.tr: xxv. Now, who is so unskilled in the Latin tongue that he cannot see that the style of writing used by the author of that instrument is far removed from the usage of that age? Platina did not pass over this point in his life of Sylvester. But Lorenzo Valla, the man of sharpest judgment in this kind, has pursued it more fully, and to his work we shall add this: anyone who considers the style in which Constantine's laws are written in the Theodosian and Justinianic codes will without any difficulty notice that this instrument came from the same workshop as the Franciscan Conformities and the Dominican fables, which we have shown above. Nor must the other wickedness of I know not what fabulist, born at I know not what time among the Greeks, be passed over in silence. For we see this instrument of donation rendered into Greek by Balsamon, the scholiast of Photius' Nomocanon, on title 8, where it is worth noting, along with the vanity of the Greeks, also the arts and cunning of the Italian popes. For thus Balsamon: "Note," he says, "that by the present edict of Constantine the Roman Pope has the right to enjoy imperial privileges, except only the crown. Therefore, in all the processions that are held everywhere, and in their divine mysteries, his head is covered in the royal manner. He is also clothed in true imperial garments and rides in the manner of the emperor, and he honours with imperial dignities those who are subject to him." But since the holy synod gave to the Archbishop of Constantinople all the privileges of the Roman Pope, some patriarchs, such as Cerularius, Lord Michael and others, tried to claim the same privileges for themselves, but it did not go well for them. Thus Balsamon, word for word, in the translation of Hervet, printed and published at Lutetia in 1561. From these passages we may see not only the levity of the Greeks (as I have said) and their vanity in affecting royal pomp, but also the craft and cunning of the Roman popes, who by this one thing have shown how far Italian arts surpass Greek levity. For they took care that this false instrument should also be turned into Greek and spread through Greece as genuine and authentic, although all the laws of Constantine are extant in the above-mentioned codes, the Theodosian and the Justinianic, written in the Latin language, even though they were also published at Constantinople, in the Greek city, and among the Greeks. Moreover, Eusebius, in book 3 of the Life of Constantine, has recorded that he spoke in Latin at the Council of Nicaea; and in book 2 he testifies that he himself translated Constantine's letters and decrees, written in Latin, into the Greek language. But enough seems to have been said about the falsity and impious fiction of the popes concerning Constantine's donation, so that it may be plain to everyone that the whole papacy, which rested on this one foundation, cannot stand much longer once that foundation is overthrown.
Another Ancient Crime of Falsehood.

units.la: COmmodissimum tamen videtur, alia quædā Papalium falsitatum ac periuriorum exempla proponere, ac potissimum ea, ex quib. intelligatur, Papam Romanum non modò contra Scripturæ sacræ, verumetiam contra veteris Ecclesiæ primitiuæ auctoritatem tyrannicum istum dominatum affectasse. Nam cùm ambitio ac libido dominandi nonnullos tum Episcopos occupasset, Nicæna Synodus anno Christi cccxxv. coacta est: in qua decretum fuit, vt in quaque pro-vincia siue dioecesi (vtroque enim vocabulo patres illi veteres vtebantur) pastor aliquis, ætate (vt credi par est) & doctrina præstans deligeretur, cui potestas permitteretur, cùm vsus veniret, collegas ad-vocādi, atque ad eos de communium Ecclesiarum negotiis referendi. Hic per ea tempora modo Patriarcha, modo Metropolitanus, modo Archiepiscopus promiscue dicebatur: ita tamen, vt neque minores Episcopi sine huius, neque hic sine illorum consensu atque auctoritate gravius quicqua administraret. Verba Synodi cap. 6. haec tuerunt:
units.tr: It seems most convenient, however, to set out some other examples of Papal falsehoods and perjuries, and especially those from which it may be understood that the Roman Pope aimed at this tyrannical domination not only against the authority of holy Scripture but also against the authority of the primitive, ancient Church. For when ambition and the lust for domination had already seized some bishops, the Nicene Synod was convened in the year of Christ 325. In it, it was decreed that in each province or diocese (for those ancient fathers used both words) some pastor, outstanding in age (as is fitting to believe) and in learning, should be chosen, to whom power would be granted, whenever the need arose, to summon colleagues and to refer to them the affairs of the common Churches. At that time he was called now patriarch, now metropolitan, now archbishop, indiscriminately; yet in such a way that neither the lesser bishops could administer anything of weight without his consent and authority, nor he without theirs. The words of the Synod, canon 6, were these:

units.la: Antiqua consuetudo valeat, quae in Aegypto, Lybia, & Pentapoli fuit, vt Alexandrinus Episcopus super his omnibus auctoritatem habeat, quoniam & Romano Episcopo haec eadem consuetudo est. Similiter autem & apud Antiochiam, & in caeteris provinciis privilegia conferuntur. Illud autem planum est, quod si quis sine consensu Metropolitani fiat Episcopus, hunc magna Synodus statuit Episcopum esse non oportere. Rufinus autē lib. io. Eccles. histor. decretum illud sic interpretatur. Apud Alexandriam, & in urbe Roma haec consuetudo seruetur, vt & ille Aegypti, & hic suburbicarum Ecclesiarum solicitudinem gerat. Ex quibus intelligitur, fines Episcopatus Romani suburbicarū Ecclesiarū terminis à Nicæna Synodo circumscriptos fuisse: tantum abest, vt ei vel principatus, vel auctoritas in omnes orbis totius Ecclesias ab Imperatore Constantino tributum fuerit. Audiamus nunc quid anno post sexto & quinquagesimo in Synodo Constantinopolitana prima eadem de re constitutum fuerit, hoc est, anno Christi cccLxxxi. Nam cap. 2. scriptum ita est: Episcopi quibus sua diæcesis attributa est, ne in Ecclesias quae extra fines suos sunt, se inferant: neue Ecclesias confundat: sed secundum canones, Alexandriae quidem Episcopus ea tantum quae in Aegypto sunt, gubernet. Orientis vero Episcopi solum Orientem administrent. Conseruetur-que sua Ecclesia Antiochina dignitas, quae in Nicæna Synodo declarata est. Et Episcopi Asiæ diœcesis siue præfecturæ, ea tantum quæ in Asia sunt, gubernet: qui in Ponto sunt, quæ in Ponto tantum. Thracii vero ea tantum quæ sunt in Thracia. Episcopi autem nisi aduocati, ne in alienam diœcesim & præfecturam se inferant: siue ad suffragia, siue ad alias ullas administrationes Ecclesiasticas. quod si prædictus canon super præfecturis & diœcesibus conseruetur, perspicuum est, quod cuiusque prouincia negotia unaquæque Synodus prouincialis gubernabit, quemadmodum a Synodo Nicæna constitutum est.
units.tr: "Let the ancient custom prevail which was in Egypt, Libya and Pentapolis, that the Bishop of Alexandria have authority over all these things, since the same custom also belongs to the Roman Bishop. Likewise, at Antioch and in the other provinces, privileges are conferred. But this is plain: if anyone is made bishop without the consent of the metropolitan, the great Synod decrees that such a man ought not to be bishop." Rufinus, however, in book 10 of his Ecclesiastical History, interprets that decree thus: "At Alexandria and in the city of Rome let this custom be kept, that the one bear care for the Churches of Egypt and the other for the suburbicarian Churches." From this it is understood that the boundaries of the Roman bishopric were fixed by the Nicene Synod to the limits of the suburbicarian Churches. So far is it from the case that either principate or authority over all the Churches of the whole world was granted to him by the Emperor Constantine. Let us now hear what was decreed on the same matter in the first Synod of Constantinople, fifty-six years later, that is, in the year of Christ 381. For canon 2 is written thus: "Bishops to whom a diocese has been assigned shall not intrude into churches that lie outside their bounds, nor confound the churches; but according to the canons, the Bishop of Alexandria shall govern only those things which are in Egypt. The bishops of the East shall govern only the East, the Church of Antioch keeping its dignity which was declared in the Nicene Synod. And the bishops of the diocese or prefecture of Asia shall govern only those things which are in Asia; those in Pontus, only those in Pontus; and the Thracian bishops, only those in Thrace. Bishops, unless summoned, shall not intrude into a foreign diocese or prefecture, either for votes or for any other ecclesiastical administration. And if this canon concerning prefectures and dioceses is kept, it is plain that each provincial synod shall govern the affairs of its own province, as was decreed by the Nicene Synod."

units.la: Quinetiam Socrates libro hiftor. Ecclefiaft. 3. his eandem rem confirmat verbis. Rursus fidem à Nicæna Synodo traditam confirmarunt, & Patriarchas de-scriptis prouinciis constituerunt: vt Episcopi certa diœcesi præpositi in alienas ecclesias ne inuaderet. Et mox, Conseruantes tamen primum honoris & dignitatis gradum Antiochorum Ecclesiæ, quæ ei qui tunc aderat Miletio dederunt. Statuerunt autem, vt quoties res postularet,de cuiusque prouincia negotiis cuiusque prouinciæ Synodus constitueret. Hæc Socrates. Atque illam i-psam Ecclesiarum descriptionem videre licet ab Imperatore Gratiano, Valentiniano & Theodosio traditam, & constitutam in l. 3. C. Theodo. de fide Cothol.Eat nunc Romanus Episcopus, & sibi principatum in omnes vniuersi orbis Ecclesias, & nominatim in sedem Antiochinam, Hierofoly-mitanam, Alexandrinam & Constantinopolitanā ab Imp. Constātino tributam fuisse glorictur. Nā hunc Ecclesiæ primitiuę statum, & conditionem usque ad annum Christi cccxxci.fuisse demonstra-uimus. Quinetiam eiusdem Synodi c. 5.ita scriptū est. Constantinopolitanus Episcopus habeat primatum honoris post Romanum Episcopum, quia ipsa est noua Roma. Roma.quod etiam relatum est,dist.22. c. Constantinopolitanæ. Vbi nuper Papa Gregorius xii i.in suo decreto interpolato, annotauit,canonem illū à Romana sede receptum non fuisse. Nec mirum: cum eo canone Papatus manifestæ falsitatis conuictus esset. Sed quid Imp. Iustinia-no respondebit,qui in l.24. C. de sacrof. ecclef. ita loquitur, Constantinopolitana ecclesia omnium aliarum est caput?itemImp.Zeno,qui in l. decernimus,16.C.eod.tit.decreuit,ut eadem Constantinopolitana ecclesia quoniam in vrbe regia est,auctoritatem ac dignitatem habeat aliis omnibus ecclesiis superiorem? Audiamus etiam Ioann. Chry-sostomi hac de re iudicium, qui circiter annum Christi ccc. floruit, & primatū illum Antiochinę Ecclesiæ perspicuè vindicat, his verbis, hom. 3. ad populum Antiochin. Ciuitatum omnium Antiochina nostra Christo est optatissima: & sicut Petrus inter Apostolos primus Christum prædicauit, sic inter ciuitates (sicut iam prædixi) hæc prima tanquam coronâ quandam admirabilem Christianorum tenet appellationem. Item, Homil. 16. Quæ vero est ciuitatis nostræ dignitas? contigit primum Antiochiæ discipulos appellari Christianos. hoc autem ciuitatum quæ sunt in mundo ciuitas habet nulla, neque ipsa Romuli ciuitas: propterea contra omnem terrarum orbem Antiochia oculos erigere potest.Atque hæc quidem (ut dixi) temporum illorum conditio fuit, cum Papa Rom. ab illa tyrannide, quam postea in Ecclesia occupauit, longè longéque abesset. Nunc, quid posterius observatum fuerit, consideremus. Nam in Synodo E-phesina,quæ quinquaginta pòst annis,hoc est anno Christi cccc xxx. habita est,cap. postremo,ita scriptum est. Visum est sancta & universali Synodo, seruando unicuique provincia pura & integraura[?], quae ad ipsam pridem & ab initio pertinent, secundum mo-rem qui iam pridem obtinuit,&c. Vbi est ille summus super universi mundi Ecclesias tributus Papae Rom. ab Imp.Constantino principatus? Audiamus insequentem universalem Synodum, xx. post annis, hoc est anno Christi CCCCLI. Chalcedone con-gregatam. Nam cum Episcopus Constantinopo-litanus propter Orientalis Imperij sedem, in urbe sua collocatam, pari eodemque ambitionis mor-bo, quo noster Romanus laboraret, artibus ac tech-nis suis perfecit, ut ea Metropolis, quae tantam dignitatem haberet, ius quoddam praeter caeteras ob-tineret: atque ut ipse Asiae, Ponti, & Thraciae Me-tropolitas solus constitueret. Unde accidebat, ut Ecclesiae Antiochinae auctoritas tantopere a Chryso-stomo celebrata, & Nicaena primum, tum deinde Constantinopolitana Synodo constituta funditus everteretur. Simul his artibus effectum est, ut Quatuor viri regundo terrarum orbi crearentur, qui Metropolitas suae praefecturae subiectos haberent.
units.tr: Socrates too, in book 3 of his Ecclesiastical History, confirms the same matter in these words: "Again they confirmed the faith handed down by the Nicene Synod, and appointed the patriarchs by describing the provinces, so that a bishop set over a certain diocese should not encroach upon foreign churches." And soon after: "Yet they preserved first the grade of honour and dignity to the Church of Antioch, which they gave to Meletius, who was then present. They also decreed that, whenever the matter required it, a synod should settle the affairs of each province." Thus Socrates. And that same description of the Churches may be seen as handed down by the emperors Gratian, Valentinian and Theodosius, and established in law 3 of the Theodosian Code, on the Catholic faith. Let the Roman bishop now boast that a principate over all the Churches of the whole world, and by name over the seats of Antioch, Jerusalem, Alexandria and Constantinople, was granted to him by the Emperor Constantine. For we have shown that this state and condition of the primitive Church lasted until the year of Christ 325. Moreover, canon 3 of the same Synod is written thus: "The Bishop of Constantinople shall have the primacy of honour after the Roman Bishop, because it is New Rome." This is also cited in dist. 22, c. Constantinopolitanae. There Pope Gregory XIII recently, in his interpolated decree, noted that this canon was not received by the Roman see. No wonder: by that canon the papacy is convicted of manifest falsehood. But what will the Emperor Justinian answer, who in law 24 C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis says: "The Church of Constantinople is the head of all other churches"? Likewise the Emperor Zeno, who in law 16, "Decernimus," C. of the same title, decreed that the same Church of Constantinople, since it is in the royal city, should have authority and dignity superior to all other churches? Let us also hear John Chrysostom's judgment on this matter. He flourished about the year of Christ 300 and clearly claims that primacy for the Church of Antioch, in these words, homily 3 to the people of Antioch: "Our city of Antioch is most desirable to Christ, and as Peter among the apostles first preached Christ, so among cities (as I have already said) this one holds the first place, like a certain admirable crown, in the name of Christians." Also homily 16: "What then is the dignity of our city? It came to pass first at Antioch that the disciples were called Christians. This city has no equal among the cities of the world, not even the city of Romulus; therefore Antioch can lift its eyes against the whole orb of the earth." These, as I have said, were the conditions of those times, when the Roman Pope was far, far removed from that tyranny which he later seized in the Church. Now let us consider what was observed afterwards. For in the Synod of Ephesus, which was held fifty years later, that is, in the year of Christ 430, it is written at the end of the last chapter: "It seemed good to the holy and universal Synod, preserving to each province its pure and entire rights, which from of old and from the beginning belong to it, according to the custom that has long prevailed," and so on. Where, then, is that supreme principate over the Churches of the whole world which the Emperor Constantine is said to have granted to the Roman Pope? Let us hear the next universal Synod, twenty years later, that is, in the year of Christ 451, assembled at Chalcedon. For the Bishop of Constantinople, on account of the seat of the Eastern Empire established in his city, laboured with the same ambitious disease from which our Roman suffered, and by his arts and devices brought it about that this metropolis, which had so great a dignity, should obtain a certain right above the others, and that he alone should appoint the metropolitans of Asia, Pontus and Thrace. Hence it came about that the authority of the Church of Antioch, so greatly celebrated by Chrysostom and established first by the Nicene and then by the Constantinopolitan Synod, was utterly overthrown. At the same time, by these arts, it was brought about that four men were created to rule the orb of the earth, each having metropolitans subject to his prefecture.

units.la: Nam Alexandrino Africa, Occidens Romano, Constantinopolitano vero pars illa Europae & Asiae prope tota tributa est, praeter per paucas Ecclesias, quae Hierosolymitano propter antiquitatem & auctoritatem vrbis, quasi dicis causa, relictae sunt. Itaque cum olim Archiepiscopi, Patriarchae, & Metropolitae iidem essent, totidemque nominibus promiscue appellarentur, deinceps Archiepiscopi (qui Patriarchae quoque dicti sunt) quatuor tantum facti sunt, qui Metropolitanis, ut diximus, praesent.
units.tr: For Africa was assigned to the Alexandrian see, the West to the Roman, and to the Constantinopolitan almost all of that part of Europe and Asia, except for a few churches which were left to Jerusalem, for the antiquity and authority of that city, as a mere formality. So although archbishops, patriarchs and metropolitans were once the same men and were called by all these names interchangeably, afterwards only four archbishops (who were also called patriarchs) were made, who presided over the metropolitans, as we have said.

units.la: Nam cap. illius Synodi 28. scriptum ita est: Vbique leges sanctorum patrum nostrorum sequentes, eadem & nos definimus, ac statuimus de dignitate atque præstatia huius sanctis. Ecclesiæ Constantinopolis, nouæ Romæ. Etenim sedi antiquioris Romæ, quia tũ ciuitas illa regnabat, patres nostri merito primum honoris gradum tribuerunt. Atque eádem consideratione moti CL. Deo amantissimi Episcopi parem honoris gradum tribuerunt nouæ Romæ (notentur hęc verba) sedi sanctissimæ: merito decernentes, ut ea ciuitas, quæ tantum honorem adepta est, ut & sedes esset Imperii, & Senatum haberet, & parē dignitatis gradum obtineret, atque antiqua sedes Imperii Rom. obtinet: etiam in Ecclesiasticis negotiis parem atque illa honorem & dignitatem obtineat, cū post illa secunda sit. Ubi tum ille Romani Papæ principatus ac dominatus summus latebat, quę Imp. Constā-tinus ei super omnes Ecclesias tribuisse dicitur? Audiamus verba secundę Synodi Cōstantinopo-litanæ, ex cap. 36. Renouantes quæ à CL. Patribus qui in hac à Deo seruata & regia urbe conuentum egerunt, & sexcetorū triginta, qui Chalcedone cōgregati fuerūt instituta sūt, definimus, ut Constantinopolis sedes parē habeat dignitatem sedi antiquioris Romæ, & in Ecclesiasticis negotiis æque atque illa magnificetur, (Notentur hæc verba) cum sit post ipsa secunda: post eā autē Alexandrinæ magnæ urbis, & post hæc Hierosolymorum Episcopus succedat. Sed post ea sensim Archiepiscoporum numerus Imperatorum arbitrio adauctus est, nam Imperator Iustinianus Iustinianæ urbi, suæ patriæ, honore illū tribuit Nouel. xi. ubi sic scribit multis & variis modis patria nostra augere cupientes, in qua Deus præstitit nobis ad hunc mundū venire, iubemus ut eius sacrosanctus antistes non solū Metropolitanus, sed etiā Archiepiscopus fiat, & certa provinciæ sub eius sint auctoritate: id est, Dacia mediterranea, Dacia Ripensis, Mysia secunda, & Dardania, & Pra-ualitana,&c.Item ad extremum:Archiepiscopum eius à venerabili concilio Metropolitanorum ordinari sancimus,Fuerunt & aliæ eodem nomine vrbes, Iusti-nianæ dictæ:in Africa, Iustiniana Carthaginensis: quam idem Imp. Romano imperio adiunxerat: in Cypro infula,Iustiniana, Theodoræ vxoris eiusdē patria: quibus parem iuris,honoris, & dignitatis prærogatiua Iustinianus tribuit.Ex his igitur multiplex Paparum Romanorum impudentia perspicitur:primùm in eo quòd quatuor tantùm Patriarchias siue Archiepiscopales sedes per ea tempora numerant:tum in eo, quòd suam sedem illis quatuor sedibus superiorem faciùt,& sibi in illas principatum ac iurisdictionem arrogant:deinde, quòd illorum patriarcharum ius ac potestatem sibi asciscunt.cùm euidentissimè appareat, Imperatorum illam auctoritatem ac potestatem fuisse.Quæ omnia quo planiùs ac dilucidiùs cognoscantur, vnico insuper eiusdem Iustiniani testimonio contenti erimus:cuius in Nouella 123.verba hæc sunt, Latinè à Iuliano antecessore conuersa. Iubemus igitur beatissimos quidem Patriarchas, id est, Papam Romanum & Constantinopolitanum & Alexandrinum & Theopolitanum,id est,Antiochinum, & Hierosolymitanum, siquidem consuetudo est,&c. Et mox, Metropolitanos autem,qui à consilio suo vel beatissimis Patriarchis, vel à Metropolitanis consecrantur.&c.Itè Nou.131. Papa Romanus, inquit, prior omnibus Episcopis & Patriarchis sedeat: & post illum Constantinopolitanæ ciuitatis Episcopus:Archiepiscopus primæ Iustinianæ habeat sibi subiectos Episcopos Dacia Mediterranea, & Dacia Ripensis,itemPrænalenos,& Dardania, & Mysia superioris,& Pannonia:sed & ille ab ipsis consecretur, & eadem iura super eos habeat, quæ Papa Romanus habet super Episcopos sibi suppositos. Perspicuum est igitur, primis Christianæ libertatis temporibus quatuor tantùm Patriarchas fuisse, pari omnes honore, dignitate, iurisdictione, auctoritate, gradu: nisi quòd in Synodis vniuersalibus Romanis, propter veterem veteris Romæ dignitatem, primus cōside-bat: deinde Patriarcharū numerum auctum fuisse, non à Papa Romano, sed ab Imperatore Romano: vt essent quinque, tum sex, tum septem, tum ad ex-tremum octo. tot enim sub Iustiniano numeraui-mus. Ex quibus simul animaduerti volumus, insignem Romani Papæ in illo Synodi Constantinopolitanæ cap.36. corrumpendo fraudem atque impudentiam. Nam apud Gratianum dist. 22.c. renouantes, verba Synodi Græca ita verterunt: Rènouantes sancti Constantinopolitani decreta concilii, petimus (imò Definimus, ὁρίζομεν ) vt Constantinopolitana sedes similia priuilegia quæ superior Roma habet accipiat. Non tamen in Ecclesiasticis rebus magnificetur vt illa: sed hæc secunda post illam existens, prius quam Alexandrina sedes numeretur, deinde Antiochena, & post eam Hierosolymitana. De qua falsitate ne cui dubiū esse possit, Græca ipsa verba proferemus: ὁρίζομεν ὡς τὸν κωνσταντινουπόλεως ὅρον τῶν ἴσων ἀπολαβεῖν πρεσβείων τῆς τῆς πρεσβυτέρας Ρώμης θρόνῳ, ἐν τοῖς ἐκκλησιαστικοῖς ὡς ἐκεῖ-νον μεγαλύνεσθαι πράγμασι. Verùtamè, dixerit fortasse quispiam, mendum istud nuper in editione Papæ Gregorij xiii. sublatum est, &, pro Non tamen, repositū Necnon. Præclarè. Nam ista ratione primum fateri Papa cogitur, apertissimæ se falsitatis conui-ctum esse: eáque falsitate & corruptela per annos amplius cccc.ad fallendam Christianā Ecclesiam improbè ac veteratorie usum esse. Præterea nũquã illam falsitatémque correcturum fuisse, nisi à nostris iam pridem falsi accusatus & convictus fuisset. Sed quid respodebit vel Gregorius xiii.vel Sixtus noster de iterata, & renovata hac eadem falsitate in c.antiqua,extra de privileg.ubi turpior etiã impostura commissa est,his verbis. Antiqua Patriarchaliũ sedium privilegia renovantes sancimus,ut post Romana Ecclesiam( quæ disponente domino super omnes alias ordinariæ potestatis obtinet principatum, utpote mater u-niversorum fidelium & magistra ) Constantinopolitana primum, Alexandrina secundum, Antiochina tertium, Hierosolymitana quartum locum obtineat: servata cuilibet propria dignitate: ita quòd postquam antistites eorum à R.Pontifice receperint pallium( quod est plenitudinis officii Pontificalis insigne)præstito sibi fidelitatis & obedientiæ juramento,licenter,&c. Ecquis est vel tam ferreo pectore, vel tam vecordi mente, quem ista tanta Paparum in corrumpedis Ecclesiæ Christianæ monimentis impudentia non moveat? Ecquis est,ex illo Jurisconsultorum numero,qui in illustri-bus parlamentis senatores sedent, qui constitutionem illã Imp.Zenonis,Conciliis illis antiquis consentaneã quã superius cõmemoravimus,nõ legerit, & ex ea Paparũ falsitate non animadverterit in l.de cernimus 16. C.de sacros.eccles. in qua scriptum ita est:Sacrosanctã huius Constãtinopolitanę civitatis ecclesiam , & matrem nostræ pietatis & Christianorum Orthodoxę religionis omnium,& eiusdem regiæ urbis sanctissimam sedem, privilegia & honores omnes super Episcoporum creationibus,& jure ante alios residendi, & cętera omnia, quæ ante nostrum imperium, vel nobis imperantib᷑s habuisse dignoscitur, habere in perpetuum firmiter, regiæ v᷑bis intuitu, iudicamus & sancimus. Q᷑inetiam, extat sub eod. tit. in l. 24. altera Iustiniani sanctio, vererib᷑us il᷑is conciliis æque consentanea, his verbis. ... id est, Constatinopolitana ecclesia omnium aliarum est caput. Item in Photij Nomocanone, & apud Balsamonem tit. 8. retertur hæc lex posita in lib. Basilic. 54. tit. 5. c. 3. ... Cōstantinopolis non solùm Italiæ, sed etiam ipsius Romæ priuilegiis fruitur. Ex quibus tum singulis tum vniuersis Paparum falsitas manifestò deprehenditur, qui ex donatione Imp. Constantini contendebant, principatum sedi suæ tributum super omnes Christiani orbis ecclesias: vti superius idoneo loco demonstrauimus. Neque verò consimilis altera impudetia silentio præterevnda est, ex c. placuit, 2. q. 6. Nam cùm in synodo Carthaginensi sexta, cui B. Augustinus interfuit, cap. 105. decretum aduersus Papam R. fuisset, ne ad ipsius Sedem ex transmarinis Ecclesiis prouocaretur: si quis prouocare auderet, anathema esset: tamen idem Papa in illo c. placuit, post hæc verba: Ad transmarina autem, qui putauerit appellandum, à nullo intra Africam in communione recipiatur: impudenter hanc exceptionem subiunxit, Nisi forte Romanam sedem appellauerit: vbi nuper Gregorius. XIII. perfidiosæ falsitatis atque imposturæ manifestò conuictus, hanc excusationem adiecit, Hæc in antiquis Codicibus scribuntur tanquam Grætiani verba.Præclarè rursus. Nam hoc modo into-leranda Paparum Rom. impudentia perspicitur, qui non modò decretum data opera contra ipsorum ambitionem scriptum illa exceptione corruperunt, verùm etiam per annos amplius quadringentos, usque dum à nostris illa falsitas atque impostura patefacta est, illo mendacio Christianam Ecclesiam circumuenerunt. Et quoniam Gallis nostris hæc potissimùm à nobis opera navatur, non alienum erit ex Doctore Bernardo quid aliquando Lutetiæ Parisiorum ex hac Romanarum appellationum ambitione accidèrit[?], verbis ipsius exponere, ex lib. de consideratione 3.Parisiis, inquit, contigit hoc, nobili Galliarum civitate, sede Regia. Quidam sibi publicè desponsaverat uxorem: adest dies celebris nuptiarum, parata omnia, invitati multi: & ecce homo concupiscens uxorem proximi sui, in vocem appellationis inopinatæ prorumpit, affirmans sibi traditam prius suam potius esse debere. Stupet sponsus, hærent aures, sacerdos non audet progredi, frustratur omnis apparatus ille, descendit quisque in domum suam, suam cœnam manducaturus. Sponsa à mensa & thalamo sponsi suspenditur, quousque Roma reditum est. Rursus in eadem Parisiorum civitate quidam sibi desponsata uxore diem constituit nuptiarum: interim emergit calumnia, dicentibus quibusdam, non debere coniungi. Ad judicium Ecclesiæ causa delata est. Sed non expectata sententia appellatum est. At ille nihilominus, quod propositum erat, contempta, sive dissimulata appellatione peregit. Age, posterioris temporis ratione consideremus. Nā anno ccccxxcv. Carthaginensis synodus, eáque universalis habita est, ad quā Episcopus Rō. tres legatos, Faustinū, Philippū, & Asellū, cū his mādatis misit, ut jus suae Sedi à synodo Nicæna tributum, nimirùm vt ab omnibus metropolitanis ad illum appellaretur, sibi conseruaretur. Tum repentè scriba, nomine Daniel, iussus est de scripto mandata illa recitare: ac simul caput illud synodi Nicænæ, quod Papa Rom. illis pro causæ suæ instrumento adiunxerat. Recitatum est quintum caput integrum synodi Sardicensis, quod Episcopus Rom. fraudulenter ac malitiosè pro Nicæna synodo supposuerat. Omnes qui tum aderant Episcopi & Archiepiscopi negarunt id se vnquam in Synodo Nicæna legisse. Itaque placuit, vt exemplar Nicænæ synodi, quod tum erat in manibus, recitaretur. Verbū de appellatione nullum.
units.tr: For chapter 28 of that synod reads as follows: In everything, following the laws of our holy fathers, we likewise define and decree the same concerning the dignity and pre-eminence of this most holy Church of Constantinople, New Rome. For the fathers rightly gave the first place of honour to the see of older Rome, because that city was then the seat of empire. And moved by the same consideration, the one hundred and fifty most God-beloved bishops gave an equal place of honour to the most holy see of New Rome (let these words be noted), rightly decreeing that the city which has obtained such honour, being both the seat of the empire and possessing a Senate, and enjoying an equal rank of dignity with the ancient seat of the Roman Empire, should also in ecclesiastical affairs have honour and dignity equal to that city's, since it is second after it. Where then was that supreme primacy and lordship of the Roman Pope, which Emperor Constantine is said to have granted him over all churches? Let us hear the words of the Second Synod of Constantinople, from chapter 36. Renewing what was established by the one hundred and fifty fathers who met in this God-preserved and imperial city, and by the six hundred and thirty who were gathered at Chalcedon, we define that the see of Constantinople shall have equal privileges with the see of older Rome, and shall be magnified equally with it in ecclesiastical affairs (let these words be noted), since it is second after it; and after it the bishop of the great city of Alexandria shall follow, and after him the bishop of Jerusalem. But after this, the number of archbishops was gradually increased at the will of the emperors. For the Emperor Justinian gave that honour to Justiniana, the city of his own homeland, in Novel 11, where he writes thus: Desiring to enlarge our homeland in many and various ways, in which God granted us to come into this world, we command that its most holy bishop shall be made not only a metropolitan but also an archbishop, and that certain provinces shall be under his authority: namely, Dacia Mediterranea, Dacia Ripensis, Moesia Secunda, Dardania, and Praevalitana, etc. Again at the end: We decree that its archbishop shall be ordained by the venerable council of metropolitans. There were also other cities of the same name, called Justiniana: in Africa, Justiniana Carthaginensis, which the same emperor had added to the Roman Empire; in the island of Cyprus, Justiniana, the homeland of his wife Theodora. To these Justinian gave an equal prerogative of right, honour and dignity. From these facts, then, the manifold impudence of the Roman Popes is plain: first, in that they count only four patriarchal or archiepiscopal sees at that time; then, in that they make their own see superior to those four sees and arrogate to themselves primacy and jurisdiction over them; and lastly, in that they claim for themselves the right and power of those patriarchs, although it is most evident that this authority and power belonged to the emperors. That all these things may be known more plainly and clearly, we shall be content with one further testimony of the same Justinian, whose words in Novel 123, translated into Latin by the jurist Julian, are these: We therefore command that the most blessed patriarchs, that is, the Roman Pope, the Constantinopolitan, the Alexandrian, the Theopolitan, that is the Antiochene, and the Jerusalemite, should be so called, since such is the custom, etc. And soon after: But the metropolitans, who are consecrated either by his council or by the most blessed patriarchs, or by the metropolitans, etc. Likewise Novel 131: The Roman Pope, he says, shall sit first among all bishops and patriarchs; and after him the bishop of the city of Constantinople; the archbishop of Justiniana Prima shall have as subject to him the bishops of Dacia Mediterranea and Dacia Ripensis, likewise of Praevalitana, and of Dardania, and of Upper Moesia, and of Pannonia; and he too shall be consecrated by them, and shall have over them the same rights which the Roman Pope has over the bishops subject to him. It is therefore clear that in the first times of Christian liberty there were only four patriarchs, all equal in honour, dignity, jurisdiction, authority and rank, except that in the universal synods the Roman one sat first, on account of the ancient dignity of old Rome. Then the number of patriarchs was increased, not by the Roman Pope but by the Roman Emperor, so that there were five, then six, then seven, and at last eight; for so many we counted under Justinian. From these things we also wish it to be noticed how remarkable was the fraud and impudence of the Roman Pope in corrupting chapter 36 of that Synod of Constantinople. For in Gratian, Dist. 22, c. Renovantes, they translated the Greek words of the synod thus: Renewing the decrees of the holy council of Constantinople, we ask (nay, we define [ὁρίζομεν]) that the see of Constantinople should receive similar privileges to those which superior Rome has. Yet it shall not be magnified in ecclesiastical affairs as that one is, but, being second after it, shall be counted before the see of Alexandria, then Antioch, and after it Jerusalem. That there may be no doubt about this falsehood, we shall set out the Greek words themselves: we define that the see of Constantinople shall receive equal privileges with the see of elder Rome, and be magnified equally with it in ecclesiastical affairs [ὁρίζομεν ὡς τὸν κωνσταντινουπόλεως ὅρον τῶν ἴσων ἀπολαβεῖν πρεσβείων τῆς τῆς πρεσβυτέρας Ρώμης θρόνῳ, ἐν τοῖς ἐκκλησιαστικοῖς ὡς ἐκεῖνον μεγαλύνεσθαι πράγμασι]. But perhaps someone will say that this error has recently been removed in the edition of Pope Gregory XIII, and that, in place of Non tamen, Necnon has been put back. Splendid! For by this reasoning the Pope is first forced to admit that he has been convicted of most manifest falsehood, and that for more than four hundred years he used that falsehood and corruption, craftily and dishonestly, to deceive the Christian Church. Moreover, he would never have corrected that falsehood, unless he had long since been accused and convicted of falsehood by our side. But what will either Gregory XIII or our Sixtus reply concerning this same falsehood, repeated and renewed in c. Antiqua, Extra, de privilegiis, where an even more shameful imposture was committed, in these words? Renewing the ancient privileges of the patriarchal sees, we decree that after the Roman Church (which, by the disposition of the Lord, holds the primacy of ordinary power over all other churches, as the mother and teacher of all the faithful), the Church of Constantinople shall hold the first place, Alexandria the second, Antioch the third, and Jerusalem the fourth; each keeping its own dignity; so that, after their bishops have received the pallium from the Roman Pontiff (which is the badge of the fullness of the pontifical office), having sworn to him an oath of fidelity and obedience, they may freely, etc. Is there anyone with a heart so iron-hard, or a mind so senseless, that such great impudence of the Popes in corrupting the monuments of the Christian Church does not move him? Is there anyone, from that number of jurists who sit as senators in the famous parliaments, who has not read that constitution of the Emperor Zeno, agreeing with those ancient councils, which we mentioned above, and who has not noticed from it the falsehood of the Popes, in law De cernimus, 16, C. De sacrosanctis ecclesiis, in which it is written thus: We judge and decree, out of regard for this imperial city, that the holy church of this city of Constantinople, the mother of our piety and of all Christians of the orthodox religion, and the most holy see of this same royal city, shall firmly hold in perpetuity all privileges and honours concerning the creation of bishops, and the right of sitting before all others, and all other things which are known to have been held before our empire, or under our emperors. Moreover, under the same title, in law 24, there is another sanction of Justinian, equally agreeing with those ancient councils, in these words: ... that is, the Church of Constantinople is the head of all the others. Likewise in Photius's Nomocanon, and in Balsamon, title 8, this law is cited, which stands in the Basilica, book 54, title 5, chapter 3: ... Constantinople enjoys privileges not only over Italy, but also over Rome itself. From these things, both taken singly and taken together, the falsehood of the Popes is manifestly exposed, for they contended that the primacy over all the churches of the Christian world had been granted to their see from the donation of the Emperor Constantine, as we have shown above in a suitable place. Nor must another, similar impudence be passed over in silence, from c. Placuit, 2, q. 6. For when, in the Sixth Synod of Carthage, at which the blessed Augustine was present, it had been decreed in chapter 105 against the Roman Pope that no one should appeal to his see from the churches beyond the sea, and that if anyone dared to appeal he should be anathema; yet the same Pope, in that chapter Placuit, after these words: But whoever thinks he should appeal to the churches beyond the sea shall not be received into communion by anyone within Africa, impudently added this exception: Unless perhaps he has appealed to the Roman see. Here Gregory XIII, having been manifestly convicted of perfidious falsehood and imposture, has added this excuse: These words are written in the ancient codices as the words of Gratian. Splendid again! For in this way is seen the intolerable impudence of the Roman Popes, who not only corrupted, with deliberate purpose and by that exception, a decree written against their own ambition, but also for more than four hundred years, until that falsehood and imposture was exposed by our people, deceived the Christian Church with that lie. And since this work is undertaken chiefly by us for our Frenchmen, it will not be out of place to set out, in the words of Doctor Bernard, from his book On Consideration, book 3, what once happened at Paris, in the city of Lutetia, from this ambition of Roman appeals. It happened, he says, at Paris, the noble city of the Gauls and seat of the king. A certain man had publicly betrothed a wife to himself; the day of the famous wedding arrived, everything was prepared, many guests were invited; and behold, a man coveting his neighbour's wife burst out with an unexpected cry of appeal, asserting that she had been given to him before and ought rather to be his. The bridegroom was astonished, their ears were struck, the priest did not dare to go on, all that preparation came to nothing, and each went down to his own house to eat his supper. The bride was kept from the table and the bed of her husband until the matter was referred back to Rome. Again, in the same city of Paris, a certain man, having betrothed a wife to himself, fixed a day for the wedding; meanwhile a false accusation arose, some saying that they ought not to be joined. The case was brought before the judgment of the Church. But before the sentence was awaited, an appeal was made. Yet he nevertheless carried out what he had proposed, disregarding or ignoring the appeal. Come, let us consider the matter from a later period. For in the year 425 the Council of Carthage was held, and it was a universal one. To it the Roman bishop sent three legates, Faustinus, Philip and Asellus, with these instructions: that the right granted to his see by the Council of Nicaea, namely that appeals should be made to him from all metropolitans, should be preserved for him. Then suddenly a scribe named Daniel was ordered to read aloud those instructions from the document, and at the same time that chapter of the Council of Nicaea which the Roman Pope had added to them as the instrument for his cause. The fifth chapter of the Council of Sardica was read out in full, which the Roman bishop had fraudulently and maliciously put forward in place of the Council of Nicaea. All the bishops and archbishops who were present then denied that they had ever read that in the Council of Nicaea. So it was agreed that the copy of the Council of Nicaea which was then at hand should be read. There was no word at all about appeal.

units.la: Decretum fit, vt certi homines Constantinopolim, Antiochiam, Alexandriam, Romam denique mitterentur, qui alia exemplaria Nicænæ synodi asportarent, sed maximè Constantinopolim: vbi authoritas ipsa, siue ἀνθέντικὸν Nicænæ Synodi asseruabatur. Anno vertente allata sunt.
units.tr: It was decreed that certain men should be sent to Constantinople, Antioch, Alexandria and finally Rome to bring back other copies of the Nicene Synod, but chiefly to Constantinople, where the authority itself, the authentic copy [ἀνθέντικον] of the Nicene Synod, was kept. Within the year they were brought.

units.la: Recitata, Nulla deinceps Episcopi Rom. priuilegio ac præcipuo iure suspicio. Scribitur epistola de communi patrum sententia Rom. Episcopo. Nusquam illud in Nicæna synodo repertum: imò ex contrario, in illa ipsa synodo decretū, vt ipse suis se finibus, item vt alij Papæ & Metropolitani, contineret. Quare si saperet, deinceps sua diœcesi & præfectura contentus esset: neque in alienam possessionem inuaderet.
units.tr: Read out: henceforth there is to be no suspicion of any privilege or special right of the Bishop of Rome. A letter is written to the Bishop of Rome in the name of the common opinion of the Fathers. Nowhere is this found in the Nicene Synod; on the contrary, that same synod decreed that he himself should keep within his own bounds, and likewise the other Popes and Metropolitans. Therefore, if he were wise, he would from then on be content with his own diocese and jurisdiction, and would not invade another's possession.

units.la: Huic sententiæ subscripserunt ducenti & triginta patres in iis, illi ipsi quos antea nominauimus, Faustinus Episcopus Potentinæ Ecclesiæ, legatus Episcopi R. Philippus, Presbyter & legatus Episcopi R. Asfellus presbyter, & eiusdem episcopi legatus. Quin-etiam illius Nicænorum patrum decreti quatuor hasce causas Synodus adscripsit,quas non alienum est exponere.Prudentissime,inquiût,iustissimeque Nicaeni patres prouiderunt,quocunque negotia in suis locis, vbi orta essent,finienda:nec vnicuique prouinciae gratia spiritus Sancti defuturam, qua aequitas a Christi sacerdotibus & prudenter videatur,& constantissime tenea-tur:maxime,quia vnicuique concessum est,si iudicio offensus fuerit cognitorum ad concilia suae prouinciae vel etiam vniuersale prouocare, nisi forte quisquam est,qui credat,Deum uni alicui cognitionis & examinis inspirare iustitiam, innumerabilibus autem in synodo congregatis sacerdotibus denegare. Aut quomodo ipsum transmarinum iudicium ratum erit, ad quod testium necessariae personae vel propter sexus, vel propter senectutis infirmitatem,vel multis aliis interuenientibus impedimentis adduci non poterunt?
units.tr: Two hundred and thirty fathers subscribed to this sentence, among them those same men we named earlier: Faustinus, Bishop of the church of Potentia, legate of the Bishop of Rome; Philip, presbyter and legate of the Bishop of Rome; and Asfellus, presbyter and legate of the same bishop. Moreover, the Synod appended to that decree of the Nicene fathers four reasons, which it is not out of place to set out. "Most prudently and most justly," it says, "did the Nicene fathers provide that matters be settled in their own places, where they arose; nor will the grace of the Holy Spirit fail any province, by which equity may be seen and firmly kept by the priests of Christ; especially since it has been granted to each man that, if he is offended by the judgement of those who heard his case, he may appeal to the councils of his own province or even to the universal one, unless perhaps there is someone who believes that God inspires justice and judgement in one single man, but denies it to the countless priests gathered in a synod." Or how will that judgement across the sea be valid, to which the necessary witnesses cannot be brought, whether because of their sex, or the infirmity of old age, or many other hindrances intervening?

units.la: De legatis autem illis tribus,Faustino præsertim, graues querimoniae in iisdem literis perscriptae sunt, quòd conuentui magnas molestias exhibuissent, cùm simularent se Rom. Ecclesiae priuilegia defendere. Videmus igitur Rom. Papae iam tùm per illud tempus patefactam improbitatem, perfidiam, falsitatem, impudentiam atq; aperte ab vniuersali synodo conuictam & condemnatam. Ecquid illum sublatis omnibus ex Africa & Asia suis vel aemulis vel certe riuali-bus fecisse arbitramur, vt potentia iam tum illis tē[?] poribus affectatam in Occidente suo constabiliret? Verùm hæc quidem hactenus de prima Nullitatis causa, & iudicis incompetentia dicta sint: quæ tamen quò magis apud clarissimos Parlamentorum regiorū senatores, & alios iurisperitos testata esse possint, authoritate Doctorum confirmabimus. Ac primùm illa peruulgata Canonistarum sententia, Papæ[?] etiam in solo hæresis crimine non esse idoneū iu-dicem,sed ab aliis iudicari oportere.c. si Papa,dist. 40.Quo casu Philippus Decius fortiter contendit, concilium auctoritate Papæ non esse congregan-dum,in c.cum venissent,num.37.extr.de iudic. Ite, Panormit. & Decius in c.significasti, num. 4. & num.9.de electi.Sed omnium copiosissimè & doctissimè Lud.Rom.in consil.vlt.num.15.&seqq.vbi ex ipsius Decreti auctoritate contendit,eum Papa qui rebelliter viuit, & discere atque agere bona re cusat,magis esse membrum diaboli,quàm Christi: & potiùs infidelē,quàm fidelem monstrari.c.nullus,dist.38.Idem,Iason in conf.95.requisitus,vol.4. Decius conf.115.quorum verba,posterius,magis i-doneo loco,proferentur.
units.tr: Concerning those three legates, and Faustinus especially, grave complaints are written in the same letters, that they caused great trouble to the assembly while pretending to defend the privileges of the Roman Church. We see, then, that the wickedness, perfidy, falsehood and impudence of the Bishop of Rome were already exposed at that time, and openly convicted and condemned by the universal synod. What do we suppose he did, having removed from Africa and Asia all his rivals or at least his competitors, so that he might establish in the West the power he was already then aiming at? But these things have so far been said about the first cause of nullity, the incompetence of the judge. So that they may be attested more strongly before the most distinguished senators of the royal Parliaments and other jurists, we shall confirm them by the authority of the Doctors. And first, that widely spread opinion of the Canonists: that the Pope is not a fit judge even in the sole crime of heresy, but must be judged by others. c. si Papa, dist. 40. In that case Philip Decius strongly contends that a council is not to be convened by the authority of the Pope: in c. cum venissent, n. 37, extra de iudiciis. Likewise Panormitanus and Decius on c. significasti, n. 4 and n. 9, de electione. But most fully and most learnedly Lud. Rom. in consil. ult., n. 15 and following, where, from the authority of the Decretum itself, he contends that a Pope who lives rebelliously and refuses to learn and to do good is rather a member of the devil than of Christ, and is to be shown to be an unbeliever rather than a believer. c. nullus, dist. 38. Likewise Jason in consil. 95, when asked, vol. 4; Decius consil. 115. Their words, the latter ones especially, will be brought forward in a more suitable place.
The Second Nullity: From the Falsity of the Allegation

units.la: Secundam igitur Nullitatis caussam in allega-tionis falsitate consistere dicimus,hoc est,in al-legata falsa caussa,quam Papa in concipienda sententia secutus est.Nota enim regula iuris est,vt sententia ex falsis caussis,falsis allegationibus,falsis instrumentis,falsis testimoniis pronunciata,ipso iure,ac sine appellatione nulla sit:præsertim vbi sententia præcipuam causam ac fundamentū habuit allegationis falsitate,l.1.& pass.C.si ex falsinstr.l.si præctor.7.D.de iudic.l.cum vero, 26.§. subuentum, De fidei c.libert.l.Seiæ.26.D.de tutor.& cur.dat.l.1.§.hæc verb.D.ne vis fiat ei.l.1. C. si ex falsi. alleg. At Papa Sixtus iccirco Regem Nauarrum & Princi-pem Condæum ab se proscriptos esse prædicat, quia sunt notorij (vt ipse loquitur) haeretici. Festiue. Nam hac ratione, si principes illi notorij sunt haeretici, tum armis & bello persequendi sunt: si non sunt haeritici notorij, tum proscriptio & execratio nullius momenti est. Videamus igitur quo nomine, & quânam allegatione supradicti Principes pro haereticis damnentur. Neque enim tantum crimen vel infimo cuiquam Christiano, sine magna & graui caussa imponendum est: nedum illis tantis principibus, & tanti Regis agnatis proximis. Imperatores Gratianus, Valent.Honor. statuerũt, vt haereticorum numero habeantur, qui vel leui argumento a iudicio catholicae religionis ac tramite detecti fuerint deuiare.l.2. C.de haeret. & Manich. Quis illam definitionem probaret? nam Augustinus eos qui sententiam suam, quamuis falsam & perniciosam, nulla pertinaci animositate defendunt, præsertim quam nō audacia sua præsumptionis pepererunt, sed a seductis atque in errorem prolapsis parentibus acceperunt, quaerunt autem cauta solicitudine veritatem, corrigi parati, cum inuenerint, nequaquam haereticos deputat: vt loquitur text.24.dist.3.c.dixit. Rursus Ioh. Auentinus lib. Annal.3.scriptum reliquit, Episcopū quendam Germanum, nomine Vergilium, Mathematicis aitibus eruditum, in crimen haeresis iccirco vocatum fuisse, & Romam a Zacharia Pontifice accersitum, quod Antipodas esse affirmasset. Pari temeritate Canonistae decreuerunt, eum haereticum habendum esse, qui non omnibus ac singulis Papae decretis obtemperaret. gloss.dist.10. c.nulli.& dist. 21. quinetiam Papa ipse decreuit, vt qui negat Imperatores, Reges, Principes, humanam denique omnem creaturam temporali & materiali gladio Romani Pontificis subesse, haereticus habeatur: quoniam hoc credere, est de necessitate salutis: hoc est, unus est ex fidei articulis.c.1.in sin.ex-trauag.de maiorit.& obed.Anno Christi cxcviii. Victor Papa Romanus Ecclesias Orientales iccirco haereticas esse pronuntiavit, quod de festo die Paschatis non idem quod ipsius Ecclesia sentiebant. Qua de causa Irenaeus Lugdunensis Episcopus Papam illum vehementer increpuit: auctore Eufeb.lib.5.26. & Epist.24. Quid opus est multa?
units.tr: Secondly, then, we say that the second cause of nullity consists in the falsity of the allegation, that is, in a false cause alleged, which the Pope followed in framing the sentence. For it is a known rule of law that a sentence pronounced on false causes, false allegations, false instruments or false testimonies is null by the law itself and without appeal, especially where the sentence had as its principal cause and foundation the falsity of the allegation. l. 1 and passim, C. si ex falsis instrumentis; l. si praetor 7, D. de iudiciis; l. cum vero 26, § subventum, De fide libellorum; l. Seiae 26, D. de tutoribus et curatoribus datis; l. 1 § haec verba, D. ne vis fiat ei; l. 1, C. si ex falsa allegatione. But Pope Sixtus declares that he has proscribed the King of Navarre and Prince Condé for this reason: that they are, as he himself puts it, notorious heretics. A witty point! For on this reasoning, if those princes are notorious heretics, then they are to be pursued with arms and war; if they are not notorious heretics, then the proscription and execration is of no moment. Let us see, therefore, under what name, and by what allegation, the aforesaid princes are condemned as heretics. For such a charge must not be laid even on the lowliest Christian without a great and grave cause, much less on such great princes, the close kinsmen of so great a King. The emperors Gratian, Valentinian and Honorius decreed that those should be counted among the heretics who, though detected by even a slight argument, deviate from the judgement and path of the Catholic religion. l. 2, C. de haereticis et Manichaeis. Who would approve that definition? For Augustine does not count as heretics those who defend their opinion, however false and pernicious, without any stubborn animosity, especially one which they have received not from their own presumptuous audacity but from parents seduced and fallen into error, and who seek the truth with cautious care, ready to be corrected when they have found it. So the text puts it, dist. 24, c. dixit, dist. 3. Again, John Aventinus, in book 3 of his Annals, has left it written that a certain German bishop named Virgilius, learned in the mathematical arts, was summoned on a charge of heresy and brought to Rome by Pope Zachary, because he had affirmed that there are Antipodes. With equal rashness the Canonists decreed that he is to be held a heretic who does not obey all and each of the Pope's decrees: gloss on dist. 10, c. nulli, and dist. 21. Moreover, the Pope himself decreed that whoever denies that emperors, kings, princes and, in short, every human creature is subject to the Roman Pontiff in the temporal and material sword, is to be held a heretic, since to believe this is necessary for salvation: that is, it is one of the articles of faith. c. 1, in fine, Extravag. de maioritate et obedientia. In the year of Christ 198, Victor, Roman Pope, declared the Eastern Churches heretical because they did not hold the same view as his own Church about the feast day of Easter. For this reason Irenaeus, Bishop of Lyons, vehemently rebuked that Pope, on the authority of Eusebius, book 5, ch. 26 and letter 24. But why say more?

units.la: Haereticus in Papatu definitur, qui non credit iis omnibus, quae in Ecclesia R.pro veris tradita sunt.
units.tr: A heretic in the Papacy is defined as one who does not believe all those things which are delivered as true in the Roman Church.

units.la: c,nulli.dist.19. At superius demonstratum est, Paparum auctoritate atque imperio traditam hanc Ecclesiae Christianae doctrinam fuisse ad credendum, Monachum Dominicum plura edidisse miracula, quam Christum, & omnes ipsius Apostolos: eundem Dominicum multo praestantiore fuisse Christo, & omnibus eiusdem Apostolis: Ioanem Baptistam, cui Scriptura sacra elogium hoc tribuit, neminem unquam mortale in terris illo maiorem extitisse, multis partibus inferiorem illo veteratore Dominico fuisse. Demonstratum est praeterea, fabulam de stigmatibus Francisci Bernardonis a Pa-pis approbatam fuisse, Ecclesiēque Romanae traditam ad credendum, & sub nota haeresis puniedum oppositum sapientem: his enim ipsis verbis Papae in suis Bullis utuntur.lib. Conformat.sol.234.col. 3.
units.tr: c. nulli, dist. 19. But it has been shown above that the Papists, by the authority and command of the Popes, handed down this doctrine of the Christian Church to be believed: that the monk Dominic performed more miracles than Christ and all his Apostles; that the same Dominic was far superior to Christ and all his Apostles; and that John the Baptist, of whom Holy Scripture gives this testimony that no greater man than he has ever arisen among mortals on earth, was in many respects inferior to that sorcerer Dominic. It has been shown moreover that the fable about the stigmata of Francis Bernardone was approved by the Popes and handed down to the Roman Church to be believed, and that whoever holds the opposite is to be punished under the mark of heresy; for the Popes use these very words in their Bulls. Liber Conformitatum, fol. 234, col. 3.

units.la: 3.Quare, inquit, hoc est firmissime, tanquam verum tenendum, & oppositum tenentem, ut haereticum ab omnibus despiciendum. Pari ratione Anton. Florentinus hist.part.3.c.1.§.3. sic scribit: Ecclesia indubie approbavit & declaravit festu de hoc celebre instituendo;quod Francisco oranti & transformato D. Iesus in modum Zeraphyn (scilicet cum sex alis) crucifixus ei impressit in manibus & latere signa suae passionis, in quibus sentiebat maximum dolorem. Iudicent nunc clarissimi & prudentissimi Regis Galliae consiliarij, satisne vera illa Haereticideﬁnitio sit, vt qui turpissima illa de Dominico & Bernardone commenta Ecclesiae Romanae auctoritate comprobata non crediderit, pro haeretico habeatur, & ab Ecclesiae communione arceatur? Si non aequum hoc Papatus R. decretum esse statuant, tum meminerint eius regulę, qua traditur, leues & temerarios accusatores, non modo calumnię damnatos, infamia notari, verum etiam talionis poena damnari. vlt. C. de accusat. ac proinde Papam Sixtum V. qui Nauarrum Regem, & Condæum Principem haeresis crimine calumniose accusauit, perspicuè pro schismatico & haeretico damnandum esse. Sed iam paulo attentius consideremus, in quos nefarium illud crimè ac nomen Haereticorum conueniat. Nam quantum ex sacrae Scripturae & veterum Ecclesiae doctorū auctoritate cognosci licet, Haereticus is demū dicendus est, qui doctrinam cū regula fidei (hoc est symbolo Christianorum) pugnantem legitimè admonitus, & conuictus, tamen & contumaciter tuetur, & seditiosè disseminat. Sic enim Augustinus, lib. de ciuit. Dei. 18. c. 51. Qui in Ecclesia Christi, inquit, morbidu aliquod prauumque sapiut, si correpti vt sanu reclumque sapiant, resistunt contumaciter, suaque pestifera & mortifera dogmata emedare nolunt, sed defensare perfistunt, haeretici fiunt, & foras exeuntes habentur in exercentibus inimicis. Iam verò de Symbolo Christianorū, quā fidei regulam Tertullianus appellat, praepræclarum eiusdem Tertulliani hoc testimonium extat in libro de præscript. hæret. Regula fidei est, inquit, qua creditur unum omnino Deum esse (notetur hæc pia Christiani symboli paraphrasis) nec alium præter mundi creatorem, qui universa de nihilo produxerit per verbum suum. Id verbum Filium eius appellatum, varie visum patriarchis, a prophetis semper auditum, postremo delatum a Spiritu Patris Dei & virtute in virginem Mariam, carnem factum in utero eius, & ex ea natum egisse (exisse) Iesum Christum, exinde prædicasse novam legem, & novam promissionem regni cælorum, virtutes fecisse, fixum cruci, tertia die resurrexisse, in cœlis ereptum sedere ad dexteram patris, misisse vicariam vim Spiritus Sancti, qui credentes agat, venturum cum claritate ad sumendos sanctos in vita æterna & promissorum cœlestium fruitionum, & ad prophanos iudicandos igni perpetuo: sed utriusque partis resuscitatione cum carnis restitutione. Hæc regula a Christo instituta nulla habet apud nos quæstiones, nisi quas hæreses inferunt, & quæ hæreticos faciunt. Hæc Tertullianus. Ex quibus intelligitur, Hæreticos ab eo defi-niri, qui doctrinam Christianorum Symbolo contrariam in Ecclesiam inducunt: quod illi Pauli Apostoli præcepto consentaneum est: Qui aliud vobis Evangelium attulerit, quàm quod nos attulimus, anathema esto. Itaque Tertullianus alio eiusdem libri loco, Unde, inquit, extranei & inimici Apostolis hære-tici, nisi ex diversitate doctrinæ, quâ unusquisque de suo arbitrio adversus Apostolos, aut protulit aut recepit? Illic igitur & Scripturarum & expositionum adulteratio deputanda est, ubi diversitas inuenitur doctrinæ. Item alio loco: Hæ-retici edat origines Ecclesiarū suarū, euoluant ordinem Episcoporum suorum, ita per successiones ab initio decurrentem, vt primum ille Episcopus aliquem ex Apostolis, vel Apostolicis viris, qui tamen cum Apostolis perseveraverit, habuerit auctorem & antecessorem. Apostolicos Tertullianus diserte appellat, neque alios hoc nomine appellari patitur, quam qui cum Apostolorum doctrina consenserint, & in ea perseuerauerint: vt facile intelligatur, Apostolicos non ex sedis & loci, sed ex doctrinæ successione & perpetuitate æstimados esse. Itaque alio loco: Hæreticorum doctrina, inquit, cum Apostolica comparata, ex diuersitate & contrarietate sua pronuntiabit, neque Apostoli alicuius auctoris esse, neque Apostolici: quia, sicut Apostoli inter se diuersa inter se docuissent, ita & Apostolici non contraria Apostolis edidissent, nisi illi qui ab Apostolis defecerunt, & aliter prædicauerunt. En, vt aperte Tertullianus ostendit, eos qui doctrinam cum Christianorum Symbolo pugnantem inducunt, Hæreticos proprie appellandos esse, quamuis se Apostolicos nominent: quandoquidem, inquit, ab Apostolis desciuerunt: & (vt aliquanto ante dixit) ex suo arbitrio, id est, ingenio & commento, aliquid præter sacram Scripturam effinxerunt. Animaduertendum præterea, dici à Tertulliano Apostolicos, non proprie ac præcipue qui Petro, sed generaliter qui alicui ex ipsius Coapostolis successerunt: neque id præcise: vt referri ad locum & ciuitatem certam oporteat: sed connexè, qui Apostolis eorumque muneri & functioni in Christi doctrina per manus tradenda successerunt. Ex quo Papatum impudentia perspicitur, qui non modo Apostolici nomen proprie ad Romanum Episcopum restrinxerunt, verum etiam stolidis rebus nomen illud imposuerunt, veluti: Sedes apostolica ftolica,Legatus apostolicus, Nuntius apostolicus, Notarius apostolicus,Cancellaria apostolica ,Pœ-nitétiaria apostolica, Camera apostolica, Priuile-gium apostolicum,Prouifio apostolica,Bulla apo-ftolica:ut tandem aliquando(fit honos auribus) di catur,Mulus apostolicus, Matellio apostolicus, & fiquid eiusmodi. Verùm,ut ad inftitutù redeamus, quo planiùs discrimen inter Hæreticum & Apostolicum intelligeretur,exemplū Tertullianus subiungit apertisimum, & valde ad id quod agimus accommodatum:Paulus, inquit,Timotheum institues, nuptiarum interdictores inter hæreticos suggillat. Quid ita, Tertulliane? Nempe, quoniam Apostolorum doctrinæ interdictum illud contrarium est, qui diserte docuerunt matrimonium esse omnibus omnium generum atque ordinum hominibus, non modo decorum, & honorabile, verùmetiam plerumque necessarium. Ex quo intelligitur, prohibitionem matrimonij non esse apostolicam, sed hæreticam: quoniâ hæretici ex Tertulliani sententia definiuntur, qui doctrinam apostolorum scriptis contrariam inuehunt. Apostolici verò & Orthodoxi, & Catholici, qui scriptis Apostolorum contenti, eos qui de his quicquam detrahunt, aut aliquid affingunt, vnà cum Apostolo execrantur. Porrò huic hæreticorum definitioni consentanea alte ra illa est, quâ B. Augustinus tradit in lib. de utilit. creden.Hæreticus est, inquiens, qui ob amorem lucri aut principatus nouas aut gignit, aut sequitur opiniones, ubi Principatum intelligit factionis & fcecefsionis ab Ecclesia, cuius fe Ducem ac Principem aliquis quasi sublato signo profitetur. Et hac eadem mente Paulus, Philetum & Hymenæum Hæreticos appellat, quòd non modò à fide aberrassent, sed etiam quorundam fidem subvertissent: quos e-tiam alio loco πλανῶντας, ἢ[?] πλανωμένους appellat: id est, errantes, & alios in errorem inducentes. 1. Timoth. 2. 2. Tim. 3. Sed & Petrus Hæreticos de-scribens, ait eos leuium & infirmorum hominum mentes inescare. Item alio loco: Inter vos, inquit, e-runt falsi doctores, qui clàm inducent hæreses, siue sectas exitiales. 2. Pet. 2. Quantum autem ad formam de-clarandorum hæreticorum attinet, Paulus eam his demonstrat verbis: Hæreticum post unam & alteram admonitionem devita. 1. Tit. 3. quam ad formam ille quoque ordo pertinet, quê[?] Christus Math. 18. præ-scribit, ut apud Ecclesiam accusetur, & si se contu-macem præbuerit, pro ethnico & profano habea-tur. Et in hanc eandem sententiam videmus étiam Doctores scholasticos consentire: in his Magistr. in 4. dist. 18. ca. 7. vbi sic scribit: Excommunicationem fieri debere, cum quis secundum Canonicam disciplinam tertio vocatus ad emendationem manifesti delicti, & satisfacere vilipendens, sententia Ecclesiæ à loco orationis & sacramentorum communione, & fidelium consortio præciditur ut erubescat, & pudore sceleris conversus pœ-niteat, ut spiritus eius salvus sit. qui si pœnitentiam prosi-tens resipuerit, negatæ communioni admittitur, & Ecclesiæ reconciliatur. Quibus etiam consentaneum est quod traditur à Canonistis 1.24. q. 1. c. aperte, &c. hæc est, eum qui paratus est corrigi, non debere dici hæreticum, quamuis erret in fide. Ex quibus omnibus perspicuè intelligitur, tres Hæreticorum esse notas, quibus ab orthodoxis internoscuntur: si quid à regula fidei alienum in Ecclesiam inducant, si secessionem faciant, & si solenniter admoniti contumaciter perseverent. Sed quoniam ad Regios Se-natores Iurisperitos magna ex parte hæc disputatio Pertinet, non alienum videtur, alteram ex Iustiniani libris Haereticorum definitionem proponere. Nam in l. 1. C. de sum. tri. Catholici definiuntur, qui vnam patris, filij, & Spiritus sancti Deitatem credunt, Haeretici vero, qui eandem non credunt. Rursus Imp. Iustinianus in Nouel. 115. §. si quis, vbi inter legitimas liberorum exheredandorum causas haeresim enumerat, Iuliano antecessore interprete, haec subiungit: Orthodoxos autem dicimus eos, qui communicant in sacrosancta Ecclesia Catholica, in quam omnes Patriarchae vna conspiratione & concordia colliguntur: & quatuor sancta concilia praedicantur: Nicaenum, Constantinopolitanum, Ephesinum primum, & Chalcedonense. Haereticos autem dicimus eos, qui Catholicis non communicant. His igitur ita constitutis, videamus nunc, quo iure supradicti Principes nostri a Papa Sixto V. pro haereticis damnentur. Nam sive priorem, sive posteriorem definitionem sequamur, supradicti Principes quanta maxima possunt contentione profitentur, ac praedicant, Deumque & Angelos, atque omnes omnium ordinum ac generum homines, coelum denique & terra contestatur, se neque quicquam a regula fidei & vsitato Christianorum Symbolo, & recepta de summa trinitate doctrina, neque ab illis antiquissimis quatuor conciliis alienum in Ecclesia inuehere, sed eorum doctrina & confessione, qualis in Synodo Nicaena, Constantinopolitana, Ephesina, Chalcedonensi concepta est, ex animo amplecti, neque ab vsitata Athanasij formula, vel latiū (vt dicitur) vnguem discedere. Profitentur praeterea, se nullam ab iis Ecclesiis, quae in illa fidei regula, & confessionum formula permanserunt (quales sunt illustrissimorum & potentissimorum Electorum, & Principum Augustanae confessionis Ecclesiae) secessionem fecisse, aut facere velle. Postremo nunquam vsque adhuc ab vlla huius generis Ecclesia, quae in Apostolorum doctrina perseuerarit, admonitos, aut reprehensos fuisse. Quod si Parisiensis carnificinae cruore & caedibus infinitis adolescentuli conterriti, Regisque potentissimi conspectu ac praesentia permoti, multis postea mili-tum armatorum gladiis circumuenti, ea quae vel facere, vel pronuntiare iussi sunt, inuiti fecerunt, ac pronunciarunt, non hanc legitimam ac solennem, & qualem Christus instituit, Apostoli & Apostolici seruarunt, Ecclesiasticae comonefactionis formam habendam esse: praesertim cum aliquanto post, recuperata libertate, protestati sint, se, quicquid illius fecerant, inuitos ac minis compulsos fecisse: fuegue illius infirmitatis veniam a Deo, & Christianis palam, pro concione in Ecclesia reformata postularint.
units.tr: 3.Therefore, he says, this is to be held most firmly as true, and whoever holds the opposite is to be despised by all as a heretic. In the same way Antoninus of Florence writes in his History, part 3, chapter 1, §3: The Church has undoubtedly approved and declared that a famous feast is to be instituted for this, because, while Francis was praying and transfigured, Jesus Christ, crucified, appeared to him in the form of a seraph (that is, with six wings) and imprinted on his hands and side the marks of his passion, in which he felt the greatest pain. Let the most distinguished and wise councillors of the most renowned King of France now judge whether that definition of heresy is true, namely that whoever does not believe those most shameful fictions about the Lord and Bernardone, fictions approved by the authority of the Church of Rome, is to be held a heretic and shut out from the communion of the Church. If they judge that the decree of the Roman Papacy is not fair, let them remember this rule of law, which teaches that light and rash accusers, condemned for slander, are not only branded with infamy but are also punished with the penalty of retaliation (Code, last title, on accusers). And so Pope Sixtus V, who slanderously accused the King of Navarre and the Prince of Condé of the crime of heresy, must plainly be condemned as a schismatic and a heretic. But let us now consider a little more carefully against whom that wicked charge and name of heretics properly applies. For, so far as can be learned from the authority of Scripture and of the ancient teachers of the Church, he alone is rightly called a heretic who, when lawfully admonished and convicted of teaching a doctrine at odds with the rule of faith (that is, the creed of the Christians), nevertheless stubbornly defends it and spreads it seditiously. For Augustine says this in The City of God, book 18, chapter 51: Whoever, he says, savours of some diseased and perverse thing in the Church of Christ, and when corrected so that he may savour what is sound and right, resists stubbornly, and refuses to amend his pestilent and deadly dogmas but persists in defending them, becomes a heretic, and is regarded as an enemy going out from us, as those who practise enmity. Now, concerning the creed of the Christians, which Tertullian calls the rule of faith, there is this most excellent testimony of the same Tertullian in his book on prescription against heretics: The rule of faith is this, that we believe there is one God only (let this pious paraphrase of the Christian creed be noted), and no other besides the Creator of the world, who brought all things out of nothing through his Word. This Word, called his Son, was variously seen by the patriarchs, was always heard by the prophets, and was at last sent down by the Spirit and power of God the Father into the virgin Mary, was made flesh in her womb, and was born of her as Jesus Christ; thereafter he preached a new law and a new promise of the kingdom of heaven, performed miracles, was fixed to the cross, rose again on the third day, was taken up into the heavens and sits at the right hand of the Father, and sent in his place the power of the Holy Spirit to guide believers; he will come with glory to take the saints to eternal life and the enjoyment of the heavenly promises, and to judge the profane with eternal fire; and both parts will rise again with the restoration of the flesh. This rule, instituted by Christ, has among us no questions except those which heresies introduce and which make heretics. So Tertullian. From these words it is understood that heretics are defined as those who introduce into the Church a doctrine contrary to the creed. This agrees with the precept of the Apostle Paul: If anyone brings you a gospel other than that which we have brought, let him be anathema. Hence Tertullian, in another place of the same book, says: Whence came strangers and enemies of the Apostles, heretics, except from the diversity of doctrine by which each one, by his own judgment, has either put forward or received something against the Apostles? Therefore the corruption of both Scriptures and their interpretations is to be charged where diversity of doctrine is found. Likewise in another place: Let heretics set out the origins of their churches, let them unroll the order of their bishops, running down from the beginning through successions in such a way that the first bishop had as his author and predecessor one of the Apostles, or some apostolic man who nevertheless persevered with the Apostles. Tertullian plainly calls men apostolic, and does not allow others to be called by that name except those who agreed with the doctrine of the Apostles and persevered in it. So it is easily understood that apostolic men are to be judged not by the seat or place, but by the succession and continuity of doctrine. Thus in another place he says: The doctrine of the heretics, when compared with the apostolic, will show by its diversity and contrariety that it belongs to no Apostle nor to any apostolic man; for just as the Apostles taught different things among themselves, so the apostolic men would not have published things contrary to the Apostles, unless those who had fallen away from the Apostles and preached otherwise. See, as Tertullian clearly shows, that those who introduce a doctrine at odds with the creed of the Christians are properly to be called heretics, even though they call themselves apostolic; since, he says, they have departed from the Apostles, and (as he said a little earlier) have fashioned something of their own judgment, that is, of their wit and invention, apart from Holy Scripture. It should also be noted that Tertullian calls men apostolic not properly or chiefly those who succeeded Peter, but generally those who succeeded any of the Apostles' fellows; nor is this to be understood so strictly that it must refer to a particular place and city, but in the sense that they succeeded the Apostles, and their office and function of handing down the doctrine of Christ. From this one sees the shamelessness of the Papists, who have not only restricted the name apostolic properly to the Roman bishop, but have also attached that name to silly things, such as: the apostolic see, apostolic legate, apostolic nuncio, apostolic notary, apostolic chancery, apostolic penitentiary, apostolic camera, apostolic privilege, apostolic provision, apostolic bull; so that at last (let it be a pleasure to the ears) we hear of an apostolic mule, an apostolic chamber-pot, and whatever else is of that kind. But, to return to our purpose, so that the difference between a heretic and an apostolic man may be understood more clearly, Tertullian adds a most manifest example, very well suited to what we are doing: Paul, he says, in instructing Timothy, Timotheum institues, nuptiarum interdictores inter hæreticos suggillat. Why so, Tertullian? Clearly because that prohibition of marriage is contrary to the doctrine of the Apostles, who plainly taught that marriage is not only proper and honourable but often necessary for men of every kind and rank. From this it is understood that the prohibition of marriage is not apostolic but heretical, since, in Tertullian's judgment, heretics are defined as those who bring in something contrary to the writings of the Apostles. Apostolic, orthodox and catholic men, however, who are content with the writings of the Apostles, curse together with the Apostle those who take anything away from these or add anything to them. Moreover, another definition of heretics, which agrees with this one, is given by Blessed Augustine in his book On the Advantage of Believing: A heretic is, he says, one who, for love of gain or of power, begets or follows new opinions, where by power he understands the leadership of a faction and secession from the Church, when someone, as if having raised a standard, professes himself its leader and prince. And in this same sense Paul calls Hymenaeus and Philetus heretics, because they not only had strayed from the faith but had also subverted the faith of some; elsewhere he calls them wandering and leading others astray [πλανῶντας, πλανωμένους], that is, erring and inducing others into error. 1 Timothy 2; 2 Timothy 3. And Peter, describing heretics, says that they entice the minds of light and unstable men. Likewise in another place: Among you, he says, there will be false teachers, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies or sects. 2 Peter 2. As for the manner of declaring heretics, Paul sets it out in these words: Avoid a heretic after one or two admonitions. Titus 3. To this form also belongs the order that Christ prescribes in Matthew 18, that the matter be brought before the Church, and if he shows himself stubborn, he is to be regarded as a heathen and a profane person. And we see that the scholastic teachers agree with this same opinion; among them the Master of the Sentences, on book 4, distinction 18, chapter 7, where he writes thus: Excommunication ought to be pronounced when someone, called three times according to the canonical discipline for the amendment of a manifest offence, scorns to make satisfaction; by the sentence of the Church he is cut off from the place of prayer, from communion in the sacraments, and from the fellowship of the faithful, so that he may blush, and, turned by shame at his wickedness, may repent, that his spirit may be saved. If he repents and returns to his senses, professing repentance, he is admitted to the communion he had been denied and is reconciled to the Church. To this also agrees what the canonists teach in Decretum I, distinction 24, chapter 'Aperte', etc.: that one who is ready to be corrected ought not to be called a heretic, even though he errs in faith. From all these things it is plainly understood that there are three marks of heretics by which they are distinguished from the orthodox: if they introduce into the Church anything alien to the rule of faith; if they make a secession; and if, when solemnly admonished, they persist stubbornly. But since this discussion pertains in large part to the royal senators who are lawyers, it seems not out of place to set forth another definition of heretics, from the books of Justinian. For in Code 1, title 'On the Holy Trinity', Catholics are defined as those who believe in the one Deity of Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and heretics as those who do not believe it. Again, the Emperor Justinian, in Novella 115, §'si quis', where among the lawful causes for disinheriting children he lists heresy, adds these words, following the interpretation of the jurist Julian: We call orthodox those who communicate in the most holy Catholic Church, into which all patriarchs are gathered in one agreement and concord, and the four holy councils are proclaimed: the Nicene, the first Constantinopolitan, the first Ephesine, and the Chalcedonian. We call heretics those who do not communicate with the Catholics. Having set these things down, let us now see by what right the aforesaid Princes of ours are condemned as heretics by Pope Sixtus V.
