For whether we follow the earlier or the later definition, the aforesaid Princes profess and proclaim with the utmost earnestness, and God and the angels, and all men of every order and rank, heaven and earth at last bear witness, that they introduce into the Church nothing alien to the rule of faith and the customary Christian creed, nor to the doctrine of the Trinity received, nor to those most ancient four councils; but they embrace from the heart the teaching and confession which was framed at the Synods of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon, and they do not depart by a hair's breadth (as they say) from the customary formula of Athanasius. They further profess that they have made no secession, nor wish to make one, from those Churches which have remained in that rule of faith and in the form of confession (such as the Churches of the most illustrious and most powerful Electors and Princes of the Augsburg Confession). Lastly, they have never until now been admonished or rebuked by any Church of this kind which has persevered in the doctrine of the Apostles. But if young men, terrified by the blood and countless slaughters of the Parisian butchery, and moved by the sight and presence of the most powerful King, and afterwards surrounded by the swords of many armed soldiers, did unwillingly what they were ordered to do or say, and said it unwillingly, this should not be held to be the lawful and solemn form of ecclesiastical admonition, such as Christ instituted and the Apostles and apostolic men observed; especially since, some time afterwards, having recovered their liberty, they protested that whatever they had done under that compulsion, they had done unwillingly and under threats; and they openly asked God and the Christians, in a sermon in the reformed Church, for pardon for that weakness.

units.la: Ex contrario vero demonstrant, Papa Romanum iudicio maximae partis Europae, no modo inter haereticos, sed etiam tanquam Haeresiarcham, & factionis principem auctorem, duce damnatum esse. Primum quia fabulas impias, & blasphemas de falsis monachorum miraculis in Ecclesia inuexit, & traditiones ab illis quatuor antiquis conciliis alienissimas: quales superius protulimus de commentitio Purgatorio, de inuocatione mortuorum, de veneratione imaginum, de quotidiana renouatione sacrificij Christi in missa, de idololatrica panis & calicis veneratione, de prohibitione coiugij, de monachis Dominicanis sub virginis Mariae stola occultis, de pluribus & maioribus miraculis a Dominico & Francisco factis quam aut a Christo, aut ipsius apostolis: quae sunt blasphemiae adeo nefariae, sceleratae, atque impiae, vt illarum commemoratione piorum omnium animi cohorrescant. Deinde quoniam dominatu ac potentatu regio in Ecclesiam vniuersam occupato, adhibitisque ad eum tuendum & ornandum administris & satellitibus, satrapis, & Cardinalibus purpuratis, nouæ se factionis & Synagogæ ducem ac principem professus est. Postremo quoniam quadringentis hisce annis continuis, omnium Christianorum Principum precibus rogatus atque admonitus, vt emendationem & reformationem aliquam admitteret, superbè postulata & preces illorum repudiauit. Cuius rei, ne longius testimonia petantur, patrum certè atque aliorum nostrorum memoria testis esse poterit, ex concilio Constantiensi, Basiliensi, Florentino, & Tridentino: in quo postremo, non modò falsæ & adulterinæ doctrinæ sublatæ non sunt, verùmetiam magis ac magis confirmatæ: vt iam dubium nemini esse possit, quin tres illæ notæ, quibus paulò ante dicebamus Hæreticum ab Orthodoxo internosci, euidentissimè in Papa Romano apparreant. Quæ cùm ita se habeat, satis iam perspicuum esse arbitramur, quanti momenti hæc apud Regis Galliæ consiliarios esse debeat Papæ Sixti accusatio, iampridem à maxima Europæ parte instituta simúlque intelligi, cuius auctoritatis esse apud eosdem debeat hæc ab illo contra Regem Nauarrum & Principem Condæum insana criminatio. Nam, vt illum suo(vt dici solet)gladio iugulemus, ecce in ipsius Decret.24.distin.1.multis passim testimoniis traditur, lapsum in hæresim non posse alium officio priuare, vel sententia innodare: velut in c.acasius. Si ergo episcopus, inquit, in hæresim iam damna-tam lapsus est, antiqua excommunicatione damnatus, ahos damnare non potest. Excommunicatus enim alios excommunicare non valet. Quod idem seq.confirma-tur, hac subiecta ratione: Ligandi namque vel soluendi potestas veris, non falsis sacerdotibus a Domino tradita est, &c. seq. Manet Petri priuilegium, vbicunque ex ipsius æquitate fertur iudicium. Facit quod scribit Ias. in consil. 145. requisitus, num. 3. vol. 2. quod Papa non potest sine caussa quemquam in dignitate constitutum deponere: quia potestas data Petro, ad pascendas oues Christi non extenditur ad necandum eas. c. in no-uo 21. dist. manet enim potentia Petri, dum vere indicat, & clauis non errat. d. c. manet. &c. hoc idem scribit Abb. in c. vlt. col. pen. & vlt. de confirm. vel tanto & in c. constitutus, col. 3. de religios. dom. & in c. vlt. de postul. prælat. & in c. de multa. de præbend. quinetiam is qui iniuste quempiam excommunicat, teneri dicitur pœna sacrilegij. 24. q. 3. c. non in perpetuo. Planius etiam Ias. in consil. 95. requisitus vol. 4. Quando Papa, inquit, impeteretur de hæresi, cum ab hoc ordine possit deponi: c. si Papa, 40 dist. per hoc definit esse Papa, cum sit extra Ecclesiam catholicam: iuxta not. per Innocent. in c. ex parte, de verb. signif. & eodem modo quando Papa esset criminosus notorius, & grauibus criminibus irretitus, ita quod Ecclesiam scandalizaret, &c. Item col. 3. Sed fortius tenuit glossa trita, quam totus mundus allegat in d. c. si Papa, quod etiam de alio crimine, puta simoniæ, vel adulterii quod sit notorium, & admonitus Papa est incorrigibilis, ita vt scandalizet Ecclesiá Dei, potest accusari cum habeatur pro hæretico: & sic Papa non solu pro caussa hæresis, sed etiam pro quocunque alio crimine in quo Papa committit excessu scandalizante Ecclesia, si sit notoriu, & Papa sit incorrigibilis, potest accusari & puniri: quia notoria inotoria inobedientia habetur pro hæresi. Vnde sicut Papa potest pro hæresi accusari, & dánari, ita etiá pro quocun-que notorio crimine in quo sit incorrigibilis, quinetia Fe-lin.in c.ego N.de iureiur.Papa nõ Canonicè electus est diabolus, non habens claues regni cœlorum, sed inferni.
units.tr: On the contrary, they show that the Roman Pope, by the judgement of the greater part of Europe, has been condemned not only among heretics but also as a heresiarch and the author and leader of a faction. First, because he has introduced into the Church impious and blasphemous fables about the false miracles of the monks, and traditions wholly alien from the four ancient councils: such as we set out above concerning the fictitious Purgatory, the invocation of the dead, the veneration of images, the daily renewal of Christ's sacrifice in the Mass, the idolatrous veneration of bread and chalice, the prohibition of marriage, the Dominican monks hidden under the stole of the Virgin Mary, and the many and greater miracles wrought by Dominic and Francis than by Christ or his apostles. These blasphemies are so wicked, villainous and impious that the hearts of all the pious shudder at their mention. Second, because, having seized lordly and royal power over the whole Church, and having taken as ministers and guards to defend and adorn it satraps and purple-robed cardinals, he has professed himself the leader and prince of a new faction and synagogue. Last, because for these four hundred continuous years, though asked and urged by the prayers of all Christian princes to admit some amendment and reformation, he has arrogantly rejected their demands and prayers. As witness of this, lest we seek testimonies from afar, the memory of the fathers and of others of our own time can bear witness, from the councils of Constance, Basel, Florence and Trent; at the last of which not only were false and adulterated doctrines not removed, but were more and more confirmed, so that no one can now doubt that those three marks by which we said shortly before that the heretic is distinguished from the orthodox appear most evidently in the Roman Pope. Since this is so, we think it is now clear enough how great weight the accusation of Pope Sixtus, begun long ago by the greater part of Europe, ought to carry with the counsellors of the King of France, and also how much authority with the same men ought to be given to this mad accusation made by him against the King of Navarre and the Prince of Condé. For, to slit his throat with his own sword, as the saying goes, see: in his own Decretum, distinction 24, part 1, it is handed down in many places that one who has fallen into heresy cannot deprive another of office or bind him by sentence; as in c. Acasius: If therefore a bishop has fallen into a heresy already condemned, and has been condemned by an ancient excommunication, he cannot condemn others. For one who is excommunicated cannot excommunicate others. The same is confirmed in what follows, with this reason added: For the power of binding and loosing was given by the Lord to true priests, not to false ones, etc. and then: Peter's privilege remains wherever judgement is pronounced in accordance with his equity. Jason agrees with what he writes in consilium 145, when asked, no. 3, vol. 2: that the Pope cannot depose anyone who is placed in dignity without cause, because the power given to Peter to feed Christ's sheep does not extend to slaying them. c. in novo, 21 dist.: for Peter's power remains so long as he judges truly, and the key does not err. d. c. manet, etc. Abbas writes the same on c. vlt., penultimate and last column, de confirm. vel tanto, and on c. constitutus, col. 3, de religios. dom., and on c. vlt., de postul. praelat., and on c. de multa, de praebend. Moreover, he who unjustly excommunicates anyone is said to incur the penalty of sacrilege: 24 q. 3, c. non in perpetuo. Jason speaks even more plainly in consilium 95, when asked, vol. 4: When the Pope, he says, is charged with heresy, since he can be deposed by this order: c. si Papa, 40 dist.; by this he ceases to be Pope, since he is outside the Catholic Church, according to the note of Innocent on c. ex parte, de verb. signif.; and in the same way when the Pope is a notorious criminal, entangled in grave crimes, so that he scandalises the Church, etc. Likewise, col. 3: But the worn-out gloss, which the whole world cites on the said c. si Papa, holds more firmly that even for another crime, such as simony or adultery, if it is notorious, and the Pope is admonished and incorrigible, so that he scandalises the Church of God, he can be accused, since he is held to be a heretic; and thus the Pope can be accused and punished not only for the cause of heresy, but also for any other crime in which the Pope commits an excess that scandalises the Church, if it is notorious and the Pope is incorrigible; because notorious and manifest disobedience is held to be heresy. Hence, just as the Pope can be accused and condemned for heresy, so also for any notorious crime in which he is incorrigible; indeed Felinus, on c. ego N., de iureiur.: a Pope not canonically elected is a devil, not having the keys of the kingdom of heaven but of hell.

units.la: TERTIA NVLLITAS EX DEFECTV ORDINIS iudicialis.
units.tr: THE THIRD NULLITY, FROM A DEFECT OF JUDICIAL ORDER

units.la: Veniamus iam ad tertiam Nullitatis caussa quam esse dicebamus, defectum formę & ordinis iudicialis. Nam, vt quondam ab Oratore sumo dictū est, quid indignius, quā qui neq; adesse iussus fit neq; citatus, neq; accusatus, de eius capite ac fortunis omnibus iudicare? Demostratū est superius, formam hanc atq; ordinē ecclesiastici iudicij à Christo & ipsius Apostolis in hæreticis declarandis institutū fuisse, primū vt aliquoties erroris sui cōuincerentur:tū si monitis Ecclesiæ non vnis sed pluribus ac repetitis non parerēt, sed (vt Augustinus loquitur) cōtumaciter resisterent, atq; in errore perseuerarēt, tū in hostiū ac profanorum numero haberētur. Monitionibus igitur opus est, & causę cognitione solenni, ac legitima. Cuius rei satis multa exempla ex literis sanctis proferre possumus. Nō ignorabat Deꝰ, quid cōtra suū interdictū Adamus & Eua cōmisisset euocauit, tamē vtrūq;, & quasi quæstione causæq; cognitione instituti ac tū demū in illos cōuictos sententiā pronūtiauit. Nō ignorabat idem seuerissimus flagitiorum vindex Deus, quanto se scelere, & quàm nefario Sodomitæ, & Gomorrhæi polluissent. Verūmtamen vt mortalibus iurisdictionem exercentibus æquitatis exemplum præberet, causæ cognitionem suscepit, descensurúmque fe & cogniturum dixit. quod etiâ Canonistæ multis verbis tradiderunt in 1.q.2. passim, sed præsertim in c. Deus omnipotens. Sed & eadem scriptura alio loco testatur, Seniores populi Iudaici, qui ad radices montis Sinai res iudicabant, non nisi vtraque parte audita, & causa vtrinque perorata sententiam pronuntiasse. Quinetiam Iudæi quamuis malitiose perniciem atque interitu Chri-sto molirentur, tamen vsitatum iudiciorum ordinem conseruarunt, vt illum apud Caiapham Pontificem maximum & iudicem competentem reum facerent: tum eundem comprehensum ad eiusdem Pontificis tribunal adducerent, simulque testes in suam accusationem produceret. Causa igitur vtrinque dicta est: rogatæque confessorum sententiæ: ac tum demum, ordine iudiciali seruato, pronuntiata condemnatio est. Sed quid opus est plura? Cum in adulterio deprehensa mulier fuisset, vt Scriptura loquitur, ἑαυτῷ[?], neque quisquam esset, qui aduersus eam accusationem institueret, ac testes produceret, tum Christus, Nec ego, inquit, te non cōuin-ctam damnabo. Ioh.8. Item alio loco: cum Iudæi quodam die Christum inauditum condemnare vel-lent, tum eos Nicodemus his verbis increpuit: An lex nostra vllum hominem condemnat, quin prius auditus sit, & de eius facto cognitum? Denique nihil est de quo veteres Christianorum patroni, in his Tertullianus, Arnobius, Augustinus, Lactan-tius tantopere querantur, quàm quòd Ethnici Christianos inauditos, atque indicta causa passim ac temere damnabant. At horum Ethnicorum temeritatem Papa Sixtus & eius assessores Cardina-les les in hac insanissima DECLARATIONE fecut{1} sunt, cùm supradictum Serenissimū Navarræ Regem & Illustrissimum Principem Condæum, non dico inauditos, sed ne adesse quidem iussos aut citatos, barbara & Cyclopica quadam arrogantia condemnarūt. qua de re si clarissimi Parlamentorū senatores ex suis libris iudicare volent, regulam habent in Nouell.123.cap.ii[?]: vbi sic scriptum est: Omnibus episcopis & presbyteris interdicimus segregare & excommunicare aliquem, priusquam causa monstretur, propter quam sanctæ regulæ hoc fieri iubent. At enim dixerit fortasse quispiam, condemnati sunt illi Principes, non simpliciter tanquam hæretici: sed connexè, tanquam hæretici notorij, & manifesti. Sic enim multis locis in illa furiali Declaratione appellātur. Est autem inter Canonistas hoc ius receptum, ut in manifestis & notoriis criminibus accusatione, & ordine iudiciali opus nō fit. c. manifesta, & ccc. seqq. 2. q. 1. Ex quo concludi volunt, cùm supradicti Principes palàm atque apertè se ab Romana sede descivisse profiteantur, nulla vel citatione, vel accusatione, vel causæ cognitione ad eos condemnandos opus fuisse.
units.tr: Let us now come to the third cause of nullity, which we said was the defect of form and judicial order. For, as the orator once said, what is more unworthy than to pass judgment on a man's life and all his property when he has not been summoned to appear, nor cited, nor accused? It has been shown above that Christ and his Apostles instituted this form and order of ecclesiastical judgment for declaring heretics. First, they were to be convicted of their error several times. Then, if they did not obey the admonitions of the Church, not once but many times and repeatedly, but (as Augustine puts it) resisted stubbornly and persisted in error, they were to be counted among the enemies and the profane. Admonitions are therefore needed, and a solemn and lawful examination of the case. We can bring forward many examples of this from holy writ. God did not ignore what Adam and Eve had done against his prohibition, yet he summoned both of them, and, as if by inquiry and examination of the case, he then pronounced sentence on them once they were convicted. The same most severe avenger of crimes, God, did not ignore how deeply and how wickedly the Sodomites and Gomorrhites had defiled themselves. Yet, so that he might give an example of equity to mortals who exercise jurisdiction, he undertook an examination of the case, saying that he would go down and inquire. The canonists have also related this at length in 1 q.2 passim, but especially in c. Deus omnipotens. The same Scripture elsewhere testifies that the elders of the Jewish people, who judged matters at the foot of Mount Sinai, pronounced sentence only after hearing both parties and having the case pleaded on both sides. Moreover, the Jews, though they maliciously plotted Christ's ruin and death, nevertheless kept the customary order of trials. They made him a defendant before Caiaphas the high priest, the competent judge, and then brought the man, once seized, before the tribunal of that same high priest, and at the same time produced witnesses against him. The case was therefore argued on both sides, the judges' verdict was asked for, and only then, the judicial order having been observed, was condemnation pronounced. But why say more? When a woman was taken in adultery, as Scripture says [ἐν μοιχείᾳ κατειλημμένην], and there was no one who brought an accusation against her or produced witnesses, Christ said: "Neither do I condemn you, although you have not been convicted." John 8. Likewise, elsewhere, when the Jews wished to condemn Christ one day without a hearing, Nicodemus rebuked them with these words: "Does our law condemn any man unless he has first been heard and it is known what he has done?" Finally, there is nothing about which the early defenders of the Christians, among them Tertullian, Arnobius, Augustine and Lactantius, complain so bitterly as that the heathen condemned Christians unheard, without a hearing of the case, carelessly and everywhere. Yet Pope Sixtus and his assessor cardinals have imitated the rashness of those heathen in this most insane DECLARATION. With a certain barbarous and Cyclopean arrogance they condemned the aforementioned most serene King of Navarre and the most illustrious Prince Condé, who were not only unheard but not even summoned to appear or cited. If the most distinguished senators of the Parlements wish to judge this from their own books, they have a rule in Novel 123, chapter 2, where it is written: "We forbid all bishops and presbyters to separate or excommunicate anyone before the cause is shown for which the holy rules order this to be done." But perhaps someone will say that those princes were condemned not simply as heretics but as notorious and manifest heretics, for so they are called in many places in that frenzied Declaration. Among the canonists the law is accepted that in manifest and notorious crimes no accusation or judicial order is needed (c. manifesta, and ccc. seqq., 2 q.1). From this they wish to conclude that, since the aforesaid princes openly and plainly profess that they have withdrawn from the Roman see, no citation, accusation or examination of the case was needed to condemn them.

units.la: Sed facilis ad hanc obiectionē responsio est, eaque duplex: prior est, quòd Papa pro concesso id sumit, quod ei à maxima Christianitatis parte fortiter negatur, Religionem supradictorum principū ac tam multorum aliorū Regum ac procerum, idem sentientium esse hæreticam[?]: ex quo intelligitur, absurdum esse, Notorios hæreticos appellari eos, qui ne hæretici quidē sunt. Altera responsio est, quòd omnia illa Decreti Gratiani capita 1. q. 1. quæ obiici nobis possent, nulla ex parte ad crimē hæresis pertinent:sed (ut Nicolaus Papa c.16. loquitur) ad opera carnis: quæ (quemadmodum ex Apostolo eodem loco subiungit) manifesta sunt: veluti homicidium, latrocinium, stupium, incestum, adulterium, & cetera consimilia. Neque omnibus illis locis vox vlla de hæresis crimine reperietur: quod crimen à carnis operibus, & ceteris maleficiis eo discrepat, quod in hæresi damnanda, personæ correctio & emendatio quæritur: quam Paulus iccirco [illegible, ~10 letters] appellat, eodem ipso vocabulo, quo Plato eam castigationem nominat, quæ adhibetur emendandi gratia. nam in reliquis pœnis non personæ delinquentis emendatio quæritur, sed aliis exemplum datur: ut homines consimilis pœnæ metu à maleficio deterreantur. Qua de causa [illegible, ~9 letters] ab eodem Platone nominatur. Plato Gorgia. Agell.6.c.4. Quamuis igitur quis in aliquo religionis articulo caliget, manifesto etiam erret, ac labatur, non tamen continuò vel ab Ecclesiæ communione arcendus est, vel in hostium, atque (ut Augustinus loquitur) inimicorum exercentium numero habendus: sed semel ac sæpius admonendus, castigandus, edocendus, neque prius à fidelium communione submovendus, quàm se contumacem ac pertinacem offenderit: atque (ut eiusdem Augustini verba usurpemus) contumaciter Ecclesiæ restiterit. Quare, cùm supradicti Principes, neque ullam doctrinam profiteantur, à fidei regula (ut superius diximus) aliena, sed quatuor superius à nobis nominata Cocilia studiosissimè amplectantur: neque ab ulla Ecclesia Apostolica, quæ (ut Tertullianus definit) in Apostolorum doctrina perseuerarit, sint reprehensi, neque se in discendo contumaces præbuerint: sed si alicuius erroris con-uincanvincantur,emendare parati sint: sine ulla cūstatio- ne cōcludimus,Nullitatis caussæ à nobis tertio lo- co propositę abundè satisfactum fuisse.Nam etiam Canonistarum iure tota hæc Papæ declaratio iniu- sta,& irrita esse cōuincitur: quandoquidem ubi vel non iusta ex caussa,vel non seruato iudiciali ordine emissa excommunicatio est,tum ipsa excommuni- cationis maledictio, in caput maledicentis redun- dare dicitur. De iniusta caussa testimonia extat ex scriptis Augustini in c.temerarium,eod.ubi sic scri- bit:Temerarium iudicium plerumque nihil nocet, ei de quo temerè iudicatur, ei autem qui temerè iudicat ipsa temeritas necesse est noceat. Item c.seq. Quid obest ho- mini quod ex illa tabula vult illum delere humana igno- rantia,si de libro viuentium non deleat iniqua conscien- tia?Senti de Augustino,quicquid libet. Sola me in oculis Dei conscientia non accuset,&c. Etsi,ex eodem Au- gustino hæc proferuntur: Etsi ad tempus damnaris ab homine,aliud est sella terrena, aliud est tribunal cæ- leste: ab inferiori accipit sententiam, à superiori coro- nam. Item in c.illud plane, ex eodem Augustino. Illud plane, non temerè dixerim,quod si quisquam fide- lium fuerit anathematisatus iniustè, potiùs ei oberit qui facit, quàm qui hanc patitur iniuriam. Spiritus enim sanctus habitans in sanctis, per quem quisque ligatur, aut soluitur, immeritam nulli ingerit pœnam. In ordi- ne autem iudiciali primò requiritur citatio, & ci- tati contumacia, 11.q.3.c. Episcopi, c. nemo, c.cer- tum,c. ex partę, cap. cùm olim. De senten.excom- mun. ut puta, inquit Hostiensis,si aliquis iussus vel monitus noluerit maleficium emedare. Host.in Summ. tit.de sent. excommunic.num.7. glos.in c. Statui- mus.eod[?].tit.in vj. Requiritur præterea ut excommunicator sit iudex competens:alioqui iudicis in-congrui excomunicatio[?] nulla est. cap. ad nostram. De consuetud. ubi concord. in gloss. Tertiò si excommunicatus legitimè appellauit, aut appellationis loco idoneè sit protestatus. c. solet, & c. venerabilem, &c. per tuas. eod. tit. in vj. Nā allegans sententiam nullam, quamuis non petat se absolui, sed (ut in hac causa usuvenit) legitimas nullitatis causas proferens, præsertim tanto numero, & tam legitimas, audiendus est: atque interea sententia suspenditur: ut communiter iidem Canonistæ tradunt in d.c. per tuas, & in d.c. solet. Pari modo si sententia continet errorem intolerabilem: ut per eosdem Canonistas in d.c. solet, & d.c. per tuas. velut in hac causa nostra, ubi Bulla Sixti Papæ manifestissimis erroribus convincitur: quemadmodum in postre-ma Nullitatis causa demonstrabimus. præsertim ubi sententia perspicuè continet errorem facti: ut notat Ang. in Sum. contra gloss. in d.cap. per tuas. Nam sententia ex falsis allegationibus pronuntiata ipso iure nulla est: ut paulò antè copiosè docuimus.
units.tr: But the answer to this objection is easy, and it is twofold. The first is that the Pope assumes as granted what the greater part of Christendom strongly denies: that the religion of the aforesaid princes, and of so many other kings and nobles who think the same, is heretical. From this it follows that it is absurd to call notorious heretics those who are not even heretics. The second answer is that none of those chapters of Gratian's Decree, 1 q.1, which might be thrown at us, pertains in any way to the crime of heresy. They deal instead (as Pope Nicholas says in c. 16) with "the works of the flesh," which (as the same passage goes on to say from the Apostle) are manifest: such as murder, robbery, fornication, incest, adultery and the like. Nor will any word about the crime of heresy be found in all those passages. This crime differs from the works of the flesh and other wrongdoings in this respect: in condemning heresy what is sought is the correction and amendment of the person, which Paul therefore calls [illegible] by the very word Plato uses for the chastisement that is applied for the sake of amendment. For in other penalties what is sought is not the amendment of the offending person but an example given to others, so that men are deterred from wrongdoing by fear of a similar punishment. For this reason [illegible] is so named by Plato himself (Plato, Gorgias; Gellius 6.4). Therefore, although someone may be in darkness on some article of religion, and even err and stumble manifestly, he is not at once to be shut out from the communion of the Church, or counted among its enemies and (as Augustine puts it) among those who wage war on it. He is to be admonished, corrected and taught once and again, and he is not to be removed from the communion of the faithful until he has shown himself stubborn and obstinate and (to use Augustine's own words) has stubbornly resisted the Church. Accordingly, since the aforesaid princes profess no doctrine foreign to the rule of faith (as we said above), but most eagerly embrace the four councils named above by us, and have not been rebuked by any Apostolic Church, which (as Tertullian defines it) has persevered in the teaching of the Apostles, and since they have not shown themselves obstinate in learning but are ready to amend if they are convicted of any error, we conclude without hesitation that the third cause of nullity proposed by us has been fully satisfied. For by the law of the canonists too this whole declaration of the Pope is shown to be unjust and void, since where an excommunication has been issued either for no just cause or without the judicial order being observed, the curse of excommunication is said to recoil on the head of the one who curses. Testimony to the unjust cause is found in Augustine's writings in c. temerarium, same title, where he writes thus: Rash judgment usually does no harm to the one about whom it is rashly passed, but the rashness itself necessarily harms the one who judges rashly. Likewise in the next chapter: What harm does it do a man that human ignorance wants to erase his name from that tablet, if an unjust conscience does not erase it from the book of the living? Feel about Augustine whatever you like. Let only the conscience in the eyes of God not accuse me, etc. And these words are cited from the same Augustine: Even if you are condemned for a time by a man, it is one thing the earthly chair, another the heavenly tribunal: he receives sentence from the lower, a crown from the higher. Likewise in c. illud plane, from the same Augustine: Certainly I would not say rashly that if any of the faithful has been anathematized unjustly, the harm falls rather on the one who does it than on the one who suffers the injury. For the Holy Spirit dwelling in the saints, through whom each is bound or loosed, inflicts no undeserved penalty on anyone. In the judicial order, however, a citation is first required, and the contumacy of the one cited (11 q.3, c. Episcopi; c. nemo; c. certum; c. ex parte; cap. cum olim, De sententia excommunicationis). For instance, says Hostiensis, if someone, ordered or admonished, has been unwilling to amend his wrongdoing. (Hostiensis, Summa, title De sententia excommunicationis, n. 7; gloss on c. Statuimus, same title, in VI.) Moreover, it is required that the excommunicator be a competent judge; otherwise an excommunication by an unsuitable judge is void (c. ad nostram, De consuetudine; where the gloss agrees). Thirdly, if the excommunicated person has lawfully appealed, or has properly protested in place of an appeal (c. solet; c. venerabilem; c. per tuas, same title, in VI). For a man who pleads that a sentence is void, even if he does not ask to be absolved but, as happens in this case, sets out lawful grounds of nullity, especially so many and so lawful, must be heard, and in the meantime the sentence is suspended, as the same canonists commonly teach in the said c. per tuas and c. solet. Likewise, if a sentence contains an intolerable error, as the same canonists teach in the said c. solet and c. per tuas, as in this case of ours, where the Bull of Pope Sixtus is convicted of the most manifest errors, as we shall demonstrate in the last cause of nullity. This holds especially where a sentence plainly contains an error of fact, as Ang. notes in his Summa against the gloss on the said c. per tuas. For a sentence pronounced on false allegations is void in law itself, as we taught at length a little earlier.
THE FOURTH NULLITY, FROM THE FORM OF THE SENTENCE.

units.la: Superest quarta nullitatis causa, ex stulta con-ceptæ sententiæ formula. nam, ut dici solet, stul-titia sermonis, mentis stultitiam indicat. l.pen. D.de cond. & demonst. l.1. § pen. & vlt. D.de ædil. edict. Itaque Iudex incipè, stultè & absurdè sententiam pronuntiās, stultus appellatur. l.vlt. C.de fideic. lib. qualè hunc monachū Francisci Bernardonis discipulū. ex ipsius sententia & monachali bulla demonstrabi-mus. Sic enim exorditur: Ab immensa aeterni regispote-tia B. Petro eiusque successoribus tradita auctoritas, omnes terrenorum Regum & Principum supereminet Potestates. Ut sententias loquitur carnifex! At vetus Dialecticorum praeceptum est, comparationes non nisi in rebus quae generis eiusdem sunt, usurpari. Quid verò commune est inter auctoritatem Apostolis tributā, quę ad res spirituales, hoc est, religione & conscientias pertinet: & potestatem regibus concessā, quae in temporalibus, hoc est, in civilibus & politicis rebus versatur? Itaque proinde Bardocucullus noster loquutus est, quasi dixisset: Stultitia discipuli Bernardonis supereminet auriculas omnium onagrorū, qui sunt in Arcadia. Verūmtamen ut serio aliquid respondeatur, prodeat haec in medium conclusio. Non plus habet successor iuris, quàm quatum [?] auctor suus habuit. Petrus non habuit auctoritatem supereminentem potestates regum, sed iis tanquam superioribus parere iussus est. Ergo etiamsi Papa esset Petri successor (quod superius falsum esse docuimus) tamen Regibꝰ inferior parere illis deberet. Assumptio perspicua est ex illis verbis. Omnis anima Potestatibus supereminentibus subiecta esto. Quisquis opponit se potestati, Dei ordinationi resistit: Rom.13. Suggere ipsis, ut se subiiciant Principatibus ac Potestatibus, ut obtemperent. Tit.3. Subiecti estote cuiuis humanae ordinationi, propter Domini: sive Regi, ut qui supereminet [?]: sive Praesidibus, ut qui per eum mittuntur. 1. Pet.2. Sed quid apud Papā Scripturae sacrae auctoritas valebit? nam uno jā hoc verbo refellitur: Costātinus omnia Papae Occidetis [?] regna donavit, statuitq;ut Imperatores & Reges ei in equum ascendenti strepam teneant, af-feclas eidem fe prebeant, denique vt humi pro-strati, osculum ipsius pedibus ferant. Hæc est illa quam hoc loco significat, Paparum super-eminentia: qualis Dei fui Francifci, vel fuit quon-dam in terris cum in mediam aëris regionem sub latus familiariter cum Christo fabulabatur: vnde frigoris illius vitandi caussa, cucullatum veftimen-tum induit: vel hodie est in cœlis vbi super Cheru-bin sedere diuaricatus dicitur, sed iam sequentia vi-deamus Stabilis in petra consistens, nec vllis aduerfan-tibus, veletiam fecundis flatibus à recto cursu deflectit. Ecquis antehac audierat, vel Auctoritatem in pe-tra positam nauigare, vel Nauem aliquam fecun-dis flatibus, recto cursu deflecti. Verùmtamen vt-cunque nauis ista nauiget, superius demonstratum est, ei qui fe in eius puppi sedere clauum que tene-re gloriabatur, ne in ima quidem sententia locum relictum esse. Consimile illud est quod sequitur: Si quos ordinationi Dei resistentes inuenit, sæuiore hos vin-dicta vlciscitur. Quasi verò vel in vrbe Roma, quod flagitiorum omnium domicilium est, nullis ordi-nationibus Dei resistatur: vel Papa vllos iiftiufmo-di resistentes sæuiore vindicta vlciscatur. At Pe-trarcha Mantuanus, Sannafarius, & alij complures Itali Romam appellant scelerum omnium offici-nam, Babylonem, Sodomam, scholam errorû, tem-plum hærefeum, scortum perfrictæ frontis.
units.tr: There remains a fourth ground of nullity, from the foolish form of the sentence he has framed. For, as the saying goes, the foolishness of the speech shows the foolishness of the mind. l.pen. D.de cond. & demonst. l.1. § pen. & vlt. D.de ædil. edict. So a judge who pronounces his sentence foolishly and absurdly from the very start is called a fool. l.vlt. C.de fideic. lib. This is the kind of man the monk, the disciple of Francis Bernardone, is. We shall show this from his own sentence and from the monkish bull. It opens thus: The authority handed down by the boundless power of the eternal King to Blessed Peter and his successors surpasses all the powers of earthly kings and princes. What a butcher's way of talking about sentences! But there is an old precept of the dialecticians that comparisons are to be drawn only between things of the same kind. What in common is there between the authority given to the Apostles, which pertains to spiritual matters, that is, to religion and consciences, and the power granted to kings, which is exercised in temporal matters, that is, in civil and political affairs? So our Bardocucullus has spoken, as though he had said: the folly of Bernardone's disciple surpasses the ears of all the asses that are in Arcadia. But, to answer seriously, let this conclusion be brought forward. A successor has no more right than his predecessor had. Peter did not have an authority that surpasses the powers of kings; he was commanded to obey them as his superiors. Therefore, even if the Pope were Peter's successor (which we have shown above to be false), he would still owe obedience to kings as their inferior. The minor premise is clear from these words: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. Whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God: Rom. 13. Remind them to submit themselves to princes and powers, and to obey: Tit. 3. Be subject to every human ordinance for the Lord's sake, whether to the king, as supreme, or to governors, as sent by him: 1 Pet. 2. But what authority will Holy Scripture have with the Pope? For he refutes it at once with one word: Constantine gave all the kingdoms of the Western world to the Pope, and decreed that emperors and kings should hold his stirrup when he mounted his horse, should act as his grooms, and finally, prostrate on the ground, should kiss his feet. This is that superiority of the Popes which the passage means: such as that of his god Francis, who once on earth, when he was chatting familiarly with Christ in the middle region of the air, put on a hooded garment to ward off that cold; or such as he is said to enjoy today in heaven, where he sits astride above the Cherubim. But let us now see what follows: Standing firm on the rock, and not deflected from its straight course by any opposing or even by favourable winds. Has anyone ever heard before of an authority set on a rock sailing, or of a ship being turned from its straight course by favourable winds? However, however that ship sails, it has been shown above that no place is left even in the lowest rank of judgement for the man who boasts that he sits at her stern and holds the helm. What follows is similar: If he finds any who resist God's ordinance, he avenges himself on them with a more severe punishment. As if, forsooth, in the city of Rome, which is the home of every crime, no one resists God's ordinances; or as if the Pope took vengeance on any such resisters with more severe punishment! But Petrarch, Mantuan, Sannazaro and many other Italians call Rome the workshop of all crimes, Babylon, Sodom, the school of errors, the temple of heresies, a harlot of brazen forehead.

units.la: 1 Pudor in villas: fi non patiuntur easdem Et villæ vomicas.Roma est iam tota lupanar. inquit Mantuanus: Item, alio loco:
units.tr: 1 Modesty has gone out to the villages, if they do not suffer the same. And the villages are the sores of the nation. Rome is now wholly a brothel, says Mantuan. Likewise, in another place:

units.la: Venalia Romæ Templa, sacerdotes, altaria, sacra, coronæ. Ignis,thura,preces,cœlum est venale,Deusque.
units.tr: At Rome the temples, priests, altars, sacred rites and garlands are for sale. Fire, incense, prayers, heaven is for sale, and God too.
Likewise, Alberico of Rosate, under the word Rome:

units.la: Curia Romana non petit ouem sine lana, Dantes exaudit:non dantibus ostia claudit,
units.tr: The Roman Curia does not ask for a sheep without its wool; it hears those who give, and shuts its doors on those who do not give.

units.la: Item,R.Bernardus lib.quarto de consid. ad Eugenium Papam,cap.1. Quem dabis mihi de tota maxima urbe,qui te in Papam receperit,pretio seu spe pre-tii non intervenient. Hi invisi terra & cœlo,utrinque iniecere manus:impii in Deum:temerarii in sancta : seditiosi in invicem.Item, Petrarcha in Epistol. Quicquid de Assyria,vel AEgyptia, Babylone,quicquid de Labyrinthis,quicquid denique de Auerni limine,déque Tartareis syluis sulphuribus legitur,huic Tartaro admotum fabula est. Hic turrificus simul & terrificus Nimrod.hic Pharetrata Semiramis. hic inexorabilis, Minos. hic Rhadamantus.hic Cerberus, universa denorans. Hic Tauro suppositá Pasiphae,mixtúmque genus,quod Maro ait,prolesque biformis, Minotaurus inest Veneris monumenta nefanda. Hic postremo quicquid confusum, quicquid atrum, quicquid horribile usquam est,aut fingitur,aspicias:&,ut breviter dicam, scelerum ac dedecorum omnium sententia.Quid ad hęc Papa noster? Audiamus elogium urbis Romæ ex cap. fundamenta, 17. De elect. in vj. Roma,inquit, est gens sancta,populus electus,civitas sacerdotalis, & regia,per sacram B. Petri sedem caput totius orbis effecta. Ecquod fuit unquam tam perfricta fronte prostibulū, cuius ex ore dictum impudentius prodierit? aut quid de monacho Bernardonico nostro dicemus,qui quæ trans-Alpes fiunt,curat:quæ domi gerūtur,negligit?cùm Paulus statuerit,ne qui familiā suam regere nō potest,ei regimen Ecclesiæ committatur. Sequitur. Quamuis potentiores de solio deiiciens, velut superbientis Luciferi ministros ad infima terræ deturbatos prosternit. Quam amenter monachus temulentus incurrit in locum Isaiæ ex cap. 14. qui proprie in Papas Romanos,& universales istos Ecclesiæ sa-cerdotes convenit?Nam Gregorius Magnus dilu-cidè testatur, sub persona Nabuchadnosoris Papæ vniuersalem describi. Inducuntur quippe in infe-ris Reges & Principes damnati, quasi Papæ mor-tuo ad se venienti gratulandi caussa obuiam pro-cedentes eíque sic illudentes: Infernus expauit pro-pter te. In occursum aduentus tui, exurgunt tibi mortui omnes Principes terræ. Exsurgunt ex solis suis omnes reges gentium,tèque his affantur verbis:Etiámne tu in-firmatus es,sicut nos,& nobis similis fastus es? Detra-sta est ad inferos superbia tua.Quando cecidisti de cœ-lo Lucifer,fili Aurorœ,& succisus es ad terram, qui ter-ritabas gentes? At tu dicebas in corde tuo, Cœlum asce-dam:super stellas cœli exaltabo solium meum , ascenda super altitudinem nubis, & similis fiam altissimo. Qui te videbunt, dicent, Num hic est qui conturbabat ter-ram,& concutiebat regna? Nunc Gregorium audia-mus ex lib. 4. epist. cap. 82.ubi locum illum Isaiæ ad eum qui se Papam & Episcopum vniuersalem profitebatur,accommodans,Ascendam, inquit,su-per altitudinem nubiu:similis ero Altissimo. Quid enim fratres tui omnes vniuersalis Ecclesiæ Episcopi, nisi a-stra cœli sunt? quibus dum cupis temetipsum vocabulo elationis præponere, eorúmque nomen tui comparatione calcare,quid aliud dicis,nisi,in cœlum ascendam :super astra cœli exaltabo solium meum? quos dum vestra fraternitas despiciens sub se premere conatur,quid aliud dicit.nisi hoc quod ab antiquo hoste dicitur, Ascendam super altitudinem nubium? Quæ[?] cuncta ego cum flens respicio, respicie, &c. Quibus ex verbis intelligitur, locum Isaiæ de Lucifero in infima terræ præcipitato, & eius ferocitate in inferos depressa, non ad Serenissimum Regem Navarrenum (quo nihil masuetius, nihil clementius sol intuetur) sed ad Polyphemum nostrum Sixtum quintum & eius in conculcanda Regum maiestate superbiam pertinere. Quod si suo Cyclops ille gladio iugulandus est, ecce text.in suo Decreto dilucidum, de poenit.distinct. 2.§.qui vero reprobi, ubi scriptum ita est: Lucifer dum de se superbiendo præsumpsit, ex Paradiso deiectus est in infernum. Item 23.q.5.§.hinc notandum: Nabuchodonosor dum in corde suo superbiendo diceret, Nonne hæc est Babylon, quam ego condidi? &c. statim mutavit Deus rationabilem eius mentem, & immutavit eum in formam bestialitatis, ut ab hominibus fugiens cum bestiis viveret. Quæ verba Ludovicus Romanus (id quod subrumpere adnimaduerti videmus, laudans & commemorans diserte ad Papam Romanum refert, in consil.ult. num. 2. sed iam ad reliqua pergamus, si modo, quoniam de sede Luciferi instituta commemoratio est, illud ex libri Conformitatum sol. 38. ascripserimus: Frater Pacificus raptus in cœlum, sive, corpore, sive extra corpus Deus novit (considerent lectores quam impie verba Pauli nefarius monachus irrideat) & vidit in cœlo multas sedes, inter quas unam vidit eminentiorem aliis, ornatam lapide pretio-so. Et audivit vocem dicentem sibi, Hæc sedes fuit Luciferi, & loco eius sedebit humilis Franciscus. Atque hoc nimirum est, quod superius diximus, Franciscum Bernardonem una cum cæteris suis histrionibus & comœdis locum apud Luciferi regnum habiturum, ut non magnopere quærendum sit, utri dignior fella debeatur, Francisco, aut Papæ Sixto quinto, Franciscanici ordinis antistici. Sequitur in Bulla: Pro incumbenti nobis Ecclesiarum omnium, populorum, ac gentium solicitudine. Papæ! quantum in se Pandocucullus nosler onus suscepit, cum & Ecclesiarum omnium & populorum ac gentium curam ac solicitudinem in suos humeros sustulit? deinceps mirari desinemus, quid sit, quod Pictores in ipsius imagine nitentis formam effinxerint. Vix Atlas, quem suis humeris cœlum sustinuisse fabulantur, gravius in se onus susceperat. Quid igitur nobis fiet, si Papa sub onere isto tanto, quod sibi uni incumbere queritur, labascere ac succumbere incipiat? quam ægritudinis causam melancholico cuidam fuisse aiunt, metuenti assiduè ne Atlas, qui tandiu tantum onus sustinuerat, aliquando succumberet. Sed iuuat nos Guillielmi Budæi viri, non minus (ut iam ante dixi,) patriæ amantis quàm eruditi, de his Atlantibus facetam quandam narrationem, hoc loco proponere, ex ipsius quinto de Asse libro: Concionator quidam perlepidus, inquit, & facetus cauillari non ita pridem in eos solebat, ut diceret eos sibi tales videri, quales sunt in ædibus sacris mutulares statuæ, quæ pilis aut columnis imponuntur. Ut enim illa simulachra quædam veluti oneri cedentia videmus, quæ vel mutulorum vicem sustinent, vel extra abacos mutulorum porrectα sunt, eámque speciem intuenti præbent, ut magnopere niti operiferundo atque insudare videantur, cum reuera sensu sint carentia: ac nihil ipsa facie nitentium saxeam adiuuent firmitatem: ita Atlantes istos sanctos summis scapis columnarum in fano Domini superpositos, fabulosa quidem illa amplitudine, appellationúmque maiestate venerandorum senum instar, sanctissanctitatemque praeferre, moris est, speciemque luculentam praebere grauissimorum Patrum, sanctuarium Domini fulcientium: stupidam autem eorum ignorantiam aut incuriam dissolutam intuentibus patere, eos nihilo vtiliores statuis lapideis esse. Haec Budaeus. Quin ne illud quidem permittendum videtur, quod Antoninus Archiepisc. Florent. qué superius aliquoties commemorauimus, nos docuit, cum oneri tanto Papa iampridem succumbere coepisset, repertos esse, qui eum labentem suis humeris fulcirent, ne-pe Monachos Dominicanos. Nam Historiar. part. 3.tit.23.§.3.sol 191.sic scribit:Dominicus Papam Innocentium adiit, & ab eo petiit, vt suum praedicatorium ordinem confirmaret. Papa primitus se difficilem exhibuit, at noctè quadam Deo sibi reuelante, vidit in somnis quod Lateranensis Ecclesia quasi suis compagibus resoluta, grauem subito minaretur ruinam. quod cū tremens simul ac mœrens aspiceret, ex aduerso vir Dei Dominicus occurrebat, qui humeris suppositis, totam illam casuram fabricam sustentabat: cuius quidem visionis & nouitatem admirans & significationem prudenter intelligens, Dominici petitionem hilariter acceptauit:anno Domini MCCX. Haec ille. Sed quid si etiam Dominicani, qui annos iam amplius trecentos suis humeris ruentem Papatum sustinuerunt, ipsi quoque labascere ac debilitari coeperint? Repertum est alterum columen subsidiarium. Nam Iesuitae nuper exorti sunt, qui defessis Dominicanis integri ac recentes succurrerent. Ita res (vt in vetere prouerbio est) ad triarios rediit, quibus iam debilitatis Papa summae rei diffisus, ad hoc brutum excommunicationum fulmen descendit. Sequitur in bulla:Vt non solum FAMVLATVS nostri, sed etiam omnia futura tempora cunctis Christiani orbis partibus pacem afferant. De hoc FAMVLATVS genere superius dictum est: quod in eo versari docuimus, ut Reges & Imperatores Papę ex equo descendenti strepam teneant, ut eidem in oppida ingredienti seruilem pedisequi operam praestent: ut eidem in regali solio considenti venerationem & cultum diuinum praebeant: soloque prostrati, & ad pedes ipsius iacentes, ad testificandam seruitutem calceis ipsius osculum ferant. Sed quid hoc verbi est:Hoc tempore damnamus Hereticos, ut futura tempora orbi Christiano pacem afferant? Nunquid nisi pransus, potus, ebrius Sixtus noster fuisset, scripturus potius fuerat,Vt futuris temporibus orbi Christiano pacem afferamus? Sed pergamus ad reliqua huius Bullae oracula. Sic enim subiungit: In Gallia regno Christiana religio omni tempore viguit, tantaque regum illorum pietas, fides ac devotio fuit, tot in Romanam Ecclesiam merita, ut Christianissimorum cognomen ab ea sint consecuti. Si omni tempore religio Christiana a Regibus Gallorum tantopere culta est, quid ita tot Papae, toties suis istis insanissimis execrationibus & proscriptionibus tantum Regum Gallorum nu merum insectati sunt? Merces scilicet haec fuit & gratia, quam Papae pro tantis Gallorum Regum in se & sedem suam meritis ipsis retulerunt. Nā [?]quic-quid potentiae Pontifices obtinent, id omne ex Gallorum Regum beneficiis & largitionibus immensis eos consecutos constat, ac praecipuē Regis Pipini & Caroli Magni, & Ludouici cognomento Pij: ut superius demonstratum est. Sequitur, Arma nostra, quae non carnalia sunt in duos IRAE FILIOS Henricum quondam Regem Navarrum, & Henricu olim Principe Condefem exercere cōpellimur. Carnalia c[?]rtè Paparū arma non esse, sed ferrea, & (vt Bonifacius octauus loquitur) materialia, si quis ex Iulij secundi gladio, quem superius commemorauimus, non meminit, at ex his eiusdem Bonifacij verbis cognoscet: ex c. vnam sanctam, Extrauag. de maiorit. & obed. Certè, inquit, qui in potestate Petri temporalem gladium esse negat, male verbu Domini attendit proferentis, Conuerte gladium tuum in vaginæ. u-terque ergo gladius est in potestate Ecclesiæ: spiritualis scilicet gladius & materialis. Ecquis Sannio magis ridiculus in comœdia vlla fuit, quâ Bonifacius, qui gladium Petri, quem piscator forte tum ad zonam alligatū gerebat[?], dicit eiusmodi gladiū fuisse, qualem Paulus scribit à Deo tributum esse magistratibus, vt in facinorosos & damnatos animaduertant? praeterea quāta ista est stoliditas, Ex eo quod Christus vetat Petrum vti suo gladio, eúmque iubet di-stri&tum ab se gladium in vaginam recondere, sic concludere: Licere ergo Papis vti gladio materiali? Videat igitur Sanio noster, qua ratione ab ista sese extricet repugnantia: Paparum arma non esse carnalia: & Papam habere ius gladij temporalis, materialis, ferrei. Arma Paparū non esse ferrea: sed Regem Galliæ à Papa iuberi ferro, armis & castris Nauarrum Regem, agnatum suum proximum, insectari: & hanc suam sententiam sic exequi, vt incendiis & caedibus vniuersa Gallia compleatur. Nam hoc illud est, quod eodem loco Bonifacius scribit: Spiritualem gladium ab Ecclesia, temporalem pro Ecclesia exerceri, illum Sacerdotis, hunc manu Regum & militum, sed ad nutum & patientiā Sacerdotis. Hæc sunt totidem literis exscripta Bonifacij Papæ verba ex d.c.j.de maiorit.& obed.ne quis forte dubitet,quin Reges ad nutum Papae, tanquā gladiatores ad nutum lanistae ,parati in armis esse debeat, & eadem ad eiusdem nutum deponere:ne cui,inquā,dubium fit,quin crudelissimus & immanissimus tyrannus Papa Sixtus V.qui hoc loco Nauarrum Regem & Condaeum Principem nouo & inaudito contumeliae genere IRAE FILIOS appellat, Gallis omnibus,gladios,incendia,cruciatus,tormenta,pestem, perniciem,exitium denuntiet.Omnes quidem irae filij natura fumus:vt ait Paulus Rom.3. & Ephes.2. Sed Papa irae filius est iudicio, malitia, & voluntate.Sed quid illud est,quod identidem in hac Bulla inculcat:QVONDAM REGEM?Posterius de regno videbimus. Sed quo iure Henricus noster Regis nomen amisit?an quo Scarabeus Francisci Bernar-donis discipulus in hac Bulla sese Monarcham ecclesiae appellat? Vae tuo capiti,trifurcifer execran-de,& Antichriste facerrime.Tu DEUM te appella-ri gloriaris,& gaudes:vt superius demonstrauimus. Tu Imperatores & Reges mancipiorum habes loco:tibi diuinos honores ab iis praeberi postulas.An siquis seruilem istam idololatriam tibi deneget, continuo Regis aut Principis nomen amittet? Audiamus quantopere hunc Antichristum B.Bernar-dus detestetur in sermone sexto,ad Psalm.xcı.Ipsa quoque,inquit, Ecclesiae sacrae dignitatis officia, in turpem quaestum & tenebrarum negotium transfuere. nec in his salus animarum, sed luxus quaeritur diuitiarum. Propter hoc tundentur, propter hoc frequentant Ecclesiasticas celebrant, Psalmos decantant. Pro episcopatibus, archidiaconatibus, abbatiis, aliisque dignitatibus impudenter hodie decertatur, ut Ecclesiarum reditus in superfluitatis & vanitatis usu dissipentur. Superest ut reveletur homo peccati, filius perditionis, daemonium non modo diurnum, sed & meridianum, quod non solum transfiguratur in Angelum lucis, sed extollitur super omne quod dicitur Deus, aut quod colitur. Quibus verbis Sixtus nostep non HERI aut QVONDAM aut OLIM Antichristus esse osteditur[?], sed HODIE, cras, perendie, & quandiu occupatam in Ecclesia Dei tyrannidè impiè ac scelerate retinebit. Sequitur in Bulla: Errores & haereses ab ineunte adolescentia secutus est, quoad multorum hortationibus ad Ecclesiam Romanam (ut existimabatur) conversus, haereses omnes Parisiis in Ecclesia publicè abiurauit. Quid hoc verbi est, Ab ineunte adolescentia? cum illam religionem fere ab incunabulis ac prope cum lacte imbiberit, quam hic noster Carnifex Haeresim appellare audet. Sed illud multo absurdius, Quifalso ab haeresibus conversus existimabatur, eas haereses damnauit. Nam qui falso existimatur conversus, quomodo dici potest priorem sententiam mutasse? Quod vero de abiuratione Bardocucullus noster fabulatur, paulo planius explicandum est. Adolescentulus vix annos unde viginti natus, hospitio à Rege affine suo exceptus, multo ante lucem, è geniali thoro euocatus, inter cruentos ac madentes sanguine gladios adductus, quae facere ac pronuntiare iussus est, tremebundus ac gemens fecit, ac pronuntiauit: quae Papae Gregorio per legatos nuntiare iussus est, nuntiauit. Ecqua unquam in Barbaria ius illud receptum fuit, ut quae hoc modo gesta essent, vel rata & firma haberentur, vel ex animi sentetia[?] gesta esse crederentur? Vetus illud est Doctoris Baldi, & verum, Spiritus sanctus posuit in ore Praetoris, Quod metum gestum est,ratum non habebo: Item illud, Praesentia & multò magis comminatio Principis & potentioris inducit verum metum. Haec Angel.in consil.223. Et rursus in consil.378.Abb.Sicul.in consil.3.vol.2. Itaque Scriptura sacra testatur, Petrum Apostolum mulierculae voce territum, etiam cum execratione Deum abnegasse:sed cum id metu ac terrore factū esse constaret, facile veniam ab eodem impetrasse. Canonistae narrant,Marcellinum Papam Paganorum terrore permotum in idolorum sacrificiis thura incendisse: sed tamen facti ac sceleris illum sui poenitu isse.c.nunc autem,distinct.21.Cur in Papa, qui se Christianae religionis columen profitetur,terrore gestum excusabitur:in adolescete cruē-tis & stillatibus sanguine gladiis circumuento ratum haberi oportebit? Sequitur in Bulla: Idem Gregorius literis Regis Navarrae, vtpote Regis, fidem habens, cum a censuris incursis absoluit, omni inhabili-tate ab eo sublata, Pondus esse Papa voluit in his verbis:Vtpote regiis: quasi firmissima debeat esse re-giarum literarum diplomatum & edictorum au-ctoritas. Quo loco primum ex illo scire cupimus, semperne auctor ac suasor fuerit, vt sua Regis edictis & literis firmitas maneret? cuius rei sempiter-na manebit apud nationes ac gentes orbis terrarū omnes, memoria dicam, an infamia foedissima? Sed cum Gregorius XIII, tantus Iuris Doctor ac pro-fessor fuisse dicatur, an non meminisse debuerat, nullam literis,& instrumentis, vi ac metu extortis, auctoritatem tribui oportere? l.si donationis, 7.C. de his quae vi aut met. causa l. interpositas.13. C. de tranf.Sequitur : Dispensauit vt non obstantibus impedimentis tertii & aliorum forsan inter eos graduum consanguinitatis matrimonium inter se contrahere possent, prout in facie Ecclesia contraxerunt. Vix dici potest, quam multa in his paucis verbis stultitiæ & fatuitatis Papalis signa appareant.Primū est in eo quod ait, matrimonium Regis Nauarri suo concessu ac dispensatione cōtractum fuisse post abiurationem religionis ab eodem Rege factam. Redeamus ad Ephemerides.Cardinalis Borbonius eiusdem Regis patruus, anno 1572, decimo septimo die mensis Augusti, post missam in summo Parisiensi tēplo, summa cum pompa & solennitate, hora tamē post meridiem quarta mis[?]ficatam, matrimonium illud in Regis Galliæ Caroli noni, duorúmque ipsius fratrum conspectu, summáque principū frequentia celebrauit. Sequuta est carnificina Parisiēsis festo Bartholomæi die, hoc est, eiusdem Augusti mensis die xxiv. Abiuratio vero à Rege Nauarro cō-pluribus post diebus facta est. Quomodo Papa matrimonio consensit propter factam abiurationem: cum matrimonium tanto ante abiurationem factum fit? Sed dixerit fortasse quispiam: At post illā-abiurationem dispensatio Papæ Gregorij, postulatu Cardinalis Borbonij, allata est. Utrum igitur allata est, ut contrahere matrimonium liceret, quod tanto ante cōtractum & consummatum fuerat: an vero, ut priùs non iure contractum, nunc auctori-tate, & dispensatione Papæ confirmaretur? Si ut contrahere liceret, maior Papæ potestas est, quàm quantam & Theologi, & Philosophi, & Iurisconsulti omnipotenti Deo tribuunt, ut præterita mutari possint, ut quod factum est infectum reddatur: auctoribus Augustino libr. aduersus Faustum 25.Platone lib.de Legibus.ij.Aristot.moral.ad Nicomach.6.c.2.Nouel.de æqualit.dot.§.1.l.in bello. 12.§.facta.D.de capt.l.verba. C. de testam.l.verum, D.de reg.iur.Audacter dicam, inquit Hieronymus, cum omnia possit Deus, tamen suscitare virginem non potest post ruinam.c.si[?] Paulus.3 2.quæst.5. Maior igi-tur[?], ut dixi, Papæ quàm Deo, potestas tribuitur: qui matrimonium iam contractum, perfectum, celebratum, consummatum, facit tamen, ut neque cōtra-ctum, neque celebratum fuerit. Sin autem Papa dif pensavit, ut matrimonium nefarium & contra leges Ecclesiæ contractum, celebratum, & consummatum, accedente sua auctoritate ratum haberetur: videamus, ne atrocissimi sceleris potentissimū Galliæ Regem illustrissimos ipsius fratres & Reginam ipsorum matrem condemnet: quibus auspicibus, auctoribus, suasoribus[?], matrimonium illud contractum fuerat. Damnat præterea Principes regij sanguinis omnes, & summos quoque regni Galliæ proceres, qui & illi contractui, & missæ quarta post meridiē hora missificatæ interfuerunt, suaque præsentia festivitate illius matrimonii cohonestarunt. Sed Papa his verbis neminem æque vehementer atque acriter vulnerat, ut supradictum illustrissimum Principem Cardinalem Borbonium: quem ait, matrimonium illud inter suum ex fratre nepotem & Regis Galliæ sororem, contra sacros Canones celebrasse: ut omittā Episcopū, qui missam illā in summo Parisiensi templo, tanta cum solennitate occentavit: Diaconum, & Subdiaconū qui succentavit: Canonicos eiusdem templi, & cæteros symphoniacos atque organistas omnes qui concentarunt: quos omnes, si nefarium & incestū illud erat matrimonium, vel excommunicare coniunctim iunctim & per accersione Papa debuit, vel certe ab incursis (ut ipse loquitur) censuris & poenis absoluere. Ecquis est fidelis Regni Galliæ consiliarius, qui barbaram & immanem istam arrogantiam ferat, ut Francisci Bernardonis discipulus Regem, quem ipse Christianissimum ab se appellatum gloriatur, tanti sceleris damnare audeat: ac dicere, illum incestas ac nefarias sororis & agnati sui nuptias cō ciliasse[?]? Iam vero quis est in tanto Cardinalium numero, qui hanc superioris Papæ Gregorii memoriæ contumeliam æquo animo fieri ab isto Bernardonico patiatur, ut eum dicat sorori Regis Christianissimi veniam dedisse contrahendi cũ hæreti co notorio matrimonii·hæretico potestate illa aut nō fecisse, aut non nisi post abiurationem fecisse? An non his verbis perspicuè defuncto Papæ Gregorio illudit: quasi fuerit alter Cælestinus Papa, qui Ioa. Andreas, Baldus, Iason & alii, scribunt fuisse unum pecus, in eo quod de manè faciebat gratiâ, & de ferro revocabat: unde Cardinales, licèt scirent quod per fatuitatè renuntiarat Papatui, tamen quia erat unū pecus, lubenter acceptarunt renuntiatione: & creauerunt Bonifacium octauū, qui depingitur vulpes in ingressu, leo in accubitu, & canis in occasu. Hæc totidem verbis Bal.in c.1. De natur. feud.Ias. in cons.145.circa primū,num.2.vol.2.Quōd si propius accedendum est. Ecquid tandem Excucullatus noster, de vetere illa & famosa Paparum contentione statuet: quorum alter, nimirum Cœlestinus tertius, potestatem facit coniugi, nouum matrimonium contrahendi, si alter in hæresin lapsus esset: alter, nimirum Innocentius tertius, non cōcedit?c.quāto, Extr.de diuort.Sed fanaticus impudens respondebit primum.id,quod supra diximus,raro reperiri mo-nachos, qui sint boni Canonistae: deinde quanuis Papa Bonifacius octauus dixerit,Papas iura omnia in scrinio pectoris continere: c.1. de constitut. lib. 6. non tamen minus vere Bald m [?] sub uxisse,quod licet Papa,ex eo quod est Papa, est Doctor vtriusque iuris, tamen plerunque est Doctor auctoritate,sed non scientia:vt dicit Iason in l. praescriptione,col.2.C.si contra ius vel vtil.publ.Prima igitur huius articuli stultitia ex eo demonstrata sit, quod Papa dicere ausus est,nefarium matrimonium voluntate,studio & auctoritate Regum & Reginae ipsorum matris contractum fuisse. Secunda ex eo intelligitur quod scribit se dispensasse,vt matrimonium illud propter precedentem abiuratione contrahcretur, quod erat tanto ante illam peractum. Tertia ex eo, quod ait semel contractum matrimonium vt iterum contraheretur dispensasse:proinde quasi actus legitimi, quale matrimonium esse constat,iterentur [?].contra l. si solus,§ vlt.D.de acq. hered.l.adoptare,D.de adop.l.2.C.de manum.vind. l.serui,D. de legit.2. Nam quod de secundo consanguinitatis gradu subiungit,hoc quale sit, posterius magis idoneo loco demonstrabimus. Deinceps alia videamus Misit Iohannem Duratii, Dominum oratorem suum,qui de poenitentia & conuersione in sedis Apostolicae conspectu sponderet. Qua ex officina literae prodierunt,ex eadem legatus ille profectus est:nimirum ab iis qui capto & armis territo adolescenti mortem,nisi dicto pareret,minabantur. Sed quod tandem istud aenigmatis videtur genus,In conspectu sedis Apostolicae? Vtrum illo sedes aliqua conspicatrix,& oculata delata est, an illa quam Papae ipsi in libro Pontificali Stercorariam, alij Testiculatri-cem appellant, ex qua de inaugurati Papae, vel habilitate vel inhabilitate pronũtiatur? Et sane iuvat nos ioculare illud de Stercoraria sede acroama re-citare, ex lib. Caeremon. Pontifical. i. sectio. 2. c. 3.
units.tr: Likewise, Bernard, in the fourth book of his On Consideration to Pope Eugenius, chapter 1: Whom will you find in all the great city who has received you as Pope without intervening for a price or in hope of a price? These men are hated by earth and heaven alike. They have laid hands on both sides: impious against God, reckless against holy things, and seditious against one another. Likewise, Petrarch in an epistle: Whatever is read about Assyria or Egypt, about Babylon, about the labyrinths, about the threshold of Avernus and the sulphurous Tartarean woods, is a fable compared with this Tartarus. Here is the tower-building and terror-bringing Nimrod. Here is the quiver-bearing Semiramis. Here is the inexorable Minos, here Rhadamanthus, here Cerberus devouring everything. Here is the offspring of Pasiphae, joined with the bull, the mixed breed that Virgil speaks of, the two-formed Minotaur, the monument of unspeakable lust. Here, in short, you will see whatever is confused, whatever is dark, whatever is horrible anywhere, or is imagined: in a word, the sum of all crimes and disgraces. What does our Pope say to this? Let us hear the eulogy of the city of Rome from the chapter Fundamenta, 17, On Elections, in the Sixth Book: Rome, it says, is a holy nation, a chosen people, a priestly and royal city, made the head of the whole world through the holy see of Blessed Peter. Was there ever a brothel-keeper with so brazen a forehead whose words came out more shamelessly? Or what shall we say of our monk Bernardon, who takes care of what happens beyond the Alps and neglects what is done at home, when Paul has laid down that a man who cannot rule his own household shall not be entrusted with the rule of the Church? It goes on: Casting down the more powerful from their thrones, he strikes them prostrate, like the ministers of the proud Lucifer, dragged down to the lowest parts of the earth. How foolishly the drunken monk runs into the passage of Isaiah, chapter 14, which applies properly to the Roman Popes and to these universal priests of the Church! For Gregory the Great plainly bears witness that under the person of Nebuchadnezzar a universal Pope is described. Indeed, the condemned kings and princes are introduced in hell, as though going out to meet the dead Pope coming to them, to congratulate him, and mocking him in these words: Hell was astonished at you. At your coming all the princes of the earth rise up to meet you; all the kings of the nations rise from their thrones and address you in these words: Have you too become weak, as we have, and have you become like us? Your pride is brought down to hell. How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, son of the morning, and been cut down to the earth, you who did terrify the nations? Yet you said in your heart: I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven, I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High. Those who see you will say: Is this the man who troubled the earth and shook kingdoms? Now let us hear Gregory, in book 4 of his epistles, chapter 82, where, applying that passage of Isaiah to the man who called himself Pope and universal bishop, he says: I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High. For what are all your brothers, the bishops of the universal Church, but the stars of heaven? While you wish to set yourself above them by the name of pride, and to trample their name under your own pretension, what else do you say but, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven? And when your fraternity, despising them, tries to put them under you, what else does it say but what is said by the ancient enemy: I will ascend above the height of the clouds? Looking back on all these things, I weep, I look back, and so on. From these words it is understood that the passage of Isaiah about Lucifer thrown down to the lowest parts of the earth, and his pride brought down to hell, refers not to the most serene King of Navarre (than whom the sun sees nothing gentler or more merciful), but to our Polyphemus Sixtus V and his pride in trampling on the majesty of kings. But if that Cyclops must be slain with his own sword, here is a clear text in his own Decretum, De Poenitentia, distinction 2, §. Qui vero reprobi, where it is written: Lucifer, while he presumed to be proud of himself, was cast out of Paradise into hell. Likewise, 23, q. 5, §. Hinc notandum: Nebuchadnezzar, while in his heart he said proudly, Is not this Babylon which I have built? etc., God immediately changed his rational mind and turned him into the form of a beast, so that he fled from men and lived with the beasts. Ludovicus Romanus quotes these words and, praising and mentioning them expressly, refers them to the Roman Pope (a thing we see he has slipped in), in his last consilium, number 2. But let us go on to the rest, since, as mention has been made of the seat of Lucifer, I will add this from the book of the Conformities, folio 38: Brother Pacificus was caught up into heaven, whether in the body or out of the body God knows (let the readers consider how impiously the wicked monk mocks the words of Paul), and he saw in heaven many thrones, among which he saw one higher than the others, adorned with a precious stone. And he heard a voice saying to him: This was the throne of Lucifer, and in his place the humble Francis shall sit. And this is surely what we said above, that Francis Bernardon, together with his other actors and comedians, will have a place in the kingdom of Lucifer, so that there is no great need to ask which of them deserves the higher seat, Francis or Pope Sixtus V, the chief of the Franciscan order. The bull continues: On account of the care that rests on us for all the Churches, peoples and nations. Pope! How much of a burden our Pandocucullus has taken on himself, when he has lifted onto his shoulders the care and concern of all the Churches, peoples and nations! Henceforth we will cease to wonder why painters have shaped his image as a man straining under a load. Atlas, whom they fable as having borne heaven on his shoulders, scarcely took on a heavier burden. What then will happen to us if the Pope, under this so great a load, which he complains rests on him alone, begins to totter and sink? They say this was the cause of illness in a certain melancholy man, who constantly feared lest Atlas, who had borne so great a weight for so long, should at some point give way. But it pleases us to set forth here a witty story about these Atlases from the fifth book of Guillaume Budé, a man no less (as I said before) a lover of his country than learned, from his book On the As: A certain very charming and witty preacher, he says, used not long ago to jeer at them, saying that they seemed to him like those mutule statues in sacred buildings which are set on pillars or columns. For as we see those figures yielding, as it were, to a weight, which either bear the place of the mutules or are thrust out beyond the abacus of the mutules, and give the viewer the impression that they seem to strain and sweat greatly in bearing, although in reality they lack sense, and by the very look of their shining faces they do nothing to support the stony firmness: so these Atlases, placed on the high capitals of the columns in the Lord's temple, are customarily, in their fabulous magnitude and the majestic titles of venerable old men, to show the holiness and sanctity of very grave Fathers who hold up the sanctuary of the Lord, and to present a splendid appearance; but to those who look closely, their dull ignorance or dissolute carelessness is evident, and they are no more useful than stone statues. So says Budé. Nor does it seem right to pass over what Antoninus, archbishop of Florence, whom we have often mentioned above, has taught us: when the Pope had already begun to give way under so great a burden, there were found men who held him up, propping him on their shoulders when he was sinking, namely the Dominican monks. For in part 3 of his Histories, title 23, §. 3, page 191, he writes thus: Dominic went to Pope Innocent and asked him to confirm his preaching order. At first the Pope showed himself unwilling, but one night, God revealing it to him in sleep, he saw that the Lateran church, as though its joints were loosened, threatened a sudden and heavy collapse. While he looked on this, trembling and grieving, the man of God, Dominic, came to meet him from the opposite side, and placing his shoulders under it, held up that whole falling building. The Pope, wondering at the strangeness of the vision and wisely understanding its meaning, gladly accepted Dominic's petition: in the year of the Lord 1210. So he. But what if the Dominicans too, who for more than three hundred years have borne the falling Papacy on their shoulders, have themselves begun to totter and grow weak? Another supporting pillar has been found. For the Jesuits have recently arisen, who might come to the aid of the wearied Dominicans, fresh and whole. So the matter (as the old proverb says) has come down to the triarii, and since the Pope, now that his strength is failing, has no confidence in the outcome of the affair, he has resorted to this brutal thunderbolt of excommunications. The bull continues: So that not only our FAMVLATVS, but all future times, may bring peace to all parts of the Christian world. We have said above what this class of FAMVLATVS consists in: that they are to see to it that kings and emperors hold the stirrup for the Pope when he dismounts from his horse, that they perform servile service as attendants when he enters towns, that they give him reverence and divine worship when he sits on his royal throne, and that they lie prostrate at his feet and kiss his shoes to attest their servitude. But what kind of phrase is this: At this time we condemn heretics, so that future times may bring peace to the Christian world? Had our Sixtus not been fed, drunk and drunken, would he not rather have written: so that in future times we may bring peace to the Christian world? But let us proceed to the other oracles of this bull. For it adds: In the kingdom of France the Christian religion has always flourished, and such was the piety, faith and devotion of those kings, and so many were their merits toward the Roman Church, that they gained the name of Most Christian from it. If the Christian religion has always been so greatly cherished by the kings of the French, why then have so many Popes, so often, with their insane curses and proscriptions, harassed so many kings of France? This, of course, was the reward and thanks that the Popes gave back for the great merits of the French kings toward themselves and their see. For it is well established that whatever power the Pontiffs possess, they have all obtained from the benefits and immense largesse of the French kings, and especially of King Pepin, Charlemagne, and Louis surnamed the Pious, as has been shown above. It continues: Our arms, which are not carnal, we are compelled to use against the two SONS OF WRATH, Henry, formerly King of Navarre, and Henry, formerly Prince of Condé. That the arms of the Popes are certainly not carnal, but iron and (as Boniface VIII puts it) material, anyone who does not recall the sword of Julius II, which we mentioned above, will learn from these same words of Boniface, in the chapter Unam sanctam, Extravagants, On the Majority and Obedience: Certainly, he says, whoever denies that the temporal sword is in the power of Peter misreads the word of the Lord who said: Put up your sword into its sheath. Both swords, therefore, are in the power of the Church: the spiritual sword and the material. What buffoon was ever more ridiculous in any comedy than Boniface, who says that the sword of Peter, which the fisherman happened to wear tied at his belt, was of the kind Paul writes was given by God to magistrates to punish evildoers and the condemned? Moreover, what great stupidity it is to conclude from the fact that Christ forbids Peter to use his sword, and orders him to put the drawn sword back into its sheath, that therefore it is lawful for the Popes to use a material sword! Let our buffoon see, then, by what reasoning he can extricate himself from this contradiction: that the arms of the Popes are not carnal, and yet that the Pope has a right to the temporal, material, iron sword; that the arms of the Popes are not iron, but that the King of France is ordered by the Pope to harass with iron, arms and camps the King of Navarre, his nearest kinsman, and to carry out this sentence so that all France is filled with fires and slaughter. For this is what Boniface writes in the same place: The spiritual sword is to be wielded by the Church, the temporal for the Church; the one by the hand of the priest, the other by the hand of kings and soldiers, but at the nod and sufferance of the priest. These are word for word the words of Pope Boniface from the same chapter, On the Majority and Obedience, so that no one may doubt that kings ought to be ready in arms at the nod of the Pope, as gladiators at the nod of the trainer, and to lay them down at his nod. Let no one, I say, doubt that the most cruel and monstrous tyrant, Pope Sixtus V, who in this passage calls the King of Navarre and the Prince of Condé by a new and unheard-of kind of insult the SONS OF WRATH, threatens all the French with swords, fires, torments, plague, ruin and destruction. All sons of wrath are indeed by nature, as Paul says in Romans 3 and Ephesians 2. But the Pope is a son of wrath by his judgment, his malice and his will. But what is that which he keeps hammering into this bull, over and over: FORMER KING? We will see later about the kingdom. But by what right has our Henry lost the name of king, or by what right does this Scarab, the disciple of Francis Bernardon, call himself in this bull the Monarch of the Church? Woe to your head, accursed three-forked fellow, and most wicked Antichrist! You glory and rejoice in being called God, as we have shown above. You have kings and emperors in place of slaves, and you demand that they render divine honours to you. If anyone should deny this servile idolatry to you, would he at once lose the name of king or prince? Let us hear how greatly St Bernard detests this Antichrist in his sixth sermon on Psalm 91: The very offices of the sacred dignity of the Church have passed over into shameful gain and a business of darkness. Salvation of souls is not sought in them, but luxury and the riches of this world. For this reason men are struck, for this reason they frequent the churches, sing the psalms. For bishoprics, archdeaconries, abbacies and other dignities men now contend shamelessly, so that the revenues of the churches are squandered on superfluous and vain uses. It remains that the man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition, a demon not only of the day but of midday, who is not only transformed into an angel of light, but is raised above everything that is called God or is worshipped. By these words it is shown that our Sixtus is not Antichrist yesterday, or formerly, or once upon a time, but today, tomorrow, the day after, and for as long as he impiously and wickedly keeps hold of the tyranny he has seized over the Church of God. The bull continues: He pursued errors and heresies from his earliest youth, until, at the urging of many, he was converted (as it was thought) to the Roman Church, and publicly at Paris, in the church, abjured all heresies. What does this phrase mean, from his earliest youth, since he almost drank in from the cradle, and nearly with his milk, that religion which this our executioner dares to call heresy? But that is much more absurd: He who was falsely thought to be converted condemned those heresies. For how can someone who is falsely thought to have been converted be said to have changed his former opinion? As for the abjuration which our Bardocucullus tells his tale about, it must be explained a little more plainly. A young man, barely twenty years old, received into the house of the king, his kinsman, was called out long before dawn from the marriage bed and led in among swords bloody and dripping with blood, and trembling and groaning he did and pronounced whatever he was ordered to do and to say; and he announced to Pope Gregory through envoys whatever he was ordered to announce. Was there ever any law among the barbarians that what was done in this way should be held valid and firm, or be believed to have been done with a free mind? That old saying of Doctor Baldus is true: The Holy Spirit placed in the mouth of the praetor: What is done under fear I will not hold as valid. Likewise: The presence, and much more the threat, of a prince or a more powerful man induces a true fear. So says Angelus, in consilium 223; and again in consilium 378; Abbas Siculus in consilium 3, volume 2. Thus Holy Scripture testifies that the Apostle Peter, frightened by the voice of a little maidservant, denied God even with an oath; but since it was clear that this was done from fear and terror, he easily obtained pardon from him. The canonists tell how Pope Marcellinus, moved by terror of the pagans, burned incense in sacrifices to idols; but nevertheless he repented of the deed and the crime, Distinction 21, chapter Nunc autem. Why, then, should in a Pope, who professes himself the pillar of the Christian religion, a deed done through terror be excused, while in a young man surrounded by swords dripping with blood it must be held valid? The bull continues: The same Gregory, since he regarded the letters of the King of Navarre as the letters of a king, absolved him from the censures he had incurred, with all incapacity removed from him. The Pope wanted weight in these words: as of kings, as though the authority of royal letters, diplomas and edicts ought to be most firm. Here we would first like to know whether he himself was always the author and promoter that the edicts and letters of kings should remain firm; and whether the memory of that everlasting thing will remain among all nations and peoples of the whole world, shall I say as a memory or as the most foul infamy? But since Gregory XIII is said to have been so great a Doctor and professor of law, ought he not to have remembered that no authority should be granted to letters and instruments extorted by force and fear? Digest, law Si donationis, 7, Code, On those things which are done by force or fear; law Interpositas, 13, Code, On transactions.
