The bull continues: He dispensed so that, notwithstanding the impediments of the third and other degrees of consanguinity perhaps between them, they might contract marriage with one another, as they did contract it in the face of the Church. It can hardly be said how many signs of Papal stupidity and folly appear in these few words. The first is that he says the marriage of the King of Navarre was contracted with his consent and dispensation after the king's abjuration of religion. Let us return to the chronicles. The Cardinal of Bourbon, uncle of the same king, on the seventeenth day of August in 1572, after Mass in the great church at Paris, with great pomp and solemnity, though at four o'clock in the afternoon, celebrated that marriage in the presence of King Charles IX of France and his two brothers, and in the company of a great crowd of princes. The Parisian slaughter followed on the feast day of St Bartholomew, that is, on the twenty-fourth day of the same month of August. But the abjuration by the King of Navarre was made several days later. How could the Pope have consented to the marriage because of an abjuration made after it, when the marriage had been contracted so long before that abjuration? But someone may perhaps say: Yet after that abjuration Pope Gregory's dispensation was brought, at the request of the Cardinal of Bourbon. Was it brought, then, so that it would be lawful to contract a marriage that had been contracted and consummated long before; or rather so that what had not been lawfully contracted before should now be confirmed by the authority and dispensation of the Pope? If it was to make it lawful to contract, then the power of the Pope is greater than that which theologians, philosophers and jurists attribute to almighty God, namely that past things can be changed, and what has been done can be undone: authorities being Augustine, Against Faustus, book 25; Plato, Laws, book 2; Aristotle, Ethics to Nicomachus, book 6, chapter 2; Novel, On equality of dowry, §. 1; Digest, law In bello, 12, §. Facta, On captives; law Verba, Code, On wills; law Verum, Digest, On rules of law. I will say boldly, says Jerome, that although God can do all things, yet He cannot raise a virgin after her fall. Canon Si Paulus, 32, q. 5. A greater power, therefore, as I said, is attributed to the Pope than to God: he makes a marriage already contracted, perfected, celebrated and consummated to be as if it had not been contracted nor celebrated. But if the Pope dispensed so that a nefarious marriage, contracted against the laws of the Church, celebrated and consummated, might be held valid by the addition of his authority, let us see whether he condemns the most powerful King of France for the most atrocious crime, along with his most illustrious brothers and their mother the Queen, under whose auspices, authority and encouragement that marriage was contracted. Moreover, he condemns all the princes of royal blood, and also the chief nobles of the kingdom of France, who were present at that contract and at the Mass celebrated at four o'clock in the afternoon, and by their presence graced the festivity of that marriage. But the Pope, with these words, wounds no one so bitterly and sharply as the aforesaid most illustrious Prince, Cardinal of Bourbon, whom he says celebrated that marriage between his nephew, the son of his brother, and the sister of the King of France, against the sacred canons; not to mention the bishop who sang that Mass with such solemnity in the great church at Paris; the deacon and subdeacon who assisted him; the canons of the same church, and all the other choristers and organists who sang together. All of these, if that marriage was nefarious and incestuous, the Pope ought either to excommunicate together and by summons, or at least absolve them from the censures and penalties (as he himself puts it) they have incurred. Is there any faithful counsellor of the kingdom of France who can bear this barbarous and monstrous arrogance, that a disciple of Francis Bernardon should dare to condemn for so great a crime the King whom he boasts of calling Most Christian, and say that he counselled the incestuous and nefarious marriage of his sister and his kinsman? Indeed, who among so great a number of Cardinals will bear with equanimity that this Bernardon should insult the memory of the late Pope Gregory by saying that he gave the sister of the Most Christian King leave to contract marriage with a notorious heretic, or that he did not do so with that power, or did so only after the abjuration? Does he not clearly mock the dead Pope with these words? As if he were another Pope Celestine, who, as Joannes Andreas, Baldus, Jason and others write, was one sheep in this: that in the morning he made a grace and in the evening took it back again; whence the Cardinals, although they knew that by his folly he had renounced the Papacy, nevertheless, because he was a single sheep, gladly accepted the renunciation and created Boniface VIII, who is painted as a fox on entering, a lion on his couch, and a dog at his setting. These are the very words of Baldus, on c. 1, De natura feudi; Jason, in consilium 145, on the first point, number 2, volume 2. But if we must come closer: what will our Excucullatus at last decide about that old and famous contention between the Popes, one of whom, namely Celestine III, gave a wife power to contract a new marriage if the other had fallen into heresy, while the other, namely Innocent III, did not allow it? Chapter Quanto, Extra, On divorce. But the shameless fanatic will first answer what we said above: that monks who are good canonists are rarely found; and then, although Pope Boniface VIII said that the Popes keep all laws in the chest of their breast (chapter 1, On constitutions, Book 6), Baldus nevertheless rightly observed that although the Pope, by the very fact that he is Pope, is a Doctor of both laws, nevertheless for the most part he is a Doctor by authority, but not by knowledge, as Jason says on law Praescriptione, column 2, Code, If against law or public advantage. The first folly of this article is therefore shown by the fact that the Pope dared to say the nefarious marriage was contracted by the will, zeal and authority of the Kings and of their mother the Queen. The second is understood from the fact that he writes that he dispensed so that the marriage might be contracted on account of a prior abjuration, though it had been celebrated so long before that. The third is that he says he dispensed so that a marriage once contracted might be contracted again: as though lawful acts, which marriage is plainly to be, could be repeated; contrary to the law Si solus, §. last, Digest, On acquiring an inheritance; law Adoptare, Digest, On adoption; law 2, Code, On manumission by vindication; law Serui, Digest, On legitimacy. For what he adds about the second degree of consanguinity, what kind of thing that is we will show later in a more suitable place. Let us now look at other matters. He sent John of Duratius, his lord ambassador, who was to promise repentance and conversion in the sight of the Apostolic See. From what workshop these letters came, from the same workshop that envoy set out: namely from those who threatened a young man, captured and terrified by arms, with death unless he obeyed their word. But what sort of riddle is this, in the sight of the Apostolic See? Is it some seeing and observant seat, or is it that which the Popes themselves in the Pontifical book call the Stercoraria, and others the Testiculatrix, from which the fitness or unfitness of a newly inaugurated Pope is pronounced? Indeed, it is a pleasure to recite that jesting story about the Stercoraria seat, from the book of Pontifical Ceremonies, part 1, section 2, chapter 3.

units.la: Pontifex creatus ducitur à priore & Canonicis Ecclesiae Lateranensis ad marmoream sedem, quae STERCO-RARIA appellatur, & ibi eum sedere faciunt: qui ita tamen sedet, ut magis iacere videatur: ad quem mox accedentes Cardinales elevant eum honorificè, dicentes: Suscitat de puluere egenum: & de stercore erigit pauperem: ut sedeat cum principibus, & solium gloriae teneat. Tum surgens Pontifex accipit de gremio Camerarii sibi assistentis, quantum pugno potest complecti pecuniarum, ubi tamen nihil prorsus sit argenti, aut auri, & spargit inter populum, dicens: Argentum & aurum nō est mihi: quod autem habeo, hoc tibi do. Utrum hæc risu excipienda Paparum stultitia videtur, an potius execranda profanandi verbi Dei consuetudo? Sed pergamus in Bulla, fortasse stultiora reperiemus.
units.tr: The newly elected Pontiff is led by the prior and canons of the Church of the Lateran to a marble seat called the STERCORARIA, and there they make him sit. He sits in such a way that he seems rather to be lying down. Then the cardinals approach at once and lift him up with honour, saying: "He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the needy from the dunghill, that he may sit with princes and inherit the throne of glory." Then the Pontiff, rising, takes from the lap of the chamberlain who stands by him as much money as he can grasp in his fist, although there is absolutely no silver or gold in it, and scatters it among the people, saying: "Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have, I give unto thee." Does this folly of the Popes seem to be a matter for laughter, or rather a custom of profaning the Word of God that deserves to be cursed? But let us go on in the Bull; perhaps we shall find things more foolish still.

units.la: Sequitur: Sed ille ut erat vario & inconstanti animo, paulo post à Catholica fide & debita erga sedem Apostolicam obedientia defecit. Utrum igitur hæc stultitia an potius insania dicenda est? Rex Nauarrus falso existimatus est, ad sedis Romanae obedientiam rediisse: & idem inconstanti animo ab eadem defecit.
units.tr: The Bull continues: But he, being of a fickle and inconstant mind, shortly afterwards fell away from the Catholic faith and from the obedience owed to the Apostolic See. Should this be called folly or rather madness? The King of Navarre was falsely supposed to have returned to obedience to the Roman See, and by the same inconstancy he fell away from it again.

units.la: Imò verò summa & planè singularis apparuit in tali adolescente constantia, qui dies ac noctes armatis hominibus circunsessus, tamen fugiendi facultatem assiduè captavit, ut quod vi metuque coactus gesserat, liber & solutus detestaretur.
units.tr: Indeed, a supreme and quite singular constancy showed itself in such a young man, who, surrounded day and night by armed men, nevertheless constantly sought the means of escape, so that he might be free and renounce what he had done under compulsion of force and fear.

units.la: Sequitur: Sapius hæreticos perduelles & seditiosos ad arma contra Regem Christianissimum aduersus ipsum, & reliquos catholicos concitauit. Latinitas ista Papalis cum reliquis ipsius argutiis consentanea est.Rex Nauarrus concitauit hæreticos contra Regem Christianissimum, aduersus ipsum & reliquos Catholicos. Sed sententiam potius attendamus. Non enim contra, nec aduersus Regem Christianissimum arma vnquam Rex Nauarrus cepit: sed aduersus Papæ coniuratos, & Papalis tyrannidis socios, adiutores, administros: periuriorum denique ac perfidiarum auctores: quemadmodum Rex ipse quamplurimis edictis Pacificatoriis planissimè testatus est. Itaque nefariam hoc loco Protocucullus noster potentissimis Galliæ regibus iniuriam facit: cum eorum Maiestatem mendacij arguere ausus est: à quibus toties in edictis Pacificatoriis declaratum est, bellum à Nauarrenis & Condianis non aduersus se, sed pro sua dignitate & statu suo conseruando suscept um fuisse.Sequitur, Cives & incolas ad eandem impietatem capessendam minis verberibusque coegit. Capessere impietatem, genus est eloquentiæ Papalis. Coactum autem quenquam hisce viginti annis ad mutandam religionem, vel à Nauarrenis, vel à Condianis fuisse, tam verum est, quam certum & exploratum, nullum vnquam in lupanaribus vrbis Romæ prostibulum impudetius Sixto quinto in profundendis mendaciis fuisse. Quanquam bene habet, & est huic Papæ habenda gratia, quòd eos accusat, à quibus miseri captiui minis & verberibus ad mutandam religionem adiguntur. Nam, vt verissime Lactantius scripsit, religio cogi non potest: verbis potius quàm verberibus res agenda est. Sed quoniam Lactantius illo loco ita disputat, vt de industria & Nauarri Regis, & Gallicarum Ecclesiarum caussam agere videatur, operæpretium est illum differentem audire, Aduersarii, inquit, fingunt se hominibus piis consulere, & illos ad bonam mentem velle reuocare. Num igitur hoc sermone, aut aliqua ratione reddita facere nituntur? minime: sed vi atque tormentis, ô mira & caca dementia! in iis putatur mala mens esse, qui fidem seruare conantur: in carnificibus autem bona, in iisne mala mens est qui contra ius humanitatis, contra fas omne lacerantur? an potius in iis, qui ea faciunt in corporibus innocentium, qua, nec sæuissimi latrones, nec iratissimi hostes, nec immanissimi barbari, aliquando fecerunt? Et mox: Et quoniam vi nihil possunt (augetur enim religio Dei quanto magis premitur)ratione potius & hortamentis agant: Procedant in medium Pontifices, quique sunt sacerdotes, & Antistites religionum. Conuocent nos ad concionem: (Postulata hæc sùt[?] Regis Nauarræ quotidiana, & sæpe Gallorum Regi delata) Distringant aciem ingeniorum suorum: si ratio eorum vera est, asseratur, parati sumus audire si doceant: tacentibus certè nihil credimus, sicut ne sæuientibus quidem cedimus. imitentur nos, aut rationem rei totius exponant. Nos enim non illicimus, ut ipsi obiectant: sed docemus, probamus, ostendimus. itaque nemo a nobis retinetur inuitus. Inutilis est enim Deo, qui devotione ac fide caret. Et tamen nemo discedit, ipsa veritate retinente. Doceant isti hoc modo si qua illis fiducia veritatis est, loquantur, discant, audeant inquam disputare nobiscum aliquid eiusmodi, iam profecto ab aniculis, quas contemnunt, & pueris nostratibus error illorum ac stultitia irridebitur. Quid potuit à Lactantio scribi pro Rege Nauarro, & Gallicis Ecclesiis aptius, & ad horum nostrorum temporum rationem accommodati[?]us?Pergit idem:Longè diuersa sunt, inquit, Carnificina & pietas:nec potest aut veritas cum vi,aut iustitia cum crudelitate coniungi. Hactenus Lactantius. ex quibus quantopere inter se veterum illarũ & nostrarum Ecclesiarum iura conueniant, perspicuè intelligitur.Sequitur in Bulla Papæ: Intimum quèdam suum nefarius artibus suis instructum extra Gallarum fines misit, per quæ cũ primarius hæreticis impia consilia sua communicauit: eorumque vires & arma contra religionem catholicam, & Romani Pontificis potestatem prouocauit. Quem his verbis Cucullatus noster designet, nihil attinet dicere: vnum hoc subiungemus, quanquam is quem Nauarri Regis intimum appella[?], inter præcipuæ nobilitatis Gallicæ viros, dignum suo genere locũ obtineat, Papa autem Sixtus quintus nuper ex cucullatorum mendicitare ac sordibus emerserit, non tamè Nobilem illum grauaturum impudentis illum mendacij arguere: & hanc illi si quam requirat, duelli chartulam mittere (honor sit auditorum auribus) sumptam ex Conformitatum suarum sol. 51. Diabolus tentauit Ruffinum, dicens: Tu es damnatus, & ipse Franciscus est damnatus, & quicunque eum sequitur, decipitur. Quod cum Ruffinus Francisco dixit, respondit Franciscus,Si iterum apparuerit, & iterum aliquid dixerit, dicas ei, scilicet Diabolo, Aperi os tuum, & ego stercorisabo in illud. Postea Ruffinus cum oraret, iterum apparuit ei Diabolus in specie Christi, dicens, Frater Russine, nonne dixi tibi, quod non crederes filio Petri Bernardonis? cur te affligis? Et statim frater Ruffinus sibi dixit. Aperi os tuum & ego in ipsum stercorisabo. Tunc Diabolus indignatus cum furia & tempestate ab eo recessit. Honor, vt præfati sumus, auditorũ fit auribus. Sed istius os impudens monachi breui hac responsione verberandum fuit. Neque enim unquam nobilis ille apud ullos vel Reges vel Principes verbum ullum de bello cuiquam inferendo interposuit: sed tantum de constabilitâ inter Ecclesias reformatas charitate & fraterna benevolentia. Quanquam quis non videt, quanti totius Christianitatis interfit, impium istum & sanguinarium Ecclesiae Christianae parricidam, fictarum religionum auctorem ac defensorem, conculcatae Regum maiestatis convictum, & certissimum patriae nostrae incendiarum radicitus e terra viventium auer-runcari? Doluit quidem illi tatis vectigalibus spoliari, quae ex Dania, Suetia, Anglia, Scotia, Germania, & Helvetia superioribus seculis auferebat. Sed nobilis quem hoc loco perstrinxit, ait illum nunquam aeque insanisse ut nunc, cum in periculum amittendi Galliae regni adductus est: idemque fecisse, quod asini cicuta pasti, facere in Thuscia dicuntur: quos Matheolus scribit, tam arcto somno consopiri, ut plane mortui videantur, adeo ut rustici plerunque ad pellem detrahendam accedant, & partem eius prope dimidiam detrahant, priusquam asini excitentur. Verum ubi ad media tergoris partem ventum est, tum illos repente in pedes exilire, & dimidia pellis parte propendente, foedu faucibus russis rudorem edere: sic, ut rustici interdū magno terrore afficiantur. Simillimum hoc tempore Papae Sixti vlulatum videri, dimidia prope regnorum suorum parte spoliati, & de reliqua desperantis, ac iam collum in laqueum inseretis, nisi potentissimi Reges ac Principes, restituēdę ipsius potentiae causa, miseram Galliā caedibus atque incendiis
units.tr: The Bull continues: Often he stirred up heretics, rebels and seditious men to take up arms against the Most Christian King, against him and the rest of the Catholics. That Papal Latinity agrees with the rest of his quibbles. The King of Navarre stirred up heretics against the Most Christian King, against him and the other Catholics. But let us rather consider the sense. The King of Navarre never took up arms against or towards the Most Christian King, but against the conspirators of the Pope, and the allies, helpers and agents of Papal tyranny; in short, against the authors of perjuries and treacheries, as the King himself has plainly attested in very many Peace edicts. So our Hooded Protoscoundrel here does a wicked wrong to the most powerful kings of France, since he has dared to accuse their Majesty of lying, when it has so often been declared in the Peace edicts that the war was undertaken by the men of Navarre and of Condé not against the King, but to preserve their own dignity and standing. The Bull continues: He compelled citizens and residents by threats and blows to take up the same impiety. "To take up impiety" is a kind of Papal eloquence. But that anyone in these twenty years has been compelled to change his religion, either by the men of Navarre or by those of Condé, is as true as it is certain and established that no prostitute in the brothels of the city of Rome has ever lied more shamelessly than Sixtus V. Still, it is well, and this Pope deserves thanks, that he accuses those by whom wretched captives are driven to change their religion by threats and blows. For, as Lactantius wrote most truly, religion cannot be forced: the matter must be handled by words rather than by blows. But since Lactantius argues in that place as if he were deliberately pleading the cause of the King of Navarre and of the Gallican Churches, it is worth hearing him speak: "Our adversaries," he says, "pretend that they are caring for pious men and wish to call them back to a good mind. Do they then attempt this by argument, or by any reasoned means? Not at all: but by force and torments, O wonderful and blind madness! Among them the mind is thought to be evil in those who strive to keep the faith, but good in the executioners. Is the mind evil in those who are torn against every law of humanity and every divine right, or rather in those who do to the bodies of the innocent what the most savage robbers, the most enraged enemies and the most monstrous barbarians never did?" And soon: "And since they can do nothing by force (for the religion of God grows the more it is pressed), let them rather act by reason and exhortation. Let the Pontiffs come forward into the midst, and those who are priests and chief men of religions. Let them summon us to a sermon." (These demands of the King of Navarre are made every day and have often been laid before the King of France.) "Let them sharpen the edge of their wits. If their reasoning is true, let it be set forth; we are ready to listen if they teach. Certainly we do not believe those who keep silent, nor do we yield to those who rage. Let them imitate us, or set out the reasoning of the whole matter. For we do not entice, as they object; we teach, prove and show. So no one is kept among us against his will, for he who lacks devotion and faith is useless to God." And yet no one departs, the truth itself holding them. Let them teach in this way, if they have any confidence in the truth; let them speak, let them learn, let them dare, I say, to dispute with us about such matters. Then indeed their error and folly will be mocked by old women, whom they despise, and by our own boys. What could have been written by Lactantius for the King of Navarre and the Gallican Churches more fitting, and more suited to the circumstances of our own times? He goes on in the same place: "Butchery and piety," he says, "are wholly different, and neither truth can be joined with force, nor justice with cruelty." So far Lactantius. From these words it is clearly seen how far the rights of those ancient Churches and of our own agree with one another. The Bull of the Pope continues: He sent an intimate of his, instructed in his own wicked arts, beyond the borders of France, through whom he communicated his impious plans with the chief heretics, and stirred up their strength and arms against the Catholic religion and the power of the Roman Pontiff. Whom our Cowled friend means by these words it is not worth saying. We will add only this: although the man whom he calls an intimate of the King of Navarre holds a place, among the men of the chief nobility of France, worthy of his birth, and Pope Sixtus V has lately risen up from the beggary and filth of the friars, I do not think that noble man will be troubled to prove the shameless lie of this man; and if he should ask for a proof of it, I will send him a small sheet from the Conformities of his own (let it be an honour to the ears of the hearers), taken from page 51: "The devil tempted Ruffinus, saying: 'You are damned, and Francis himself is damned, and whoever follows him is deceived.'" When Ruffinus said this to Francis, Francis replied: "If he appears again and says something again, tell him, namely the devil: 'Open your mouth, and I will defile it.'" Afterwards, when Ruffinus was praying, "the devil appeared to him again in the likeness of Christ, saying, 'Brother Ruffinus, did I not tell you that you should not believe the son of Peter Bernardone? Why do you torment yourself?'" And immediately Brother Ruffinus "said to him: 'Open your mouth, and I will defile you.'" Then the devil, indignant, departed from him with rage and tempest. As we have said before, let this be an honour to the ears of the hearers. But the shameless mouth of this monk ought to have been beaten down with this short answer. For that noble man never, before any kings or princes, put forward a word about waging war on anyone, but only about the firm charity and brotherly goodwill between the reformed Churches. Yet who does not see how greatly it concerns all of Christendom that this impious and bloodthirsty parricide of the Christian Church, the author and defender of feigned religions, convicted of trampling on the majesty of kings, and the certain firebrand of our fatherland, be torn up by the roots from the land of the living? He grieved, to be sure, at being robbed of the tributes which in earlier centuries he drew from Denmark, Sweden, England, Scotland, Germany and Switzerland. But the noble man whom he has here assailed says that he was never so mad as now, when he was brought into danger of losing the kingdom of France; and that he did what asses fed on hemlock are said to do in Tuscany, which Matthiolus writes of: they are lulled into so deep a sleep that they seem plainly dead, so that the peasants often come to strip off their hide and take away almost half of it before the asses are roused. But when they have come to the middle of the back, the asses suddenly leap to their feet, and with half the hide hanging down they bray with foul red jaws, so that the peasants are sometimes struck with great terror. The howling of Pope Sixtus at this time seems very like this: he is stripped of almost half of his kingdoms, and despairs of the rest, and is already putting his neck into the noose, unless the most powerful kings and princes, for the sake of restoring his power, fill wretched France with slaughter and fires.

units.la: n. j. nouis compleant. Verum, hęc quidem quantum ad Serenissimi Nauarrorum Regis protestationem attinet, hactenus dicta sint. Quæ vero deinceps in eadem Bulla contra Illustrissimi Principis Côdæi dignitatem proprie ac seporatim dicuntur, communi hoc responso, satis refutata esse arbitramur.
units.tr: ...fill up with new matter. But these things have now been said as far as the protest of the most Serene King of Navarre is concerned. As for the points that the same Bull goes on to make specifically and separately against the dignity of the most Illustrious Prince of Condé, we think they have been sufficiently refuted by this common answer.

units.la: Criminatur eum Papa, quòd utroque parente hæretico sit natus. Sicuti præclarum est laudari, sed a laudato viro: ita præclarum est vituperari, si modo a vituperato & vituperabili nebulone id fiat: qualem & hunc cucullatum ganeonem, & nescio quos ipsius assecias Cardinales esse constat: a quibus ita fulmen istud Romæ fabricatum est, ut quondam a Cyclopibus fulmina in Ætna monte Ioui fabricabantur. Quis enim non intelligit, quorsum hęc nefaria de utroque parente hæretico cōtumelia, proprie in Condæum Principem coniecta, pertineat?
units.tr: The Pope accuses him of having been born of two heretical parents. It is an honour to be praised, but only by a man who is himself worthy of praise; in the same way, it is an honour to be reviled, but only when the reviler is a worthless scoundrel and a reviler of decent men. Such is this hooded glutton, and certain Cardinals of his, as everyone knows. The thunderbolt was forged at Rome by them much as the Cyclopes once forged Jove's thunderbolts on Mount Etna. For who does not see what this wicked insult, that both parents were heretics, aims at when it is directed specifically against the Prince of Condé?

units.la: Nam apud Canonistas regula est, ne filiis Hæreticorum usque ad secundam generationem dignitas ullaEcclesiastica mādetur. c. quicunque, §. Hæretici, &c. statutum, De hæretic. in vj. gloss. in c. 1. in verb. Regnum; Extrauag. de præbend. Itaque nõ dubium est, quin Sixtus noster hac sibi viam Marranorum quorundam consilio munitet, ad Cardinalatum & Sacerdotia illustrissimo Principi Carolo, Condæi Principis fratri, & iisdem hæreticis parentibus genito eripienda: quod illum speramus, qua prudetia est, perfacile animaduersurum. Sed iam ad reliquas Sixtinæ Bullæ sententias pergamus. Nam paucis versibus interiectis, Papa eidem Principi Condęo suam dispensationem exprobrat, ut ei liceret matrimonium cum illustrissima consobrina sua contrahere. Quanta mentis cæcitas in tam impudenti mendacio cernitur? Princeps matrimonium illud, aliquam multis ante dispensationem illam Romæ allatam mensibus, contraxerat. Dispensatione ipse petiit nunquam: sed armatis hominibus circumuentus, qui ei imperabant, ut Epistolæ ab ipsis scriptæ, & dispensationem postulanti manu sua subscriberet, paruit inuitus: eadem prorsus ratione, quam superius in Rege Nauarro, Principis ipsius patruele, commemorauimus. Sed operæpretium est, considerare, qualis tandem hæc Papæ liberalitas fuerit, ut Principi consobrinam suam ducere liceret: quod matrimonium neque diuino, neque ciuili iure interdictum esse constat. Nam in eo libro cuius supra mentionem fecimus, cui titulus est, Taxæ Pœnitentiariæ Apostolicæ, absolutio Papæ, pro eo qui in quarto gradu contraxit, taxata est grossis duntaxat decem & septem. Sic enim pag.37. scriptum est: Dispensatio super quarto gradu consanguinitatis de contrahendo vel contracto ignoranter, groff. 17. Super tertio & quarto gradu 27. Super quarto & quinto, groff. 27. & debet concordare cum camera apostolica. Si vero contraxerint scienter, & consummauerint. groff. 21. & eodem modo de affinitate. gr. 29. Quid? an non Papa iam aliquoties contra manifestum diuinarum legum interdictu dispensauit, ut & patruo & auunculo cum fratris sororisve filia contrahere matrimonium liceret? quod tamen eo minus debet mirum videri, quia Papa Martin[?] v. habita (ut historicus loquitur) cum suis Doctoribus & Theologis consultatione, cum quoda dispensauit, ut sororem suam germanam impune in matrimonium haberet. Nam hoc sacrilegium literis mandauit Anton. Floren. in summa 3. par. tit. 1. cap. 11. §. quod Papa, quem refert & sequitur Angel. de Claua. in sua summa in verbo Papa, & Nicol. Boerius in confil. 20. Vtrum Papa, num. 26.
units.tr: For the canonists have a rule that no ecclesiastical office is to be entrusted to the sons of heretics down to the second generation (c. Quicunque, §. Haeretici, etc.; the statute De haereticis in VI, gloss on c. 1, s.v. Regnum; Extravagante De praebendis). It is therefore beyond doubt that our Sixtus is paving this way, with the advice of certain Marrano men, for stripping the Cardinalate and priesthoods from the most Illustrious Prince Charles, brother of the Prince of Condé, who was born of the same heretical parents. We hope he will perceive this easily, as his prudence allows. But let us now proceed to the remaining sentences of the Sixtine Bull. For after a few intervening verses the Pope upbraids the same Prince of Condé with his dispensation, which allowed him to marry his most illustrious cousin. What blindness of mind is seen in so shameless a lie! The Prince had contracted that marriage many months before that dispensation was brought from Rome. He never sought the dispensation; rather, surrounded by armed men who ordered him to sign with his own hand the letters written by them and the petition for the dispensation, he complied unwillingly, by exactly the same means as we mentioned above in the case of the King of Navarre, the Prince's cousin. But it is worth considering what sort of generosity this Papal favour was, to allow him to marry his cousin. It is well known that this marriage is forbidden neither by divine nor by civil law. For in the book I mentioned above, entitled Taxae Poenitentiariae Apostolicae, the absolution granted by the Pope for one who contracted a marriage in the fourth degree is priced at only seventeen groats. For thus it is written on page 37: A dispensation for the fourth degree of consanguinity, for contracting or for having contracted in ignorance, 17 groats. For the third and fourth degree, 27. For the fourth and fifth, 27 groats, and it must agree with the Apostolic Chamber. But if they contracted knowingly and consummated the marriage, 21 groats. In the same way for affinity, 29 groats. What then? Has the Pope not already on several occasions, against the plain prohibition of divine laws, dispensed so that a man might marry his uncle's daughter, or his aunt's, by a brother or sister? Yet this ought to seem the less strange, since Pope Martin V, after consultation (as the historian puts it) with his Doctors and Theologians, dispensed one man to take his own full sister in marriage with impunity. For Antoninus of Florence committed this sacrilege to writing in his Summa, part 3, title 1, chapter 11, §. Quod Papa, which Angelus de Clavasio, in his Summa under the word Papa, reports and follows, and Nicolaus Boerius in Consilium 20, Utrum Papa, n. 26.

units.la: Et quoniam Papa sermonem de suis dispensationibus intulit, non praetereunda, ne illa quidem altera memorabilis dispensatio videtur, vt monacho liceat, deposito ad tepus cucullo, vxorem ad certum tepus ducere: nempe vsque ad procreationē sobolis: ne stirps nobilis fine prole deficiat: ea lege, vt simulatque proles suscepta fuerit, tum pater patratus demissis auriculis ad suum cucullum redeat. qua de re videre Baldi testimonium licebit in l. fi tibi filius, & l. fi paterfamilias, §. in arrogationibus, D. de adopt. Iohann. Andr. in c. actus legitimi, & in c. semel Deo, de reg. iur. in vi. Innocen. in c. cum ad monasterium, in verb. licentiam. & ibi Panorm. qui & alios antiquiores producit, De stat. monach. Petr. Anchar. in confil. 339. parum dubitationis Mariam confi. 13. praesens cosultatio, & confi. 28. circa primu. Guill. Benedict. in c. Raynutius, in verb. Qui cum alia, num. 26. part. 3. vbi notat Papae potestatem esse, dispensare vt matrimonium temporale contrahatur quo nihil vel ftultius, vel a sanctissimo matrimonij instituto alienius dici potest.
units.tr: And since the Pope has brought up his own dispensations, there is also another memorable dispensation that ought not to be passed over: that a monk may, for a time, lay aside his cowl and take a wife for a set period, namely until children are produced, so that a noble stock may not die out without offspring; on condition that as soon as the offspring has been begotten, the father then returns to his cowl with his ears drooping. On this matter one may consult the testimony of Baldus on l. Fi tibi filius and l. Fi paterfamilias, §. In arrogationibus, D. de adoptionibus; John Andreas on c. Actus legitimi and on c. Semel Deo, De regulis iuris in VI; Innocent on c. Cum ad monasterium, s.v. licentiam, and there Panormitanus, who also cites older authors, De statu monachorum; Peter Anchoran, Consilium 339 (parum dubitationis); Marianus, Consilium 13 (praesens consultatio), and Consilium 28, circa primum; Guillelmus Benedictus on c. Raynutius, s.v. Qui cum alia, n. 26, part 3, where he notes that the power of the Pope is to dispense so that a temporary marriage may be contracted, than which nothing can be said to be more foolish, or more alien to the most holy institution of marriage.

units.la: Verumtamen talis Papae fuit liberalitas in permittendo monachis temporali matrimonio, quod ex Apostolo Paulo didicerat esse inter omnium ordinum homines maxime honorabile. Sed ecce alia ex aduerso mirifica eiusdem fiue parsimonia, fiue seueritas.Nam Papa Calliftus III. (inquit Boerius) recusauit dispensare super coniugio Diaconi, qui allegabat se continentiae domum non habere, neque legi carnis posse resistere, atque vxore carere: quamuis pro eo intercederet, tunc Cardinalis Senensis, qui postea successit Callisto, ut in suis epistolis in Car-dinalatu compositis testatur: scribens illi suo amico, alterum Papam expectandum esse qui melior sit. quam hi-storiam idem Nicol. Boerius in eodem illo cósil. 20. memoriæ prodidit. Hæc igitur ad illam dispen-sationis exprobrationem responsa sunto. Nā quod ad postremam Papalis Declarationis partem attinet, in qua coniunctim supradicti Principes bombis Papalibus conquassantur, excommunicantur, proscribuntur, eorumque regna, ditiones, ducatus, principatus, & iurisdictiones, primo cuique occupanti adiudicantur, satis iam superius demonstratum est, totum hoc nugarum genus eodem loco iampridem à maxima Christianitatis parte habitū fuisse, quo Bernardonis & Dominici miracula hodie à plerisque Pontificiæ religionis studiosis habentur: quæ tamen religio ita Franciscanorum & Dominicanorum ordinibus, tanquam firmissimis columnis sustinetur, ut si columnas illas subrui paterentur, actum de sua religione existimarent. Sed de brutis illis Paparum fulminibus, iampridem contemptis, ac pro nihilo habitis paulò vberius differendum videtur.
units.tr: Yet such was the Pope's generosity in permitting monks a temporary marriage, which he had learned from the Apostle Paul to be the most honourable of all among men of every order. But look, on the other side there is another wonderful stinginess or severity of the same man. For Pope Callistus III, as Boerius says, refused to dispense concerning the marriage of a deacon, who pleaded that he did not have a house of continence, nor could he resist the law of the flesh and go without a wife; although at the time the Cardinal of Siena, who later succeeded Callistus, interceded for him, as he testifies in his letters composed while still a Cardinal, writing to his friend that another Pope was to be awaited who would be better. The same Nicolaus Boerius has handed down this story in that same Consilium 20. Let these be the answers to that reproach of the dispensation. As for the last part of the Papal Declaration, in which the aforesaid Princes are together battered with Papal thunderbolts, excommunicated, proscribed, and their kingdoms, lordships, duchies, principalities and jurisdictions are adjudged to the first who seizes them, it has already been sufficiently shown above that this whole kind of trifling was long ago held in the same place by the greater part of Christendom in which the miracles of Bernardone and Dominic are today held by most devotees of the Papist religion. Yet that religion is sustained by the orders of the Franciscans and Dominicans as by the firmest of pillars, so that if they allowed those pillars to be undermined, they would think their religion undone. But concerning those brutish thunderbolts of the Popes, long since despised and held for nothing, it seems right to discuss more fully.

units.la: DE BRUTIS ET CONTEM-PTIS PAPARUM FUL-MINIBUS.
units.tr: ON THE BRUTE AND DESPISED THUNDERBOLTS OF THE POPES.

units.la: NAm, ut pauca è variis testimonia proferamus, cum Papa Bonifacius VIII. Regem Galliæ Philippum Pulchrum hac eadem inveterata audacia proscripsisset, Rex coactis Regni sui comitiis, de ordinum sententia decrevit, ut legati Papæ sordidati, omni dedecore infamiaque affecti regni sui finibus exterminarentur. Boni-facium Papa, inquit Laurentius Valla, qui Celestinũ tubis parieti infertis decepit, Regem Franciæ regno pri-vauit, regnumque ipsum (quasi donationem Constantini exequi vellet) Ecclesiæ Romanæ fuisse, & esse subiectu indicauit. Sed comodius [?] videturreferre verba ipsa, Ioanis Tiliani, Parifiefis Parlameti scribæ primarij, & testis in hoc historiarum genere minime su-specti. Cardinalis quidam, (inquit pag. 172) denun-tiauit indicias [?] imperatas à Papa Bonifacio octauo inter Philippum Pulchrum & reges Romanorum atque Anglorum: adiecta poena siue comminatione censuræ. Philippus Pulcher anno 1297. consilio suorum Principū & consiliariorum respondit, se paratum esse sedi Apostolicæ parere in iis rebus quæ ad suam animam & ad spiritualitatem pertinerent: sed neminem præter Deum agno-scere superiorem se in ijs, quæ ad res sui regni tem-porales pertinerent. neque velle se in temporali-bus sui regni negotijs cuiq; mortali subiicere. Qui-bus rebus cognitis, Bonifacius bulla Regi Philippo missa, denuntiauit eum sibi subiectum esse æ-que in temporalibus, ut in spiritualibus: simulque pronuntiauit hæreticos esse, qui aliter crederet, cui denuntiationi fortiter reclamatum est: simul bulla Lutetiæ combusta in præsentia Regis & Principū, atque consiliariorum. Hæc Tilianus in Historia Gallica. Bullæ autem exemplum, & Philippi Regis ad eam responsum, superius sub crimine Maiestatis protulimus. Neque vero Rex fortissimus contentus fuit illius tyranni insaniam scripto retundere: sed acrius illam ulciscendam putavit. Cuius rei historiam commodius videtur Platinæ verbis gnoscere:Bonifacius (inquit Platina) misit Narbo-nensem Archidiaconum qui Regi nuntiaret, ut missum faceret Episcopum Apamensem. Id si non impetraret, diceret audientibus omnibus, Regnum Franciæ ad Ecclesiam devolui,adderetque anathema,& omnes Francos iuramento Regio absolueret. An non hanc eandē-proscriptionis formulam agnoscimus, quam fanaticus noster Sixtus,in Rege Nauarro & Principe Condæo proscribendis usurpauit? Pergit Platina:Interim verò,inquit,Philippus Rex Franciæ Bonifacii arrogantiam iniquo animo ferens, habito apud Parisios Ecclesiasticorum & nobilium magno concentu, commemoratisque iniuriis à Bonifacio acceptis, & eius ambitione ac malis artibus ad occupandum Pontificatum,quem iniuste teneret, ad sedem Apostolicam,tum (ut ipse dicebat)vacatem,futurumque concilium appellauit.Qua quidem re percitus Bonifacius, habito generali concilio,Philippum eiusque regnum Alberto Imperatori subiicit,quem initio Pontificatus sui repulerat. Tum verò Philippus superbia hominis domiturus,Sarrā Columnensem in parte Massiliæ cognitum,à Pyratis redeptū cum Nogaretio Gallo Equite fidissimo Romam mittit,hac ratione(ut ipse palā dicebat)ut appellationesua publicarent.Verum ei longè alia mens fuit.Nam Sarra servili habitu Latium ingressus,collectis undique amicis Nogaretum cum ducentis Equitibus Gallis mercede conductis à militia Caroli V alesii Ferentinū praemittit,qui inde ei,si opus esset,praesidium ferret. Ipse verò Anagniam clam noctu ingressus,adiuuantibus Gibellinis,quos Bonifacius diu multumque vexarat, Pontificem nihil tale metuentem in domo paterna capit, refractis valuis,captiuumque Romam perducit:vbi quinto & tricesimo die post, dolore animi confectus, periit. Hæc Platina:vbi etiam illud Johannis Andreæ & Baldi subiungit, eum esse ut canem mortuum, qui ut vulpes ingressus, ut leo imperarat. Baldus in c.1, de nat.feud. Quo loco praetermittendum non videtur, quod Bardocucullus nosterin suo Conformitatum libro folio 103[?].(scriptum reliquit his verbis: Papa Urbanus Quintus iurauerat destruere ordine nostrum, sed paulo post obiit: Papa Bonifacius octauus bullas innumeras fieri fecit, omnes eiusdem tenoris, ut de fratribus minoribus fieret, sicut de Templariis, ut ordo noster destrueretur totus una die. Antequam ipsas mitteret, captus fuit, bulla combusta, & Papa infeliciter obiit. Sed omissis nugis caetera videamus. Ex his certe intelligitur, iam tum per ea tempora, id est, anno MCCCVI[?], Papārum insanas istas & furibundas praescriptiones, à Regibus Gallis contemptas, ac pro nihilo habitas fuisse. Quod ut certius Regis Galliae consiliariis innotescat, & quae pulchra sunt bis & ter, ex veteri proverbio, repetatur, commodissimum videtur eandem illam historiam exponere verbis ipsissimis Thomae VValsingha-mij, historici Angli veteris, & monachi papisticis superstitionib. deditissimi. Celestin. Papa, vir vitae anachoriticae, subdole à Benedicto Caietano inductus est, ut ei Papatum cederet: & constitutionem ederet, ut Papa quilibet cedere suum Papatum posset: quam tamen constitutionem Benedictus ille (postea Bonifacius Papa factus) revocavit, de quo vere Celestinus prophetavit in hunc modum. Ascendisti ut vulpes: regnabis ut leo: morieris, ut canis. Bonifacio Papae creato Rex Francorum Philippus in multis resistebat. Papae fauebat Gallus Appamensis Episcopus, qui propterea de conspiratione contra Regem Franciæ accusatus, & ad Regis vocatus curiam, in custodia detentus est, Mense vero Februario ad mandatum Domini Papæ liberatus, jubetur vnà cum nuncio domini Papæ regnum evacuare. Papa talibus novis exasperatus, omnes gratias à se, vel à suis prædecessoribus Francorum regibus concessas revocauit: & in eundem Regem cito post excommunicationis sententiam fulminauit. Quam tamen Regi nemo est ausus nūtiare: vel in regno Franci[?] publicare. Fecit etiam citari prælatos omnes de regno Franciæ, necnon & omnes magistros in Theologia, & in iure, tam canonico quàm civili, vt coram eo Romæ Kalend. Novemb. comparerent. Rex verò Franciæ publico prohibuit edicto, nequis aurum, vel argentum seu merces quascunque Romam asportaret de regno suo: fecit etiam omnes exitus & introitus diligentissimè custodire. Prælati Franciæ, misis ad Papam tribus Episcopis, de non veniendo ad diem citationis præfixum, se per eosdem excusarunt. Papa verò Prælatis Franciæ non comparentibus, misit in Franciam Joannem Monachum Cardinalem, qui convocatis prælatis Parisiis, secretum consilium habuit cū eisdem. Postea, circa festum S. Joan. Baptistæ, milites quidã in præsentia cleri & populi Parisiis congregati, Papæ Bonifacio multa imposuerunt enormia, puta hęresim, simoniam, homicidia, propter quę per Regem Franciæ appellatū est contra eum, ad illum cuius interest: donec, convocato concilio, se à criminibus purgaret obiectis. Circa festum natiuitatis beatæ Virginis, videlicet in vigilia natiuitatis eiusdem, venit summo mane magnus exercitus hominum armiatorum missus ex parte RegisFræciæ repēte ad portas ciuitatis Ana-gninę,in quā Papa confugerat pro tutela:quia ibi-dem natus fuerat. Inuenietes igitur portas apertas ingresi sunt ciuitate,& mox dederūt insultū Pala-tio domini Papæ.Cōmunitas vero villæ cōperto, cp VVillelmus de Lōgarecto(legēdū estNogaret-to)senefchallus RegisFræcię aduenisset,vt Papā de poneret vel necaret, statim pulsata cōmuni cāpa-na,& tractatu habito,elegerūt sibi capitaneū quē-dāAdnulphū,qui quidē ill s ignorātibus extitit do-mini Papæ capitalis inimicus.Hi omnes cōmuni-bus votis tantū irruerūt in Papā, & nepotē suū, & tres Cārdinales(q a tergo per latrinā euaserunt) cp diu(vt putabatur)eis resistere non valerent.Ob quā caussam Dominus Papa timēs sibi,treugas petiit. Quib' finitis, exercitus per vim ad Papā est ingref sus: quē tūc permulti verbis cōtumeliōsis sunt ag-gressi. Cū aūt ad rationē positus esset,an vellet re-nuntiare Papatui,cōstāter respōdit.Nō:imō citius vellet perdere caput suū,dicēs in suo vulgari Ecco il colo:Ecco il capo:quōd est dicere,Ecce collū,Ecce caput.Et statim ptestatus est cora omnibus,quōd Papatui nunquā renūtiaret, quādiu posset habere vitā, exercit' verò postquā irrupit palatiū,mox de spoliauit Papā,& eius camerā,atq; thefauraria suā, & asportauit vestimenta cum ornamentis,& au-rum atque argentum,cū omnibus aliis rebus inuē tis ibidem.Et reuera creditur, quod omnes reges mundi non possent tantum de thesauro reddere, infrā vnum annum, quantum fuit de papali pala-tio asportatum.Remansit autem papa sub custodia militum & custodum vsque ad diem tertiā:sed po-pulus Anagū,fācta conuocatione secreta vsque ad decem millia hominum concurrunt, & Papa deliberauerunt. Sed ante hæc omnia sciendum, quod cum illi primo Papam comprehendissent, in equum posuerunt effrenem, facie ad caudam versa, & sic coegerunt discurrere, fere ad inouissimum[?] halitum, & tandem pene fame necauerunt: donec eum populus Anagum (vt præmittitur) liberasset. Tunc populus fecit Papam deportari in magnam plateam, vbi Papa lachrymando populo prædicauit: & tandem in fine sermonis dixit: Boni homines & mulieres, constat vobis, qualiter inimici mei venerunt, & abstulerunt omnia bona mea, & non tantū mea, sed etiam bona Ecclesiæ, & me ita pauperem, sicut Iob fuerat, dimiserunt. Propter quod dico vobis veraciter, quod nihil habeo ad comedendum vel bibendum, & ieiunus remansi, usque ad pręsens. Et si sit aliqua bona mulier, quæ me velit de sua iuuare eleemosyna, in pane vel vino, & si vinum non habuerit, de aqua permodica, dabo ei benedictionem Dei & meam, & omnes qui quicquam portauerint, quantulumcunque modicum, absoluo eos ab omnibus peccatis suis. Tūc omnes hæc audientes ex ore Papæ, clamabat, VIVAS PATER SANCTE. Et mox cerneres mulieres currere certatim ad Palatium, ad offerendum sibi panem, vinum, vel aquam: in tantum, quod statim camera Papæ victualibus repleta fuit. Et cum non inuenirentur vasa ad capiendum allata, fundebant vinum & aquam in area cameræ Papæ, in maxima quantitate. Et tunc potuit quisque ingredi, & cum Papa loqui, sicut cum alio paupere, qui volebat. Tunc Papa exiens absoluit omnes existentes in ciuitate ab omnibus peccatis eorum. His itaque geftis, Papa subitò & inopinatè, recessit de villa Anagnum progrediens, versus Romam, cum maxima multitudine armatorum. Et cùm peruenisset ad sanctum Petrum, ex timore, quem conceperat, quādo fuit captus, & mœrore rerū inæstimabilium perditarum, cito defecit, & sic completa est prophetia prædecessoris sui, quæ dixit: Ascendisti vt vulpes: regnabis vt leo: morieris, vt canis. Hæc VValsinghamius, totidem verbis: primùm in Historia sub Eduardo primo, deinde in Annalib. quin etiam sub anno 1307. hæc adscribit: Rex Franciæ per hoc tempus petiit per suos nuntios à domino Papa Benedicto, ossa prædecessoris sui Bonifacij, ad comburendum, tanquam hæretici.
units.tr: To cite a few testimonies from among many: when Pope Boniface VIII had outlawed Philip the Fair, King of France, with the same long-standing audacity, the King, having called together the assemblies of his realm, decreed by the judgment of the estates that the Pope's legates, dressed in mourning and laden with every disgrace and infamy, should be driven out of his kingdom. Boniface the Pope, says Lorenzo Valla, who deceived Celestine by putting tubes into the wall, deprived the King of France of his kingdom, and showed that the kingdom itself (as if he wished to carry out the Donation of Constantine) belonged to and was subject to the Roman Church. But it seems more fitting to quote the words of John Tillet, chief clerk of the Parliament of Paris and a witness in this kind of history least open to suspicion. A certain cardinal (he says on p. 172) announced the truces imposed by Pope Boniface VIII between Philip the Fair and the kings of the Romans and of the English, with the penalty or threat of censure added. In 1297, with the advice of his princes and counsellors, Philip the Fair replied that he was ready to obey the Apostolic See in those matters which pertained to his soul and to spiritual affairs, but that he acknowledged no superior in those matters which pertained to the temporal affairs of his kingdom except God, and that he did not wish to subject the temporal business of his kingdom to any mortal man. When these things became known, Boniface sent a bull to King Philip declaring that he was subject to him in temporal affairs just as in spiritual ones, and at the same time pronounced that whoever believed otherwise was a heretic; to this declaration strong protest was made, and at the same time the bull was burned at Paris in the presence of the King, the princes and the counsellors. So Tillet in his Gallic History. The text of the bull, and King Philip's reply to it, we have already set out above under the charge of treason. Nor was that most brave king content to repel the madness of that tyrant with a written answer; he thought it right to take a sharper revenge. The history of this affair seems best recalled in the words of Platina: Boniface (says Platina) sent the archdeacon of Narbonne to tell the King to release the bishop of Pamiers. If he did not obtain this, he was to tell everyone present that the kingdom of France had fallen to the Church, and to add an anathema, and absolve all the French from their oath of allegiance to the King. Do we not recognise here the same formula of proscription which our fanatical Sixtus has used to proscribe the King of Navarre and the Prince of Condé? Platina continues: Meanwhile Philip, King of France, bearing Boniface's arrogance with an angry mind, held a great assembly of clergy and nobles at Paris, recounted the injuries he had received from Boniface, and his ambition and wicked arts for seizing the papacy, which he held unjustly, and appealed to the Apostolic See, then (as he himself said) vacant, and to a future council. Stirred by this, Boniface called a general council, placed Philip and his kingdom under the Emperor Albert, whom at the beginning of his pontificate he had repulsed. Then Philip, wishing to tame the man's pride, sent Sciarra Colonna, whom he had met in part of Marseilles and ransomed from pirates, with Nogaret, a most faithful French knight, to Rome, with the plan (as he openly said) of publishing his appeals. But his mind was far otherwise. For Sciarra entered Latium in servile dress, gathered friends from every side, and sent Nogaret ahead to Ferentino with two hundred French knights hired from the army of Charles of Valois, to give them protection there if need be. Sciarra himself secretly entered Anagni at night, aided by the Ghibellines whom Boniface had long and greatly harassed, and seized the Pope, who suspected nothing of the kind, in his father's house; the doors being broken down, he led the captive to Rome, where on the thirty-fifth day afterwards, worn out by grief of mind, he died. So Platina; where he also adds the saying of John Andrea and Baldus, that he went in like a fox, reigned like a lion, and died like a dog. Baldus on c. 1, de nat. feud. Here it does not seem right to pass over what our Bardocucullus wrote in his book of Conformities, folio 103 (?), in these words: Pope Urban V had sworn to destroy our order, but shortly afterwards died. Pope Boniface VIII had countless bulls made, all of the same tenor, that the Friars Minor should be dealt with as the Templars were, so that our order would be utterly destroyed in a single day. Before he could send them he was seized, the bull was burned, and the Pope died unhappily. But, leaving aside trifles, let us consider the rest. From these things it is certainly understood that already at that time, that is, in the year 1306 (?), those insane and furious proscriptions of the Popes were despised and held as nothing by the Kings of France. So that this may become more certainly known to the counsellors of the King of France, and so that what is fine is repeated twice and thrice, as the old proverb has it, it seems most convenient to set out the same history in the very words of Thomas Walsingham, an old English historian and a monk most devoted to papist superstitions. Pope Celestine, a man of anchoritic life, was craftily induced by Benedict Caietanus to cede the papacy to him, and he issued a constitution that any Pope might resign his papacy; which constitution that Benedict (afterwards made Pope Boniface) revoked; of him Celestine truly prophesied in this manner: You have ascended like a fox, you will reign like a lion, you will die like a dog. When Boniface had been created Pope, King Philip of the Franks resisted him in many things. The Bishop of Pamiers, who favoured the Pope, was on that account accused of conspiracy against the King of France, and, being summoned to the King's court, was held in custody; in February, however, at the Pope's command he was released, and ordered to leave the kingdom together with the Pope's messenger. The Pope, exasperated by such news, revoked all the favours granted by himself or by his predecessors to the kings of the Franks, and soon afterwards thundered the sentence of excommunication against the same King. Yet no one dared to announce it to the King or to publish it in the kingdom of the Franks. He also had all the prelates of the kingdom of France summoned, and all the masters in theology and in law, canon and civil, to appear before him at Rome on the Kalends of November. The King of France, however, by public edict forbade anyone to carry gold, silver or any wares whatsoever out of his kingdom to Rome; he also had all exits and entrances most carefully guarded. The prelates of France, sending three bishops to the Pope, excused themselves from not coming on the day appointed for the summons. The Pope, since the prelates of France did not appear, sent into France John, a monk and cardinal, who, having called the prelates together at Paris, held a secret council with them. Afterwards, about the feast of St John the Baptist, certain soldiers, gathered at Paris in the presence of the clergy and the people, brought many monstrous charges against Pope Boniface, namely heresy, simony and murders; on account of which an appeal was made by the King of France against him to the one whose concern it was, until, a council being convoked, he should purge himself of the charges laid against him. About the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin, that is, on the eve of her Nativity, early in the morning a great army of armed men, sent on the part of the King of France, suddenly came to the gates of the city of Anagni, where the Pope had taken refuge for protection, because he had been born there. Finding the gates open, they entered the city, and soon attacked the palace of the lord Pope. But the community of the town, having discovered that William of Longarec (it should be read Nogaret), seneschal of the King of France, had come to depose or kill the Pope, at once rang the common bell, and after deliberation chose as their captain one Adulph, who, unknown to them, had been the Pope's chief enemy. All of these, with the common consent, rushed upon the Pope and his nephew and three cardinals (who escaped by the latrine at the back), so that they could not for long (as was thought) resist them. For this reason the lord Pope, fearing for himself, asked for a truce. When this was concluded, the army forced its way into the Pope's presence, and many then attacked him with insulting words. When he was put to the question whether he would resign the papacy, he answered firmly: No; indeed he would sooner lose his head, saying in his own vernacular: Ecco il collo, ecco il capo, that is, Here is my neck, here is my head. And at once he declared before everyone that he would never resign the papacy as long as he could have life. But the army, after bursting into the palace, at once despoiled the Pope, his chamber and his treasury, and carried off the vestments with their ornaments, and the gold and silver, with all the other things found there. And indeed it is believed that all the kings of the world could not return so much treasure within a year as was carried off from the papal palace. The Pope remained under guard of soldiers and jailers until the third day; but the people of Anagni, having held a secret assembly, gathered up to ten thousand men and deliberated about the Pope. But before all this it must be known that when those men first seized the Pope, they put him on an unbridled horse, facing the tail, and so forced him to run, almost to the last breath, and at last nearly starved him to death, until the people of Anagni (as has been said) freed him. Then the people had the Pope carried into a great square, where the Pope preached to the people in tears, and at last at the end of his sermon said: Good men and women, you know how my enemies came and took away all my goods, and not only mine but also the goods of the Church, and left me as poor as Job was. Therefore I tell you truly that I have nothing to eat or drink, and have remained fasting until now. And if there is some good woman who wishes to help me from her alms, with bread or wine, or if she has no wine, with a little water, I will give her the blessing of God and mine, and I absolve from all their sins all who have brought anything, however small. Then all who heard these words from the Pope's mouth cried out: Long live the Holy Father! And straightway you could see women running eagerly to the palace, to offer him bread, wine or water, so much that the Pope's chamber was at once filled with provisions. And since no vessels were found to receive what was brought, they poured the wine and water into the courtyard of the Pope's chamber in the greatest quantity. And then anyone who wished could enter and speak with the Pope, as with any other poor man. Then the Pope, going out, absolved all who were in the city from all their sins. These things having been done, the Pope suddenly and unexpectedly left the town of Anagni, setting out for Rome with a great crowd of armed men. And when he had come to St Peter's, from the fear he had conceived when he was taken, and from grief at the inestimable goods lost, he quickly sank, and so the prophecy of his predecessor was fulfilled, which said: You have ascended like a fox, you will reign like a lion, you will die like a dog. So Walsingham, in the very same words: first in his History under Edward I, and then in the Annals; indeed under the year 1307 he also records this: At this time the King of France, through his messengers, asked the lord Pope Benedict for the bones of his predecessor Boniface, to burn them as those of a heretic.

units.la: ALTERUM CONTEMPTÆ A REGIBUS GALLIAE PAPALIS fulminationis exemplum,
units.tr: ANOTHER EXAMPLE OF A PAPAL THUNDERBOLT SCORNED BY THE KINGS OF FRANCE,

units.la: Hactenus præclarum contemptæ à Rege Philippo Pulchro Papalis fulminationis exemplum commemorauimus. Neque verò minor fuit Regis Caroli VI. virtus, circiter annum MCCCCXVIII. Nam, ut ex Senatus Parisiensis Archiis & Gallicis ac Germanicis annalibus intelligitur, ut primùm Martinus V. in concilio Constantiensi Papa factus est, non contentus tot, támque magnis vectigalibus ac tributis, quibus freti duo superiores Antipapæ, tres item superiores Antipapæ, aliquanto etiam antè quatuor Antipapæ, funesta inter se bella, per quadraginta prope annos aluerant, noua insuper in Ecclesiis ac præsertim Gallicis, tributa imperare coepit. Quo nuntio Rex accepto, confestim regni comitia de more habere instituit. In eo conventu, re diu multúmq; cognita deliberata, decretu fit, ut nouu illud exactionu Pa-paliu gen' inhiberetur. Quod ubi Martin' Papa cognouit, repente legatos e suo comitatu in Galliam misit, qui Lugdunensi praecipue civitati sacris omnibus interdicerent. Horum Papae interdictorum (si quis forte id nesciat), vis esse in illorum tempo-rum caligine haec solebat, ut templorum omnium valvae praecluderentur, sacra nulla fierent, nullus es-[?]set religionis ullius usus aut exercitatio, campanarum etiam sonitus conquiesceret. tantumne? Imo vero etiam mortuis caemeteriorum sepultura de-negaretur. Quibus rebus dici vix potest, quanto-pere hominum animi superstitione imbuti perter-rerētur. Quid igitur factum est? statim de publici concilij auctoritate, & Parisiensis Senatus decreto pronuntiatum est, anathema illud pro nihilo ha-bendum esse. Sed commodius videtur, rem to-tam ex historici Galli, Engerantij Monstreletti commentariis proponere. Sic enim fere ad ver-bum sub cap. xl. & aliquot sequentibus scriptum reliquit: Rex Carolus v i. per legatos denuntiavit Petro de Luna, Bonifacio xiii. per papificationem nominato, nisi intra tempus illud quod de communi Christianorum Principum sententia praestitutum erat, fine illi funesto certamini imponeret, ac de Papatu cum aemulo suo transfigeret, fore, ut ipse, suique omnes Gallie populi sibi consilium caperent: ac neutri Antipaparum obedientiam praestarent. Hac denuntiatione Papa Benedictus graviter indignatus, animi tamen offensionem vultu atque oratione tegens, blanda oratione legatos dimisit, confirmans se propediem responsum per certum hominem ac nutium Regi missurum, Pauculis post diebus diploma quam Bullam appellant, Regi per emissarium quendam misit, qua & Regem & omnes ipsius imperio subiectos excommunicabat, sacrisque omnibus tanquam impios ac profanos arcebat. Ea bulla perlecta, eiusque rei fama per universam Galliam disseminata, Rex Cōcilium publicum Lutetiam Parisiorum indicit: quo in conventu de communi ordinum sententia decreta haec fuerunt: primum ut Benedictus Papa deinceps pro schismatico, haeretico, & Ecclesiae Christianae perturbatore haberetur: neve illi obedientia ulla praestaretur: utique acta illius omnia irrita essent: tum ut bulla Regi missa pronuntiaretur impia, scelerata, & in regiam Maiestatem contumeliosa: atque iccirco palam inspectante populo lacera-retur.postremo, ut tam atrox illata Regi & regno iniuria tum adversus Papam, ipsius auctorem, tum etiam adversus omnes ipsius factionis socios vindicaretur. His decretis palam in conventu pronuntiatis confestim Re-ctor Academiae Parisiensis e sella exsurgens, bullam cepit, eamque inspectante Rege in procerum delectorumque omnium conspectu suis manibus discidit. Nuntius autem Papae qui eam attulerat, atque alter quidam eiusdem Pontificis emissarius talaribus amicti togis, in quibus inversa Papae insignia depicta erant, mitra capitibus imposita, in qua grandibus literis elogium hoc scriptum erat:HI SVNT IN ECCLESIAM ET REGEM PERFIDI:e carcere usque ad palatii Parisiensis aream adducti sunt: atque in cōtabulato ex tempore extructo destituti, summa cum Papae infamia ac dedecore catamidiati [?], omnium irrisui ac ludibrio expositi, ioculare Parisiensibus spectaculum praebuerunt. Tertio denique post die iterum in plaustrum impositi, ac per urbis vias circumvecti, convitiis, sibilis, clamoribus omnium vexati, vix e populi insultantis manibus effugerunt. Hæc recor-detur, hæc cogitent, hæc meditetur, si qui in Gallia nostra, vel tā ignari atq; imperiti rerū, vel tam malè erga summos Principes animati sunt, vt istam stul-tam & ridicula Bardocuculli nostri monachi pro-scriptione alicuius esse momenti arbitrentur: præ-fertim hoc tempore, quo Paparū hypocrisis tota fe rè Europa patefacta est. Nā idem fecit PERETVS noster, quod limaces solent hyeme præterita, quæ vbi sentire Solem coeperūt, tūm è suis cochleis tu-midas ceruices, & bina cornua protendunt, quibus nonnunquam infantuli terretur. Sic ille complures annos in suo monachali latibulo tacitꝰ delituit, fa-mem suam hostiatim mendicando miserè toleras. Nunc vbi se in tantum honorem collocatū videt, reiecto de capite cucullo cornua insoleter ostetat, iisque se terrore Principibus, ac Regibus illaturum sperat. Verùm, vt diximus, iā pridē Principes pleri-que Christiani belluarū istarum cæcitatem norūt. iampridē quid inter leonem & asinum Cumanum interfit, didicerunt: neq; Manduci late dehiscētibus malis, & clarè crepitatibus dētibus, aut aliis generis eiusdē puerilibus terriculamētis mouetur. Memo-riæ proditū est, eum quē modò dicebamus Galliæ nostræ Regem, Carolum vi. circiter annum MCCCCXXX. pari animi magnitudine brutum Papæ fulmen despexisse. Nā cùm propter prohibitas no-uas quasdā & inusitatas Papæ Benedicti xiii. exa-ctiones, ab illo proscriptus fuisset, de publici cóci-lij, & ordinū sententia decreuit, vt Legati Papę, qui bullā illam pueris & mulierculis horribile, in Gal-liam attulerant, Lutetiæ hac ignominia damnare-tur: primum vt hora ante meridiem decima, quo tempore dimitti Senatus Parisiensis solet, ad Pala-tij gradus adducti adstantibus Episcopis aliquot, & magno sacerdotum numero, nudi ardente dextra tædam tenentes,palam admissum ab se facinus confiterentur: eiusque veniam supplices peterent. Tum ut à carnifice pictis ad ignominiam vestibus induti ac mitellati, cum illius Papæ insignibus ad ignominiam inversis, per celebriores urbis vias lutulento plaustro circumvecti, plebis ludibrio exponerentur. quod & factum, & celeriter executioni mandatum fuisse, Parisiensis Senatus monimenta declarant, & refertur à Paponio in libro Arrest. I. tit.5.articul.27.
units.tr: Hitherto we have recalled a notable example of the papal thunderbolt scorned by King Philip the Fair. Nor was the courage of King Charles VI any less, around the year 1418. For, as is understood from the archives of the Parisian Senate and from the French and German annals, as soon as Martin V was made pope at the Council of Constance, he was not content with the great revenues and taxes on which the two earlier antipopes, three others, and even four antipopes before them had relied, and which had fed their deadly wars among themselves for nearly forty years. He began to impose new taxes on the churches, especially the French ones. When the king received this news, he at once called an assembly of the realm, as was customary. In that gathering, after the matter had been long and thoroughly considered, it was decreed that this new kind of papal exaction be forbidden. When Pope Martin learned of this, he suddenly sent legates from his retinue into France, who were to lay an interdict especially on the city of Lyons. (If anyone does not know, the force of these papal interdicts in those dark times was usually this: the doors of all churches were shut, no sacred rites were performed, there was no use or practice of any religion, and even the ringing of the bells fell silent. Indeed, even burial of the dead in cemeteries was refused.) It can scarcely be said how greatly men's minds, steeped in superstition, were terrified by such measures. What then was done? Immediately, by the authority of the public council and by decree of the Parisian Senate, it was pronounced that this anathema was to be counted as nothing. But it seems more convenient to set out the whole matter from the commentaries of the French historian Enguerrand de Monstrelet. For he left it written almost word for word under chapter 40 and several following: King Charles VI sent word by envoys to Peter de Luna, named Benedict XIII by the papists, that unless within the time fixed by the common judgment of the Christian princes he put an end to that deadly strife and settled the papacy with his rival, then he himself and all the people of France would take counsel for themselves, and they would render obedience to neither of the antipopes. Pope Benedict, deeply offended by this announcement yet concealing his resentment in his face and speech, dismissed the envoys with soft words, assuring them that he would shortly send the king a reply by a trusted man and messenger. A few days later he sent the king, by a certain emissary, a document which they call a bull, by which he excommunicated both the king and all his subjects and barred them from all the sacraments as impious and profane. When this bull had been read, and the report of it had spread through all France, the king called a public council at Paris. In that assembly, by the common opinion of the orders, these decrees were issued: first, that Pope Benedict should henceforth be regarded as a schismatic, a heretic, and a disturber of the Christian Church, that no obedience be rendered to him, and that all his acts be void; then, that the bull sent to the king be declared impious, wicked, and insulting to the royal majesty, and therefore be torn up in full view of the people; lastly, that so grave an injury inflicted on the king and kingdom be avenged both against the pope, its author, and against all his partisans. When these decrees had been publicly announced in the assembly, the rector of the University of Paris at once rose from his seat, took up the bull, and, with the king watching and before all the nobles and chosen men, tore it apart with his own hands. The papal messenger who had brought it, and another emissary of the same pontiff, dressed in gowns reaching to the heels on which the papal insignia were painted upside down, with mitres placed on their heads bearing this inscription in large letters, were led from prison to the courtyard of the Parisian palace, and there, placed on a scaffold hastily built, were exposed to the greatest shame and disgrace of the Pope, made the laughingstock and mockery of all, and offered a comical spectacle to the Parisians. Finally, on the third day after, they were put back on a cart and carried through the streets of the city, assailed by the insults, hisses and shouts of everyone, and barely escaped from the hands of the jeering people. Let those in our France who are either so ignorant and inexperienced of affairs, or so ill-disposed toward the highest princes, recall these things, consider them and reflect on them, if they think that this foolish and ridiculous proscription by our monk Bardocucullus is of any importance, especially now, when the hypocrisy of the popes has been laid bare over almost the whole of Europe. For our Peretus has done what snails are wont to do after the winter is past: when they begin to feel the sun, they stretch out their swollen necks and two horns from their shells, with which they sometimes frighten little children. So he lay hidden for many years in his monastic lurking-place, miserably sustaining his hunger by begging from door to door. Now that he sees himself placed in such high honour, he throws back his cowl from his head, displays his horns insolently, and hopes to strike terror into princes and kings with them. But, as we have said, most Christian princes have long known the blindness of these beasts; they have long since learned what lies between a lion and the Cumaean ass, and they are not moved by the wide-gaping jaws and loudly clattering teeth of Manducus, or by other similar childish bugbears. It is recorded that the king of our France whom we have just mentioned, Charles VI, around the year 1430, with equal greatness of spirit despised the brutish thunderbolt of the pope. For when he had been proscribed by Pope Benedict XIII on account of certain new and unusual exactions which he had forbidden, it was decreed by the public council and the assembly of the orders that the legates of the pope, who had brought that bull, terrifying to boys and old women, into France, should be condemned to this disgrace at Paris: first, that at the tenth hour before noon, when the Parisian Senate is usually dismissed, they should be led to the steps of the palace, and standing before several bishops and a great number of priests, naked and holding a burning torch in the right hand, they should openly confess the crime they had committed and humbly beg pardon for it. Then that they should be clothed by the executioner in garments painted for disgrace, with mitres on their heads, the insignia of that pope turned upside down as a mark of shame, carried in a muddy cart through the more crowded streets of the city, and exposed to the mockery of the common people. That this was done, and quickly carried out, the records of the Parisian Senate declare, and it is reported by Papon in the book of Arrests, title 5, article 27.

units.la: Quinetiam extat Doctoris Baldi auctoritas adversus illam Benedicti xiii.temeritatem, in c.olim, col. penult. Ext. de rescript. vbi animosè atque acriter in illius temporis Antipapas invehitur: quorum hic Benedictus Avenione, alter Bonifacius Romæ sedem occuparat: illumque bovem boantem, hunc belluam bellantem appellat: atque utrumque acerrimè ac liberrimè insectatur.
units.tr: Moreover, there is the authority of the jurist Baldus against that rashness of Benedict XIII, in c. olim, col. penult., Ext. de rescript., where he attacks with spirit and sharpness the antipopes of that time. One of them, Benedict, held the see at Avignon, and the other, Boniface, at Rome. Baldus calls the one a bellowing ox and the other a warring beast, and assails both most bitterly and most freely.

units.la: Quinetiam extat epistola universitatis ac studij Parisiensis apud Theod. Nihemium, tract.6.c.17. ubi hæc prima requesta proponitur. Quod laceretur & frangatur litera Papæ ad Bullæ modum confecta, tanquam iniuriosa, seditiosa, fraudulenta, ac Regiæ maiestatis offensiua, cum protestatione ad maiora procedendi: & capiantur & detineantur omnes suggestores, fautores, receptores pro puniendo & corrigendo secundum Canones. Par Florentinorum civium virtus enituit adversus Papam Sixtum IIII. cuius hic noster Sixtus v. & nomen sibi asciscendum, & exemplum imitandum putavit: quippe, qui ex eodem Bernardonicorum seminario prodierit.
units.tr: Moreover, there is a letter of the University and schools of Paris, cited by Theodoricus Niemius, tract. 6, c. 17, in which this first demand is put forward: That the letter of the Pope, drawn up in the form of a Bull, be torn and broken, as injurious, seditious, fraudulent, and offensive to the royal majesty, with a protest that they will proceed to greater measures; and that all its promoters, supporters, and harbourers be seized and detained, to be punished and corrected according to the canons. The Florentine citizens showed a similar courage against Pope Sixtus IV, whose name and example this our Sixtus V thought fit to claim for himself, since he came out of the same nursery of the Bernardoni.

units.la: Nam cum Florentinos ob illum proditorem Episcopum, de quo supra commemorauimus, è curiæ fenestra suspensum, proscripsisset, eósque Ferdinando Siciliæ Regi in prædam addixisset, Florentini, contépto Papæ bruto fulmine, ac Duce Ferrariæ in belli societatem ascito, furibundi ac ferocis excucullati vesaniam compresserunt: cúmque ad obliterandum suum anathema bello atque armis compulerunt. Quam historiam Raphael Volaterranus lib.Geographi.v.commemorat. Quinetiam extat consiliū Franc. Aretini Iurisconsulti,per id tempus in primis clari ac nobilis: in quo Florentinorum causā defendens, his verbis vtitur: Crimen quod infertur magnifico Laurentio de Medicis, de rebellione, adeo manifeste refellitur,vt erubescam vocem summi Pontificis in hac parte. Nam ex literis suis scriptis ad eundem magnificum virum,de mense Septembris præteriti, declaratur quod de crimine illo habet eum pro innocente & innoxio, & quod nihil sinistri de eo suspicatus est. Vnde ergo beatissime pater, post paucos menses etiam multa & enormia crimina in eum congeris, tu videris. Meum non est ponere os in cœlum. hoc tantū dixerim, In eo qui sedet in throno Dei non est satis honestū tanta varietate vti.Hæc Aretin.consil.163.sicut Iohannes,num.3.Dies nos deficeret, si Principes ac proceres,qui proscriptiones istas & inania tonitrua, fulmina, fulgetra Papalia, etiam superioribus seculis, in tanta temporum caligine,cæcísque tenebris contempserunt,persequi conemur.Imperator Ottho IIII.ab Innocentio proscriptus est. Henricus IIII.à Gregorio VII. Henricus V. à Paschali secundo. Fridericus primus Suenus ab Adriano quarto,& Alexandro tertio. Philippus Friderici primi filius,ab Innocētio II I.Fridericus secundus à Gregorio IX.non semel, non iterum,sed tertiū excōicatus est.Cōradus IIII. ab Innocentio quarto. A quo vero primum istius audaciæ ac su-roris initium natum fucrit, non fatis inter historicos Germanos constat. Ottho quidem Frisingen-sis refert ad annum CIↄ LXVI. quo Guill. Angliæ Rex à Papa Alexandro fecundo proscriptus est, lib. Chron. 6. c. 35. lego, inquit, & relego Romanorum Re-gum & Imperatorum gesta, & nusquam invenio quen-quam eorum ante hunc à Romano Pontifice excommu-nicatum. At Iohan. Tritemius in Chronic. Hirsaug. cap. 4. de Imper. Henrico IIII. scribens: Is à Grego-rio VII. inquit, excommunicatus, & ab Imperio Synodali Episcoporum decreto fuit depositus : quamvis non curaret. Ipse autem primus est, inter omnes Imperatores per Papam depositus. Verum, utcunque fit, (neq; enim ad id quod agimus magni interest, quo tempore hæc Paparum insolentia cœperit) costat omnibus seculis cordatos complures viros extitisse, qui to-nitrua ista Papalia, tanquam bruta fulmina, & aniles bobos, ac puerorum terriculameta[?] contempserunt.
units.tr: For when Sixtus had outlawed the Florentines on account of that traitor bishop, whom I mentioned above as hanged from the window of the court, and had handed them over as plunder to Ferdinand, King of Sicily, the Florentines, despising the Pope's brutish thunderbolt and having taken the Duke of Ferrara into alliance for the war, crushed the madness of that furious and fierce man in his hood, and compelled him to erase his anathema by war and arms. Raphael Volaterranus records this history in book 5 of his Geography. Moreover, there is the opinion of Francis Aretinus, a jurist especially distinguished and noble at that time, in which, defending the cause of the Florentines, he uses these words: The charge brought against the magnificent Lorenzo de' Medici, of rebellion, is so plainly refuted that I blush at the voice of the Supreme Pontiff in this matter. For it is made clear from his letter written to the same magnificent man in last September that he holds him innocent and blameless of that crime, and that he suspected nothing sinister of him. Whence, then, most blessed Father, after a few months you heap many enormous crimes upon him as well; see to it yourself. It is not for me to lift my mouth to heaven.
