I will say only this: it is not fitting for one who sits on the throne of God to use such great inconsistency. Thus Aretinus, opinion 163, and likewise John, num. 3. Time would fail us if we tried to pursue all the princes and nobles who, even in earlier centuries, amid such thick darkness and blind shadows, despised those proscriptions and empty thunders, lightnings and flashes of the Papacy. The Emperor Otto IV was outlawed by Innocent. Henry IV by Gregory VII. Henry V by Paschal II. Frederick I, the Swabian, by Adrian IV and Alexander III. Philip, son of Frederick I, by Innocent III. Frederick II was excommunicated by Gregory IX, not once, not twice, but a third time. Conrad IV by Innocent IV. Where the first beginning of this audacity and fury arose is not sufficiently agreed among the German historians. Otto of Freising indeed refers it to the year 1066, when William, King of England, was outlawed by Pope Alexander II. Book 6 of his Chronicle, chapter 35: I read and re-read, he says, the deeds of the Roman kings and emperors, and nowhere do I find any of them excommunicated by the Roman Pontiff before this one. But John Trithemius, writing in his Chronicle of Hirsau, chapter 4, on the Emperor Henry IV: He was excommunicated by Gregory VII, he says, and deposed from the Empire by a synodal decree of the bishops, although he did not care. He, however, was the first of all the emperors to be deposed by the Pope. But however that may be (for it matters little to our purpose at what time this insolence of the Popes began), it is clear that in every age there have been many sensible men who despised those Papal thunders as brutish thunderbolts, as the bellowing of old oxen, and as bugbears for children.

units.la: DE NAVARRÆ REGNO A PAPA PRODITO.
units.tr: Concerning the Kingdom of Navarre, Betrayed by the Pope.

units.la: NEque vero prætereunda hoc loco videtur xecratio qua Rex Galliæ Ludovicus XII. unà cum Iohanne Navarro Rege, cognato ac populari suo proscriptus est. Nam anno MDCXI. quo tempore bellum illud, de quo superius commemoravimus, inter Papam Iulium secundum & Regem Galliæ Ludovicum XII. patriæ suæ paren-tem appellatum, vehementissimè exarserat, ac tyrannus ille furiosus, eundem Regem brutis suis fulminibus terrere conabatur, eiusque regnū præ-dæ ac dæ ac direptioni exposuerat, regnabat in Navarris Iohannes huius Henrici nostri proavus. Is cũm & in Galliæ regno natus effet, & Galli Regis propinquus & propter magna quæ in ipsius regno possi-debat feuda, eiusdem cliens ac vassalus, rogatus à Rege Ludovico est, pro senioris iure & clientelarum feudalium institutis, ut sibi adversus hostem suum auxilium adduceret. Navarrus sui erga Regem officij non immemor, maturè coactis in suo regno peditum equitumque copiis, tātum in Galliæ fines adduxit exercitum, ut regnum suum viris prope nudatum ac destitutum relinqueret. Qua re cognita Papa Iulius confestim cum Hispanorum Rege Ferdinando (cui tum primum Catholici cognomentum anno 1492. imposuit) per internuntios agere instituit, ut celeriter copias compararet, pollicetúrque se, & Navarrum pro hæretico ac schismatico proscripturum, & ipsius regni eidem pro præmio addicturum. Ferdinandus tantam rei gerendæ occasionem nactus, sibi non deesse statuit: Promulgatain Navarrum Regem execratione, manus cogit: atque in vicini Regis fines ingressus, primùm urbem primariam, nomine Pompeiopo-lim, tum deinde maximam totius Regni partem occupat, auctore, (ut dictum est) Papa Iulio, bono & sine ulla dubitatione idoneo: si modo in regula iuris, qua dicitur, eum iuste possidere, qui prætore auctore possidet: pro Prætore auctore, scriptum esset, Papa auctore. Aliquanto post Rex Galliæ non ignorans Seniorem suo vassallo periculum illius eventus præstare oportere, (quod etiam Bel-laius Langæus, Galliæ quondam clarissimum lu-men, lib. Commentariorum primo dilucidè testatur) exercitum suum ad recuperandam Pompeiopolim misit, cui ducem praefecit Aquitaniæ praefectū Dunosium, Longo villanum Ducem. Sed quidnam & illo tempore & multis post annis acciderit, commodius visum est in aliud tempus differre, & in libellum iis de rebus institutum conferre. Nunc enim satis est intelligi, Regè Nauarrum, huius nostri proauum, non alia de causa Regno suo spoliatum fuisse, quàm quia Regi Galliæ, propinquo suo vicino suo, Semori suo, à Papa Iulio excommunicato, proscripto, hæretico ac schismatico pronunciatio, debitum subsidium adduxerat. Cuius rei nō modo Galli omnes historici testes sunt, in his Arnoldus Ferronus, & Bertrandus Helias, verumetiã Itali & Hispani, ac præcipuè Stephanus Garibaius, lib.29. Franciscus Tarapha, & Antonius Nebrisse-sis[?] lib. de bello Nauarrensi, 1. cap.1.2.3. quibus locis non prætereunda videtur Hispani (ut vulgò loquimur) Pedantis arrogantia, qui Regem Gallum omnium qui vnquam fuerunt & prudentissimum & moderatissimum, tamen hoc verborum honore affecit (cap.2.) Ludouicus, inquit, Gallorum Rex, homo more gentis suæ leuissimus, non contentus se intra pelli-culam suam, hoc est, intra regni sui fines continere, animum in Italiam iniecit, Et paulo post. Igitur Pontifex Iulius secundus, ira percitus, gladium ex Petri manibus corripit, in rebelles contumaces que stringit: ipsos schismaticos ac proinde hæreticos declarat: bona publicat: ad cuius sententiæ executionem Christianos Principes inuocat, atque imprimis nostrum. Item cap.3. Igitur Hispani orbis moderator, verens Gallorum rabiem, Henricum Britannorum Regem (ad quem Aquitania per-tinebat) hortatur vt repetat bello: atque vt iustior esset repetendit repetendi causa, Apostolica intercedit auctoritas, qua Gallum Aquitania priuat, (attendant senatores & consiliarij Regij in Gallia) Britannoque occupanda proponit. Et mox eo loco vbi Papam cum Cardinalibus colloquentem inducit: Iuuandus est, inquit, Rex Hispaniae. In communes bonorum omnium hostes Gallum & Nauarrum Reges, noster vterque stringendus est gladius: atque dum secularem alterum acuimus, interim spiritualem alterum in schismaticorum ceruices intentemus. Itaque communi Cardinalium decreto, Rex Nauarrus declaratus est schismaticus ac proinde haereticus: quia identidem admonitus pertinacius agebat, & se ita non obscure Gallu[?] profitebatur. mulctatur regno & omnibus fortunis: non modo ipse sed & vxor & filij cum omni posterirate sua, & in Hispania omne ius regnandi transfertur. Haec totidem verbis Hispanus Nebrissensis ex quib' intelligitur, quo iure, quo auctore, & qua de causa Rex Nauarrus regno suo spoliatus fuerit. Guicciardinus quidem lib. Histor. Italic. xi. his verbis suum ea[?]dem re iudicium exponit: Hispanorum Rex, inquit, cum se Nauarra regnum legitime possidere alio nomine affirmare non posset, occupationem iure Pontificii imperii factam esse sacrosanctae sedis auctoritate, differebat.
units.tr: Nor should the curse by which King Louis XII of France was proscribed, together with his cousin and fellow countryman John, King of Navarre, be passed over here. In the year 1511, when the war I mentioned above had broken out violently between Pope Julius II and King Louis XII of France, who had been called the father of his country, and that furious tyrant was trying to terrify the king with his brute thunderbolts and had exposed the king's realm to plunder and devastation, John, the great-grandfather of our Henry, was reigning in Navarre. Born in the kingdom of France, a kinsman of the French king, and his vassal and client on account of the great fiefs he held in that kingdom, he was asked by King Louis, according to the rule of seniority and the customs of feudal clientage, to bring him aid against his enemy. Mindful of his duty to the king, Navarre quickly gathered foot and horse from his own kingdom and led an army across the borders of France, so that he left his own realm almost stripped of men and defenceless. When this became known, Pope Julius at once began negotiating through intermediaries with the Spanish king Ferdinand (to whom he had given the title Catholic in 1492), so that he might quickly assemble troops, promising that he would proscribe Navarre as a heretic and schismatic and award the same kingdom to Ferdinand as his reward. Ferdinand, having found such an opportunity for action, judged that he should not let it slip. Having published the curse against King Navarre, he gathered an army and, entering the neighbouring king's territory, first seized the chief city, called Pompeiopolis, and then the greater part of the whole kingdom, on the authority (as has been said) of Pope Julius, a good and undoubtedly sufficient authority, provided that the rule of law which says that one who possesses by the authority of the praetor possesses justly were read, not "by the authority of the praetor," but "by the authority of the Pope." Some time later the King of France, not unaware that a lord must answer for the danger his vassal incurs in such an event (as Bellay Langey, once the most famous light of France, clearly attests in the first book of his Commentaries), sent his army to recover Pompeiopolis, placing over it as commander Dunois, governor of Aquitaine, and the Duke of Longueville. But what happened at that time and in the many years after, it seemed more fitting to defer to another occasion and to a separate little book devoted to those matters. For now it is enough to understand that King John of Navarre, my Henry's great-grandfather, was stripped of his kingdom for no other reason than that he had brought the aid owed to the King of France, his neighbour, his kinsman and his lord, who had been excommunicated, proscribed and pronounced a heretic and schismatic by Pope Julius. Of this not only all the French historians are witnesses, among them Arnold Ferron and Bertrand Élie, but also the Italians and Spaniards, and above all Stephen Garibay (book 29), Francis Tarafa, and Antonio de Nebrija in his book on the Navarrese war, chapters 1 to 3. In these passages the arrogance of the Spanish pedant (as we say colloquially) deserves not to be passed over, for he bestowed this verbal honour on the French king, the most prudent and moderate of all who have ever lived (chapter 2): "Louis, king of the French, a man most frivolous after the manner of his people, not content to keep himself within his own skin, that is, within the bounds of his kingdom, cast his mind upon Italy." And a little later: "Therefore Pope Julius II, stirred to anger, snatches the sword from the hands of Peter and draws it against the rebellious and contumacious; he declares them schismatics and therefore heretics; he confiscates their goods; he calls upon the Christian princes to carry out the sentence, and above all our own." Likewise in chapter 3: "Therefore the ruler of the Spanish world, fearing the fury of the French, urges Henry, king of the Britons (to whom Aquitaine belonged), to make war again; and so that the renewal of war might be more just, the apostolic authority intervenes, by which it deprives the Frenchman of Aquitaine (let the senators and royal counsellors in France consider this) and proposes that it be seized by the Briton." And soon after, in the place where he introduces the Pope conferring with the cardinals: "The King of Spain must be aided," he says, "The Kings of France and Navarre, enemies common to all good men, must both be struck with our sword; and while we sharpen the one that is secular, we should meanwhile aim the other, spiritual, at the necks of the schismatics." Accordingly, by common decree of the cardinals, the King of Navarre was declared a schismatic and therefore a heretic, because, though repeatedly admonished, he persisted obstinately and openly professed himself to be on the side of France; he is punished with the loss of his kingdom and all his property, and not only he but his wife and sons, with all their descendants, and the whole right to reign is transferred to Spain. The Spaniard Nebrija says these things in just these words, from which it is clear by what right, on whose authority, and for what cause the King of Navarre was despoiled of his kingdom. Guicciardini, in book 11 of his History of Italy, sets out his own judgement on the same matter in these words: "The King of Spain," he says, "since he could not otherwise affirm that he legitimately possessed the kingdom of Navarre, was putting off the occupation, which had been made by the right of papal power, by the authority of the holy see."

units.la: Pontifex enim rebus in Italia feliciter gestis minime contentus paulo ante edictum in Gallia regem promulgarat, quo illum non amplius Christianissimum, sed illustrissimum appellans eum & quotquot illi studerent, omnibus Haereticorum & schismaticorum poenis subiiciebat: cuius fortunas, regnum, resque illorum omnes iure occupandi facta potestate damnatos declarabat. In eandem quoque sententiam Arnoldus Ferronus doctissimus rerum Gallicarum historicus, & Burdegalensis quondam parlamenti senator his scribit verbis: Ferdinandus, inquit, Rex Hispa-nus vbi fœdus inter Gallum & Nauarrum Reges ini-tum intellexit, instructas copias quas in Galliam ductu-rus erat, vertit in Nauarrum: atque hæc causa fuit Fer-dinando vicini Regis eiiciendi: quamuis alteram etiam prætexuit, quod edicto Pontificio & Gallorum Rex, & qui auxilium ei ferrent, impii pronuntiati essent, eorum-que regna publicata. Hæc Ferronus, ex quibus fie-ri conjectura potest, quantum illustriss. Germaniæ Principibus, atque adeo Regibus Europæ omni-bus, ex illa tam arcta Paparum, & Maranicæ inqui-sitionis conspiratione periculi impendeat. Nam ista compediaria ratione, monachus aliquis, dum-modo vafro & callido ingenio sit, aliquandiu in Hispania (vt Sixtus hic noster) commoratus, & cum Inquisitoribus Maranicis versatus, facere cum il-lis fœdus & pactionem huiusmodi poterit, vt si eo-rum gratia & commendatione consequi Papatum possit, tum primum quemque Regem aut Princi-pem, arrepta undecunque occasione, schismaticum & hæreticum pronuntiet: regnum ipsius quasi seu-dum sedi Romanæ apertum & commissum illis adiudicet. Optandum est igitur, vt nobis tandem Rex aliquis heroico animo diuinitus detur, qui meretricem istam Babylonicam è sua sede detur-bet, & Christianam Ecclesiam ex tam diuturna, ac misera seruitute, in pristinam suam libertatem ac dignitatem vindicet: quam animi magnitudinem Ludouicus ille Rex noster xii. parens patriæ no-minatus, ac seruitutis illius pertæsus, susceperat[?], cum post illam Papæ Iulij furibundam execratio-nem nummos aureos in Gallia, cum hac inscrip-tione tione cudi iussit: LVD. XII. D. G. FRANC. REX: DVX MEDIOLANI. tùm ex altera parte insignia Franciæ & Mediolani coniuncta, cum hac inscriptione: PERDAM BABYLONEM. Quod nomen, si quis forte non intelligit, cósulat Apocalypsim Iohan. cap.17. & Hieronymum in catalogo, vbi Maci meminit, & aperte scribit, Romam à Petro in Epistola priore, cap.5. Babylonis nomine figuraliter intellecta. Itémque in prologo lib. de Spiritu sancto, vbi Romam aperte Babylonem appellat, & purpuratam illam meretricem, quæ in Apocalypsi designatur. Quod idem etiam confirmat in Esaiam c.14. & iterum c.47. & ad Aglasiam in xi.quæst.qua de causa Paula quoque & Eustochium in ea Epistola, quam ad Marcellum scripserūt[?], similiter Babylonis nomine Romam appellant: nec obscurius idem Hieronymus in Epist. Cùm apud Babylonem, inquit, essem purpuratæ meretricis colonus, &c. Sed & Prosper Aquitanicus Episcopus Regiensis, qui ante annos mille de futuro & regnaturo Romæ Antichristo scripsit, in lib. de promiss. & prædict. Dei secundo, cap. 7. vbi locum Apocalypsis de Babylonica meretrice interpretatur: Quis est, inquit, qui non intelligat, quam dicat Meretricem, ferentem poculum plenum execrationibus immunditiæ, & fornicationis totius terræ? æterna cum dicitur civitas, quæ temporalis est, vtique nomen est blasphemiæ. Cùm mortales (licet Reges) in ea dicantur Diui, eisque supplices dicunt, Numini vestro, Altaribus vestris, perennitati vestræ, & cętera, quæ vanitas, non veritas tradidit, atque execrabilia sunt. Hæc vetus ille Theologus, Romam apertissimè sedem ac domicilium Antichristi futurum ostendens, cū æternam ciuitatem appellat: quo nomine Romam significari, nemo in Iustiniani, aut Ammiani libris versatus ignorat,idque vel ex vno illo Ausonij versu intelligi potest : Ignota æterna ne sint tibi tem-pora Romæ. Quod autem Prosper in Cæsaribus reprehendit, qui sibi dici patiebantur, NUMINI VESTRO, quanto detestabilius est, quod Papa Romanus dici sibi non tantum patitur,verū etiam iubet, SANCTITATI VESTRAE.
units.tr: For the Pontiff, by no means content with his successes in Italy, had a little before promulgated an edict against the King of France. In it, no longer calling him Most Christian but merely Most Illustrious, he subjected him and all who favoured him to every penalty of heretics and schismatics. He declared that, with the power of occupation granted, their property, their kingdom and all their affairs were condemned. Arnoldus Ferronus, the most learned historian of French affairs and once a senator of the parlement of Bordeaux, writes to the same effect in these words: "Ferdinand, King of Spain, when he learned that an alliance had been made between the Kings of France and Navarre, turned the forces he had prepared to lead into France against Navarre. This was the reason Ferdinand gave for driving out his neighbouring king, although he also put forward another pretext: that by the Pontifical edict both the King of France and those who gave him aid had been declared impious, and their kingdoms made forfeit." So far Ferronus. From this one may conjecture how great a danger hangs over the most illustrious princes of Germany, and indeed over all the kings of Europe, from that close conspiracy of the Popes and the Marrano Inquisition. For by this short method any monk, provided he has a crafty and cunning mind, after living for some time in Spain (as this our Sixtus did) and dealing with the Marrano Inquisitors, will be able to make such an alliance and bargain with them. If he can obtain the papacy through their favour and recommendation, then at once, seizing whatever occasion offers, he declares each king or prince a schismatic and heretic, and adjudges his kingdom to them, as if it were a fief laid open and committed to the Roman see. It is to be wished, therefore, that God may at last give us some king of heroic spirit, who may drive that Babylonian harlot from her seat and vindicate the Christian Church from so long and wretched a servitude into her former liberty and dignity. That greatness of spirit our King Louis XII, named father of his country, had taken up, weary of that servitude, when after Pope Julius's furious execration he ordered gold coins to be struck in France with this inscription: LVD. XII. D. G. FRANC. REX: DVX MEDIOLANI. On the other side were the arms of France and Milan joined, with this inscription: PERDAM BABYLONEM. If anyone does not understand this name, let him consult the Apocalypse of John, chapter 17, and Jerome in the catalogue, where he mentions Mark and openly writes that Rome was figuratively called Babylon by Peter in his first Epistle, chapter 5. Likewise in the prologue to his book On the Holy Spirit, where he openly calls Rome Babylon and that purple harlot who is depicted in the Apocalypse. He also confirms the same on Isaiah, chapter 14, and again chapter 47, and in the letter to Algasia, question 11. For this reason Paula and Eustochium, in that letter which they wrote to Marcella, likewise call Rome by the name of Babylon. Nor does Jerome himself say it less plainly in the Epistle: "When I was in Babylon, he says, a colonist of the purple harlot, etc." But Prosper of Aquitaine, bishop of Riez, who a thousand years ago wrote of the future Antichrist who was to reign in Rome, in book 2 of his work On the Promises and Predictions of God, chapter 7, where he interprets the passage of the Apocalypse about the Babylonian harlot, says: "Who is there who does not understand what the harlot means, bearing a cup full of the abominations of uncleanness and fornication of the whole earth? The city is called eternal, though it is temporal, and that is surely a name of blasphemy. When mortals, even kings, are called divine in it, and suppliants say to them, to your Divinity, to your Altars, to your Eternity, and the rest, which vanity, not truth, handed down, and which are execrable." That old theologian, showing that Rome would openly be the seat and dwelling of Antichrist, calls it the eternal city. Anyone versed in the books of Justinian or Ammianus knows that by this name Rome is meant, and this can be understood even from that single line of Ausonius: "Let not the eternal times of Rome be unknown to you." But if Prosper in the Caesars rebukes those who suffered themselves to be called YOUR DIVINITY, how much more detestable is it that the Roman Pope not only suffers himself to be called, but even commands, YOUR HOLINESS.
Conclusion of the Previous Protestation.

units.la: His igitur ita constitutis, superest, ut conclusa nobis hæc sit ratio: CUM PAPA SIXTUS v.septem grauissimorum scelerum nomine, a maxima Christianitatis parte damnatus sit, nimirum impietatis, occupatę in Ecclesia tyrānidis, corruptæ religionis, sacrilegij, maiestatis, perduellionis, & falsi: cumque superiorum suorum insolentiam, audaciam, ac ferocitatem secutus, insanissimum hoc decretum contra omnia diuina, & humana iura, falsis vsus allegationibus, sine vllo iudiciali ordine, stultè, stolidè, atque impudenter aduersus Serenissimum Navarræ Regem & Illustrissimum Principem Condæum promulgarit, eosque spurcis & inauditis verborum contumeliis onerarit, cum eos Iræ filios, Hæreticos pertinaces, notorios, relapsos, in cœno volutatos, contra Regem Christianissimum rebelles, Ecclesiæ persecutores, prolem detestabilem, læsæ diuinæ atque hu-manæ manæ maiestatis reos appellaret:atque his de cauf-sis eosdem suis principatibus,ducatibus,dominiis,feudis,honoribus omnibus,& iure legitimæ in re-gno Galliæ successionis priuaret: cúmque hæc il-lius abiudicandorum & adiudicandorum regno-rum inueterata atque effrenata audacia, perspicuè ad omnes Europæ Reges,Principes,ac potentatus pertineat, periculúmque sit, ne qui alienorum regnorum cupidi atque appetentes erunt, deinceps per hane excommunicationum & proscriptionum machinam,aliis pacatis & crudeli & tru-culento Ecclesiæ Christianæ parricida,importuno ac scelerato religionis hoste, certissiméque Anti-christo habendum esse:rogandósque & imploran-dos Christiani orbis Monarchas omnes , Reges, Principes,potentatus,quíque cum aliquo imperio vel legitima potestate sunt, ut iisdem Serenissimis Principibus ad cōprimendos huius immanis tyrā-ni furores, frangendósque crudeles ac furibundos ipsius impetus,auxilium ferre velint : suáque con-silia & arma conferre ad illam humani generis pe-stem extinguendam,Rémque publicam Christia-nam ab illo prodigioso atque exitiali monstro li-berandam.Interea supradictum Papam Sixtum V. pro intolerandis verborum immanium contume-liis,quas vecordi mente adversus supradictos no-stros Principes effudit, haberi diciq; à cūctis[?] Chri-stianis oportere,prodigium immanissimum , por-tentum fœdissimum,ac monstrum non in ultimas terras exportādum, sed ex humanæ naturæ finibus exterminandū, tanquam certissimum, notorium, ac manifestum Antichristum: cuius exsecrato capiti, malā omnes Christiani pestem, exitiū atque interitū imprecari debeant, vt quādiu anima maledicta in ipsius cadauere spirabit, tandiu piis omnibus fit (vt spiritus sanctus loquitur) ANATHEMA MARA-NATA. Ac ne cui forte nostrum hoc imprecationis genus nouum & inusitatum videatur, rogatos le-ctores volumus, primùm vt eorum locorū memi-nisse velint, quos superius ex Diui præsertim Ber-nardi libris deprompsimus: vbi Papatus Romanus, diserte, dilucidè, nominatim appellatur Antichri-stus, Filius perditionis, Homo peccati, Dæmonium non modo diurnum, sed etiam meridianū, quod nō solum transfiguratur in angelum lucis, sed extollitur super omne quod dicitur Deus, aut quod colitur. Hieronymus autem Romam appellat Babylonem & Purpuratam meretricē. Deinde vt legant, atq; attentè cōsiderent sanctionem Decreti Pontificalis sanctissimam, in c. 2. dist. 23. &c. si quis pecunia, dist. 79. vbi statuitur, vt qui vel pecunia vel gratia humana, (qualem huius monachi gratiam Occidentalem fuisse cōstat) vel popularī tumultu vel quolibet ingenio (id est ambitione & malis artibus) Papatum adeptus erit, is non Apostolicus, sed Apostaticus habeatur, & cum suis fautoribus & sequacibus à liminibus S. Dei Ecclesiæ separatus abiiciatur, sicut ANTICHRISTVS & innuasor & destructor totius Christianitatis. in quam sententiam audacter Canonistæ summo consensu scribere, ac palam profiteri ausi sunt, Papam aliter quàm Canonicè electum, esse Diabolum, & habere claues non cœli, sed inferni. Nam hęc Felini verba sunt,in c.Ego N.de iureiur.Consideret prę-terea Papas,Cardinales, & Episcopos omnes, qui annis ab hinc amplius centum in Ecclesia Romana dominati sunt,ex certissimo schismaticorum,& A-postatarum seminario profectos esse. Nam annus jam agitur supra centesimum prope quinquagesi-mus,ex quo Basiliense concilium summo Christia-norum omnium studio ac voluntate celebratum fuit. Hoc concilio nullum unquam aliud constat in Ecclesia Romana maiore adhibita solennitate indictum, habitum, & celebratum fuisse. Nam & duorum Paparum decreto indictum erat,nimirum Martini quinti,& Eugenij quarti, & eorum legatis praesidentibus habitum ac celebratum. Per idem concilium soleniter citatus & euocatus Eugenius, tandem adhibita summa & solenni causae cognitione,fraudum,praestigiarum,machinationum , ac factionum aduersus eius concilii libertatem, con-victus,tādem Papatu suo abdicatus est,& pro schismatico[?] & Apostatico,unà cum Cardinalibus & E-piscopis omnibus,qui partes ipsius secuti erant,ex-auctoratus. Amedæus autem Sabaudorum Dux in ipsius locum suffectus.Audiamus cuiusmodi fuerit istius exitus tragœdiæ.Breui post tempore,ille ipse Eugenius damnatus, abdicatus ,exauctoratus, ta-men Principum quorundam gratia & contentio-ne in suam sedem restitutus, Cardinales & Epis-copos suarum partium omnes secum pariter resti-tuit. units.tr: Having thus laid down these points, it remains for us to conclude the argument. Pope Sixtus V has been condemned by the greater part of Christendom on seven most grave charges: impiety; tyranny exercised over the Church; corruption of religion; sacrilege; treason against the majesty of the realm; treason against the public peace; and forgery. Following the arrogance, audacity and savagery of his predecessors, he has issued this most insane decree against all divine and human law. Relying on false allegations, without any judicial process, he has foolishly, stupidly and shamelessly promulgated it against the most Serene King of Navarre and the Most Illustrious Prince Condé. He has loaded them with foul and unheard-of verbal abuse, calling them "sons of wrath," obstinate, notorious and relapsed heretics, men wallowing in the mire, rebels against the Most Christian King, persecutors of the Church, a detestable brood, and guilty of violating the majesty both of God and of man. For these reasons he has stripped them of their principalities, duchies, lordships, fiefs and all their honours, and of their lawful right of succession to the kingdom of France. Since this long-standing and unbridled audacity of his, in pronouncing and adjudging kingdoms away, plainly concerns all the kings, princes and potentates of Europe, and since there is a danger that, through this machinery of excommunications and proscriptions, those who covet and aim at other men's kingdoms will hereafter plot against other princes who are at peace and quiet: FOR THESE REASONS the aforesaid most Serene Princes declare that the same Pope Sixtus V is to be held as an impious, perjured and sacrilegious tyrant, the author of fabricated religions, a cruel and savage parricide of the Christian Church, an importunate and wicked enemy of religion, and most certainly Antichrist. They ask and entreat all the Monarchs of the Christian world, all kings, princes and potentates, and all who hold any rule or lawful power, to be willing to bring aid to these Most Serene Princes, to restrain the rages of this monstrous tyrant and to break the cruel and furious assaults of his attacks; and to join their counsels and arms to extinguish that plague of mankind and to free the Christian commonwealth from that prodigious and deadly monster. Meanwhile, because of the intolerable insults which he poured out in his frenzied mind against our aforesaid Princes, the said Pope Sixtus V ought to be regarded and called by all Christians as a most monstrous prodigy, a most foul portent and a monster, not to be exported to the farthest lands but to be banished from the bounds of human nature; he is to be held as the certain, notorious and manifest Antichrist. On his accursed head all Christians ought to call down every evil plague, ruin and destruction, so that, for as long as the cursed soul breathes in his corpse, he may be, as the Holy Spirit says, "ANATHEMA MARANATA" to all the pious. And lest this kind of imprecation seem new and unusual to anyone among us, we wish the readers, first, to remember those passages which we have above drawn especially from the books of the divine Bernard, where the Roman papacy is plainly, clearly and by name called Antichrist, the Son of perdition, the Man of sin, a demon not only of the day but even of noon, who not only transforms himself into an angel of light but is exalted above everything that is called God or is worshipped. Jerome, moreover, calls Rome Babylon and the purple-clad harlot. Next, let them read and carefully consider the most holy sanction of the Pontifical Decree, in c. 2, dist. 23, etc., and "si quis pecunia," dist. 79, where it is laid down that whoever has obtained the papacy by money or human favour (such as, it is well known, was the western favour of this monk) or by popular tumult or any contrivance (that is, by ambition and wicked arts) is to be regarded not as an Apostolic but as an Apostate, and, separated together with his supporters and followers from the thresholds of the holy Church of God, is to be cast out, just as ANTICHRIST and the assailant and destroyer of all Christianity. To this opinion the Canonists have boldly agreed with one voice and have dared openly to profess that a pope who is not elected canonically is the Devil, and holds the keys not of heaven but of hell. For these are the words of Felinus, in c. Ego N., de iureiur. Let them consider further that all the popes, cardinals and bishops who for more than a hundred years have held dominion in the Roman Church have come forth from the most certain seminary of schismatics and apostates. For it is now a year, a little more than one hundred and fifty years, since the Council of Basel was held with the greatest zeal and goodwill of all Christians. It is established that no other council was ever convened, held and celebrated in the Roman Church with greater solemnity. It was convened by the decree of two popes, namely Martin V and Eugenius IV, and was held and celebrated with their legates presiding. Eugenius, solemnly summoned and cited by the same council, was at last, after a full and solemn hearing of the case, convicted of frauds, deceits, machinations and factions against the freedom of that council; finally he was deprived of his papacy and, as a schismatic and apostate, was struck from office together with all the cardinals and bishops who had followed his party. Amadeus, Duke of Savoy, was put in his place. Let us now hear what the outcome of this tragedy was. Shortly afterwards, that same Eugenius, though condemned, deposed and struck from office, was nonetheless restored to his see through the favour and contention of certain princes, and he restored all the cardinals and bishops of his party together with himself. Amadeus, however, although not of his own accord, was given the cardinal's hat and renounced the papacy. Let grave and judicious men now consider, according to that most holy sanction of the Pontifical Decree which we have just mentioned, whether those who have arisen from that seminary of the Eugenians and now rule in the Roman Church during these times are to be held in the place of Apostolics or rather of Apostates; whether they hold the keys of heaven or rather those of hell. So that this may be judged more conveniently, it is worth our while to learn the opinions of the teachers and jurists who have written on this matter, and above all of Ludovicus Romanus, who attended the Council of Basel, where he wrote his last opinion, whose words in number 15 are these: If a minister of ministers, governing the Church scandalously and handling it in a disorderly way, does not at once repent when admonished by the Church, but persists in his insolence of governing, he can and must be stripped of his office. For since he does not honour the Church, he will not deserve to be honoured by the Church in return when he admonishes it wholesomely. So the Church must tolerate him as a scandalous and incorrigible ruler, following the argument of the orator Domitius: and Jerome, in his letter to Nepotianus, reports it, speaking thus: Why then should I regard you as a prince, when you do not regard me as a senator? dist. 95, c. esto subiectus. It is therefore true that a pope who notoriously scandalises the Church by his crimes, and even remains incorrigible, can be accused before the Church and stripped of the papacy by it. This conclusion is further demonstrated thus: a pope who persists in a notorious crime that scandalises the whole Church, and is unwilling to desist, falls under suspicion of heresy, c. nullus, 38 dist., where it says: He who lives rebelliously, and refuses to learn and to do good, is shown to be a member of the devil rather than of Christ, and is shown to be an unbeliever rather than a believer. So says Ludovicus Romanus, who, as we have said, attended the Council of Basel with great authority. Where now are those who argue that those who oppose the tyranny of the popes are to be counted among the heretics? Who think that the unbridled audacity of the popes in proscribing kings should no longer be endured? Who detest the impiety of Sixtus V in defending the fabricated Bernardine and Dominican orders? But let us now bring forward another authority of the same great man from the same council; for a little later, in number 17, he speaks thus: If natural reason dictates that an incurable member which infects the whole body must be cut off for the health of the body, then civil reason must likewise dictate that an incurable member which infects the whole mystical Church must be cut off, lest the rest of the body be infected or scandalised; and consequently the Pope (let fairness of mind be applied in reading these things, and let these words of Ludovicus Romanus be compared with our curse and detestation) who, though he is the chief part of the Church, is nonetheless a member of the body of the Church itself, according to the gloss on c. ecce, 93 dist. The reason of divine Scripture also persuades this, approving the saying of Caiaphas, the high priest, who said: It is expedient that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish: though, even if the Pope were placed over the government of peoples, he ought not on that account to be the ruin of those peoples. The text in 11 q. 3, c. ita corporis, says so. Indeed he deserves as many deaths as he sends out examples of destruction to his subjects, says the same text in the same cause, and q. in c. praecipue. For just as it is praiseworthy and discreet to show reverence and honour to those who come before us, so it belongs to uprightness and the fear of God to set aside, without any concealment, those things in them which need correction, lest the disease invade the whole body if the sickness is not cured in the head, says the text 2 q. 7, c. sicut inquit. This conclusion is strengthened also by the text in c. in canonibus, 16 q. 1, and in d.c. sed illud, likewise: and that error must be removed from the Church which is not corrected by the Church's admonition, the Lord saying: Take away the evil from among you. For wounds which do not feel medicinal fomentations must be cut with iron. 82 dist., c. quia aliquanti; 1 q. 1, c. reperiuntur. These are the words of Ludovicus Romanus, word for word. By comparing them with our detestation, fair readers will be able to judge whether we have rightly or wrongly so boldly cursed the tyrannical audacity of this pope. Indeed, the complaint of Ludovicus Romanus is in agreement with what Cardinal Zabarella wrote about the year 1406 in his treatise on the schism, number 20: Concerning any notorious crime of the Pope, he says, if he is incorrigible and scandalises the Church, he can be accused, because he is held to be a heretic, see the gloss on dist. 40, c. si Papa; for this incorrigibility concerns the cause of faith, as in the same gloss. And if it happens that they defend themselves by temporal power, they can in fact be restrained even by secular authority, see de iudic., c. cum non ab homine. So Zabarella. But Baldus says it more briefly, in c. olim, col. penultimate, extra, de rescriptis, where he writes thus: Against a pope who abuses his power, one must first use words (that is, admonitions), secondly herbs (that is, threats), thirdly stones; and where the cleverness of virtue is not enough, there the protection of arms ought to avail. And to the same effect Jason, in consilium 95, asked in column 4: It is lawful, he says, to resist a pope who scandalises the Church, and he is not to be tolerated, c. etsi illa, 1 q. 7, and c. sunt quidam, 25 q. 1. Innocent on c. inquisitionis, de sent. excommun., and on c. quanto, de consuetud. Abbas on c. cum teneamur, de appellat. Likewise Jerome, speaking of a pope in c. non omnes episcopi, 2 q. 7, says that salt that has lost its savour is good for nothing except to be cast out and trampled by pigs. So says Jason, and no less vigorously, as is plain, than either Ludovicus Romanus or Zabarella, although they wrote these things in Italy and in such darkness of the Christian Church.

units.la: [Note: the running head reads FVLMEN. with V for U, normalised to FULMEN.] stolicorum, an potius Apostaticorum loco habendi sint: utrum coeli, an potius inferni claues habeant, qui orti ex illo Eugenianorum seminario in Ecclesia Romana per haec tempora dominatur. Quod ut commodius iudicari possit, operæpretiū est, Doctorum & Iurisconsultorum sententias cognoscere, qui aliquid hac de re scripserunt, atque imprimis Ludouici Romani, qui Basiliensi cōcilio interfuit, ubi consilium scripsit ultimum, cuius num.15.verba hæc sunt: Si pastor pastorum Eccle-siam scandalose regens & inordinate tractans, per Ec-clesiam monitus, non mox resipiscat, imo in sua perseue-ret insolentia regendi, officio potest & debet exui. Cum enim ipse Ecclesiam non honoret, ipsum salubriter admonentem, nec tunc merebitur ab Ecclesia honorari: ita ut toleret ipsum scandalose regentem, atque incorrigibilem, argumento eius, quod dicit Orator Domitius: & refert Hieronymus in epistol. ad Neapol. sic inquiens: Cur ergo te habeam ut Principem, cum tu me non habeas ut Senatorem? dist.95.c.esto subiectus[?]. Est ergo veritas, Papam suis criminibus Ecclesiam notorie scandalisantem, ac etiam manentem incorrigibilem, posse apud Ecclesiam accusari, atque per illam denudari Papatu. Quae conclusio demonstratur ulterius sic: Papa stans in crimine notorio scandalisante totam Ecclesiam, nec desistere volens, incidit in suspicionem haeresis. c.nullus, 38. dist. sic dicente: Qui rebelliter uiuit, & discere atque agere bona recusat, magis diaboli, quam Christi membrum esse ostenditur: & potius infidelis, quam fidelis esse monstratur. Haec Lud.Rom. qui Basilensi, ut diximus, concilio magna cum auctoritate interfuit. Ubi sunt qui disputant, Haereticorum numero habendos, qui Paparum tyrannidi aduersantur? qui effrenatà ipsorum in proscribendis Regibus audacia diutius feredam esse non putant? qui Sixti quinti impietatem in confictis Bernardonicis & Dominicanis religio-nibus tuendis detestantur? Sed iam alteram eius-dem summi viri auctoritatem ex eodem Concilio proferamus: nam aliquanto post num.17.ita loqui-tur: Si ratio naturalis dictat, membrum incurabile to-tius corporis infectivum pro salute corporis amputadum: pariter quoque dictare debet civilis ratio, membrum in-curabile, quod est totius Ecclesiae mysticae infectivum, am-putandum fore, ne reliquum corpus inficiatur aut scan-dalisetur: & consequenter Papam: (adhibeatur in his legendis animorum aequitas, & comparentur haec Lud. Romani verba cum illa nostra imprecatione ac detestatione) qui etsi pars sit Ecclesiae praecipua, ta-men etiam est membrum de corpore ipsius Ecclesiae, se-cundum gloss. in c.ecce, 93.dist. Hoc etiam suadet ra-tio divinae scripturae, approbantis assenerationem Caiphae principis sacerdotum, dicentis: Expedit ut unus homo moriatur pro populo, & non tota gens pereat: cum etsi fo-ret Papa positus ad gubernationem populorum non ta-men esse deberet ruina illorum: dicit text. 11.q.3. c.ita corporis. Imo tot mortibus dignus est, quot ad subditos suos perditionis exempla trasmittit, dicit text.ead.cauf. & q.in c.praecipue. Sicut enim laudabile & discretum est, reverentiam & honorem exhibere prioribus, ita rectitu-dinis & Dei timoris est, quae in eis sunt, quae indigeant correctione, nulla dissimulatione postponere: ne totu cor-pus morbus invadat, si languor non fuerit curatus in ca-pite, dicit text.2.q.7.c. sicut inquit. Et hanc conclusio-nem corroborat text.in c.in canonibus, 16 q.1. & in d.c. sed illud.sic similiter, & ille exrors debet fieri ab Eccleclesia,qui Ecclesiae admonitione nō corrigitur: dicete Domino, Auferte malum ex vobis. Ferro enim secada[?] sunt vulnera quae non sentiunt medicina fomenta. 82. dist.c. quia aliquanti. 1.q. 1. c. reperiuntur. Haec ad verbum Ludouicus Romanus. Ex quibus, cum illa nostra detestatione comparatis, aequi lectores diiudicare poterunt, iurene an iniuria tam animose tyrannicam istius Papae audaciam execrati simus. Quinetiam illi Lud. Romani querimoniae consentanea sunt, quae Cardinalis Zabarella, circa annum MCCCCVI.scripsit in tractatu de schismate, num.20 De quolibet, inquit, notorio crimine Papae, si est incorrigibilis, & scandalizat Ecclesiam potest accusari, quia censetur pro haeretico, not. in glos. 40. distinct. c. si Papa. nam haec incorrigibilitas concernit causam fidei: ut in ead. gloss. Et si contingat, quod isti tueantur se per potentiam temporalem, poterunt de facto coerceri, etiam per secularem potestatem, arg. de iudic. c. cum non ab homine. Haec Zabarella. Sed breuius Baldus in c. olim, col. pen. extr. de rescript. vbi sic scribit: Contra Papam sua potestate abutentem, primo vtendum est verbis (id est admonitionibus) secundo herbis (id est comminationibus) tertio lapidibus: & quod vbi non sufficit virtutis ingenium, ibi valere debet armorum praesidium. Et in eandem sententiam Iason in consil. 95.requisitus col. 4. Papae, inquit, scandalizanti Ecclesiam, licitum est resistere, & non est tolerandus, c. etsi illa, 1. q. 7. & c. sunt quidam 25. q. 1. Innocentius in c. inquisitionis de sent. excommun. & in c. quanto, de consuetud. Abbas in c. cum teneamur, de appella. Item Hieronymus loquens de Papa in c. non omnes Episcopi, 2. q. 7. dicit quod infatuatum sal ad nihilum prodest, nisi ut proiciaproiiciatur foras, & a porcis conculcetur. Hæc Iason nihilo, vt apparet, segnius, quàm aut Lud. Romanus, aut Zabarella: cùm tamen & in Italia, & in tā-tis Ecclesiæ Christianæ tenebris hæc scriberent.
units.tr: Let us now consider, grave and wise men, whether, by the most holy pontifical sanction of the Decree I have just cited, those men are to be counted Apostolic or rather Apostate; whether they hold the keys of heaven or rather of hell. The brood sprung from that nursery of Eugenians has ruled the Roman Church down to our own times. To judge this more fairly, it is worth knowing the opinions of the doctors and jurists who wrote on this matter, and above all of Ludovicus Romanus, who attended the Council of Basel, where he wrote his last opinion. Its fifteenth number reads: If the shepherd of shepherds, ruling the Church scandalously and managing it disorderly, does not at once repent when admonished by the Church, but persists in his arrogant way of ruling, he can and ought to be stripped of his office. For since he does not honour the Church, he will not deserve to be honoured by the Church when he admonishes it wholesomely; so that she may tolerate him ruling scandalously and incorrigibly, by the argument of the orator Domitius: and Jerome, in his letter to Nepotianus, relates it, saying: Why then should I regard you as my prince, when you do not regard me as your senator? Dist. 95, c. esto subiectus[?]. It is therefore true that a Pope who notoriously scandalises the Church by his crimes, and remains incorrigible, can be accused before the Church and deprived of the papacy by her. This conclusion is further proved thus: a Pope who stands in a notorious crime that scandalises the whole Church, and is unwilling to desist, falls under suspicion of heresy. C. nullus, 38 dist., which says: He who lives in rebellion, and refuses to learn and to do what is good, is shown to be a member of the devil rather than of Christ, and is shown to be an unbeliever rather than a believer. So writes Ludovicus Romanus, who, as we have said, attended the Council of Basel with great authority. Where now are those who argue that they should be counted among heretics who oppose the tyranny of the Popes? Who think that the unbridled audacity of the Popes in proscribing kings should no longer be endured? Who detest Sixtus V's impiety in defending the spurious religious orders of the Bernardines and Dominicans? But let us now bring forward another authority of the same great man from the same Council, for a little later, in number 17, he speaks thus: If natural reason dictates that an incurable member which infects the whole body must be cut off for the body's health, then likewise civil reason ought to dictate that an incurable member, which infects the whole mystical Church, must be cut off, lest the rest of the body be infected or scandalised; and consequently the Pope: (let fairness of mind be brought to reading these words, and let Ludovicus Romanus's words be compared with that curse and detestation of ours) who, although he is the chief part of the Church, is nonetheless a member of the body of the Church itself, according to the gloss on c. ecce, 93 dist. This too is suggested by the reasoning of divine Scripture, which approves the saying of Caiaphas, the chief priest, who said: It is expedient that one man die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish; although, even if the Pope were set over the government of peoples, he ought not to be the ruin of those peoples: the text says so at 11 q. 3, c. ita corporis. Indeed he deserves as many deaths as he sets forth examples of perdition to his subjects, says the same text in the same cause, and in q. in c. praecipue. For as it is praiseworthy and proper to show reverence and honour to superiors, so it belongs to uprightness and the fear of God not to neglect, through any dissimulation, what is in them that needs correction, lest disease invade the whole body if the sickness is not cured in the head, says the text at 2 q. 7, c. sicut, he says. And the text in c. in canonibus, 16 q. 1, and in the same c. sed illud, confirms this conclusion in like manner: and that member ought to be cut off by the Church which is not corrected by the Church's admonition, the Lord saying: Take away the evil from among you. For wounds that do not feel medicine must be cut with iron. Dist. 82, c. quia aliquanti; 1 q. 1, c. reperiuntur. These are the words of Ludovicus Romanus, word for word. From them, when they are set beside that detestation of ours, fair readers will be able to judge whether we have cursed the tyrannical audacity of this Pope rightly or wrongly so boldly. Indeed, the complaint of Ludovicus Romanus is in agreement with what Cardinal Zabarella wrote about the year 1406 in his treatise on the schism, number 20: Concerning any notorious crime of the Pope, he says, if he is incorrigible and scandalises the Church, he can be accused, because he is counted as a heretic; see the gloss at dist. 40, c. si Papa. For this incorrigibility concerns the cause of faith, as in the same gloss. And if it happens that they defend themselves by temporal power, they can in fact be restrained, even by secular power; cf. de iudiciis, c. cum non ab homine. So Zabarella. But Baldus says it more briefly, in c. olim, last column, de rescriptis, where he writes thus: Against a Pope who abuses his power, one must first use words (that is, admonitions), second herbs (that is, threats), third stones: and where the ingenuity of virtue is not enough, there the protection of arms ought to avail. And to the same effect Jason, in consilium 95, requested, col. 4: It is lawful, he says, to resist a Pope who scandalises the Church, and he is not to be tolerated; c. etsi illa, 1 q. 7, and c. sunt quidam, 25 q. 1. Innocent in c. inquisitionis de sententia excommunicationis, and in c. quanto de consuetudine. Abbas in c. cum teneamur de appellationibus. Likewise Jerome, speaking of the Pope in c. non omnes episcopi, 2 q. 7, says that salt that has lost its savour is good for nothing, except to be cast out and trodden underfoot by swine. Jason writes this, as is plain, no less boldly than either Ludovicus Romanus or Zabarella, although they wrote these things in Italy, and in such darkness of the Christian Church.

units.la: Philippus autem Decius in eandem sententiam loquitur in consil.151.maximi pōderis, num.4.vol.
units.tr: Philip Decius also speaks to the same effect in his consilium 151, of very great weight, n. 4, vol.

units.la: 1. Quando Papa, inquit, est incorrigibilis in aliquo notorio delicto, pro quo Ecclesia scandalizatur, glo. in terminis in c.si Papa, 40. dist. tenet quod Papa accusari possit, & de illa glossa maximum fuit factum fundamentum contra Eugenium iv. in concilio Basiliensi: & illa glossa communiter tenetur per omnes, vt Abbas dicit in c.significasti.de electi.& in disput. Episcopus & quidam rector: vbi inquit, quod totus mundus approbat illa gloss. & illam glossam pluribus rationibus comprobat Ludovicus Romanus in consil.523. Primo quia Papa qui in notorio crimine persistit, & non vult corrigi, in suspicionem hæresis incidit.38.dist.c.sin.86.dist.c.si qui sint.& c.sin.de pœnit. Sed pro hæresi Papa accusari potest.d.c.si Papa. Ergo pro tali crimine. Secundo quia remouetur Episcopus ab Ecclesia particulari vt scandalum tollatur, vt notat Innocent.in c.cum pridem,de renunt. idem a fortiori videtur dicendum in summo Pontifice, in quo est periculum vniuersalis Ecclesiæ. Tertio per auctoritatem Eua-ge-lii, Si oculus tuus aut pes scandalizauerit. de quo text.elegantur loquitur in c.illud sane, 24. q. 3. Expedit enim vt vnus homo moriatur pro populo, ne tota gens pereat. Ergo Papa incorrigibilis moriatur ciuiliter, ne tota Ecclesia pereat, quia Papa positus ad gubernationem populorum, non debet esse ruina illorum, vt text.dicit ii. q.3. in cita corporis. Nam tot mortibus dignus est. quot exempla perditionis ad suos transmittit, c.precipue. ii.q.3.
units.tr: 1. When the Pope, he says, is incorrigible in some notorious offence for which the Church is scandalised, the gloss in terminis on c. si Papa, dist. 40, holds that the Pope can be accused. The greatest foundation was laid on that gloss against Eugenius IV at the Council of Basel, and it is commonly held by all, as Abbas says on c. significasti, de electione, and in the disputation "Episcopus et quidam rector," where he says that the whole world approves that gloss and confirms it by many reasons Ludovicus Romanus, in consilium 523. (1) First, because a Pope who persists in a notorious crime and will not be corrected falls under suspicion of heresy (38 dist. c. sin; 86 dist. c. si qui sint; and c. sin, de poenitentia). But the Pope can be accused for heresy (d. c. si Papa). Therefore he can be accused for such a crime too. (2) Second, because a bishop is removed from a particular Church so that scandal may be taken away, as Innocent notes on c. cum pridem, de renunciatione. The same should be said, a fortiori, of the supreme Pontiff, in whom lies the danger to the universal Church. (3) Third, on the authority of the Gospel, "If thine eye or foot offend thee," of which the text in c. illud sane, 24 q. 3, speaks: "For it is expedient that one man die for the people, lest the whole nation perish." Therefore an incorrigible Pope should die civilly, lest the whole Church perish, since a Pope set over the government of peoples ought not to be the ruin of them, as the text says in ii q. 3 in the cited body of law: "for he deserves as many deaths as the examples of perdition he sends to his own people" (c. precipue, ii q. 3).

units.la: Quæ cùm ita se habeant, iterū sine cunctatione concludimus, non modò anathema[?] supradicti Papæ Sixti v, propter temerarij iudicis incompetentiā, falsæ caussæ allegationem, defectum ordinis iudicialis, & conceptæ sententiæ stultitiam pro nullo habendum esse: verūmetiam, vt execrationes eiusdem Sixti in ipsius caput redundent, cum ipsum septem atrocissimis criminibus certissimisque testimoniis cōuictum, cunctis Christianis esse, dein-eps[?] oportere EXECRABILE ET DETESTAN-DVM ANATHEMA MARANATA.
units.tr: Since these things stand thus, we conclude again, without hesitation, that not only must the aforesaid anathema of Pope Sixtus V be held as nothing, on account of the incompetence of a rash judge, the false allegation of a cause, the defect of judicial order, and the folly of the sentence pronounced; but moreover, that the curses of the same Sixtus must fall back upon his own head, since he has been convicted of seven most atrocious crimes by most certain testimonies, and that henceforth all Christians ought to regard him as an EXECRABLE AND DETESTABLE ANATHEMA, MARANATHA.
AMEN.

units.la: ROBERTI BELLARMINII SOCIETATIS IESV, DISPUTATIONIS de primatu sedis Romanæ, CAPUT XXV.
units.tr: ROBERT BELLARMINE OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS, DISPUTATION ON THE PRIMACY OF THE ROMAN SEE, CHAPTER XXV.
And the reply to it,

units.la: EDITA nuper est disputatio Rob.Bellar-minii, Iesuitæ inter primos summi, de primatu Episcopi R. cui dū plenior responsio paratur, visum est hanc ad caput illius disputationis quintum & vicesimum, responsiunculam, quasi alterius plenioris præcursorem, emittere. Summa quæstionis quæ sub illo capite tractatur, hæc est: An iure divino liceat Episcopis à suæ dioecesis Archiepiscopo condemnatis ad Episcopum R. appellare[?]: utpote ab inferiore iudice ad superiorem, ut Episcopus R. eam sententiam retractare ac rescindere pro suo iure possit. Hoc enim appellationum ac provocationū ius esse, nemo ignorat. Bellarminius contendit iure divino licere episcopis omnibus, etiam si qui apud Antipodas à suæ provinciæ Synodo condemnati essent, ad Episcopi R: tribunal provocare. Nos qui religionem reformatam tuemur, fortiter negamus: & quanvis non ei qui negat, sed ei qui affirmat, probationis onus incumbat, tamen bonitate causæ nostræ freti, ultrò ac lubenter onus probationis in nos suscepimus.Primũ igitur probationis caput hoc erit. Ne-fas est dicere, quicquā iure diuino licere, nisi quod vel disertis legis diuinæ verbis permissum est, vel ex ipsius sententia & mente permissum intel-ligitur.Deut. 4.5,6.Matth. 15.Marc. 7. Ioann. 14.2. Timot.3. Atqui nulla in Scriptura sacra istius li-centiæ vel ad Episcopum R.ex omnibus terrarum partibus appellandi, vel cuiusuis Episcopalis & prouincialis cōuentus sententiasrescindedi mentio reperitur.Id quod vel ex eo constat, quòd ne Ap-pellationis quidem, in causis ecclesiasticis aut Pro uocationis, aut Rescindendę sententiæ vocabulum vsquam in literis sanctis inuenitur. Quare, patet euidens consequentia, falsū esse quod Bellarminius contendit, licentiam illam iure diuino introductã fuisse. Nam de sententia & mente Scripturæ S. imò vero quod ista licetia iuri diuino aduersetur, vel hinc potest intelligi, quòd Christus Apostolos omnes suos pari iure, dignitate, potestate esse voluit: neque cuiquam eorum iurisdictionem, siue (ut quondam loquebantur) audientiam alterius audientia maiorem aut superiorem attribuit: ex quo secundum vulgatam regulam sequitur euidentissima conclusio, Pari in parem nullum esse imperium, nullam iurisdictionem, nullam alterius retractandæ aut rescindendæ sententiæ potestatem. Pascite greges vestros, inquit Petrus, non dominantes clero: sed alii se aliis demisse subiicientes: [?]πάντες ἀλλήλοις ὑποτασσόμενοι. 1. Pet.5. Cùm spiritus Dei linguarum ignearum forma in Apostolorum capita descendisse dicitur, nulla fit mentio linguæ alicuius cæteris amplioris aut insignioris, quæ capiti Petri, quasi principis & coryphæi insisteret. Cùm PePetrus aliquandiu vnà cū præputiatis Christianis libentiùs versatus fuisset, eáque re offensi qui ex Iudæis Christiani facti erant, grauiter cum eo expo-stulassent, modestissimè facti sui ratione illis red-didit, neque se ἀνυπεύθυνον aut ἀνεγκλήτον[?] haberi voluit. Act. 11. Cùm in Apocalypsi coelestis Hierofo-lyma duodecim columnis fundata dicitur, hoc est, duodecim Apostolis, non aliqua columna memo-ratur cæteris firmior & stabilior, sed omnes pares & æquales fuisse significantur: quid multa? Paulus non modò se Petro exæquat, neque se illo vlla re inferiorem esse ostendit, verum etiam cùm in cul-pa esset, grauiter illum tanquam parem & collegam, & eiusdem muneris socium coarguit. Nam epist. ad Galat. cap. 2. ita scribit: Euangelium mihi apud gentes concreditum est, sicuti Petro apud Iudæos. Nam qui efficax fuit per Petrum ad Apostolatum Iudæorum, idem per me fuit efficax erga gentes. Cùmque Iacobus, Cephas, & Ioannes qui videban-tur esse columnæ, gratiam mihi datam cognouis-sent, tù mihi & Bernabæ societatis dexteras dede-runt: vt nos quidem apud Gentes, ipsi vero apud circuncisos prædicarent. Quinetiam cùm Petrus Antiochiam venisset, ei in os restiti: quia reprehēdendus erat. Quibus ex locis omnibus perspicuum est, Petrum nulla re cæteris Apostolis superiorem, aut præstantiorem habitum fuisse: sed omnes à Christo pari iure, dignitate, potestate constitutos fuisse. Itaque veteres veterum ecclesiarum Episco-pi in Carthaginensi concilio cap. 42. statuerunt, ne primæ sedis Episcopus appellaretur Princeps sa-cerdotum, vel summus sacerdos, aut aliquid eius-modi: sed tantùm primæ sedis episcopus, quem canonem Episcopus R.in suum Gratianicum Decretum imprudens(vt postea constabit)referri passus est,99.c.primæ sedis.sibi enim soli Christus & summum ius summumque principatu in Ecclesia excepit: & singulare nomen retinuit, vt Princeps sacerdotum, & Princeps pastorum appellaretur: ἀρχιερεύς, inquā, & ἀρχιποίμην [?], 1.Pet.2.5.Heb.6.& 7. item Caput Ecclesiæ, Caput corporis Ecclesiæ. 1. Col.18,Ephe.15.&16,1.Pet.2.& 5.Quæ cùm ita sint, aperta conclusio sequitur, licentiam retractandorum iudiciorum, quæ vel ab aliis episcopis, vel à prouincialibus conciliis pronuntiata sunt, non modò iure diuino introductam non esse, sed aduersus ius diuinum Romanorum Episcoporum ambitione vsurpatam fuisse.
units.tr: Robert Bellarmine's disputation, by one of the first of the Jesuits, on the primacy of the Bishop of Rome, has recently been published. While a fuller reply is being prepared, I have thought it right to send out this short answer to the twenty-fifth chapter of that disputation, as a forerunner of the fuller one. The main question treated under that chapter is this: whether by divine right bishops condemned by their own archbishop may appeal to the Bishop of Rome, so that a lower judge may be brought before a higher, and the Bishop of Rome may retract and annul the sentence at his own discretion. Everyone knows that this is the right of appeals and of provocations. Bellarmine maintains that by divine right all bishops, even those condemned by the synod of their own province in the land of the Antipodes, may appeal to the tribunal of the Bishop of Rome. We who uphold the reformed religion firmly deny this. Although the burden of proof lies on the one who affirms, not on the one who denies, yet, trusting in the goodness of our cause, we willingly and gladly take up the burden of proof ourselves. The first head of our proof, then, will be this. It is wrong to say that anything is permitted by divine right unless it is either allowed in the plain words of the divine law, or is understood to be allowed by its own meaning and intent (Deut. 4:5–6; Matt. 15; Mark 7; John 14; 2 Tim. 3). Yet nowhere in Holy Scripture is there any mention of such a licence, either to appeal to the Bishop of Rome from every part of the world, or to annul the decisions of any episcopal or provincial assembly. This is shown even by the fact that the very word "appeal," or "provocation," or "annulling of a sentence," is found nowhere in the sacred writings in connection with ecclesiastical causes. Therefore the consequence is plain: what Bellarmine contends, that this licence was introduced by divine right, is false. As for the meaning and intent of Holy Scripture, indeed that this licence is opposed to divine right may be seen from this: Christ willed that all his Apostles should have equal right, dignity and power, and he gave none of them jurisdiction, or what they used to call "hearing," greater or superior to another's hearing. From this, according to the common rule, there follows a most evident conclusion: among equals there is no command, no jurisdiction, and no power of retracting or annulling another's sentence. "Feed your flocks," says Peter, "not lording it over the clergy, but humbly subjecting yourselves to one another" [πάντες ἀλλήλοις ὑποτασσόμενοι] (1 Pet. 5). When the Spirit of God is said to have descended on the heads of the Apostles in the form of tongues of fire, no tongue is mentioned as greater or more distinguished than the rest, standing upon the head of Peter as prince and chief of the choir. When Peter had for some time freely associated with uncircumcised Christians, those of the Jews who had become Christians were offended and sharply remonstrated with him. He answered them most modestly, giving an account of his conduct, and he did not wish to be regarded as [ἀνυπεύθυνον] unaccountable or [ἀνεγκλήτον] beyond reproach (Acts 11). When in the Apocalypse the heavenly Jerusalem is said to be founded on twelve columns, that is, the twelve Apostles, no column is recorded as firmer or more stable than the others; rather, they are all signified as equal and alike. Why say more? Paul not only places himself on a level with Peter, and shows himself in no way inferior to him, but even, when Peter was at fault, rebuked him sharply as an equal and colleague, and as a partner in the same office. For in his Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 2, he writes: "The gospel has been entrusted to me for the Gentiles, just as to Peter for the Jews. For he who was effective in Peter for the apostleship to the Jews was also effective in me for the Gentiles. And when James, Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, had recognised the grace given to me, they gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship, so that we should preach to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. Moreover, when Peter came to Antioch, I withstood him to his face, because he stood condemned." From all these passages it is clear that Peter was held to be in no way superior or more eminent than the other Apostles, but that all were appointed by Christ with equal right, dignity and power. Accordingly, the ancient bishops of the ancient churches, in the Council of Carthage, canon 42, decreed that the bishop of the first see should not be called "Prince of priests," or "chief priest," or anything of that kind, but only "bishop of the first see." Bellarmine, unwittingly (as will later be established), allowed this canon to be cited in his Gratian's Decretum, distinction 99, chapter "primæ sedis." For Christ alone reserved to himself the highest right and the highest principate in the Church, and he kept the unique name, so that he is called Prince of priests and Prince of shepherds: [ἀρχιερεύς], I say, and [ἀρχιποίμην] (1 Pet. 2:5; Heb. 6 and 7); likewise the Head of the Church, the Head of the body of the Church (Col. 1:18; Eph. 1:15–16; 1 Pet. 2 and 5). Since these things are so, the plain conclusion follows that the licence to retract judgements pronounced either by other bishops or by provincial councils was not only not introduced by divine right, but was usurped by the ambition of the Roman bishops in opposition to divine right.

units.la: Sequitur secundum argumentum. Prima & vetustissima concilia Christiana, summam cuique Archiepiscopo in sua prouincia audientiam, iurisdictionem, ac potestatem tribuerunt: ac vetuerunt ne quis Archiepiscoporum vllum sibi ius in alterius dioecesim vsurpâret. Quare, neque cuiquam ab Episcopis suæ Prouinciæ damnato ad Episcopum R. appellare, neque Romano Episcopo illam appellationem recipere, & aliorum Episcoporum sententiam rescindere licuit. Antecedens multis testimoniis probatur, quorum primum est ex Niceni Concilij can.6.his verbis. Antiqui mores seruentur, qui sunt in AEgypto, Lybia, & Pentapoli, vt Alexandrinus Episcopus horum omnium potestatem habeat: quandoquidem & Episcopi R. hoc idem est consuetum. Similiter & in Antiochia, & in aliis prouinciis sua priuilegia & sua dignitates & auctoritates ecclesiis seruentur. Quod decretum Rufinus lib.hist.eccl.10. his verbis expo suit: Apud Alexandriam & in urbe Roma, hæc consuetudo seruetur, vt & ille Ægypti, & hic suburbicarum ecclesiarum sollicitudinem gerat. Secundum testimonium proferri potest ex Concilio Constantin vbi eadem de re ita decretum est: Episcopi ad Ecclesias quæ sunt vltra suam diœcesim, ne accedant, nec Ecclesias confundant: sed secundum canones, Alexandriæ quidem Episcopus Ægyptum solum regat: Orientis autem Episcopi Orientem solum administrent, seruatis priuilegiis ac præeminentiis quæ sunt in Niceni Concilii canonibus Antiochenæ Ecclesiæ. Et Asianæ diœcesis Episcopi, quæ sunt in sola Asia administrent & Thraciæ Episcopi Thraciam tantum regant. & Pontanæ Pontanam. Quibus ex locis perspicue intelligitur, Ecclesiæ primitiuæ temporibus seruatam illam, quam diximus à Christo institutam inter Episcopos æquabilitatem: neque cuiquam licuisse ius aut potestatem vllam sibi in alterius diœcesim vsurpare [?]: tantum abest, vt Episcopo R. iure diuino licuerit appellationes ex longinquis & transmarinis ecclesiis recipere, & aliorum Episcoporum res iudicatas rescindere. Itaque pari eodemque modo Antiochina Synodus habita imperante Constantio, Constantini magni filio, can. 15. hanc Episcoporum in iudicando æquabilitatem seruauit: Si quis episcopus, inquit, aliquorum criminum accusatus fuerit ab omnibus prouinciæ episcopis condemnatus, & omnes vnam consentientem aduersus eius sententiam tulerint, is ne amplius ab aliis iudicetur: sed illius prouinciæ episcoporum firma maneat sententia. Vbi tum fuit Episcopi R. suprema illa potentia & dignitas, vt de rebus in quauis orbis terrarum parte iudicatis, iterum cognoscere, & aliorum episcoporum sententias retractare posset? Quartum testimonium est ex Mileuitani Concilij can. 22. vbi sic scriptum est: Si presbyteri, Diaconi, & caeteri clerici de iudicijs episcoporum suorum questi fuerint, vicini episcopi eos audiant, & inter eos quicquid est finiant, adhibiti ab eis ex consensu Episcoporum suorum. quod si & ab iis prouocandum putauerint, non prouocet nisi ad Africana Concilia, vel ad primates prouinciarum suarum. Ad transmarina autem qui putauerit appellandum, a nullo intra Africam in communione recipiatur. Hoc Mileuitani concilij decretum est, Imperatibus Arcadio & Honorio AA. coss. quo loco non praetereunda silentio est Episcopi R. terrima impudentia, qui cum illum canonem in suum Decretum a Gratiano referri passus esset, impudentissima hanc exceptionem adiecit: NISI FORTE ROMANAM SEDEM APPELLAVERIT. 2. q. 6. c. placuit. Quid n. impudentius, quam cuius potissimum prohibendi causa Canon ille scriptus est, eū solum a prohibitione excipere? Sequitur tertiū argumetum, quod ex eorūdem Conciliorū decretis & Imperatorum Christianorum constitutionibus sumemus, de Constantinopolitana sede Romanae sedi sic exaequarat ut ei nulla omnino in re cederet, extraquam ut Romanus Episcopus in conuentibus ecclesiasticis primus, in ijsdem tamen sedibus, consideret: proxime vero Constantinopolitanus ei assideret, ac deinceps caeteri, neque vlla re alia sese Romanus a liis anteferret. Nam Constantinopolitanae synodi can. 3. ita decretum est. Constantinopolitanus episcopus habeat primas honoris partes (πρεσβεῖα) post Romanum episcopum, eo quod haec vrbs est noua Roma. Rursus Chalcedonēsis Concilij can.28.Sanctorū Patrum decreta vbique sequentes, & canonem centū & viginti episcoporum agnoscentes, eadem quoque & nos decerni-mus, ac statuimus de priuilegiis sanctissimæ ecclesiæ Co-stantinopolis[?] nouæ Romæ. Etenim antiquæ nouæ throno, quoniam vrbs illa imperabat, iure patres priuilegia (πρεσβεία) tribuere. Et eadem consideratione moti centum quinquaginta episcopi sanctissimo nouæ Romæ thro-no æqualia priuilegia tribuere: recte iudicantes vrbem quæ & imperio & senatu honorata sit, & æqualibus cum antiquissima regina Roma priuilegiis fruatur, etiam in rebus ecclesiasticis, nonsecus ac illa extolli ac magni fieri, se cundam post illam existentem. Sed & in ean-dem sententiam extat Imperatoris Zenonis con-stitutio in Cod.Iustiniano,l.decernimus,16. C. de sacrof.eccles.his verbis:Sacrosanctam huius Constantinopolitanae religiosissimae ciuitatis ecclesiam,& matrem nostrae pietati & Christianorum orthodoxae religionis omnium,& eiusdem Regiae vrbis sanctissimam sedē priuilegia & honores omnes super Episcoporum creationi-bus,& iure ante alios residendi,& cætera omnia quae ante nostrum imperium, vel nobis imperantibus habuisse dignoscitur, habere in perpetuum firmiter, Reginae vrbis intuitu, iudicamus & sancimus. Hæc Ze-no, cuius sententiam Imperator Iustinianus secu-tus in l.24,C.eod.ita sanxit:ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει ἐκκλησία πασῶν τῶν ἄλλων ἐστὶ κεφαλή. Constantinopolitana ecclesia omnium aliarum est caput. Sequitur quartum argumentum. Vetus iuris regula est, vbi de consuetudine ambigitur, vt ea potissimum valeat, de qua contradicto iudicio disceptatum est. Atqui Epis-copus R. illam appellationum & rescindendarum sententiarum potestatem sibi vindicans, à generali Carthaginensi Concilio(in quo B.Augustinus in-terfuit) re per quinquennium quaesita & deliberata, summo patrum omnium consensu condemnatus est.Quare, non licet Episcopo R.sibi ius vllum ex illa damnata consuetudine arrogare. Assumptione hoc modo probabimus. Anno Christi 485. cum esset indictu generale totius Africae Cöcilium in vrbem Carthaginem,Episcopus R. tres-cò legatos Italos misit,qui nomine ipsius peterent, vt ius illud appellationum sibi conseruaretur: simulque titulum atque instrumentum sui iuris legatis illis commisit,Nicęni nempe Concilij auctoritate,quo in Concilio ius illud sibi tributum fuisse contendebat.Omnes qui aderant Episcopi continuò responderunt,nihil se vnquam eiusmodi in Nicaeni Concilij actis legisse,simulque legatos illos iussenrunt, si canonem illum habebant, Danieli scribae publico tradere, vt ilud palam recitaret. Exhibuerunt caput Sardicensis quidem Concilij tertium, sed mutilum & contaminatum. Nam in authentico scriptum ita est: εἰ τις ἐπίσκοπος[?] ἐν τινι πράγματι[?] καταχρίνεσθαι, ἢ ὑπολαμβάνει ἑαυτῷ μὴ σαθρὸν, ἀλλὰ καλὸν ἔχειν τὸ πρᾶγμα, ἵνα ἡ αὐτῆς ἡ κρίσις ἀνανεωθῇ, εἰ δοκεῖ ὑμῖν, τῇ ἀγάπῃ Πέτρου τοῦ ἀποστόλου τὸ μνήμιον τιμήσωμεν, ἢ γράφειν, ὡς τῶν κρινάντων Ἰουλίῳ τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ ῥώμης[?], ὡς διὰ τῶν γειτνιώντων τὴν ἐπαρχίαν ἐπισκόπων, εἰ δέ τινες ἀνανεωθῆναι τὸ δικαστήριον[?], ἢ ἐπιγνώμονας αὐτῆς[?]. hoc est : Siquis episcopus in aliqua causa condemnatus fuerit,& existimet se non malam, sed bonam causam habere, vt iterum iudicium renouetur,Si VOBIS VIDETVR, PROPTER CHARITATEM HONOREMVS MEMORIAM PETRI APOSTOLI,vt scribatur ab iis qui iudicarunt IVLIO Episcopo R. ut per vicinos episcopos illius prouinciae, si iudicium re-tractari oporteat, retractetur: & ipse iudices det. Haec Sardicense concilium. At Episcopus R.omissis il-lis verbis, Propter charitatem honoremus Petri apostoli memoriam, & ad Iulium Romanum episcopum scriba-tur: decurtatum caput his misit verbis: Si episcopus accusatus fuerit, & propriae eius prouinciae qui conuene-rant Episcopi eum condemnauerint, & visum sit appel-lare, & ad beatissimum Romae episcopum confugerit, & ipse eum audiri voluerit, & aequum existimauerit, ut re-nouetur examinatio, scribere dignabitur ad Episcopos qui sunt in finitima prouincia, ut ipsi diligenter etiam in-quirant, & ex vero & aequo peragant. Et ideo si quis ve-lit negotium suum rursus audiri, & episcopum R.sua sup-plicatione monuerit, ut alatere[?] suo legatum mittat, in sua sit potestate quod vult & quod melius existimat. Haec ille, unde intelligitur quam perfidiose & quam im-pudenter Concilio Carthaginensi fucum facere conatus sit: nobis autem fucum fecerit in suo De-creto Gratianico, ubi simili fallacia & calliditate visus illa eadem verba prætereiit. 6.q.4.c.Osius. quae verba iccirco suae causse aduersari intelligebat, quia si ius illud omnino ad se pertinuisset, non illum parasitastrum Osium appos-uisset, qui priuilegium illud precibus eblandiretur: sed directis verbis illud sibi vindicasset: quandoquidem rei suae precarium nullum est, ut Iurisconsulti loquuntur. Sed iam reliqua videamus. Nam ubi Carthaginefes patres ad unum omnes ac sine vlla varietate professi sunt, se nunquam illud caput in Niceni Concilij actis legisse, ac decreuerunt ut ab Episcopo Constantinopolitano, Antiochino, Alexandrino, atque etiam ipso Romano, vera Niceni Concilij exemplaria peterentur,si forte in illis canon ille reperiri posset,neque per annos quinque perpetuos quic-quam eiusmodi peruestigari potuisset,tum de co-cilij sententia literæ ad Episcopum R. his verbis scriptæ sunt,quibus os ipsius impudens acriter, vt decuit, verberatum est.Sequemur autem Gentiani Herueti Catholici Romanensis interpretationem, quam in superioribus quoque locis omnibus accu-ratè secuti sumus , ne cui alterius interpretatio creare suspicionem possit. Petimus , ne deinceps ad vestras aures eos qui hinc veniunt , facilè admittatis , nec qui à nobis excommunicati fue-rint in communionem velitis deinceps recipere. Nam hoc quoque in Nicæna synodo definitum vestra facile inueniet beatitudo.Si enim etiam de inferioribus clericis & laicis illic seruari videtur, hoc vult multo magis etiam de episcopis seruari.Ne ergo qui in propria prouincia à communione suspensi sunt, à tua sanctitate dedita opera, &, vt non oportet, communioni restituti videatur.Præsbyterorum autem similiter & consequen-tium clericorum impudentes fugas,vt te dignum est,per-sequetur tua sanctitas. Nā neque per vllu patrū decre-tū hoc Africanicæ ecclesiæ est prohibitū:& Nicænæ synodi statuta,siue clericos inferioris gradus,siue ipsos episcopos propriis metropolitanis apertissime commiserunt. Sapiē-ter enim & iuste perspexerunt,quacunque fuerint exor-ta negotia ea in propriis locis terminari debere. Neque enim vnicuique prouinciæ sancti spiritus gratiam deesse putarunt , per quam iustitia à sacerdotibus & videtur prudenter & stabiliter tenetur.maxime quod vnicuique concessum est,si ei videatur , de iudicum sententia ad synodos propriæ prouinciæ, vel præterea etiam ad vni-uersalem synodum appellare. nisi vbique est aliquis qui credat, uni cuipiam, quicunque is sit, posse Deum nostrū-iudicii iustitiam inspirare, innumerabilibus autem sa-cerdotibus in synodo cogregatis, denegare. Quomodo ergo firmum erit hoc transmarinum iudicium, ad quod testiū necessariæ personæ, vel propter naturam, vel propter senii imbecillitatem, vel propter nulla alia impedimenta, de-duci non possunt. Nam de mittendis quibusdam veluti à latere vestræ sanctitatis, à nulla patrum synodo con-stitutum inuenimus. Nam quod per Faustinum tanquam ex parte Nicænæ synodi istius missum fuerat, in verio-ribus descriptionibus Nicænæ synodi, nihil eiusmodi inuenire potuimus. Itaque ne velitis permittere ut su-mosum mundi fastum in Christi ecclesiam inducere vi-deamur. Hactenus Carthaginenses episcopi ex qui-busfacile quiuis perspicit, non modo quàm im-pudens Episcopi impostura, in illo sacro Patrum conuentu patefacta, & manifesto deprehensa fue-rit, verùm etiam quàm multis quámque iustis ra-tionib⁹ ab iisdē refutata, cōdēnata, & repudiata sit.
units.tr: Now for the second argument. The first and most ancient Christian councils gave each archbishop, within his own province, the highest hearing, jurisdiction and power, and they forbade any archbishop to usurp any right in another's diocese. It therefore was not lawful for anyone condemned by the bishops of his own province to appeal to the Roman bishop, nor for the Roman bishop to accept such an appeal and overturn the sentence of other bishops. The antecedent is proved by many testimonies, of which the first is the sixth canon of the Council of Nicaea, in these words: The ancient customs shall be observed which are in Egypt, Libya and Pentapolis, so that the bishop of Alexandria has authority over all these, since the bishop of Rome also has this same custom. Likewise at Antioch and in the other provinces, the privileges, dignities and authorities of the churches shall be preserved. Rufinus, in his Ecclesiastical History, book 10, explained this decree in these words: At Alexandria and in the city of Rome, this custom shall be kept, that the one has care of Egypt and the other of the churches in the suburbicarian region. A second testimony can be brought from the Council of Constantinople, where the same matter was decreed as follows: Let bishops not go to churches beyond their own diocese, nor confuse the churches; but according to the canons, the bishop of Alexandria shall govern Egypt alone; the bishops of the East shall administer the East alone, the privileges and pre-eminences of the church of Antioch which are in the canons of the Council of Nicaea being preserved. And the bishops of the Asian diocese shall administer only what is in Asia, and the bishops of Thrace shall rule Thrace only, and those of Pontus, Pontus. From these passages it is plainly understood that in the time of the primitive Church that equality among bishops which we have said was instituted by Christ was maintained, and that no one was permitted to usurp any right or power in another's diocese. So far is it from the case that the bishop of Rome had a divine right to receive appeals from distant and overseas churches and to rescind the judgements of other bishops. Likewise, the Synod of Antioch, held under the emperor Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, kept this equality of bishops in judging, in canon 15: If any bishop, it says, has been accused of some crimes and has been condemned by all the bishops of the province, and all have pronounced one sentence in agreement against him, he shall not be judged again by others; but the sentence of the bishops of that province shall stand firm. Where, then, was that supreme power and dignity of the bishop of Rome, by which he could take up again matters judged in any part of the world and retract the sentences of other bishops?
