A fourth testimony is from canon 22 of the Council of Milevis, where it is written thus: If presbyters, deacons and other clergy have complained of the judgements of their bishops, the neighbouring bishops shall hear them, and settle whatever is between them, with those whom they have called in with the consent of their bishops. But if they think they must appeal even from these, they shall appeal only to the African councils or to the primates of their provinces. Whoever thinks he must appeal overseas shall not be received into communion by anyone within Africa. This decree of the Council of Milevis was made in the consulship of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius. At this point we must not pass over in silence the most shameless impudence of the Roman bishop, who, when he allowed that canon to be cited by Gratian in his Decretum, added this most impudent exception: UNLESS PERHAPS HE HAS APPEALED TO THE ROMAN SEE. (2 q. 6, c. Placuit.) For what could be more impudent than to exempt from the prohibition the very person against whom that canon was written to prevent such appeals? A third argument follows, which we shall take from the decrees of the same councils and the constitutions of Christian emperors. It holds that the see of Constantinople was so equated with the Roman see that it yielded to it in nothing at all, except that the Roman bishop was first in ecclesiastical gatherings and took the first seat, while the bishop of Constantinople sat next to him, and the others after, and the Roman bishop was preferred to the others in no other respect. For in canon 3 of the Synod of Constantinople it was decreed thus: The bishop of Constantinople shall have the primacy of honour (πρεσβεῖα) after the bishop of Rome, because that city is New Rome. Again, canon 28 of the Council of Chalcedon: Following everywhere the decrees of the holy Fathers, and acknowledging the canon of the one hundred and twenty bishops, we too decree and establish the same things concerning the privileges of the most holy church of Constantinople, New Rome. For the Fathers rightly gave privileges (πρεσβεία) to the throne of Old Rome, because that city ruled. And moved by the same consideration, the one hundred and fifty most holy bishops gave equal privileges to the most holy throne of New Rome, rightly judging that the city which is honoured with empire and senate, and enjoys privileges equal to those of ancient Rome, the queen, should also be exalted and magnified in ecclesiastical matters, being second after her. The same opinion is also found in a constitution of the emperor Zeno in the Code of Justinian, law 16, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, in these words: We, by reason of the regal city, judge and decree that the sacrosanct church of this most religious city of Constantinople, mother of our piety and of all Christians of the orthodox religion, and the most holy see of the same royal city, shall have firmly and in perpetuity all the privileges and honours concerning the creation of bishops, and the right of sitting before others, and all the other things which are known to have been had before our empire or under our rule. So Zeno. The emperor Justinian, following his opinion, enacted in law 24, C. of the same title: ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει ἐκκλησία πασῶν τῶν ἄλλων ἐστὶ κεφαλή. The church at Constantinople is the head of all the others. A fourth argument follows. It is an old rule of law that where custom is in doubt, that custom should prevail which has been disputed in a contested trial. But the bishop of Rome, claiming for himself the power of appeals and of rescinding sentences, was condemned by the general Council of Carthage (in which St Augustine took part), after the matter had been sought and deliberated for five years, with the unanimous consent of all the Fathers. Therefore it is not lawful for the bishop of Rome to claim for himself any right from that condemned custom. We shall prove the assumption as follows. In the year of Christ 485, when a general council of all Africa had been called to the city of Carthage, the bishop of Rome sent three Italian legates, who were to ask in his name that the right of appeals be preserved for him; and at the same time he entrusted to those legates a title and an instrument of his right, namely by the authority of the Council of Nicaea, in which council he contended that this right had been granted to him. All the bishops present at once replied that they had never read anything of the kind in the acts of the Council of Nicaea; and at the same time they ordered those legates, if they had that canon, to hand it over to Daniel, the public scribe, so that he might read it aloud openly. The legates produced the third chapter of the Council of Sardica, but it was mutilated and corrupted. For in the authentic text it is written thus: εἰ τις ἐπίσκοπος ἐν τινι πράγματι καταχρίνεσθαι, ἢ ὑπολαμβάνει ἑαυτῷ μὴ σαθρὸν, ἀλλὰ καλὸν ἔχειν τὸ πρᾶγμα, ἵνα ἡ αὐτῆς ἡ κρίσις ἀνανεωθῇ, εἰ δοκεῖ ὑμῖν, τῇ ἀγάπῃ Πέτρου τοῦ ἀποστόλου τὸ μνήμιον τιμήσωμεν, ἢ γράφειν, ὡς τῶν κρινάντων Ἰουλίῳ τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ ῥώμης, ὡς διὰ τῶν γειτνιώντων τὴν ἐπαρχίαν ἐπισκόπων, εἰ δέ τινες ἀνανεωθῆναι τὸ δικαστήριον, ἢ ἐπιγνώμονας αὐτῆς. That is: If any bishop has been condemned in some matter, and thinks that he has not a bad but a good cause, so that the judgement may be renewed, IF IT SEEMS GOOD TO YOU, LET US HONOUR, OUT OF CHARITY, THE MEMORY OF THE APOSTLE PETER, and let it be written to Julius, bishop of Rome, that through the neighbouring bishops of the province, if the judgement ought to be retried, it may be retried, and that he may appoint the judges. So the Council of Sardica. But the bishop of Rome, omitting those words, Out of charity let us honour the memory of the apostle Peter, and let it be written to Julius, bishop of Rome, sent the chapter to us abridged, in these words: If a bishop has been accused, and the bishops of his own province who had gathered have condemned him, and he thinks fit to appeal, and has taken refuge with the most blessed bishop of Rome, and he wishes to be heard, and thinks it fair that the examination be renewed, he will deign to write to the bishops who are in the neighbouring province, that they themselves may inquire carefully and conclude according to truth and justice. And therefore, if anyone wishes his case to be heard again, and by his supplication admonishes the bishop of Rome to send his legate to his side, it is in his power to do what he wishes and what he thinks best. So he. From this it is understood how treacherously and how impudently he tried to deceive the Council of Carthage; and he deceived us also in his Gratian Decretum, where, with the same trickery and cunning, he omitted those very words. (6 q. 4, c. Osius.) He understood that those words were against his cause, because if that right had wholly belonged to him, he would not have brought in that parasite Hosius, who flatters that privilege with prayers, but would have claimed it for himself in direct words; since, as the jurists say, there is no grant at will (precarium) in one's own affair. But now let us look at what remains. For when the Carthaginian Fathers, all together and without any dissent, declared that they had never read that chapter in the acts of the Council of Nicaea, they also decreed that the true copies of the Council of Nicaea should be sought from the bishops of Constantinople, Antioch and Alexandria, and even from the Roman bishop himself, in case that canon might perhaps be found in them; and when for five full years nothing of the kind could be found, then by the sentence of the council a letter was written to the bishop of Rome in these words, by which his impudent face was sharply, as was fitting, rebuked. We shall follow the translation of Gentian Hervet, the Catholic of Rome, which we have followed carefully in all the earlier passages as well, so that no one may suspect that another's translation creates doubt. We ask that you no longer readily admit to your ears those who come hence, nor be willing to receive into communion those who have been excommunicated by us. For your blessedness will easily find that this too was defined at the Synod of Nicaea. For if it appears to be observed there even concerning the inferior clergy and laity, it is wished much more to be observed also concerning bishops. Therefore let not those who have been suspended from communion in their own province be restored to communion by your holiness, deliberately and, as is not proper, as if it were right. But the shameless flights of presbyters and of the clergy in their train, your holiness will pursue, as is fitting for you. For this has not been forbidden by any decree of the Fathers in the African Church; and the statutes of the Synod of Nicaea have most plainly committed to their own metropolitans both the clergy of the lower grade and the bishops themselves. For they wisely and justly perceived that whatever disputes arise should be settled in their own places. Nor did they think that the grace of the Holy Spirit was lacking to each province, by which justice is seen to be prudently and steadily upheld by the priests. Especially since it has been granted to each one, if he thinks fit, to appeal from the judgement of the judges to the synods of his own province, or even further to the universal synod. Unless there is anyone everywhere who believes that God our Lord can inspire the justice of judgement in any single person, whoever he may be, and deny it to innumerable priests gathered in a synod. How then will this overseas judgement be valid, for which the necessary witnesses cannot be brought, either because of their nature, or because of the weakness of old age, or because of other impediments? For concerning the sending of certain persons as if from the side of your holiness, we have found nothing decreed by any synod of the Fathers. For what was said to have been sent through Faustinus on behalf of that Synod of Nicaea, we could find nothing of the kind in the more accurate copies of the Synod of Nicaea. Therefore, do not let us seem to permit the proud pomp of the world to be introduced into the Church of Christ. Thus far the Carthaginian bishops; from which anyone may easily see not only how impudent the bishop's imposture was, once it was laid open and plainly caught in that holy assembly of the Fathers, but also how many and how just were the reasons by which it was refuted, condemned and rejected by them.

units.la: Sequitur vt videamus quibus argumentis Iesui-ta Bellarminius Romanum suum Episcopum, cui hanc operam nauauit, excusare, & contrariam sē-tentiam tueri conetur. Nam verba illius hæc sunt.
units.tr: It follows that we should see with what arguments the Jesuit Bellarmine tries to excuse his Roman Bishop, for whom he has undertaken this labour, and to defend the opposite opinion. For his words are these.

units.la: ¶Primū argumentum hæreticorum nostri tē-poris est huiusmodi. Si iure diuino Papa est summus iudex Ecclesiæ totius, quare Pontifices non ex iure diui-no, sed ex Concilio Niceno ius suum de appellationibus ad Apostolicam sedem confirmare nituntur? Et cur tot Catholici, sanctique Patres Carthaginensis Concilii, ius illud admittere nolunt, nisi in Cōcilio Niceno reperiatur?
units.tr: The first argument of the heretics of our time is of this kind. If by divine right the Pope is the supreme judge of the whole Church, why do the Pontiffs strive to confirm their right of appeal to the Apostolic See not by divine right but by the Council of Nicaea? And why do so many Catholics and holy Fathers of the Council of Carthage refuse to admit that right, unless it is found in the Council of Nicaea?

units.la: Ad hoc eorum argumentum breuiter respondemus, iure quidem diuino ad summum Pontificem appellari semper potuisse: tamen an expediret ea potestate uti, &c. omnibus in locis,non sine causa dubitatum esse. Nam utrinque rationes adferri possunt. Horum utrunque falsum est. nam neque unquam iure divino ad Episcopum R.vlla ex altera dioecesi appellare licuit: neque in Concilio Carthaginensi dubitatum est, an omni tempore id facere expediret. Prioris testimonio est paritas illa & aequabilitas a Christo inter coapostolos,& consequenter inter coepiscopos instituta, quemadmodum supra demonstratum est. Posterioris documento est illa patrum omnium Carthaginensium concors, prompta, & expedita responsio, negantium se in synodi ullius actis legisse, potestatem illam Episcopo R. tributam fuisse. deinde Nicaeni Concilii auctoritas apertissima, quae suam cuique Archiepiscopo provinciam ac dioecesim certis ac propriis finibus circumscripsit.
units.tr: To this argument of theirs we reply briefly: that by divine right appeal could always be made to the supreme Pontiff; yet whether it was expedient to use that power, etc., has been doubted in all places, not without cause. For reasons can be brought on both sides. Both of these claims are false. For by divine right it was never lawful to appeal to the Bishop of Rome from another diocese, and the Council of Carthage did not doubt whether it was expedient to do so at all times. The proof of the first is that parity and equality which Christ established among the fellow apostles, and consequently among the fellow bishops, as has been shown above. The proof of the second is the unanimous, prompt and ready reply of all the Carthaginian fathers, who said that they had not read in the acts of any synod that this power had been granted to the Bishop of Rome. Next comes the most evident authority of the Council of Nicaea, which marked out to each archbishop his own province and diocese within fixed and proper limits.

units.la: Si enim passim omnibus appellatio concedatur facile fiet ut multi effugiant legitima iudicia, ut immerito vexentur Episcopi, qui primo iudicarunt, ut causae, alioqui faciles, & perspicuae, in longum tempus protrahantur. Atque hinc sanctus CYPRIANUS libro primo, epistola tertia & quarta, non semel conqueritur de iis, qui semel legitime iudicati, & damnati, Romam ad Pontificem provocabant. Et sanctus BERNARDUS lib. tertio de consideratione, multa enumerat incommoda, quae ex nimia frequentia appellationum oriuntur. Nugatores[?] hunc non patiemur aut leves aut falsas causas Patribus Carthaginensibus affingere: sed eas ipsas quas in epistola Episcopo R. scripta attulerunt, exponemus. prima est, quod Nicaena synodus suam cuique Archiepiscopo ac proinde Romano, dioecesim definiens & iurisdictionem in suos tantum provinciae clericos attribuens, tacite vetuisse intellitelligetur, ne quis sibi ius vllum in alienam prouinciam arrogaret. Hoc quoque, inquit, vt ne qui ab nobis excommunicati sunt, a vobis in communionem recipiuntur, in Nicæna synodo definitum vestra facile inueniet beatitudo. Item, Nicænae synodi statuta a} imeclericos inferioris gradus, sine ipsos episcopos propriis metropolitanis apertissime commiserunt. Secunda causa est, quod absurdum esset existimare, spiritus sancti gratiam & recte iudicandi prudentiam omnibus praeter Episcopum R. sacerdotibus & episcopis denegata fuisse. Tertia est, quod cum satis sit bis appellare, facultas est volentibus appellare a sententia sui episcopi, prouocare ad synodum prouincialem, & rursus ab hac ad synodum vniuersalem.
units.tr: For if appeal were granted to everyone indiscriminately, it would easily come about that many escape lawful judgments, that bishops who first judged are unjustly harassed, and that causes which are otherwise easy and clear are dragged out for a long time. And hence Saint Cyprian, in the first book, epistles three and four, more than once complains of those who, once lawfully judged and condemned, appealed to the Pontiff at Rome. And Saint Bernard, in the third book On Consideration, lists many inconveniences that arise from the excessive frequency of appeals. These triflers we will not allow to attribute to the Carthaginian Fathers either trivial or false reasons; rather we will set out those very reasons which they gave in their letter to the Bishop of Rome. The first is that the Nicene synod, in defining to each archbishop, and therefore to the Roman, his diocese, and in assigning jurisdiction only over the clergy of his own province, is understood to have tacitly forbidden anyone to claim for himself any right in another's province. This also, it says, that those who have been excommunicated by us should not be received into communion by you, your holiness will easily find decreed in the Nicene synod. Likewise, the decrees of the Nicene synod most clearly entrusted the lower clergy, and the bishops themselves, to their own metropolitans. The second reason is that it would be absurd to think that the grace of the Holy Spirit and the prudence to judge rightly had been denied to all priests and bishops except the Bishop of Rome. The third is that since it is enough to appeal twice, those who wish to appeal from the sentence of their own bishop have the option of calling the matter to a provincial synod, and again from that to a universal synod.

units.la: Quarta est, quod cum in sententiis retractādis testium praesentia & depositio requiratur, iniquissimum esset testes ex quauis longinquis atque etiā transmarinis regionibus vsque Romam euocari: praesertim aut senio, aut valetudine, aut aliis causis quae innumerabiles esse possunt, impeditos. Quinta est, ꝑ[?] ista ratione & πλεονεξία[?] videretur fumosus mundi fastus in ecclesiam Christianam introduci. His vsi rationibus Carthaginenses patres illam Episcopi R. petitionem repudiarunt: quemadmodum ex eorum epistola paulò ante prolata cuiuis cognoscere licebit.
units.tr: The fourth is that since the presence and testimony of witnesses is required in the retrial of sentences, it would be most unjust to summon witnesses from any distant and even overseas regions all the way to Rome, especially when they are hindered by old age, ill health, or other causes which can be innumerable. The fifth is that by this reasoning and covetousness the proud pomp of the world would seem to be introduced into the Christian Church. Using these reasons the Carthaginian fathers rejected that petition of the Bishop of Rome, as anyone may learn from their letter set out just above.

units.la: ¶Contra vero si nulli concedatur appellatio, dabitur occasio particularibus Episcopis, vt facile & temere iudicent, & tyrannice populos opprimant, nec non, vt existiment, nullum se habere superiorem, nullirationem esse reddendam: quod nihil esset aliud, quam vnum corpus Ecclesiae in tot partes scindere quot sunt Episcopatus. Itaque, cum res dubia esset, Concilium SARDICENSE generale, ipso etiam consentiente Pontifice,declarauit, expedire, vt ordinarie Presbyteris, & aliis minoribus Clericis appellatio con-cedatur ab Epi-scopis ad Concilium prouinciale, Episcopis autem, ad sedem Apostolicam. Esse autem hanc declarationem non nouam concessionem, testantur ex-empla eorum, qui ante Concilii Sardicensis & Nicæni tēpora omnibus atatibus ad Romanum Pontificem ap-pellarunt. ¶ Imò remedium aliud, & cōmodius, & sa-pientius a Conciliis vniuersalibus in spiritu Dei cōgregatis repertum est, vt ab Episcopis ad ꝓuinciale Cōciliū, a ꝓuinciali ad vniuersale appellare liceret. neq; ferri vel arrogātia vel impudentia illa potest, si Romanꝰ Episcopus contenderet vel dis-ceptādi prudentiā, vel spiritus sancti benignitatem sibi vni concessam, cæteris omnibus conuentibus ecclesiasticis denegatam fuisse. Quinetiam Theo-dorus Balsamon Antiochinus Patriarcha longe a-liter illud Sardicense decretū interpretatur. Si E-piscopus, inquit, controuersiam aliquam habeat cū suo coepiscopo, synodus statuit eos a prouincialibus episcopis iudicandos: neque vllum debere alium episcopum ex alia prouincia ad illud iudicium euocare, ne omnes illius prouinciae episcopi (attende lector atq; animū aduer-te) vel ignorantiae vel iniustitiae condemnari videantur: Prouinciales tamen, vt honos tribuatur memoriae Petri Apostoli, eam rem ad Iulium qui per id tempus Episcopus R. erat, deferre. Quibus verbis & synodus & Bal-samon nō obscurè significā, decretum illud & personale & temporale fuisse, vt neq; Iulij per id tempus episcopi personam, neque tempus ipsius episcopatus excederet. quid amplius? subiungit Balsamon hoc decretum pugnare cum Antiochina sy-nodo, quæ sub eodem Imperatore Constantio Constantini magni filio habitum fuisse, quinto post Constantini mortem anno, idem Balsamon testatur. verba patrum Antiochinorū can. 15. haec sunt: Si quis episcopus aliquorum criminum accusatus fuerit ab omnibus provinciae episcopis condemnatus, & omnes unam consentientem adversus eum sententiam tulerint, is ne amplius ab aliis iudicetur, sed provinciae episcoporū firma maneat sententia. Sed commodius est concilij illius Sardicensis historiam ex Nicephori libro ix. exponere: praesertim ut intelligamus quo ore Bellarminius Concilium illud Nicaeno aequiparare, & illius geminum facere sit ausus. Scribit igitur Nicephorus Iulium illum Episcopum R. cui Hosius noster Sardicae supparasitatus est, arrogantia & ambitione tumidum in eam confidctiam venisse, ut sacerdotes omnes cuiusuis criminis damnatos & ab Orietalibus episcopis eiectos in communionem recipere, atque in sedes suas restituere auderet, contendens episcoporum omnium curam summumque arbitrium ad se pertinere: quam illius insolentiam cum caeteri ferre non possent, Antiochinum illud Concilium instituisse, quo in Concilio de Patrum omnium sententia publice ad illum literae scriptae sunt, quibus tantam illam confidentiam acriter atque acerbe represserunt. Breui autem post tempore sedandae illius controuersiae causa Concilium alterum in urbem Illyrici Sardicam indictum fuisse, quem in locum ex Oriente sex & sexaginta, ex Occidente trecenti episcopi convenerunt, sed partim illius Iulij artibus & machinationibus, partim Hosij nostri proteruitate & pervicacia tantam inter illos exortam seditionem fuisse, ut alij alios execrarentur, & Orientales Iulium ipsum R. episcopum sacerdotio suo exauctoratum ab eccle-siarum suarum communione arcerent. Hosium autem ubique Nicephorus ita describit, ut eum facile Romanensis sui Iulij parasitastrum & palpatorem agnosceres. Ex quo de Sardicensis concilij auctoritate, quod Bellarminius Nicæno exæquat, facilis cuiuis existimandi copia est.
units.tr: On the contrary, if appeal is granted to no one, there will be an occasion for particular bishops to judge easily and rashly, and to oppress peoples tyrannically, and also to think that they have no superior and owe an account of no reason to anyone; which would be nothing other than to split the one body of the Church into as many parts as there are bishoprics. Therefore, since the matter was doubtful, the general Council of Sardica, with the Pontiff himself also consenting, declared it expedient that appeal be granted ordinarily to presbyters and other minor clergy from their bishops to the provincial council, but to bishops to the Apostolic See. That this declaration is not a new concession is attested by the examples of those who, before the times of the Councils of Sardica and Nicaea, appealed to the Roman Pontiff in every age. Indeed, another remedy, both more convenient and wiser, has been devised by the universal councils gathered in the Spirit of God, namely that it be lawful to appeal from bishops to a provincial council, and from the provincial to a universal one. Nor can that arrogance or impudence be tolerated, if the Roman Bishop were to contend either that prudence in judging, or the kindness of the Holy Spirit, was granted to him alone and denied to all other ecclesiastical assemblies. Moreover, Theodorus Balsamon, patriarch of Antioch, interprets that decree of Sardica in quite a different way. If a bishop, he says, has some controversy with his fellow bishop, the synod has ruled that they are to be judged by the provincial bishops, and that no other bishop from another province ought to be summoned to that judgment, lest all the bishops of that province (mark, reader, and pay attention) seem to be condemned either through ignorance or injustice. Nevertheless, the provincials are to refer the matter to Julius, who was at that time Bishop of Rome, so that honour may be paid to the memory of the Apostle Peter. By these words both the synod and Balsamon clearly indicate that that decree was personal and temporary, so that it would not exceed the person of Julius, bishop at that time, nor the time of his episcopate. What more? Balsamon adds that this decree conflicts with the Synod of Antioch, which, as the same Balsamon attests, was held under the same emperor Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, in the fifth year after Constantine's death. The words of the Antiochene fathers, canon 15, are these: If any bishop has been accused of some crimes and has been condemned by all the bishops of the province, and all have pronounced one unanimous sentence against him, he is not to be judged further by others, but the sentence of the bishops of the province shall stand firm. But it is more convenient to set out the history of that Council of Sardica from the ninth book of Nicephorus, especially so that we may understand with what face Bellarmine dared to equate that council with the Nicene and make it a twin of it. Nicephorus therefore writes that that Julius, Bishop of Rome, for whom our Hosius acted as a parasite at Sardica, became so puffed up with arrogance and ambition that he dared to receive into communion all priests condemned for any crime and expelled by the Eastern bishops, and to restore them to their sees, contending that the care of all bishops and the supreme judgment belonged to him. When the others could not bear this insolence, the Antiochene council was convened, in which, by the common opinion of all the fathers, letters were publicly written to him, sharply and bitterly rebuking that great presumption. Shortly afterwards, to settle that controversy, another council was summoned in the city of Sardica in Illyricum, to which sixty-six bishops came from the East and three hundred from the West; but partly through the schemes and machinations of that Julius, and partly through the obstinacy and pertinacity of our Hosius, so great a sedition arose among them that they cursed one another, and the Eastern bishops cut off Julius himself, Bishop of Rome, deprived of his priesthood, from the communion of their churches. Nicephorus describes Hosius everywhere in such a way that you would recognise him easily as the parasite and flatterer of his Roman Julius. From this it is easy for anyone to judge the authority of the Council of Sardica, which Bellarmine puts on a level with Nicaea.

units.la: Cur igitur in Cocilio[?] Carthaginesi Romani Pontifices non ius diminuum,sed Nicaenum Concilium,ad ius appellationum stabiliendum,proferrent,causa erat, quoniam demonstrare volebant,non solum posse ad se ab omnibus appellari,sed etiam Ecclesiae expedire,ut ita fieret,quandoquidem generale Concilii idesenserat[?]. Imo si iuris divini auctoritate Episcopus R. habuisset, neque ullum certius causae suae firmamentum proferre potuisset, neque in ecclesiastico conuentu uti fere alio argumento debuisset. Nam universi Patres confestim illi auctoritati sine ulla cunctatione paruissent. Ecclesiae autem expedire iurisdictione illam sibi tribui, si Episcopus R. existimauit, at non existimarunt ducenti septemdecim Patres eiusdem coepiscopi:qui & postulatum eius repudiarunt, & iniquitatem petitionis hac ratione demonstrarunt, quod si ei soli tanta auctoritas concederetur, non modo recte iudicandi prudentia, verum etiam spiritus sancti fauor ei soli concedi, caeteris omnibus denegari videretur.
units.tr: Why, then, did the Roman bishops at the Council of Carthage bring forward the Nicene Council to establish the right of appeals, and not the decree that forbade them? The reason was that they wanted to show not only that appeals could be made to them from everywhere, but also that it was expedient for the Church that this should be so, since they believed that the general council had thought so. Indeed, if the bishop of Rome had possessed this right by divine authority, he could have offered no surer foundation for his cause, and he would hardly have needed to use any other argument in the ecclesiastical assembly. For all the Fathers would at once have obeyed that authority without any hesitation. But whether it was expedient for the Church that this jurisdiction be granted to him, the bishop of Rome thought so, but the two hundred and seventeen fathers, his fellow bishops, did not think so. They rejected his demand and showed the unfairness of the request on this ground: if such great authority were granted to him alone, it would seem that not only the wisdom to judge rightly but also the favour of the Holy Spirit were granted to him alone and denied to all the rest.

units.la: Pari ratione Africani Patres impedire cupiebant eiusmodi appellationes, quoniam existimabant eas Ecclesiae sua non expedire, tametsi neque ignorarent,neque negarent, eas absolute impediri non posse. Quocirca in utraque epistola, quam ad Pontifices Romanos de hac causa miserunt,subiectionem suam ad Apostolicam sedem testantur, dum ad eam eam referunt acta Concilii, & eius mandata accepisse se dicunt: & non habent, sed rogant, ut non facile aures appellatibus praebeat. Sed haec omnia clariora erunt, in so-lutione alterius argumenti. Imo, quia judicarunt eas non expedire, igitur dubitarunt easdem impe-dire:atque adeo absolute, praecise, & simpliciter impedire, vetare, prohibere. Causam autem & cur non expediret, & cur ipsi impedirent, aperte de-monstrarunt. ne conventus omnes ecclesiastici ex-tra urbem R. habiti, expertes Spiritus sancti judica-rentur: ne longinquarum regionum episcopi suas ecclesias relinquere, & mare transire, ac tam lon-ginquas ac periculosas & molestas & sumptuosas peregrinationes suscipere cogeretur. Denique, ne Niceni Concilij & aliorum posteriorum, quae contra licentiam illam decreverant, auctoritatem asper-nari viderentur. Quocirca in utraque epistola quam ad Pontifices R. in hac causa miserunt, non subje-ctionem ullam ad sedem R. significarunt, ut Bellarmi-nius impudenter scribere ausus est, sed modeste qui-dem attamen pro suo jure pronunciarunt, ei non li-cere tantam sibi auctoritatem asciscere. Petimus, in-quiunt, ne deinceps ad vestras aures eos qui hinc ve-niunt facile admittatis, nec qui a nobis excommunicati sunt, eos in communionem deinceps recipiatis. Nam hoc quoque in Nicæna synodo decretum, vestra facile inve-niet beatitudo. (Nota lector, appellationes istas a Sy-nodo Nicena fuisse interdictas) Si enim etiam de in-serioribus clericis & laicis illic servari videtur, hoc vult multo magis etiam de episcopis servari. Ne ergo qui in propria provincia a communione suspensi sunt, a tua sanctitate dedita opera, & ut non oportet communioni re-stituti videantur. Alterum igitur argumentum Magde-
units.tr: In the same way the African Fathers wished to prevent such appeals, because they judged that they were not expedient for their Churches, although they neither failed to recognise nor denied that they could not be prevented absolutely. Therefore, in both letters which they sent to the Roman bishops on this matter, they bear witness to their subjection to the apostolic see, in that they refer the acts of the council to it and say that they have received its commands; and they do not demand but ask that it not lightly lend its ears to appellants. But all these things will be clearer in the solution of the other argument. Indeed, because they judged that appeals were not expedient, they therefore doubted whether they should prevent them, and so they forbade, prohibited and absolutely, expressly and simply, ruled out such appeals. They clearly showed the cause both of why it was not expedient and why they themselves prevented them: lest all ecclesiastical assemblies held outside the city of Rome be judged to lack the Holy Spirit; lest the bishops of distant regions be forced to leave their churches, cross the sea, and undertake such long, dangerous, troublesome and costly journeys; and finally, lest they seem to despise the authority of the Council of Nicaea and of the other later councils, which had decreed against that licence. Therefore, in both letters which they sent to the Roman bishops on this matter, they did not signify any subjection to the Roman see, as Bellarmine has impudently dared to write, but spoke modestly yet for their own right, that it was not lawful for him to assume such great authority for himself. "We ask," they say, "that you do not readily admit to your ears those who come from here, nor afterwards receive into communion those whom we have excommunicated. For your blessedness will easily find this also decreed in the Nicene synod." (Note, reader, that these appeals were forbidden by the Synod of Nicaea.) For if this seems to be observed even for the lower clergy and laity, it wishes it to be observed much more for bishops. Therefore let not those who have been suspended from communion in their own province, by your holiness on purpose, and as it is not fitting, seem to be restored to communion. The second argument, then, of the Magdeburgers

units.la: Note: the signature "§· J·" at the foot is partly faint; its reading is doubtful. burgensium & Caluini, eiusmodi est, Zozimus, Boni-facius, & Celestinus Romani Pontifices, ius appellationum ad Apostolicam sedem ex Nicæno Concilio probare voluerunt: atqui discussa causa, falsatores & corruptores Nicænorum Canonum deprehensi sunt, igitur ne humano quidem iure, nedum divino ad eorum iudicium provocari potest.
units.tr: and of Calvin is of this kind: Zosimus, Boniface and Celestine, Roman bishops, wished to prove from the Nicene Council the right of appeals to the apostolic see; but the matter having been examined, the falsifiers and corrupters of the Nicene canons have been detected; therefore appeal cannot be made to their judgment, not even by human law, much less by divine law.

units.la: Respondendum primum, Africanos patres ex ignorantia deceptos, Magdeburgenses, & Caluinum ex malitia peccare. Nam Africani in epistola ad Celestinum bis repetunt, in nulla Patrum definitione, & in nulla Synodo se inuenisse illos Canones: ex quo apparet, eos non habuisse Canones Sardicensis Concilii, in quibus tres illi Canones diuersis verbis continentur, & si eos habuissent, sine dubio acquieuissent. Non enim minor est Sardicensis quam Nicæni Concilii auctoritas. Neque maior est error citare Nicænum Concilium pro Sardicensi, quam Matthæum pro Ioanne, vel Hieremiam pro Zacharia, vt citauit sanctus Matthæus, cap. 27.
units.tr: The first thing to answer is that the African Fathers were deceived through ignorance, while the Magdeburgers and Calvin sin through malice. For the Africans, in their letter to Celestine, twice repeat that they had found those canons neither in any definition of the Fathers nor in any synod; from which it appears that they did not have the canons of the Council of Sardica, in which those three canons are contained in different words, and if they had had them, they would undoubtedly have acquiesced. For the authority of the Council of Sardica is no less than that of the Council of Nicaea. Nor is it a greater error to cite the Council of Nicaea for the Council of Sardica than to cite Matthew for John, or Jeremiah for Zechariah, as St Matthew cited, chapter 27.

units.la: Sicut ergo non possumus vocare Matthæum falsarium, quia idem Spiritus sanctus in Hieremia & Zacharia locutus est, ita, &c.
units.tr: Just as, therefore, we cannot call Matthew a falsifier, because the same Holy Spirit spoke in Jeremiah and in Zechariah, so, etc.

units.la: ¶Imò neq; Africani patres fuerunt decepti ex ignorantia, neque nostri malitia peccarunt. At plane intolerabilis est Bellarminij insolentia condemnantis Carthaginensem synodū ignorantię, quam & Nicephorus & Balsamon & alij, testantur generalem fuisse: si non simul patiatur nos Sardicensem Synodum eodem fere tempore, & sub eodem Imperatore habitam paris ignorantiæ accusare. Patres Africani, inquit, in epistola ad Episc. R. bis repetunt sese in nulla patrum definitione & in nulla Synodo illos canones inuenisse. Satisne attendis, Bellarmini, quid voluerint, quid sequuti sint, quid verbis illis significarint? nempe se postulatum illud Osij, de B.Petri memoria in illis appellationibus honoranda, & appellationibus ad Iulium Romanum episcopum deferendis, non probare: sed Antiochinae Synodo malle obtemperare, quę veterem illarum ecclesiarum consuetudinem confirmarat. Ex quo intelligis falli te grauiter,cum ais, non minorem fuisse Sardicensis, quàm Nicęni Concilij auctoritatem: proinde quasi vllum vnquam fuerit probatum in ecclesia Concilium, quod Nicaenam Synodum sic abrogare auderet,vt Sardicense illud ab illo Antiochino, & nostro Carthaginiensi & vero etiam à Chalcedonensi abrogatum est: cuius postremi canon. 9. verba haec sunt Sardicensi plane contraria: Si episcopus aut clericus cum provincia sua metropolitano controuersiam habeat, diœcesis exarchu habeat, vel imperialis vrbis Constantinopolis thronum & apud eum litiget. Verba, inquâ, haec sunt huius synodi Oecumenicae multis post Sardicense Cocilium annis habitae, & a sexcentis triginta sanctis patribus celebratae. Quod vero de Magdeburgesibus, & Caluino abs te superatis, itemq; aliis locis de Chenitio, Illyrico, Bucero, Melanthone pari modo deuictistoties gloriaris, in eo te alterum plane Terapontigonum, aut Pyrgopolinicu agnoscimus: neque dubitamus, quin eiusmodi aduersarios tuos
units.tr: Indeed, neither were the African Fathers deceived through ignorance, nor did we sin through malice. But the insolence of Bellarmine is plainly intolerable, in condemning the Council of Carthage as ignorant, a council which both Nicephorus and Balsamon and others testify was general, unless he also allows us to accuse the Council of Sardica, held at about the same time and under the same emperor, of equal ignorance. The African Fathers, he says, in their letter to the Bishop of Rome, twice repeat that they had found those canons in no definition of the Fathers and in no synod. Do you attend sufficiently, Bellarmine, to what they meant, what they followed, what they signified by those words? Namely, that they did not approve that demand of Osius, that the memory of St Peter be honoured in those appeals, and that appeals be carried to Julius, bishop of Rome; but they preferred to obey the Synod of Antioch, which had confirmed the ancient custom of those churches. From this you understand that you are gravely mistaken when you say that the authority of the Council of Sardica was no less than that of the Council of Nicaea; as if there had ever been any council approved in the Church that dared so to abrogate the Nicene Synod that the Sardican council was abrogated by that Synod of Antioch, and by our Council of Carthage, and indeed also by Chalcedon, whose last canon, the ninth, has these words, plainly contrary to Sardica: "If a bishop or clergyman has a dispute with his metropolitan of his own province, let him take it to the exarch of the diocese, or to the throne of the imperial city of Constantinople, and let him litigate there." These words, I say, are those of that ecumenical synod held many years after the Council of Sardica, and celebrated by six hundred and thirty holy fathers. But as for the Magdeburgers and Calvin, whom you so often boast of having overcome, and likewise in other places Chemnitz, Illyricus, Bucer and Melanchthon, in this respect we recognise you as another Terapontigonus or Pyrgopolinices; and we do not doubt that your adversaries of this kind,
fifty at once,
If it were a sword of Nihebes, you would kill him with one blow.

units.la: Summae autem impudentiae est, dicere Romanum episcopum pari lapsu memoriae Nicaenum Concilium, pro Sardicensi meminisse, quo Matthaeus cap.27. Hieremiam pro Zacharia nominarat, primum quia iam a nostris demonstratum est, cùm in editione Syriaca prophetæ nomē fit omis-sum, probabilius esse illud quoq; à Matthæo suis-se præteritum, quàm ullum Matthæi ἀμαρτήμα[?] μνη-μονικὸν fuisse. tum vero quid simile? nam s[?]perius di-ctum est, quod etiam Bellarminius fatetur, non unius Episcopi R. mendum & peccatum illud suis-se, sed triū ordine Romanorū episcoporū pertinacē ac perpetuam per annos ipsos quinque fallaciam atque imposturam. Quod si Papæ sui errore hunc malit Bellarminius appellare, non magnopere lu-ctabor, modo illum simul fateatur à conuetu Carthaginensi conuictum & reductum in viam fuisse.
units.tr: Moreover, it is the height of impudence to say that the Roman bishop, by the same slip of memory, recalled the Nicene Council in place of the Sardican, just as Matthew in chapter 27 named Jeremiah in place of Zechariah. First, because it has already been shown by our side that, since the name of the prophet was omitted in the Syriac edition, it is more probable that this too was passed over by Matthew, rather than that there was any memory-slip [ἀμάρτημα μνημονικόν] on Matthew's part. And then, what is similar about it? For it was said above, and Bellarmine himself admits, that that error was not the fault and sin of one Roman bishop, but of three Roman bishops in succession, a stubborn and continuous deceit and imposture over five years. But if Bellarmine prefers to call this a mistake of their Pope, I shall not greatly struggle, provided that he also admits that they were convicted by the Council of Carthage and brought back to the right path.

units.la: ¶At Magdeburgenses nouerunt Sardicense Cocilium, & tanquam legitimum in suam quartam centuriā trans-stulerunt: ergo, necesse est fateantur Africanos deceptos, & caussa excidisse: ergo, cum illis nihilominus obstina-te victoriam tribuunt, secum pugnant, & ex malitia peccant.
units.tr: But the Magdeburgers knew the Council of Sardica, and transferred it into their fourth century as a legitimate council; therefore it must be admitted that the Africans were deceived and the cause has fallen; therefore, when they stubbornly attribute victory to them nonetheless, they contradict themselves and sin through malice.

units.la: ¶Imò qua prudetia Magdeburgenses in veteribus Conciliis recensendis, Sardicense nō præterierunt, eadem prudentia vbi Antiochinum, Carthaginē-se, & Chalcedonense Concilia suum in ordinem retulerunt, quanti postulatum illud Osij Sardicensis facerent, quod ab illis Cociliis fuit abrogatum, non obscure demonstrarunt: neque vel errore vel malitia peccarunt: vt Bellarminius loquitur: sed Bellarminium manifestas sycophantiæ & aucupij alicuius Episcopalis, vel potius mendacij contra spiritum Sanctum prolati aperte condemnarunt.
units.tr: Indeed, by the same prudence with which the Magdeburgers, in listing the ancient councils, did not pass over the Council of Sardica, by that same prudence, when they put the Synods of Antioch, Carthage and Chalcedon in their proper order, they clearly showed how much they valued that demand of Osius at Sardica, which those councils abrogated; and they did not sin either through error or through malice, as Bellarmine says, but they plainly condemned Bellarmine as a manifest sycophant and some kind of episcopal fowler of favours, or rather as the liar who has spoken against the Holy Spirit.

units.la: ¶Sed DICES, in isto Concilio VI. Carthaginensi, capite 6. citatur nominatim Sardicense Concilium, ergo non ignorabant illud Africani.
units.tr: ¶But you will say: in that sixth Council of Carthage, chapter 6, the Council of Sardica is cited by name, so the Africans were not ignorant of it.

units.la: Respondeo illa, verba quibus citatur Sardicense Concilium, non esse Africanorum, sed legatorum Pontificis. Ipsi enim ex commonitorio sibi dato a Pontifice Zozimo, illa verba citabant. Et praeterea existimo, omnino esse corruptum eum locum, & vel positum a Librariis, Sardicensi pro Nicaeno, vel quod magis suspicor, ex margine irrepsisse in textum illud: Ex Sardicensi Cōcilio. Ponitur enim in margine, Sardicense Concilium, quia reuera verba, quae ibi citantur, non inveniuntur nunc, nisi in Sardicensi Concilio.
units.tr: I answer that the words in which the Council of Sardica is cited were not the Africans' words but those of the papal legates. They cited those words from the memorandum given them by Pope Zosimus. Moreover, I think that passage is wholly corrupt, either because the scribes put "Sardican" in place of "Nicene," or, what I suspect more, because this gloss crept into the text from the margin: "From the Council of Sardica." For it is written in the margin, "the Council of Sardica," because the words cited there are in fact found nowhere now except in the Council of Sardica.

units.la: ¶Hoc verè est nugas agere. nam ego quoque non pugno, quominus illa verba ex margine sumpta sint: quādo[?] neque in Græco exemplari ea reperio, neque ab Herueto[?] translata sunt. quod Bellarminium neque vidisse, neque hoc loco inter alia obiecisse, mirum alicui videri possit. Sed ut ex margine sumpta sint, quid tum postea? nam omnes ad unum Africani patres summo consensu Concilio illi Sardicensi fidem atque auctoritatem abrogarunt: & Antiochini Concilii contrariam illi Concilio sententiam amplexi sunt: ac trium Romanorum episcoporum quinquennae[?] pertinax postulatum impudens aperte repudiarunt.
units.tr: This is truly to trifle. For I too do not dispute that those words were taken from the margin, since I find them neither in the Greek copy nor in the translation of Hervetus. That Bellarmine neither saw this nor objected it among his other points may seem surprising to someone. But grant that they were taken from the margin: what follows? For all the African fathers with one accord withdrew authority and credit from that Council of Sardica, embraced the opposite judgement of the Council of Antioch, and openly rejected the shameless demand of three Roman bishops, who obstinately pressed it for five years.

units.la: ¶At nihilominus non debet esse in textu nomen Sardi-censis Concilii. Siquidem verba illa citantur ex commonitorio Papæ Zozimi, quod ex Roma legati attulerant: legati autem illi ex Nicaeno Concilio se canones citare dicebant. Unde mox verbis illis recitatis, Augustinus dixit, Et haec nos seruaturos profitemur salua diligentiori inquisitione Nicaeni Cōcilij. Quibus verbis indicat se accepisse canonem citatum tanquam ex Nicaeno Concilio.
units.tr: ¶Nevertheless, the name of the Council of Sardica ought not to be in the text. For those words are cited from the memorandum of Pope Zosimus, which the legates had brought from Rome; and those legates said that they were citing canons from the Council of Nicaea. Hence, right after those words were recited, Augustine said: "We also profess that we shall observe these things, saving a more careful inquiry into the Nicene Council." By these words he indicates that he had received the canon as cited from the Nicene Council.

units.la: ¶Imo B. Augustinus sermonem illum suum retulit non ad illud Sardicense caput, in quo Iulij Episcopi R. & appellationum ad eum deferendarum mentio fiebat, sed restricte ad illud alterū quod ibi Daniel scriba recitarat de appellatione ad vicinos episcopos prouinciales, his verbis: Qui electus est, habeat potestatem appellandi ad finitimos, vt caussa eius audiatur, & diligentius tractetur. Ei enim appellanti, non est audientia deneganda. Tum illud continuò subiungitur: Et his lectis Augustinus episcopus ecclesiæ Hipponensis dixit, Hoc quoque nos seruaturos profitemur seruata diligentiori Nicæna Synodi inquisitione. Ex quibus de bona Bellarminij conscientia & fide, & summa in suo Papa defendendo sinceritate quiuis existimare poterit.
units.tr: ¶Indeed, Blessed Augustine did not refer his remark to that chapter of Sardica in which mention is made of Bishop Julius of Rome and of appeals to be carried to him, but strictly to the other chapter which Daniel the scribe had recited there, concerning appeal to neighbouring provincial bishops, in these words: "Whoever has been elected may have power to appeal to the neighbouring bishops, so that his case may be heard and more carefully examined. For a hearing must not be denied to one who appeals." Then this is immediately added: "And these things having been read, Augustine, bishop of the Church of Hippo, said: 'We also profess that we shall observe this too, saving a more careful inquiry into the Nicene Synod.'" From these things anyone may judge of Bellarmine's good conscience and faith, and of his great sincerity in defending his Pope.

units.la: Adde quod August. lib. 3. contra Cresconium, cap. 34. non agnoscit aliud Sardicense Concilium, quam quoddam hæreticum Concilium Orientalium Episcoporum contra Athanasium. Duplex enim fuit Sardicense, vt patet ex Sozomeno lib. 3. hist. cap. 10. & 11. vnum Catholicum generale supra CCC. Episcoporum, quod Augustinus nunquam vidit, alterum hæreticum LXXVI. Episcoporum, quod Augustinus vidit.
units.tr: Add that Augustine, in book 3 against Cresconius, chapter 34, recognises no other Council of Sardica than a certain heretical council of Eastern bishops against Athanasius. For there were two Councils of Sardica, as is clear from Sozomen, book 3 of his History, chapters 10 and 11: one Catholic and general, of more than 300 bishops, which Augustine never saw, and the other heretical, of 76 bishops, which Augustine did see.

units.la: Totum hoc caput plane nugatorium est. quid enim ad institutam disputationem pertinet vtrum Augustinus Sardicense illud Concilium viderit, an non viderit? dum illud maneat, quod negari non potest, caput illud Sardicensis Concilij quod tres ordines Romani Episcopi pro Nicæno supposuerunt, à generali Synodo Carthaginensi, cui Augustinus interfuit, repudiatum fuisse, quinimo Bellarminius scribens Augustinum non agnouisse Sardicense Cœcilium, confirmat illud ipsum quod superius aliquoties diximus, caput illud Sardicensis Concilij de appellationibus ad Iulium Papam deferendis ferendis, ab Antiochino Concilio contradictum, pro nullo, irrito, illegitimo à Carthaginensibus pa-tribus habitum fuisse.
units.tr: This whole chapter is plainly trifling. For what does it matter to the disputation in hand whether Augustine saw that Council of Sardica or did not? While this remains, which cannot be denied, that the chapter of the Council of Sardica which the three orders of Roman bishops put forward for the Nicene Council was rejected by the general Council of Carthage, at which Augustine was present; and indeed Bellarmine, in writing that Augustine did not recognise the Council of Sardica, confirms the very thing we have said several times above: that the chapter of the Council of Sardica concerning appeals to be carried to Pope Julius was contradicted by the Council of Antioch and was held by the Carthaginian fathers to be null, void and illegitimate.

units.la: ¶SECUNDO dico, Canones Nicæni Concilii qui sunt apud Ruffinum lib.10.hist.cap.6. & qui missi sunt ex Oriente ad Africanos, sine dubio non esse omnes canones, quos Nicænum Concilium edidit, & proinde probabile esse, hos tres canones, quos Zozimus citauit ex Nicæno Concilio, reuera in eo Concilio fuisse.
units.tr: ¶SECONDLY, I say that the canons of the Nicene Council which are in Rufinus, book 10 of his History, chapter 6, and which were sent from the East to the Africans, are without doubt not all the canons which the Nicene Council issued; and therefore it is probable that these three canons, which Zosimus cited from the Nicene Council, were really in that Council.

units.la: Quod illi Canones non sint omnes, probant nonnulli ex epistola Athanasii ad Marcum Papam, in qua petit exemplum Nicæni Concilii ex Romani Pontificis scrinio, asserens exempla quæ erant Alexandriæ, fuisse cre-mata ab Arianis.
units.tr: That those canons are not all of them, some prove from the letter of Athanasius to Pope Mark, in which he asks for a copy of the Nicene Council from the papal archive, asserting that the copies which were at Alexandria had been burned by the Arians.

units.la: ¶Imò ridicula illa conclusio est, Non omnes extant Niceni Concilij Canones: ergo probabile est tres illos Canones ab Episcopis R. missos partem Nicæni Concilij fuisse. Præterea, quanuis negatio-nis plerunque probatio nulla sit, tamen hæc nega-tio implicita in se cōtinet probationē. nā si neque in Africanis, neque in Romanis, neque in Constati-nopolitanis, neque in Alexandrinis, neque in An-tiochinis exēplaribus, reperiatur, neque alia usquā exemplaria extent, sequitur illos malitiosè cōfictos & suppositos fuisse.
units.tr: ¶Indeed, that conclusion is ridiculous: not all the canons of the Nicene Council survive; therefore it is probable that those three canons sent by the Roman bishops were part of the Nicene Council. Moreover, although proof of a negative is generally no proof, yet this negative contains proof within itself. For if they are not found in the African, the Roman, the Constantinopolitan, the Alexandrian or the Antiochene copies, and no other copies exist anywhere, it follows that they were maliciously invented and forged.

units.la: ¶Sed hoc argumentū ridetur à Magdeburgensibus, & verè non est solidum. Nam illa incensio librorum accidit tempore Constantii Imperatoris, quando Athanasio ex-pulso Georgius quidam Arianus, in locum eius ordina-tus est, ut ipse Athanasius testatur in epist. ad omnes or-thodoxos: constat autem ex chronico Hieronymi, Mar-cum Papam eo tempore iam fuisse defunctum.
units.tr: But this argument is laughed at by the Magdeburg Centuriators, and it is truly not solid. For that burning of books happened in the time of the Emperor Constantius, when after the expulsion of Athanasius a certain Arian named George was ordained in his place, as Athanasius himself testifies in his letter to all orthodox men. Moreover, it is clear from the Chronicle of Jerome that Pope Mark had already died at that time.

units.la: Deinde, si Marcus Papa exemplum misisset ad Alexandrinos ex Romano scrinio, certè cōvenissent deinceps inter se exemplaria Romanum & Alexandrinum. Quomodo in exemplari à sancto Cyrillo ex Alexandria ad Africanos misso, deerant isti canones tres, qui inveniebatur in Romano? ¶ Quoniā Bellarminius ineptire se & nugas agere fatetur, operam in illius inceptijs[?] refellendis non abutemur. nam, ut ait Arnobius, Cōtradicere rebus stultis stultitiæ est maioris.
units.tr: Next, if Pope Mark had sent a copy from the Roman archive to the Alexandrians, certainly the Roman and Alexandrian copies would thereafter have agreed with each other. How is it that in the copy sent to the Africans by Saint Cyril from Alexandria those three canons were missing, which were found in the Roman one? ¶Since Bellarmine confesses that he is playing the fool and trifling, we shall not waste effort in refuting his efforts. For, as Arnobius says, to contradict foolish things is the greatest folly.

units.la: ¶ Omissa ergo ista Athanasij epistola, probatur canones illos non esse integros. PRIMO, quia unus ex præcipuis canonibus Nicæni Concilij erat: ut Pascha die Dominico celebraretur, ut patet ex epistola Constan tini apud Eusebium lib.3. de vita Constantini, ex Epiphanio hæref.69. & ex Athanasio in epistola de Synodis Arimini & Seleuci. At iste Canō nō extat inter illos XX. Rufini.
units.tr: ¶Setting aside, then, that letter of Athanasius, it is proved that those canons are not complete. FIRST, because one of the principal canons of the Nicene Council was that Easter should be celebrated on the Lord's day, as is clear from the letter of Constantine in Eusebius, book 3 of the Life of Constantine, from Epiphanius, heresy 69, and from Athanasius in his letter on the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia. But this canon is not among those twenty canons of Rufinus.

units.la: SECVNDO, Ambros. in epist.82. docet, in Concilio Nicæno statutum, ne bigamus in Clerum asciscatur. At neque hoc in illis XX. canonibus invenitur.
units.tr: SECOND, Ambrose, in letter 82, teaches that it was decreed at the Nicene Council that a bigamist should not be admitted into the clergy. But this too is not found among those twenty canons.

units.la: TERTIO, Hieronymus præfatione in Iudith, asserit à Concilio Nicæno librum Iudith, inter Canonicos rece-ptum. At non reperitur inter Canones Ruffini.
units.tr: THIRD, Jerome, in his preface to Judith, asserts that the book of Judith was received among the canonical books by the Nicene Council. But it is not found among the canons of Rufinus.

units.la: QVARTO, Augustinus epist. iio. de designando successore asserit, in Concilio Nicæno prohibitum, ne duo Episcopi simul sedeant in eadem ecclesia contra quem canonem se imprudenter fecisse dolenter refert. At iste canon nusquam apparet inter illos XX.
units.tr: FOURTH, Augustine, in letter 110 on the designation of a successor, asserts that at the Nicene Council it was forbidden that two bishops sit at the same time in the same church; and he sorrowfully reports that he had acted rashly against this canon. But this canon appears nowhere among those twenty.

units.la: QVINTO, in Concilio Africano, canone 14. asserunt Patres ex Canone Nicæni Concilii, non licere, nisi ieiunis offerre Eucharistiam. At ubi est iste canon inter illos XX?
units.tr: FIFTH, in the African Council, canon 14, the fathers assert from a canon of the Nicene Council that it is not lawful to offer the Eucharist except to those who are fasting. But where is that canon among those twenty?

units.la: SEXTO, in fine Concilii Chalcedonensis, Atticus refert in Concilio Nicæno determinatam fuisse rationem scribendarum formatarum epistolarum, de quibus loqui-turtur Optatus lib.2.contra Parmenianum, vbi ait: Cum quo (Syricio Romano Pontifice) nobis totus orbis, commercio formatarum, in communionis societatem communicat: & Concilium Mileuitanum canone vicesimo, dum prohibet, ne sine formatis literis Clerici ad comitatum eant. At hoc nusquam apparet in illis viginti canonibus Ruffini.
units.tr: SIXTH, at the end of the Council of Chalcedon, Atticus reports that at the Nicene Council a method was determined for writing formal letters, of which Optatus speaks in book 2 against Parmenian, where he says: With him (Siricius, Roman Pontiff) all the world communicates with us, by the exchange of formal letters, in fellowship of communion; and the Council of Milevis in canon twenty, where it forbids clerics to go to the court without formal letters. But this appears nowhere among those twenty canons of Rufinus.

units.la: Denique SEPTIMO, Lutherus, Caluinus, Centu-riatores, & cateri haeretici passim obiiciunt ex Socrate lib.1.hist.cap.8.canone Nicæni Concilii, in quo dicunt, permissas coniuges Sacerdotibus. At iste canon nō inuenitur in illis XX. Ergo si Zosimus corruptor & falsator canonum Nicænorum dicitur, quia citauit nomine Ni-cæni Concilii unum canonem, qui non inuenitur in illis XX.canonibus: eadem ratione corruptores & falsatores dicendi sunt Constantinus, Athanasius, Epiphanius, Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Augustinus, Atticus, Socrates, Africani Patres, & ipsi Centuriatores, atque etiā Lutherus & Caluinus. Omnes enim isti citat canones Nicæni Concilii, qui in illis XX. non reperiuntur.
units.tr: Finally, SEVENTH, Luther, Calvin, the Centuriators and other heretics everywhere object, from Socrates, book 1 of his History, chapter 8, a canon of the Nicene Council in which, they say, wives were permitted to priests. But that canon is not found among those twenty. Therefore, if Zosimus is called a corrupter and falsifier of the Nicene canons because he cited under the name of the Nicene Council one canon which is not found among those twenty canons, by the same reasoning Constantine, Athanasius, Epiphanius, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Atticus, Socrates, the African fathers, the Centuriators themselves, and even Luther and Calvin, must be called corrupters and falsifiers. For all of them cite canons of the Nicene Council which are not found among those twenty.

units.la: Adde VLTIMO, quod in Concilio Florentino ses-sione vicesima, Ioannes quidam vir doctissimus asserit, se multis sanctorum veterum testimoniis posse ostendere Concilii VI. Carthaginensis Patres tandem agnouisse, corruptos & falsos canones Nicæni Concilii ad se ex Alexandria & Constantinopoli missos fuisse.
units.tr: Add, LAST of all, that at the Council of Florence, in the twentieth session, a certain most learned man asserts that he can show from many testimonies of the ancient saints that the Fathers of the Sixth Council of Carthage at last acknowledged that the corrupted and false canons of the Council of Nicaea had been sent to them from Alexandria and Constantinople.

units.la: Otio abundasse Bellarminiu oportet, cum hæc scribere exorsus est. quorsum enim hæc illorum enumeratio, quæ deesse dicit in actis Nicæni Cō-cilij? Multa se posse Bellarminius ostendit docta doctis dicere, & quamuis facunde historiam veterem atque antiquam eloqui: sed eo redeundum est denique[?], in quo causa consistit. Romanus episcopus in agenda sua causa protulit instrumentū quod iudices ad unum omnes spurium,falsum, & adulterium esse iudicarunt. Iussus est melius pro-ferre,si quod haberet.Quinquennium illi spatij ad conquirendum datum est. Si Bellarminius eo tempore vixisset, & iudicibus illis probasset non omnes Nicæni Canones adhuc editos fuisse,iccircone vicisset,istos tres canones in Sardicensis actu relatos,ex illis actis tollendos, & in Nicæna transferendos fuisse? At iudices non modo negarunt canones illos in Nicæno fuisse, verum etiam demonstrarunt illos cum decretis Nicænis apertissime pugnare: quibus decretis sua cuique Episcopo iurisdictio & dioecesis attributa definitaque fuerat.
units.tr: Bellarmine must have had plenty of leisure when he began to write these things. For why this list of those canons which, he says, are missing from the acts of the Council of Nicaea? Bellarmine shows that he can tell learned men many learned things, and he speaks eloquently of ancient history. But we must come back at last to the point on which the case rests. The Roman bishop, in pleading his cause, produced a document which the judges unanimously declared spurious, false and forged. He was ordered to produce something better, if he had it. He was given a space of five years to search. If Bellarmine had lived at that time and had proved to those judges that not all the canons of Nicaea had yet been published, would he have won, so that those three canons recorded in the acts of Sardica should be removed from those acts and transferred to Nicaea? But the judges not only denied that those canons were in Nicaea; they also demonstrated that they flatly contradicted the Nicene decrees, by which each bishop's jurisdiction and diocese had been assigned and defined.

units.la: ¶Dico TERTIO, mihi videri probabile admodum in Concilio Nicæno non fuisse expresse hos tres canones, de quibus agimus, sed a Zozimo, & a Bonifacio vocari hos canones Nicænos, quia Concilium Nicænum & Sardicense pro uno & eodem habebantur, & utriusque Concilii canones simul coniuncti erant in Bibliotheca Romana, tanquam si eiusdem Concilii essent. Cuius rei ignoratio Africanos patres perturbavit.
units.tr: ¶I say THIRD, that it seems to me quite probable that these three canons which we are discussing were not expressly in the Council of Nicaea, but that Zosimus and Boniface called them Nicene canons because the Council of Nicaea and the Council of Sardica were regarded as one and the same, and the canons of both councils were bound together in the Roman library as if they belonged to a single council. Ignorance of this fact troubled the African Fathers.

units.la: Rationes quæ me movent, hæ sunt, P R I M A, quo-niam iisdem verbis habentur hi canones in Concilio Sardicensi, quibus eos allegat legati Zozimi:nec est verisimile, eosdem prorsus canones fuisse in Nicæno Concilio, & tamen non iudicare ullomodo Patres Sardicenses, se canones non condere: sed renovare.
units.tr: The reasons that move me are these. FIRST, because these canons are found in the Council of Sardica in the very words in which the legates of Zosimus cite them. It is not likely that exactly the same canons were in the Council of Nicaea, and yet the Sardican Fathers nowhere judge that they are making new canons rather than renewing old ones.

units.la: Itaque existimo,in Nicæno Concilio implicitè & obscurè decretum,ut ad Pontificem appellaretur,quia,ni-mirum,Canone sexto,iubet Concilium servari antiquas consuetudines, & una est hæc de appellationibus,ut pa-tet ex Leone,epist.89.& ex exemplis supra adductis, & etiam, quia iubet idem Concilium, causam semel in-dicatam, iterum in alio loco iudicari posse, vt patet ex epist. Iulii apud Athanasium, in secunda Apologia: sed expresse, & diserte Concilium Sardicense rem totam ex-plicuit.
units.tr: Therefore I think that the Council of Nicaea decreed, implicitly and obscurely, that appeal be made to the Pope. This is because, by the sixth canon, the council orders that ancient customs be observed, and this one, concerning appeals, is among them, as is clear from Leo, letter 89, and from the examples adduced above. It is also because the same council orders that a case once judged may be judged again in another place, as is clear from the letter of Julius in Athanasius, in the Second Apology. But the Council of Sardica explained the whole matter expressly and plainly.

units.la: ¶Quis homo stamachũ habet, & ferre hoc comentum potest, Concilii Nicæni & Sardicense pro vno & eodem habitum fuisse: cũm illud celebratum fuisse dicatur imperante Constantino magno, anno cccxxv. hoc vero imperante Constantio ipsius filio, tum vero si pro vno & eodem habebantur, quasi geminum illud Nicænum Concilium fuisset, quæ fuit vel trecentorum Patrum Carthaginensium incogitantia, qui per quinquennium meminisse non potuerunt, vel Episcopi R. stultitia qui per illud idem spatium respondere patribus illis nõ potuit, quod reperire in actis Nicænis nõ poterũt, id extare scriptũ inSardicensibus, quę pro vnis iisdemque tabulis habebantur? quanquam quid verbis opus est? nam si ius hoc fuit episcopi R. si tanta ipsius in omnem terrarum orbem potentia & diuino & humano iure munita est, quid illa Nicænorum actuum conquisitione opus fuit? Cur non confestim Carthaginenses illos omnes dicto audiētes esse atque imperata facere coegit, & emisso aliquo excommunicationis fulmine pauidos parere impulit? Sed satis multa de nugis. Nã mesanè istius tantæ & impudentiæ & sycophan-tiæ & stultissimę loquacitatis pudet, pigetque, ne-que diutius in illa refellenda tædium sustinere pos-sum: sed quibus amplius otij suppetet, ijs illam ve-xandam ac ludificandam relinquam.
units.tr: ¶What man has the patience to tolerate this fiction, that the Council of Nicaea and the Council of Sardica were regarded as one and the same? The former is said to have been held under Constantine the Great in the year 325, the latter under Constantius, his son. Yet if they were regarded as one and the same, as if that Nicene council had been double, what was it? Was it the carelessness of the three hundred Carthaginian Fathers, who for five years could not remember? Or was it the stupidity of the bishop of Rome, who in that same space of time could not answer those Fathers that what they could not find in the Nicene acts was written in the Sardican acts, which were held to be on the same tablets? But why need words? For if this was the right of the bishop of Rome, if his power over the whole world is so great and fortified by divine and human law, why was there any need for that search for the Nicene acts? Why did he not at once make all those Carthaginians obey and do what was commanded, and by hurling some thunderbolt of excommunication drive the timid to obey? But enough of these trifles. I am ashamed of this man's great impudence, sycophancy and most stupid loquacity, and I am weary of bearing the tedium of refuting him any longer. I shall leave him to be harassed and mocked by those who have more leisure.
FINIS. [illegible]
