units.la: CVM aliquod pagellæ vacarent, non alienum fore putauimus eas replere disputatione non infructuosa de veritate aut falsitate l. inter claras, 8. C. de Summ. trinit. propterea quod directò pertinet ad crimè falsi de quo superius in Protestatione nullitatum explicatum est.
units.tr: Since some pages were left blank, we thought it not out of place to fill them with a useful disputation on whether the law "Inter claras" (8 C. de summa trinitate) is true or false, because it bears directly on the crime of forgery, which was explained above in the Protestation of nullities.
Alciatus, Parerga, book 5, chapter 23.

units.la: SVnt qui suspectam habeant Ioannis pontificis Epistolam quæ sub titulo de summa trinitate in Iustiniani codice sita est, dicúntque in antiquis Codicibus non inueniri. quòd, vt arbitror, eò faciunt, vt illos adiuuent qui Pontificis Romani autoritatem deprimunt: quo nomine alios quoque autores deprauatos ab eis deprehēdi, vt Othonis Phrisingensis Chronica, & Ligurini poëtæ carmina quædam. Ego in antiquis plurimis eam extare scio, nec vlla suspitione conuelli posse, quòd si vnus aut alter codex non habeat, id scriptorum incuriæ tribuendum, qui eam quandoque omiserunt, quòd non multum ad legalis scientiæ materiam pertineret. Non tamen ideo hæsitandum est, quin genuinus germanusque Ioannis XI. sit fœtus.
units.tr: There are those who regard the letter of Pope John, which stands under the title De summa trinitate in the Code of Justinian, as suspect, and say that it is not found in the ancient codices. I think they do this to help those who belittle the authority of the Roman Pontiff. By the same device I have found other authors corrupted by them, such as the Chronicle of Otto of Freising and certain poems of Ligurinus. I know that the letter is extant in very many ancient copies, and no suspicion can overturn it. If one or another codex lacks it, that should be put down to the carelessness of scribes, who sometimes omitted it because it bore little on the subject of legal learning. Still, we should not on that account hesitate to hold that it is the genuine and true offspring of John XI.
Cuiacius, Observations, book 12, chapter 26.

units.la: MErito doctissimus Alciatus nō tulit eos qui à tit. de summ. trinit. & fid. cath. conabatur abstrahere epistolam Ioannis Papæ, siue archiepifcopi Rom. ad Imperatorem Justinianum cui incerta est etiam ab ipso Justiniano ad eundem scripta fidei professio. Nec enim in eo tit. ponedæ epistolæ illius autor alius fuit quàm Justinianus ipse, qui Pontificis Rom. (cui libenter defert primas in Ecclesia) Judicio & approbationi tribuebat omnia, & omnino res ita procedit, posuit primum in eo tit. Justinianus fidei suæ professionem, quam ediderat statim ipse initio ipsi Imperii, quæ est lex v. Deinde edictu de fide sua, & hæreticorum condemnatione, propositum omnibus populis fidelibus ut Joannes ait in sua Epistola, Constantinopolitanis scilicet & Ephesiis & Cæsariensibus Cyzicenis, & Amidenis, & aliis plerisque quæ est 1.6. Tum ad Epiphanium archiepiscopum Constantinopoleos specialiter Epistolam eadem de re, quæ est lex vii. Et octavo atque ultimo loco similem aliam, præterquàm quod latinè, in rei summa, verborum serie & consequentia, parem ad Joannē archiepiscopum urbis Romæ, quam maluit una cō-firmationi & approbationi Joannis injectam nobis, quam solam exhibere, & probatur hic ordo evidenter libris Basil.in quibus ultimo loco quod Joannis Latinè exordium est huiusmodi.Inter claras Mansuetudinis vestræ laudes, ita redditur, ἐν τῇ λαμπρότητι τῆς ὑμετέρας παραθήκης [?], &c. Et de hac Epistola idem Joannes scribens illustribus viris, Avieno Senatori, Liberio, Severino, & aliis: Justinianus inquit, Imperator ut ex eius epistolæ tenore cognovistis, de his tribus quaestionibus orta certamina fuisse signavit, utrum unus ex trinitate Christus & Deus noster dici possit. An Deus Christus carne pertulerit, impassibili Deitate, An proprie veraciter mater domini Dei nostri Iesu Christi Maria semper virgo debeat appellari.Probauimus in his catholicam Imperatoris fidem,&c.
units.tr: The most learned Alciatus rightly did not tolerate those who tried to detach from the title De summa trinitate et fide catholica the letter of Pope John, or archbishop of Rome, to the Emperor Justinian, to which the profession of faith written by Justinian himself to the same man is also of uncertain date. For under that title the author of the letter was none other than Justinian himself, who attributed everything to the judgment and approval of the Roman Pontiff (to whom he gladly grants the first place in the Church). And indeed the matter proceeds thus. Justinian placed first under that title his profession of faith, which he had published at the very start of his reign, and this is law 5. Then came the edict on his faith and the condemnation of heretics, which, as John says in his letter, was set before all the faithful peoples, namely the Constantinopolitans, Ephesians, Caesareans, Cyzicenes, Amidenes and many others; this is law 6. Then came a letter on the same matter addressed specifically to Epiphanius, archbishop of Constantinople, which is law 7. And in the eighth and last place, another similar letter, except that it is in Latin, and in substance, order of words and sequence it is alike, addressed to John, archbishop of the city of Rome. He preferred to set this one before us as a single confirmation and approval by John, rather than to present it alone. This order is clearly shown by the Basilica books, in which the Latin opening of John's letter, in the last place, reads thus: Among the bright praises of your gentleness [in the Greek, "In the splendour of your deposit"], and so on. And John, writing about this letter to illustrious men, Avienus the senator, Liberius, Severinus and others, says: "Justinian, the Emperor, as you have learned from the tenor of his letter, has indicated that conflicts arose over three questions: whether one of the Trinity can be called Christ and our God; whether God Christ suffered in the flesh, in impassible Deity; and whether Mary, mother of our Lord God Jesus Christ, ought properly and truly to be called ever virgin. In these matters we have approved the Emperor's Catholic faith," and so on.
Hotomanus, Observations, book 7, chapter 2.

units.la: Multa esse video quae fraudis & impostura suspitionem aduersus istas mutuas Iusti-niani & Papae Rom.epistolas mouere possint:atque illud imprimis, quod complures eruditi & fide digni viri iampridem testificati sunt, illas in antiquis manuscriptis Iustiniani Codicibus nō inueniri:quod ne Alciatus quidem certissimus Palis celsitudinis suffragator, negare est ausus.lib. parereg.5.cap.23.
units.tr: I see many things that could raise suspicion of fraud and imposture against these reciprocal letters of Justinian and the Roman Pope. Above all there is this: several learned and trustworthy men have testified for some time that the letters are not found in the ancient manuscript codices of Justinian. Not even Alciatus, the most staunch supporter of the Papal dignity, dared to deny it. Book 5 of the Parerga, chapter 23.

units.la: Alterum est,quod cum papa R.eiusmodi fraudium & fallaciarum,quae ad suam potentiam amplificandam valere poterant,iampridem conuictus fuerit,(quod vel ex falso & confecto Constantini donationis instrumento iam in vulgus notum est) atque etiam in vetustissima Carthaginensi synodo ducentis & triginta Episcopis Iudicibus falsitatis & impostura damnatus: videtur locus esse regulae iuris ab ipso traditae,ut semel malus semper sui similis existimetur,semel malus semper praesumatur malus in eodem genere mali, praesertim cum haec impostura magnopere ad augendam & confirmandam ipsius potentiam valere potuerit: cuius rei studiosissimos seculis omnibus Papas R. fuisse,nemo vel mediocriter in illo historiarum genere versatus ignorat.
units.tr: The other point is that the Roman Pope has long been convicted of frauds and deceptions of this kind, which could help enlarge his power. This is known widely even from the false and fabricated instrument of Constantine's donation. Indeed in the very ancient Council of Carthage, two hundred and thirty bishops as judges condemned him for forgery and imposture. There seems to be room here for the rule of law laid down by the same man: that one who has once been bad should always be considered like himself, and that one who has once been bad is always presumed bad in the same kind of wickedness. This is especially so since this imposture could greatly help to increase and confirm his power. No one who has been even moderately versed in that kind of history is unaware that the Roman Popes have been eager for this in every age.

units.la: Tertium est,quod cum mendacem (ut in proverbio est) memorem esse oporteat,tamen harum Epistolarum architectus in duabus vicinis legibus (septima scilicet atque octaua) pugnantia scripsisse arguitur, vehementerque inter se dissidentia. Nam cum 1.7. Graece scripta, & anno Christi, IOXXXIII data, (nempe Iustiniano solo III.Cos. VII.Kal.April.) faciat eum scripsisse literas (vt nunc loquimur) patentes, omnibus cognoscendas, ad patriarcham suum Constantinopolitanum, quibus literis praedicat se hanc suam fidei confessionem iam ante R.Papae spectandam cognoscendamque misisse: tamen haec nostra 1.8. quae confessionem illam continet, facit eadem illas literas ad Papam R.datas, legatosque misisse auno demum insequenti, nempe IOXXXIIII, Iustiniano IIII, & Paulino, Cos.viri.Kal.april. Superiore, inquam, anno scribit, se iam misisse legatos ad Papam R. at anno vertente, duodecimo denique post mense, scribit se tum primum ac tum demum legationem & confessionem illam mittere. Quam sunt ista, quaeso, consentanea, aut inter se congruentia? priore anno edictum promulgare de sua fide & religione, quam & ab illo Patriarcha suo, Episcopisque Orientis omnibus, & item ab Ephesiis, Caesariensibus, Cyzicenis, Amidenis aliisque populis suis vniuersis obseruari iubeat, vt ex illius legis inscriptione apparet. anno vero insequente, & duodecim mensibus interiectis, legatos ad Papam R. cum illa eadem confessione mittere, per quos ipsius de illa sua religione sententiam ac iudicium exquirat? vt si ei probetur, tum illam edi atque obseruari iubeat: sin minus eam extinguat. quam tamen, vt dixi, duodecim iam ante mensibus per omnes Orientis ciuitates & Ecclesias promulgari ac recipi imperarat? Quid igitur si Romanus Episcopus eam improbas-
units.tr: The third point is that, although a liar (as the proverb has it) ought to have a good memory, the architect of these letters is shown to have written contradictory things in two neighbouring laws, namely the seventh and the eighth, which are sharply at odds with each other. For the seventh law, written in Greek and dated in the year of Christ 533, in the consulship of Justinian alone for the third time, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, makes him write, as we would now put it, an open letter to be known to all, sent to his patriarch of Constantinople. In it he declares that he has already sent this his confession of faith for the Roman Pope to inspect and examine. Yet this our eighth law, which contains that confession, makes him send the same letters and the legates to the Roman Pope only in the following year, namely 534, in the fourth consulship of Justinian and the consulship of Paulinus, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April. I say that in the previous year he writes that he had already sent legates to the Roman Pope; but then, in the year after, twelve months later, he writes that only then for the first time does he send the legation and that confession. Pray, how do these things agree with each other, or fit together? In the earlier year he publishes an edict about his faith and religion, which he commands to be observed by his patriarch and all the bishops of the East, and likewise by the Ephesians, Caesareans, Cyzicenes, Amidenes and all his other peoples, as is apparent from the inscription of that law. But in the following year, with twelve months intervening, he sends legates to the Roman Pope with the same confession, through whom he seeks the Pope's judgment and opinion on that religion of his, so that if it is approved, he may order it to be published and observed, but if not, he may suppress it. Yet, as I said, he had already ordered it to be promulgated and received twelve months earlier throughout all the cities and churches of the East. What then if the Roman Bishop had disapproved of it?

units.la: [The text continues on the next page.] probasset?nūquid se ipse Iustinianus summæ amé-tiæ condénasset, qui eam duodecim anté mē[?]bus per uniuersi Orientis ecclesias nòn modò promul-gandam curasset, uerum etiā probari ac recipi im-perasset? Quam repugnantiam si Alciato, viro do-ctissimo, per eos videre licuisset, qui legem illam Græcè scriptam per ea tempora comprimebāt, al-teram fortasse vel commodiorem vel honestiorem Papæ R. suffragandi occasionem captasset. tametsi quid de fabula donationis Constantini senserit, nō minus lepidè quam dilucidè in ijsdem parergis o-stendit: lib.7.cap.19.ubi Bonifacium octauum Ca-nem, & vulpem à Baldo appellatum, iccirco Iuri-consultum acutessimum[?] fuisse scribit, quòd verba illa Petri, Ecce duo Gladii hic-subtilius quàm omnes anteipsum Iuris utriusque doctores interpretatus sit, de spirituali & temporali: quorum utrúque sibi ea de causa pro suo iure asciuit.
units.tr: [The text continues on the next page.] Would Justinian himself not have been condemned for the greatest folly, having arranged for it to be published and not merely promulgated, but even ordered to be approved and received in all the churches of the whole East twelve months earlier? If this contradiction had been made visible to Alciatus, a most learned man, by those who were suppressing that law written in Greek at that time, he would perhaps have seized upon another occasion of supporting the Roman Pope, either more convenient or more honourable. Yet what he thought of the fable of Constantine's donation he shows no less wittily than clearly in the same Parerga, book 7, chapter 19. There he writes that Boniface VIII, called by Baldus "the dog and the fox," was a most acute jurist for this reason: he interpreted the words of Peter, Behold, here are two swords, more subtly than all the doctors of both laws before him, as referring to the spiritual and the temporal, and for this reason he claimed both for his own right.

units.la: Sed iam ad tertium argumentum veniamus.
units.tr: But let us now come to the third argument.

units.la: Nam cum & Iustinianus & superiores Impp. Patriarchæ suo Constantinopolitano vel maiorem quàm aliis omnibus, vel rectè parem potetiam[?] atque auctoritatem tribuerint, tamen* Iustinianus in hac octaua lege & Latina Epistola fingitur illum Papæ R.potestati & in constituenda religione cognitioni ac iudicio subijcere. Nam (ut alia sexcéta testimonia omittamus, neque longius quàm ex eodem primo Codicis libro testimonium petamus) extat eiusdem Imp.constitutio in l.24. C. de sacrosan. Ecclef. vbi scriptum ita est. ἡ ἐν Κωνςταντινουπόλει ἐκκλησία πασῶν τῶν ἄλλων ἐστὶ κεφαλή. Constãtinopolitana, inquit, Ecclesia omnium aliarum est caput. Extat itē altera superioris Imp. nomine Zenonis
units.tr: For although both Justinian and the earlier emperors granted to their Constantinopolitan patriarch either a greater power and authority than to all others, or at least an equal one, yet Justinian in this eighth law and in the Latin letter is made to subject him to the power and judgment of the Roman Pope, both in settling religion and in examining it. For (to omit six hundred other testimonies, and not to seek evidence from further afield than the first book of the same Code) there is an enactment of the same Emperor, in law 24 of the Code, on the sacrosanct churches, where it is written thus: "The church in Constantinople is the head of all the others" [ἡ ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει ἐκκλησία πασῶν τῶν ἄλλων ἐστὶ κεφαλή]. The Constantinopolitan church, he says, is the head of all the others. There is also another enactment, in the name of the earlier Emperor Zeno, *we decree*, law 16 of the same title. Its words are these: "The sacrosanct church of this most religious city of Constantinople, and mother of our piety (take note here, reader, and attend closely), and of all Christians of the orthodox religion, and of the same..."

units.la: * Printer's fleuron or mark before "Iustinianus" in the line "tribuerint, tamen". constitutio in l.decernimus,16.eod. tit.Cuius hæc verba sunt: Sacrosanctam huius Constantinopolitanæ religiosissimæ ciuitatis Ecclesiam, & matrem nostræ pietatis (hoc age lector,& animum aduerte:) Et Christianorum Orthodoxæ religionis omnium,& eiusdem regiæ vrbis sanctissimam sedem, priuilegia & honores omnes super Episcoporum creationibus, & iure ante alios residendi, & cætera omnia quæ ante nostrum Imperium vel nobis imperantibus habuisse dignoscitur, habere in perpetuum firmiter, Regiæ vrbis intuitu, iudicamus & sancimus. Hæc ille. Ex quibus licet intelligi, quantopere ab illorum temporum institutis abhorreat, quod hoc loco Iustinianus scripsisse fingitur, velle se Constantinopolitanum Patriarcham Romani Papæ iudicio atque potestati subijcere: præsertim cum in Nouel.131.dilucide profiteatur, priuilegium' illud quod Papa R. sibi per ea tempora vindicabat, vt in Synodis Ecclesiasticis primo loco & ante alios sederet, suo & superiorum Imperatorum beneficio illi tributum, & concessum fuisse. Sancimus, inquit, Episcopum R. priorem omnibus Episcopis & Patriarchis sedere, & post illum Constantinopolitanæ ciuitatis Archiepiscopum.
units.tr: [Printer's fleuron or mark before "Iustinianus" in the line "tribuerint, tamen".] See the constitution in the law "decernimus", 16, same title. Its words are: We hold the holy church of this most religious city of Constantinople, and the mother of our piety (here, reader, pay close attention:) and the most holy see of the Orthodox religion of all Christians and of this same royal city, we judge and sanction, with regard to the royal city, to hold firmly in perpetuity all privileges and honours concerning the appointment of bishops, and the right of sitting before all others, and all the other things which it is known to have had before our empire or under our rule. So far he. From these words it can be understood how far from the practice of those times it is that Justinian is here made to have written that he wished to subject the Patriarch of Constantinople to the judgment and power of the Roman Pope. This is especially so since in Novel 131 he plainly declares that the privilege which Pope R. claimed for himself in those times, of sitting first and before all others in ecclesiastical synods, was granted and conceded to him by his own favour and that of the emperors before him. "We decree," he says, "that the bishop of R. sits before all bishops and patriarchs, and after him the archbishop of the city of Constantinople."

units.la: Quartum argumentum est, quod cum idem Imp. fingatur tum in hac epistola, tu etiam in superiore septima Græce scripta, Papæ R. scripsisse, nullu se pati velle geri negotium ad religionem pertinens, quantumuis notum sit ac diuulgatum, de quo non continuo ad illum, exquirendæ sententiæ suæ causa, deferatur, vtpote caput existens omnium Dei Ecclesiarum: tamen extant Nouellæ constit. eiusdem Imp. quamplurimæ, in quibus liberè ac pro suo iure de rebus innumeris ad religionem pertinentibus nemtibus,fine vlla PapæR.mentione decernit,ve-lut in Nou.6.& No.11.& No.123.vbi de creatione & consecratione Episcoporum leges sanxit:Itémque de numero Patriarcharum, & archiepiscoporum, eorúmque Iurisdictione & priuilegiis.Item, vt quotannis semel aut iterum Ecclesiasticæ synodi in singulis Episcoporum dioecesibus celebrentur. Item, Nouel.3. ne clerici vna ecclesia in alteram demigrent: vt per certum numerum ab episcopis in singulis ecclesiis ordinetur. item Nouel.16.fi legitimus clericorum numerus defit,quomodo eum in ecclesiis suppleri oporteat. item Nouel. 5. vt clericis liceat matrimonium contrahere, non autem monachis. Cuius constitutionis initio scribit,consequens esse, vt cùm Episcopis & clericis leges præscripserit,nûc monachis vtriusque sexus leges imponat: Item No.3.& No.16.de clericis ordinandis & eorum numero in certis ciuitatibus definiendo. Item No.5.& 133.de monachis, & archimandritis,& aftetriis,& diaconis & diaconissis.Item Nouel.58. Ne cui sacram communionem in priuatis ædibus celebrare liceat. Item No. 137. cap. 6. vt Episcopi clara voce, quæ ab omnibus & intelligatur & exaudiatur, eas preces pronuntient, quæ in sacra communione & baptismo celebrando adhibentur. Cui tandem veriffimile fiet, Iustinianum ausum non esse inconsulto Papa R. de vllo negotio ad religionem pertinente leges condere, qui tamen de grauissimis quibúfquerebus tam liberè ac pro imperio statuerit?quinetiam extant eiusdem Imp.Nouellæ nō paucæ,quibus Papæ R.& ipsius Ecclesiæ leges imponit, veluti No.123.§.1.Iubemus, inquit,archiepifcepos & patriarchas veteris Romę & Constantinopolis & Alexan-driæ, & Theopolis & Hierosolymorum si quidè consuetudo &c. Item No. 7. ut nulla Ecclesia, quę sub Romana ditione sit, licentiam habeat alienádi res immobiles, &c. Quintum argumetum est (de quo tamen non temere quemuis iudicem admittemus) quod dicendi genus illud, quo logodędalus, harum Epistolarum auctor usus est, prorsus ab eo stylo alienum est, quo Iustinianus in latinis suis consti-tutionibus uti consuevit: quæ res apud eruditos viros plurimum ad hanc quæstionem disceptandá valere poterit. Nam primùm omnium plena hæc Epistola est indecoræ assentationis, & tanto Imp. indignæ, quam neverissimile quidem est Patriar-cham Constantinopolitanum (haud minus for-tasse quàm ille occidétalis fuit, ambitiosum) æquo aliiino laturum fuisse. Nos, inquit, reddentes honore apostolicæ sedi Romanæ. Quasi vero hæc sedes vel so-la esset Apostolica, vel propter excellentiam com-mune multarum Ecclesiarum nomen, suum fecif-set: vel tantum ei honorem Iustinianus debuisset, ut nihil ad religionem pertinens nisi de ipsius sen-tentia & auctoritate, vel sine ipsius permissu ac venia, statuere auderet quod esse salsissimum index ille Nouellarum quem modo protulimus perspi-cuè ostendit. Ex eodem genere illud est: Semper nobis in voto fuit & est, ut decet, honorare ut patrem, vestram beatitudinem, Cuius similem orationem nego in vlla Iustiniani constitutione reperiri pos-se. Quàm verò Maiestati Imperiali consentanea est illa supplex, ne dicam monachalis, clausula: Petimus vestrum paternum affectum, ut vestras ad nos de-stinetis literas? vel illa posterior: Manifestum nobis faciafaciatis, quod omnes qui prædicta recte confitentur suscipit vestra sanctitas, aut vero illa festiua:Petimus vestram beatitudinem Dei nobis acquirere prouidentiam, Sed operæpretium est, ornamenta illa orationis & florida dicendi genera obseruare, festinatoria dicam, an properatoria? Festinamus ad notitiam vestræ deferre. Properamus omnes sacerdotes Orientis tractus sedi vestræ subiicere. Properamus, per omnia honorem crescere vestræ sedis. Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus festinat in omnibus sequi sedem apostolicam beatitudinis vestræ. Quæ omnia si quis neget Curiæ Romanæ stylum, & Decretalisticum dicendi genus redolere, vehementérque ab usitata scribendi consuetudine Iustiniani abhorrere, is vel parum se in illis libris versatum esse, vel certè non magnum se in hoc genere habere iudicium ostendet. Neque tamen inficior, Iustinianum suam illam fidei cófessionem Episcopo R. misisse: sed eodem consilio misisse contendo, quo Episcopis Orientalibus antea miserat: nempe, ut illam in Latinis Ecclesiis proponendam promulgandamque curaret. Supplicem autem & propè seruilibus verbis conscriptam epistolam misisse, & Constantinopolitanum suum Archiepiscopum illius potestati subiecisse, vel totius religionis Christianæ caussam illius arbitrio iudicioque permisisse, nemo Papæ R. vel suffragator vel parasitus mihi unquam persuaserit. Neque me illius testimonium mouet, qui prædicat se in libris Basilicῶν manuscriptis legem hanc 8. Græcè conuersam legisse, cum hac præfatione: Ἐν τῇ λαμπρότητι τῆς ὑμετέρας προσότητι. Quidni enim Græcè conuertendum curàsset Papa R. epistolam quam ante Latinè confictam ediderat?annon ha-bere ad manum Græculum eundem tribus obolis conductū interpretem potuit, cuius opera in fig-mento Donationis Constantini Græcè vertendo usus antea fuerat?qua ex officina superioris quoq; legis septimæ partem eam prodiisse non dubito, in qua tantopere Papæ R. auctoritas prædicatur: cùm ea prædicatio,tum à Iustiniani consuetudine (quod antea demonstrauimus)tum ab orientalium Episcoporum & Ecclesiarum instituto nimium quantum abhorreat.
units.tr: The fourth argument is this. Although the same emperor is made to write, both in this letter and in the earlier seventh letter, which was written in Greek, that he would not allow any matter touching religion, however well known and public, to be handled without its being at once referred to Pope R. to seek his opinion, as being the head of all the churches of God, there are nevertheless very many Novels of the same emperor in which he decides freely and on his own authority about countless matters touching religion, without any mention of Pope R. Thus in Novel 6, Novel 11 and Novel 123 he enacted laws on the creation and consecration of bishops; likewise on the number of patriarchs and archbishops, and on their jurisdiction and privileges; likewise that ecclesiastical synods be held once or twice a year in each bishop's diocese. Likewise in Novel 3 that clerics not migrate from one church to another, and that the number of them in each church be fixed by the bishops for a set number; in Novel 16, at the end, how the lawful number of clerics is to be made up if it is lacking, and how this ought to be supplied in the churches. In Novel 5, that clerics may contract marriage but monks may not. At the beginning of that constitution he writes that it follows that, since he has prescribed laws for bishops and clerics, he now imposes laws on monks of both sexes. Likewise in Novels 3 and 16, on the ordination of clerics and the fixing of their number in certain cities. Likewise in Novels 5 and 133, on monks, archimandrites, abbesses, deacons and deaconesses. In Novel 58, that no one may be allowed to celebrate the holy communion in private houses. In Novel 137, chapter 6, that bishops are to recite in a clear voice, so that they can be understood and heard by all, those prayers which are used in celebrating the holy communion and baptism. Finally, who will think it likely that Justinian dared to make laws on any matter touching religion without consulting Pope R., when he decided so freely and with imperial authority on the gravest matters of every kind? Indeed there are not a few Novels of the same emperor by which he imposes laws on Pope R. and on the Church itself, as in Novel 123, §1: "We command," he says, "that the archbishops and patriarchs of old Rome, of Constantinople, of Alexandria, of Theopolis and of Jerusalem..., if custom..."; likewise Novel 7, that no church which is under Roman rule may have licence to alienate immovable property. The fifth argument (though we do not rashly admit this to every judge) is that the style of expression which the author of these letters, the logodaedalus, uses is wholly alien to the style that Justinian was accustomed to use in his Latin constitutions. This matter may count for a great deal in the debate over this question among learned men. For first of all this letter is full of unbecoming flattery, unworthy of so great an emperor, which the Patriarch of Constantinople (perhaps no less ambitious than that western one) would certainly not have tolerated with equanimity. "We," he says, "rendering honour to the apostolic Roman see..." As if this see alone were apostolic, or had taken to itself the common name of many churches because of its excellence, or as if Justinian owed it so much honour that he would not dare to decide anything touching religion except on its opinion and authority, or without its permission and consent, which that index of Novels that I have just cited clearly shows to be most false. Of the same kind is this: It has always been and is in our wish, as is fitting, to honour your blessedness as a father. I deny that a similar expression can be found in any constitution of Justinian. How consistent with imperial majesty is that suppliant, I might say monkish, clause: We beg your paternal affection to send your letters to us? Or that later one: Make it known to us, that your holiness receives all who rightly confess the aforesaid things; or that playful one: We beg your blessedness to obtain for us the providence of God? But it is worth observing those ornaments of speech and florid styles of writing, the hasty, or rather the hurried, ones: We hasten to bring to the notice of your see. We hurry to subject all the priests of the Eastern regions to your see. We hurry to increase the honour of your see in every way. The Patriarch of Constantinople hastens in all things to follow the apostolic see of your blessedness. If anyone denies that all these things smell of the style of the Roman Curia and of the decretalist manner of speaking, and that they are very far from Justinian's customary way of writing, he will show either that he has little acquaintance with those books, or certainly that he has no great judgment in this kind of writing. Nor do I deny that Justinian sent that confession of his faith to Bishop R.; but I maintain that he sent it with the same purpose with which he had earlier sent it to the Eastern bishops, namely that he might take care to have it set forth and promulgated in the Latin churches. But that he sent a letter written in suppliant, nearly servile, words, and subjected his Archbishop of Constantinople to that man's power, or left the cause of the whole Christian religion to his arbitrium and judgment, no one who is a supporter or flatterer of Pope R. will ever persuade me. Nor am I moved by the testimony of the man who declares that he read this eighth law, translated into Greek, in the manuscript Basilica books, with this preface: [In the splendour of your gentleness.] [Ἐν τῇ λαμπρότητι τῆς ὑμετέρας προσότητι.] For why should Pope R. not have had the letter, which he had earlier published in Latin, turned into Greek? Could he not have had at hand the same little Greek interpreter, hired for three obols, whose work he had earlier used in translating the forgery of Constantine's Donation into Greek? I do not doubt that from the same workshop there also came forth that part of the superior seventh law in which the authority of Pope R. is so greatly extolled; since that exaltation is far too removed both from Justinian's custom (as we have shown above) and from the practice of the Eastern bishops and churches.
Most Holy Lord,
OF POPE SIXTUS V.
DECLARATION

units.la: Contra Henricum Borbonium assertum Regem Navarre, & Henricum item Borbonium, prætensum Principem Condensem, Hæreticos, eorúmque posteros & successores: Ac liberatio Subditorum ab omni fidelitatis & obsequii debito.
units.tr: Against Henry of Bourbon, asserted King of Navarre, and likewise Henry of Bourbon, the so-called Prince of Condé, heretics, together with their posterity and successors; and the release of subjects from every debt of allegiance and obedience.
AT ROME.

units.la: Apud Hæredes Antonij Bladij Impressores Camerales.
units.tr: At the heirs of Antonio Blado, printers to the Apostolic Chamber.

units.la: AB immensa æterni Regis potentia beato Petro, eiusque successoribus tradita auctoritas omnes terrenorum Regum, & Principum supereminet potestates, stabilíque in petra consistens, nec vllis aduersantibus, vel etiam secundis flatibus à recto deflexa, inconcussa profert in omnes iudicia: & ne diuinæ maximè leges violentur, summa ope prouidet, & si quos ordinationi Dei resistentes inuenit, seueriore hos vindicta vlciscitur, & quamuis potentiores de solio deiiciens, veluti superbientis Luciferi ministros ad infima terræ deturbatos prosternit. Quare pro incumbenti nobis Ecclesiarum omnium, populorum, ac gentium solicitudine, ut animarum saluti imprimis prospiciatur, & non solum famulatus nostri, sed etiam omnia futura tempora impiis ac detestandis monstris purgata cunctis Christiani Orbis partibus pacem afferant, & quietem: & præser-tim amplissimo Galliæ Regno, in quo Christiana Religio omni tempore ita viguit; tantaque Regum illius pietas, fides, ac devotio; tot in Romanam Ecclesiam merita extiterunt; ut ij iure optimo gloriosissimum Christianissimi cognomè ab ea sint consecuti; ac etiam ne nos de neglecta officij nostri cura unquam apud Deum arguimus, arma militiæ nostræ, quæ non carnalia sunt, sed potentia Deo in destructionem munitionum, nunc contra duos potissimum iræ filios Henricum Borbonium quondam Nauarræ Regem, & Henricum Borbonium olim Principem Condensem exercere compellimur. Ille enim quondam Rex, Caluini errores, atque haereses e-tiam ab ineunte adolescentia secutus est, pertinaxque earum patrocinium tandiu exercuit, quoad clarae mem. Caroli Noni Francorum Regis, & charissimae in Christo filiae Catharinae Reginae eius matris pientissimae, atque etiam dilecti filij nostri Caroli tit. s. Chrysogoni presbyteri Cardinalis Borbonij patrui sui, & Ludouici Mopenserij Ducis, pijs frequentibusque hortationibus, apertisque eximiae virtutis ac doctrinae Theologorum demonstrationibus ad fidem Catholicam & Apostolicam Romanam (vt existimabatur) conuersus, haereticas omnes contra fidem Catholicam opiniones Parisiis publice in Ecclesia damnauit, anathematizauit, & abiurauit, fidemque ipsam Catholicam expresse professus est; datisque subinde suis ad fe.re. Gregorium Papam XIII. praedecessorem nostrum literis, quibus eundem praedecessorem supremum Catholicae Ecclesiae caput iam agnoscens, ipsum supplex deprecabatur, vt poenitentiae, conuersionis, & obedientiae suae confessionem acceptam habere, & anteactorum veniam, remissionisque gratiam concedere dignaretur: firmiter promittens se fidem ipsam Catholicam perpetuo integre, ac inuiolate seruaturum. Quibus literis, vt potè Regiis idem praedecessor credens, & paternae charitatis viscceribus commotus, ac etiam grauissimo Regis, Reginae matris, Cardinalis & Ducis praedictorum de huiusmodi conuersione testimoftimonio adductus, illum ipsum praeteritos erro-res confitentem, veniámque humiliter petentem à crimine haeresis & à censuris Ecclesiasticis propterea incursis absoluit, & in gremium Sanctae matris Ecclesiae communionémque fidelium admisit, omni inhabilitate abeo sublata. Quinetiam ut arctiori, & firmiori vinculo ligaretur, cum eo, & Margarita dicti Caroli Regis sorore, quae ex illa Christianissima stirpe nata, atque alta facilé maritum in officio, & Religionis Catholicae observantia continere posse sperabatur, dispensauit, ut non obstantibus impedimentis tertii, & aliorum forsan inter eos graduum consanguinitatis, & cognationis spiritualis, matrimonium inter se contrahere p ssent, prout in facie Ecclesiae contraxerunt; excursisque deinde aliquot mensibus, ille Johánem Duratii Dominum Oratorem suum, qui nomine suo de poenitentia, conuersione, fide, & constantia sua in sedis Apostolicae conspectu sponderet, ad dictum praedecessorem delegauit; habitóque pro eo publico, solemníque in aula Regia de more consistorio, in concessu Sanctae Romanę Ecclesiae Cardinalium, Praelatorúmque & aliorum frequentissimo concursu, professis omnibus supradictis, idem Héri-cus [?] tanquam Rex recens ad fidem conuersus, & ut Catholicus admissus est, tota Urbe exultate, & ingentes Deo de conquisita & inuenta oue gratias agente. Sed ille, ut erat vario & incostanti animo, haud multo post à Catholica fide, & debita erga sedem Apostolicam obedientia, caeterisque à se expresse, & cum Juramento professis deficiens, atque in eo, quo prius erat, cœno reuolutus, à Rege Christianissimo clam se subducens, collectoque in loco ab ipsius Regis aula satis remoto quàm potuit copiosò hæreticorum sceleratorum,aliorúmque id genus impiorum hominum numero,ibi ea omnia, quæ de Caluinismi detestatione,hæresum omnium abiuratione, ac Romanæ fidei Catholicæ & Apostolicę professione antea fecerat,palàm renocauit:testificans,se Caluinismum ipsum profiteri, prout professus est: eique hæresi, pertinaci & obdurato animo semper adhæsit:& in ea hucusque viuens,sæpius hæreticos perduelles,ac seditiosos (quorum caput, dux,& propugnator in Gallia, & etiam exterorum hæreticorum acerrimus fautor semper fuit, ad arma contra prædictum Carolum, ac etiam charissimum in Christo filium nostrum Henricum Regem Christianissimum, tametsi eum vt Regem, ac Dominium suum colere, vt sororium amare,& sequi debebat, omnis scilicet officij,ac pietatis immemor,aduersus ipsum,& reliquos Catholicos omnes concitauit, infestissimos exercitus, accitis etiam externarum nationum hæreticis contraxit, à quibus omnia passim loca cruentis piorum hominum cædibus fœdata,sacra ei templa temerata & direpta, Sacerdotes, & viri religiosi cruciatibus trucidati sunt: oppida præterea, & munitiones Catholicorum partim insidijs,partim vi, & armis occupauit: & in eis Catholicæ Ecclesiæ ritus prohibuit,ac sustulit, ministros & concionatores hæreticos constituit,Ciues & incolas ad eandem impietatem catem capessendam minis, verberibusque coegit. Sed ne haec quidem satis sibi existimans, inter alios, intimum quendam suum nefariis artibus suis instructum, extra Gallię fines ad diversa lo-ca misit, per quem cum primariis haereticis im-pia consilia sua communicavit, eorumque vires & arma contra religionem Catholicam, & Ro-mani Pontificis potestatem provocavit: conci-liabula quoque haereticorum in diversis Provin-ciis habenda curavit: quorum nonnullis (dum iniquissima illa foedera contra fidem Catholi-cam, ac praesertim contra Ecclesias,Clerum, & universos Catholicos Regni Franciae tractaban-tur) ille non solum interfuit, sed etiam praefuit: Henricus vero Borbonius Princeps Condensis, utroque parente haeretico genitus, cum illi exi-tialia Caluini dogmata, eorumque ministros pertinaciter in omni vita fovisset, eorundem, patris, ac matris secutus haereses, consimilia fa-cinora etiam adolescens perpetravit: deinde ea-dem illa, qua alter Henricus, opera, viam verita-tis poenitentia, & humilitate cordis quantum coniici potuit, arripiens, detestatisque pariter: & abiuratis publice omnibus haereticorum errori-bus & deliramentis, fidem Catholicam, ut prae-fertur, professus est. Quibus ad eundem Ponti-ficem perlatis, ac etiam pro eo similibus precib[?] porrectis, ipse praedecessor illum, ac etiam quo-dam Mariam Cliuensem praetensam conjugem suam, eodem tunc haeresis crimine infectam, si-mili modo poenitentem, detestantem, ac prosi-tentem ab haeresi & censuris huiusmodi absc [?]uit,eosque in gremium Catholicæ Ecclesiæ, fi-deliúmque consortium recepit: quinetiam ex paternę charitatis abundantia, cum eis, vt non obstante impedimento secundi gradus consan-guinitatis, quo inuicem tenebantur, matrimo-nium inter se contrahere possent, dispensauit. Sed ille paulò post ad pristinam impietatem re-diens, teterrimámque illam viam, quæ signata, & impressa erat vestigiis quondam Ludouici Có-densis patris sui impiissimi Catholicæ Ecclesiæ persecutoris ingressus, eisdémque vestigiis insi-stens, se quoque hæreticorum ac consceleratorū hominum dicti Regni Galliæ Ducem, ac defen-sorem bellorúmque ciuilium, ac seditionum au-ctorem præstitit; militum hæreticorum extero-rum copias in Galliam transduxit, Vrbes & op-pida expugnare tentauit, Templa euertit, sacra violauit & populatus est, Sacerdotes indignis modis necauit: ministrósque impietatum substi-tuens, peruersam illorum doctrinam publicari, & custodiri iussit; & denique omne feritatis & sæuitiæ genus, tam in Dei ministros, quàm in cæteros Catholicæ fidei cultores exercuit. Quæ omnia cum manifesta, publica, & notoria sint: cúmque nobis plenè, & legitimè constet, præ-sertim ex processu tempore eiusdem se.re. Gre-gorij Papæ prędecessoris nostri confecto, & aliis quàm plurimis documentis, & grauissimis testi-moniis, Henricum quondam Regem, & Henri-cum Condensem prædictos notorij, & inexcu-sabilis criminis hæresis, & in hæresim relapsos, atque etiam hæreticorum fautores reos existere:
units.tr: From the boundless power of the eternal King, an authority was handed down to the blessed Peter and his successors, and it rises above the powers of all earthly kings and princes. Fixed upon the rock, it is never turned aside by any opposing or even favourable winds, and it pronounces its judgements unshaken over all men. It takes the greatest care that the divine laws be not violated, and where it finds men resisting the ordinance of God, it punishes them with more severe vengeance. Even the most powerful it casts from their thrones, and like ministers of the proud Lucifer it strikes them down and hurls them to the lowest parts of the earth. Therefore, since the care of all the Churches, peoples and nations rests upon us, and since above all the salvation of souls must be provided for, and so that not only our own rule but all future times may be cleansed of impious and detestable monsters and bring peace and quiet to every part of the Christian world, and especially to the most ample kingdom of France, in which the Christian religion has always flourished, and whose kings have shown such piety, faith and devotion, and have deserved so well of the Roman Church, that they have rightly obtained from it the glorious title of Most Christian; and so that we may never be accused before God of neglecting the duty of our office, we are compelled to wield the weapons of our warfare, which are not carnal but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds, now chiefly against two sons of wrath: Henry of Bourbon, formerly King of Navarre, and Henry of Bourbon, once Prince of Condé. For the former king, from his earliest youth, followed the errors and heresies of Calvin, and stubbornly defended them for so long, until, by the pious and frequent exhortations of the illustrious Charles IX, King of the French, of his most devout mother, Queen Catherine, the most beloved daughter in Christ, and of our dear son Charles, Cardinal Bourbon, priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, uncle of the same Henry, and of Louis, Duke of Montpensier, and by the clear demonstrations of theologians of remarkable virtue and learning, he was converted (as was believed) to the Catholic and Apostolic Roman faith. He publicly condemned, anathematised and abjured at Paris, in the church, all heretical opinions against the Catholic faith, and he expressly professed the Catholic faith itself. Afterwards he sent letters to our predecessor, Pope Gregory XIII of happy memory, in which, already acknowledging that pope as the supreme head of the Catholic Church, he humbly begged him to deign to accept his confession of repentance, conversion and obedience, and to grant pardon for his past offences and the grace of remission, firmly promising that he would keep the same Catholic faith perpetually whole and inviolate. Our predecessor, believing these letters as coming from a king, and moved by the bowels of paternal charity, and also induced by the very weighty testimony of the king, the queen mother, the cardinal and the duke concerning this conversion, absolved him, confessing his former errors and humbly seeking pardon, from the crime of heresy and from the ecclesiastical censures thereby incurred, and admitted him into the bosom of holy Mother Church and the fellowship of the faithful, removing every disability. Moreover, so that he might be bound by a closer and firmer tie, he also dispensed him, together with Margaret, sister of the said King Charles, who was born of that most Christian stock and was hoped, by her upbringing, to be able to keep her husband in the duty and observance of the Catholic religion, so that, notwithstanding the impediment of the third and other degrees of consanguinity and spiritual kinship that perhaps lay between them, they might contract marriage with each other, as they did before the face of the Church. Then, some months later, he sent to the said predecessor John of Durfort, lord of Duras, his ambassador, who was to pledge in his name his repentance, conversion, faith and constancy in the sight of the Apostolic See. A public and solemn consistory was held for him in the royal hall, as is customary, in the assembly of the Cardinals of the holy Roman Church, of prelates and of a very large concourse of others; all the aforesaid professions were made, and the same Henry, as a king newly converted to the faith, was admitted as a Catholic. The whole city rejoiced, and gave immense thanks to God for the sheep that had been sought and found. But he, being of a changeable and inconstant mind, not long afterwards fell away from the Catholic faith and the due obedience to the Apostolic See, and from the other things he had professed expressly and with an oath. Rolling back into the mire in which he had been before, and secretly withdrawing himself from the Most Christian King, he gathered, in a place as far as possible from the king's court, a number of wicked heretics and other impious men of that kind, and there openly revoked all those things which he had earlier done concerning his detestation of Calvinism, his abjuration of all heresies, and his profession of the Roman Catholic and Apostolic faith. He testified that he professed Calvinism itself, as he had professed it before, and he has always clung to that heresy with a stubborn and hardened mind. Living in it until now, he has often stirred up heretical rebels and seditious men (whose head, leader and champion in France, and the most bitter supporter also of foreign heretics, he has always been) to take up arms against the said Charles and also against our dearly beloved son in Christ, Henry, the Most Christian King. Although he ought to have honoured him as his king and lord, loved him and followed him as a brother-in-law, he has, forgetful of all duty and piety, roused against him and all the other Catholics the most hostile armies, drawing in also heretics from foreign nations. By these armies all places have been everywhere defiled with the bloody slaughter of pious men; sacred temples have been violated and plundered; priests and religious men have been butchered with torments. Moreover, he has seized towns and fortresses of the Catholics, partly by ambushes and partly by force and arms, and in them he has forbidden and abolished the rites of the Catholic Church, has appointed heretical ministers and preachers, and has compelled citizens and inhabitants, by threats and blows, to take up the same impiety. But not thinking even this enough for himself, he sent among others a certain intimate of his, trained in his wicked arts, to various places outside the borders of France; through him he shared his impious plans with the leading heretics and stirred up their strength and arms against the Catholic religion and the power of the Roman Pontiff. He also took care that meetings of heretics should be held in various provinces; he not only attended some of these, when those most unjust treaties against the Catholic faith, and especially against the Churches, the clergy and all the Catholics of the kingdom of France, were being negotiated, but also presided over them. Henry of Bourbon, Prince of Condé, born of two heretical parents, since from his whole life he had cherished the pernicious doctrines of Calvin and its ministers, followed the heresies of his father and mother and, while still a young man, committed similar crimes. Then, by the same means as the other Henry, taking up the way of truth through repentance and humility of heart as far as could be conjectured, and likewise detesting and publicly abjuring all the errors and follies of the heretics, he professed the Catholic faith, as has been said. When these matters were brought to the same Pontiff, and similar prayers were also presented on his behalf, our predecessor absolved him, and also a certain Marie of Cleves, whom he claimed as his wife, who was then likewise infected with the crime of heresy, in the same way, as penitent, detesting and professing, from heresy and from censures of this kind, and received them into the bosom of the Catholic Church and the fellowship of the faithful. Moreover, out of the abundance of paternal charity, he dispensed them so that, notwithstanding the impediment of the second degree of consanguinity by which they were mutually bound, they might contract marriage with each other. But he, returning a little later to his former impiety, and entering that most foul path which had been marked and stamped with the footprints of Louis of Condé, his most impious father, persecutor of the Catholic Church, and following those same footprints, has made himself also the leader and defender of the heretics and criminals of the said kingdom of France, and the author of civil wars and seditions. He has led bands of foreign heretic soldiers into France, has attempted to storm cities and towns, has overturned temples, violated and plundered sacred things, and slain priests with unworthy cruelty. Appointing ministers of impiety, he has ordered their perverse doctrine to be published and preserved; and finally he has practised every kind of savagery and cruelty, both against the ministers of God and against the other worshippers of the Catholic faith. All these things being manifest, public and notorious, and it being fully and lawfully established to us, especially from the process drawn up at the time by our predecessor Pope Gregory of happy memory, and from very many other documents and most weighty testimonies, that the aforesaid former King Henry and Henry of Condé are notoriously and inexcusably guilty of the crime of heresy, relapsed into heresy, and also guilty as supporters of heretics:

units.la: Nos gladium vindictæ contra eos pro officij no-stri debito exerere coacti, vehementer indolemus, quòd illum in hanc prolem detestabilem, ac degenerem inclytæ Borboniorum familiæ, in qua spectatæ Religionis candor, & virtutis decus, ac in sedem Apostolicam obseruantia omni tempore emicuit, pro his sceleribus conuertere debeamus. Itaque in præcelso hoc solio & in plenitudine potestatis, quam ipse Rex Regum, & Dominus dominantium, licet nobis indignis tribuit, constituti, auctoritate Dei omnipotentis, ac beatorum Petri & Pauli Apostolorum eius, & nostra, ac de venerabilium fratrum nostrorum Sanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ Cardinalium consilio, pronuntiamus, & declaramus Henricum quondam Regem, & Henricum Condensem supradi-ctos fuisse & esse hæreticos, in hæreses relapsos, & impœnitentes, hæreticorum quoque duces, fautores, & defensores manifestos, publicos, & notorios, sicque læsæ Maiestatis diuinæ reos, & orthodoxæ fidei Christianæ hostes, adeò vt nulla posint se tergiuersatione, aut excusatione defendere, ac proinde eos damnabiliter incurrisse in sententias, censuras, & pœnas sacris canonibus, & constitutionibus Apostolicis, legibúsque generalibus, & particularibus contentas, ac hæreticis relapsis, & impœnitentibus debitas, & specialiter eosdem fuisse, & esse ipso iure priuatos. Henricum quondam Regem, videlicet prætenso Nauarræ Regno illiúsque parte, quam adhuc obtinuit, nec non Bearni[?]alterum verò Henricum, Condensi, & vtrumque, eorúmque poste-ros omnibus, & quibuscumque aliis Principatibus,Ducatibus,Dominiis, Ciuitatibus, & locis feudisque,& bonis etiâ emphyteoticis, & succes-sionibus,necnon dignitatibus,honoribus,munera-ribus,& officiis, etiam regus,aciurifdictionibus, & iuribus, quæ de facto detinent, & ad quæ ius quomodolibet habuerunt,seu prætendunt,eos-demque propter ea fe illis reddidisse indignos:ac fuisse,& esse inhabiles,& incapaces ad illa retinë-da,& alia huiusmodi in posterum obtinenda. Ac pariter eos ipso iure priuatos,& incapaces, ac in-habiles ad succedendum in quibuscunque Du-catibus, Principatibus, Dominiis,& Regnis, ac specialiter in Regno Franciæ, in quo tot atrocia, & nefaria crimina patrarunt, ac Regno ipsi an-nexis dominiis, iurisdictionibus, & locis, cæte-risque omnibus bonis, & rebus prædictis, & ad illa alia quomodocunque acquirendum, pro vt etiam ex abundanti,& in quantum opus est, nos illos, illorum que posteros priuamus in perpe-tuum,videlicet Henricum quondam Regem Re-gno Nauarræ, & illius parte, ac Bearni, & alte-rum Henricum Condensi,ac vtrunque,& eorum posteros aliis Principatibus, Ducatibus, Domi-niis, Feudis, ac cæteris omnibus bonis, & rebus: nonnon iure succedendi & acquerendi, aliisque prædictis vniuersis & singulis:ac etiam in perpetuū inhabilitamus eosdem,eorum que posteros ad il-la,& ad successionem in q ib suis Principatibus, Ducatibus,Dominiis,Feudis,& Regnis,& signa-ter in Franciæ Regno,& illi annexis omnib s su-pradictis,(supplétes omnes iuris & facti defectus, si qui forsan interuenerint in eisdem. Quinetiam Proceres,Feudatarios,Vassallos,Subditos, & Po-pulos Regnorum,Ducatuum , Principatuum, & aliorum Dominiorum prędictorum,etiam alium superiorem non recognoscentes,ac cæteros omnes,qui illis quomodocunque iurauerint, à iuramento huiusmodi,ac omni prorsus Dominii, fidelitatis, & obsequii debito perpetuo absolutos esse. prout nos illos omnes tàm vniuersè, quàm singulatim, auctoritate præsentium absoluimus, & liberamus, præcipiúsque[?] & interdicimus eis vniuersis & singulis,ne illis,eorúmve monitis,legibus & mandatis audeant obedire: qui secus fecerint,eos excommunicationis sententia innodamus eo ipso. Cæterum,eundem charissimum in Christo filium nostrum Henricum Fracorum Regem Christianissimum per viscera misericordię Iesu Christi hortamur,rogamus,ac etiam monemus,ut memor præstantissimæ fidei,& religionis Regum maiorum suorum, quam quasi hæreditatem longè ipso Regno potiorem ab eis accepit,memor etiam illius iuramenti,quod in eius coronatione de exterminandis hæreticis solenniter præstitit, auctoritate,potestate,virtute, atque animi magnitudine verè regia ad executionē tam iustæ huius sententiæ nostræ incumbat,ut scilicet in hoc quoque gratum se omnipotenti Deo exhibeat,& matri suæ Ecclesiæ obsequium debitum persoluat.Præterea omnibus venerabil. fratribus nostris Primatibus, Archiepiscopis,& Episcopis per Regnū Franciæ,Nauarræ,Bearni,& alia prænominata loca constitutis in virtute sanctæ obedientiæ præcipimus, & mandamus, ut cum primùm[?] harum literarum exempla ad eorum manus peruenerint, illa publicari faciant, & quantum in ipsis erit, ad effectum perduci curent. Volumus autem, quòd eædem præsentes nostræ literæ ad valuas Basilicæ Principis Apostolorum, & in acie Campi Flore de Vrbe, vt moris est, affigantur, & publicentur, quódque earum exemplis etiam impressis, ac notarij publici manu, & prælati Ecclesiastici, eiúsque Curiæ sigillo obsi-gnatis, eadem prorsus fides in iudicio, & extra illud vbique gentium habeatur, quæ haberetur ipsis præsentibus, si essent exhibitæ vel ostensæ.
units.tr: Although we are compelled by the duty of our office to draw the sword of vengeance against them, we grieve deeply that we must turn it against this detestable and degenerate offspring of the illustrious house of Bourbon, a house in which sincerity of religion, the honour of virtue and obedience to the Apostolic See have always shone forth. Therefore, seated on this lofty throne and in the fullness of the power which the King of kings and Lord of lords, though we are unworthy, has granted us, by the authority of almighty God, of his blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and our own, and with the counsel of our venerable brothers the Cardinals of the holy Roman Church, we pronounce and declare that Henry, formerly King, and Henry of Condé, named above, have been and are heretics, relapsed into heresy and impenitent, and manifest, public and notorious leaders, abettors and defenders of heretics; and thus they are guilty of violating the divine majesty and enemies of the orthodox Christian faith, so that they can defend themselves by no evasion or excuse. Consequently we declare that they have incurred, to their damnation, the sentences, censures and penalties contained in the sacred canons, the Apostolic constitutions and the general and particular laws, and due to heretics who relapse and remain impenitent; and that they have been and are specially deprived by law itself. We declare this of Henry, formerly King, namely of the pretended Kingdom of Navarre and that part of it which he still holds, as also of Béarn; and of the other Henry, of Condé; and of both, and of their posterity, with regard to all other principalities, duchies, lordships, cities and places, fiefs and goods, including those held by emphyteusis, and successions, as well as dignities, honours, offices and duties, even royal ones, and jurisdictions and rights which they now hold by fact, or to which they have in any way claimed a right or pretend it; and that by these acts they have rendered themselves unworthy of these, and are and have been unfit and incapable of retaining them and of obtaining others of the same kind in future. Likewise we declare that they are by law itself deprived, and incapable and unfit to succeed to any duchies, principalities, lordships or kingdoms, and especially to the Kingdom of France, in which they committed so many atrocious and wicked crimes, and to the lordships, jurisdictions and places annexed to that kingdom, and to all other goods and things mentioned above, and to acquire them in any other way. Moreover, so as to be abundantly sure, and insofar as it is necessary, we deprive them and their posterity forever: namely Henry, formerly King, of the Kingdom of Navarre and its part, and of Béarn, and the other Henry of Condé, and both, and their posterity, of other principalities, duchies, lordships, fiefs and all other goods and things; and likewise of the right to succeed and to acquire, and of all the other things mentioned above, one and all. We also declare them and their posterity forever incapable and unfit for these things, and for succession to those principalities, duchies, lordships, fiefs and kingdoms, and especially to the Kingdom of France and the things annexed to it, all mentioned above, supplying all defects of law and fact that may perhaps have arisen in them. Furthermore, we absolve from their oath, and from every obligation of dominion, fidelity and obedience, forever, the nobles, feudatories, vassals, subjects and peoples of the kingdoms, duchies, principalities and other lordships mentioned above, even those who acknowledge no superior, and all others who have sworn any oath to them in any way; as we do absolve and free all of them, both collectively and individually, by the authority of these presents. And we charge and forbid all and each of them to dare to obey them, their admonitions, laws or commands; and whoever acts otherwise we bind by the sentence of excommunication, by that very fact. Furthermore, we exhort, request and also admonish our most dear son in Christ, Henry, Most Christian King of the Franks, through the bowels of mercy of Jesus Christ, that, mindful of the most excellent faith and religion of his forefathers the kings, which he has received from them as an inheritance far more precious than the kingdom itself, and mindful also of the oath which he solemnly took at his coronation to exterminate heretics, he should apply himself, with the authority, power, strength and truly royal greatness of spirit, to the execution of this our so just sentence; so that in this too he may show himself pleasing to almighty God and render due obedience to his mother the Church. Moreover, to all our venerable brothers the Primates, Archbishops and Bishops established throughout the kingdoms of France and Navarre, Béarn and the other places named above, we command and order, in virtue of holy obedience, that as soon as copies of these letters reach their hands they cause them to be published and, so far as in them lies, bring them into effect. We will also that these same present letters be affixed and published at the doors of the Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles and on the Campo de' Fiori of the City, as is customary; and that copies of them, whether printed or sealed by the hand of a public notary and by an ecclesiastical prelate with the seal of his Curia, shall have everywhere among the nations, both in court and out of it, the same full faith that would be given to these present letters if they were produced or shown.

units.la: Nulli ergo omnino hominum liceat hanc paginam nostræ pronuntiationis, declarationis, priuationis, inhabilitationis, suppletionis, absolutionis, liberationis, præcepti, interdicti, innodatio-nis, hortationis, rogationis, monitionis, mandati, & voluntatis infringere, vel ei ausu temerario contraire. Si quis autem hoc attentare præsumpserit, indignationem omnipotentis Dei, ac beatorum Petri & Pauli Apostolorum eius se noverit incursurum.
units.tr: Therefore let no one at all dare to infringe this page of our pronouncement, declaration, deprivation, disqualification, supplying, absolution, liberation, precept, interdict, binding, exhortation, request, admonition, command and will, or to act contrary to it with rash audacity. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed Apostles Peter and Paul.

units.la: Dat. Romæ apud Sanctum Marcum Anno Incar-nationis Dominicæ, millesimo, quingentesimo octogesimo quinto, Quinto Idus Septembris, Pontificatus Nostri Anno primo.
units.tr: Given at Rome, at Saint Mark's, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord one thousand five hundred and eighty-five, on the fifth day before the Ides of September, in the first year of our pontificate.
A. de Alexiis.

units.la: Omnia conuerso declinant ordine Romæ, Quod verè signum est, Roma, tui interitus. Adnumerare solent Papæ, (crescentis imago Imperii quod erat) sed modo dinumerant: Dinumera subito, Sixte, atque imponito finem, Vt sis ex numero, qui fueras numerus.
units.tr: All things in Rome are sliding backward in reversed order, Rome, and this is a true sign of your ruin. They used to number the popes, an image of the growing empire, but now they renumber them. Count yourself again at once, Sixtus, and put an end to it, so that you may be of the number, you who were a number.
B.C.P.
